sections.title: LRN-M03-L05: Dual coding, and one study session that uses all six
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Combine words with maps, timelines and diagrams, and run a complete 60-minute study session that uses all six strategies on one PSC topic. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 60-minute study session plus a 15-minute check two days later).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Dual coding: words plus pictures

**Dual coding** means combining words with visuals: a map, a timeline, a flowchart, a table or a diagram. You then have two connected ways to find the memory, a verbal one and a visual one. The Learning Scientists list it among their six strategies ([dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding)).

Dual coding is **not** about learning styles (Module 2). A map helps everyone learn where places are. A timeline helps everyone learn the order of events.

Choose the visual by the content:

| PSC content | Visual | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Places | Map | Kerala's 14 districts from north to south; national parks |
| Order of events | Timeline | The Kerala renaissance: 1888, 1903, 1924, 1936 |
| Processes | Flowchart | How a bill becomes law; how a PSC rank list is made |
| Comparisons | Table | Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; rights and duties |
| Parts of a whole | Labelled diagram | Parts of the heart; layers of the atmosphere |
| Hierarchies | Tree | The court system; local government tiers |

Three rules make dual coding work:

1. **The picture must carry meaning.** A decorative photo of a temple doesn't help you remember the Temple Entry Proclamation; a timeline that places it after the Vaikom and Guruvayur satyagrahas does.
2. **Draw it from memory, then check.** Drawing a timeline from memory is dual coding and retrieval at once. Copying a diagram neatly is mostly copying.
3. **Keep it simple.** Boxes, arrows, a few words. You are not making art, and an overloaded diagram adds cognitive load (Module 1).

Be careful with one related idea: Dunlosky and colleagues rated **imagining pictures while reading text** as low utility ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). Real, meaningful visuals that you look at and draw are a different thing.

### One session, six strategies

Each strategy is good alone; together they make a study session that is hard to beat. Here is a 60-minute plan for one PSC topic:

| Minutes | What you do | Strategies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–5 | Blank-page recall of the last session's topic; check | Retrieval, spacing |
| 5–25 | Learn the new topic in chunks; ask why and how; give your own example for each idea | Elaboration, concrete examples |
| 25–35 | Close the book; draw a map, timeline or diagram of it from memory; check and fix | Dual coding, retrieval |
| 35–50 | Mixed practice: 10 questions from this topic and two older ones, options covered | Interleaving, retrieval |
| 50–55 | Check answers; note errors; add the topic to the Revision tab | Spacing |
| 55–60 | Write three margin questions for tomorrow's warm-up | Retrieval (planned) |

The same structure works in 30 minutes: halve every part.

## Local example

**Anu** chose the Kerala renaissance for her six-strategy session. She began with a five-minute recall of yesterday's topic, the Travancore kings, and fixed two errors.

Then she studied four events with why-questions: why Sree Narayana Guru's consecration of a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram in 1888 was revolutionary; why the SNDP Yogam was founded in 1903; what the Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924 demanded; and what the Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 changed. For each she wrote one line in her own words and one example of what the change meant for an ordinary person.

She closed the book and drew a timeline from memory with the four dates and the causes between them. She had placed two events in the wrong order; she fixed them in red. Next came ten mixed MCQs from the renaissance, the Travancore kings and the freedom struggle, with options covered. She scored 7, noted the three errors and added the topic to her Revision tab.

Two days later she redrew the timeline from memory, this time with no errors, and scored 9 out of 10 on new questions.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaningful visuals combined with words (dual coding) | **Moderate** | One of the Learning Scientists' six strategies; the visual must carry the meaning, not decorate. |
| Imagining pictures while reading text | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). Draw real visuals instead. |
| Combining the six strategies in one session | **Limited** | Little research on this exact package; each part has its own evidence, and the strongest parts are retrieval and spacing. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding) | Watch the video and download the dual coding poster | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: free posters, slides and bookmarks for the six strategies](https://www.learningscientists.org/downloadable-materials) | Download the six-strategy bookmarks (or posters) and keep them where you study | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 6: Studying, Memory, and Test Taking](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking) | Read 6.2 Studying, and compare its advice with the six strategies | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a new PSC topic for one 60-minute session.
2. Run the six-strategy session plan below, ticking each part as you finish it.
3. Make your visual (map, timeline, flowchart, table or diagram) from memory in the 25–35 minute part, then check and fix it.
4. Add the topic to your Revision tab.
5. Two days later, redraw the visual from memory without looking, and answer 5 new questions on the topic. Score both.

**Proof to record:** Your session plan with all six parts ticked, both versions of your visual drawn from memory, and the two-day scores.

## Template: six-strategy study session (60 minutes)

```
SIX-STRATEGY SESSION     Date: ______  Topic: ______________
[ ] 0-5    Warm-up recall of last topic (__________): recalled ___ points, fixed ___
[ ] 5-25   Learn in chunks: why/how question + my own example for each idea
           1. ______________________  2. ______________________  3. ____________
[ ] 25-35  Visual from memory: map / timeline / flowchart / table / diagram
           Errors found when checking: ___
[ ] 35-50  Mixed practice: 10 questions (this topic + __________ + __________)
           Correct ___/10, recognised only (R) ___
[ ] 50-55  Errors noted; topic added to the Revision tab
[ ] 55-60  Three margin questions for tomorrow:
           1. _____________________ 2. _____________________ 3. _____________________
Two-day check: visual redrawn with ___ errors; new questions ___/5
```

## Template: choose your visual

```
Is it about WHERE?         -> map
Is it about WHEN or ORDER? -> timeline
Is it about HOW (steps)?   -> flowchart
Is it about COMPARING?     -> two- or three-column table
Is it about PARTS?         -> labelled diagram
Is it about LEVELS?        -> tree
Rule: draw it from memory first, then check, then fix in another colour.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Decorating notes with pictures that carry no meaning.** Every visual should show where, when, how, what differs, or what the parts are.
- **Copying a diagram instead of drawing it from memory.** Look, close the book, draw, check. Copying feels productive and teaches little.
- **Cramming too much onto one visual.** One visual, one idea. Make two simple ones rather than one crowded one.
- **Skipping the mixed practice part to save time.** It is where retrieval and interleaving happen. Shorten the other parts instead.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which visual best suits the order of events in the Kerala renaissance?
    - A) A pie chart
    - B) A timeline
    - C) A labelled diagram of a building
    - D) A photo of a temple
2. Is dual coding the same as matching a "visual learning style"?
    - A) Yes, it only helps visual learners
    - B) No, it only helps auditory learners
    - C) No: meaningful visuals help everyone learn content such as places and sequences
    - D) Yes, and it harms auditory learners
3. What did Dunlosky and colleagues rate as low utility?
    - A) Interleaved practice in maths
    - B) Imagining pictures while reading text
    - C) Distributed practice
    - D) Practice testing
4. In the 60-minute six-strategy session, what happens in minutes 35–50?
    - A) Rereading the chapter
    - B) A break
    - C) Drawing decorative pictures
    - D) Mixed practice questions from this topic and older ones

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The dual coding materials, the six-strategy bookmarks and College Success 6.2 Studying
- **Action:** Run one 60-minute six-strategy session with a visual drawn from memory, and check it two days later. It is done when your proof is saved: your session plan with all six parts ticked, both versions of your visual drawn from memory, and the two-day scores.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** A timeline shows order and the gaps between events.
2. **C.** The content decides the visual, not a learning style.
3. **B.** Imagery for text learning was rated low; real, meaningful visuals are different.
4. **D.** Mixed questions combine interleaving and retrieval, with spacing for the older topics.

sections.title: Module 4: Spaced repetition from zero with AnkiDroid
sections.summary: Learn spaced repetition from zero with AnkiDroid: set it up, write good cards, use cloze and image occlusion, and keep the daily habit sustainable. Build a deck of 100 or more cards on one PSC topic and review it every day for 30 days, with a test before and after.
sections.content:
## Overview

AnkiDroid is free and open source, and it does the hard part of spacing for you: it shows each card just before you would forget it. Used well, 15 to 25 minutes a day can hold thousands of PSC facts. Used badly, with list-cards and too many new cards, it becomes a chore people abandon in a fortnight. This module teaches the good way.

Your deck starts this week, and so does your 30-day review on the **Learning system track**. On day 30 you retake a 20-question test on your topic to measure the difference.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain how spaced repetition schedules reviews and use the four answer buttons honestly
- Write one-fact cards with context cues and sources, using the card-writing checklist
- Make cloze cards and image occlusion cards from maps and diagrams
- Budget new cards, rescue a backlog and fix leeches
- Build a 100-card PSC deck and review it daily for 30 days

## Time

About 8 hours 15 minutes in total: 5 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 2 hours 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 4–5, with the module project due in week 5.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M04-L01: How spaced repetition works, and setting up AnkiDroid (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. LRN-M04-L02: Writing good cards (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
3. LRN-M04-L03: Cloze deletions and image occlusion (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
4. LRN-M04-L04: The daily review habit and managing your workload (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **card-writing checklist** (one of the six core tools)
- Your **AnkiDroid deck** and the daily review habit
- The **workload calculator** and **backlog rescue plan**
- **Cloze patterns** and **image occlusion steps**

## Module project: My 100-card PSC deck

1. Make sure your deck has 100 or more cards on one PSC topic, with a mix of Basic, Basic (and reversed) where PSC asks both ways, cloze and at least one image occlusion note.
2. Pick 20 cards at random and check each against the card-writing checklist. Fix any that fail.
3. Back up the deck: sync to AnkiWeb or export it to your Learning Folder (04 Anki).
4. Keep reviewing daily to day 30 on the Learning system track, then retake a 20-question test on the topic (new questions where possible) and compare with your pre-test.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of the deck with its card count, your 20-card checklist audit, and your pre-test score (the day-30 retest goes on the Learning system track).

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size and mix | Under 100 cards | 100 cards, one card type | 100 or more, with Basic, cloze and image occlusion used where they fit |
| Card quality | Lists and vague questions | Mostly one fact, some unclear | 20-card audit passed: one fact, context cue, source |
| Habit | Missed several days | Reviews most days | Reviews every day at a fixed time, reviews before new cards |
| Workload | Backlog out of control | Workable but uneven | Budget set from timing; backlog plan known |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Make 100 Basic and cloze cards on one topic at 10 a day; skip image occlusion.
- Never skip the daily reviews: on a bad day, 5 minutes.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Note versus card | A note is what you type in; a card is one question Anki shows. One note can make several cards. |
| The four answer buttons | Again (forgot), Hard, Good (most correct answers), Easy (too easy). |
| Young versus mature card | Young: gap under 21 days. Mature: 21 days or more. |
| The minimum information principle | One fact per card, short question, short answer. |
| What each cloze number does | Makes its own card; c1 and c2 make two cards. |
| Image occlusion mode for maps | Hide all, guess one. |
| Anki's workload rule of thumb | 20 new cards a day leads to roughly 200 reviews a day. |
| Backlog rescue | New cards to 0; a fixed amount of reviews daily until the count is normal. |
| Leech fixes | Split, add context or contrast, add a hook, relearn, or suspend. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Building a big deck fast, then quitting.** Slow and daily beats big and abandoned. Ten good cards a day is plenty.
- **Copying someone else's ready-made deck instead of making your own.** Making cards is part of learning, and other people's cards often don't match your syllabus or understanding.

sections.title: LRN-M04-L01: How spaced repetition works, and setting up AnkiDroid
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain how spaced repetition decides when you see each card, set up AnkiDroid for one PSC topic, take a 20-question pre-test, and make your first 15 cards. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 40 minutes setup and cards).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What spaced repetition does

In Module 3 you scheduled whole topics by hand. For single facts (who, when, which article, which river) there are far too many to schedule by hand. **Spaced repetition software** does it for you. Each fact is a flashcard. When you review a card, you say how well you recalled it, and the software decides when to show it next: soon if you struggled, much later if it was easy. Each card comes back just as you are about to forget it, which is when a successful recall strengthens memory most (Module 1).

The idea is older than smartphones. Nicky Case's comic shows the **Leitner box**: cards move forward through boxes that are reviewed less and less often, and back to box 1 when you forget them ([How To Remember Anything Forever-ish](https://ncase.me/remember/)). Software does the same with exact dates.

### AnkiDroid

**AnkiDroid** is the free, open-source Android version of Anki, one of the most widely used spaced repetition programs ([Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ichi2.anki); [source code and other downloads](https://github.com/ankidroid/Anki-Android)). Anki for computers is also free, and a free AnkiWeb account can sync your phone and laptop ([Anki downloads](https://apps.ankiweb.net/)).

A few words from the Anki manual ([Getting Started](https://docs.ankiweb.net/getting-started.html)):

- A **note** is the information you type in. A **card** is one question-and-answer that Anki shows you. One note can make several cards.
- A **deck** is a group of cards. Use `::` for sub-decks, such as `PSC::Constitution::Fundamental Rights`.
- **Note types** decide which cards a note makes. You will use four: **Basic** (one card), **Basic (and reversed card)** (two cards, both directions), **Cloze** (hides words in a sentence) and **Image Occlusion** (hides parts of a picture).
- A card is **young** until its gap reaches 21 days, then **mature**.

### The four answer buttons

After you try to recall, you reveal the answer and press one button ([Anki manual: Studying](https://docs.ankiweb.net/studying.html)):

- **Again:** you forgot or got it wrong. The card comes back soon.
- **Hard:** you got it, with real difficulty.
- **Good:** you got it with some effort. Use this for most correct answers.
- **Easy:** it was too easy. The gap grows a lot.

If you can't recall the answer in about 10 seconds, reveal it and press Again. Be honest: pressing Good when you were wrong only fools the schedule.

### Choose your 100-card topic

The course asks you to build one deck of 100 or more well-made cards on **one PSC topic** and review it every day for 30 days. Choose a topic that:

- **Appears in your syllabus and in previous papers** (look at the three papers you saved in week 0)
- **Is rich in facts:** the Constitution (Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, amendments, schedules), the Kerala renaissance, Kerala geography, awards and firsts, English idioms, Malayalam synonyms and antonyms
- **You actually need,** not one you already know well

Before you make any cards, take a **20-question pre-test** on the topic from previous papers or your guide, without looking anything up. You'll take a similar test on day 30, and the difference will show what the deck did.

## Local example

**Ashiq** chose the Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35) for his deck: they appear in almost every general PSC paper, and he kept mixing up the article numbers.

He picked 20 questions on the topic from previous papers and his guide and took the pre-test cold: 9 out of 20. Then he installed AnkiDroid from Google Play, made a deck called `PSC::Constitution::Fundamental Rights`, and set **New cards/day** to 15 in the deck options.

His first 15 cards were Basic cards, one fact each, such as "Constitution: which article abolishes untouchability?" with "Article 17" on the back and the textbook page in brackets. He studied them once that evening. The next morning, at the bus stop on his way to the library, AnkiDroid showed him the cards that were due. He set a daily alarm for 7:15 a.m. as his review time: day 1 of his 30 days had begun.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced repetition (spacing plus retrieval in one tool) | **Strong** | It combines the two techniques rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| The Leitner box on paper | **Strong** | The same principles without software: spaced, effortful recall with feedback. |
| Newer schedulers (FSRS) versus the older one | **Limited** | The Anki manual says FSRS estimates forgetting more accurately; either scheduler works if you review daily. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Nicky Case, "How To Remember Anything Forever-ish" (interactive comic, public domain)](https://ncase.me/remember/) | Read the comic if you have not, or reread the Leitner box part | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki manual: Getting Started (cards, decks, notes, note types)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/getting-started.html) | Read Getting Started: cards, decks, notes, fields, note types | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki manual: Studying (the four answer buttons)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/studying.html) | Read the parts on the answer buttons and what to do when you can't recall | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AnkiDroid Flashcards on Google Play (free, open source)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ichi2.anki) | Install AnkiDroid (free; open source) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AnkiDroid manual](https://docs.ankidroid.org/) | Keep it open for anything you can't find in the app | As needed | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose your 100-card topic with the checklist below, using your saved previous papers.
2. Take a 20-question pre-test on the topic from previous papers or your guide, without looking anything up. Record the score in your Study Log.
3. Install AnkiDroid. Create a deck named PSC::<subject>::<topic>, and set New cards/day to 15 in its options.
4. Make 15 Basic cards from your notes or textbook: one fact per card, a short context word at the start of each question, and the source (book and page, or paper and question number) in brackets on the back.
5. Study the 15 new cards today. Choose a fixed daily review time and set an alarm. Tomorrow is day 2 of your 30 days.
6. Optional: make a free AnkiWeb account and sync, so your deck is backed up.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your deck with its card count and of the deck options showing New cards/day, plus your pre-test score.

## Template: choose your 100-card topic

```
CHOOSE MY DECK TOPIC
Candidate topics: 1. ______________ 2. ______________ 3. ______________
For each, tick:
[ ] In my exam's syllabus
[ ] Appears in at least 2 of my saved previous papers (count: ___)
[ ] Rich in facts (enough for 100 cards)
[ ] I don't know it well yet (pre-test likely under 70%)
Chosen topic: ______________   Deck name: PSC::__________::__________
Pre-test (20 questions, no help): ___/20   Date: ______   Day-30 retest date: ______
```

## Template: AnkiDroid setup checklist

```
[ ] AnkiDroid installed from Google Play (or F-Droid)
[ ] Deck created: PSC::<subject>::<topic>
[ ] Deck options: New cards/day = 15
[ ] First 15 Basic cards made (context word + one fact + source)
[ ] Studied once today
[ ] Daily review time chosen: ______  Alarm set [ ]
[ ] Optional: AnkiWeb account made and synced (backup)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Making cards before you understand the topic.** The first of Wozniak's rules: do not learn what you do not understand. Read and make sense of it first.
- **Creating ten decks on the first day.** Start with one deck for one topic. Add subjects one at a time, later.
- **Setting 50 new cards a day.** New cards create future reviews. Start with 15; LRN-M04-L04 shows the maths.
- **Pressing Good when you were wrong.** Honest answers keep the schedule right. Wrong means Again.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the difference between a note and a card in Anki?
    - A) A note is what you type in; a card is one question-answer that Anki shows, and one note can make several cards
    - B) A card is a deck of notes
    - C) They are the same thing
    - D) A note is a deck
2. You can't recall the answer after about 10 seconds. What should you do?
    - A) Press Easy and move on
    - B) Keep thinking for five minutes
    - C) Delete the card
    - D) Reveal it and press Again
3. Which button should you use for most correct answers?
    - A) Hard
    - B) Good
    - C) Again
    - D) Easy
4. Why take a 20-question pre-test before making the deck?
    - A) To choose a deck name
    - B) To measure how much the deck helps when you retest on day 30
    - C) To find the answers to copy
    - D) Because AnkiDroid requires it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Nicky Case's comic and the Anki manual's Getting Started and Studying pages
- **Action:** Choose your deck topic, take the 20-question pre-test, set up AnkiDroid and make your first 15 cards. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your deck with its card count and of the deck options showing New cards/day, plus your pre-test score.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** For example, a Basic (and reversed) note makes two cards.
2. **D.** The Anki manual suggests revealing after about 10 seconds; forgetting means Again.
3. **B.** Good is for answers recalled with some effort, which is most of them.
4. **B.** A before-and-after test turns your 30 days into measured improvement.

Action: Choose your deck topic, take the 20-question pre-test, set up AnkiDroid and make your first 15 cards

sections.title: LRN-M04-L02: Writing good cards
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Write clear one-fact PSC cards with the card-writing checklist, rewrite bad cards, and grow your deck to 45 or more. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 50 minutes writing cards).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A deck is only as good as its cards. Bad cards are slow to review, easy to fail and hard to remember. Most rules for good cards come from Piotr Wozniak's classic "Twenty rules of formulating knowledge", written in 1999 by the creator of SuperMemo, the first spaced repetition program ([SuperMemo](https://www.supermemo.com/en/blog/twenty-rules-of-formulating-knowledge)). The most important ones for PSC:

### 1. Understand first, then memorise

"Do not learn if you do not understand" and "learn before you memorise" are rules 1 and 2. A card should capture something you already understand. If you don't understand Article 32, read and explain it first (Module 8), then make cards.

### 2. One fact per card: the minimum information principle

Compare:

| Bad card | Why it is bad | Good card(s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12–35: equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural and educational, constitutional remedies, with article ranges | A whole list on one card: you will fail it even when you know most of it | Constitution: right to constitutional remedies is in which article? → Article 32 (and one card per right) |
| Periyar → longest river, 244 km, ends in the Arabian Sea, ... | Many facts, no clear question | Kerala rivers: the longest river? → Periyar (244 km) |
| Important features of the Preamble? | No single correct answer | Preamble: which words were added by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, secular, integrity |

Short questions with short answers are fast to review and easy to grade honestly.

### 3. Avoid sets and lists

"Name the six Malayalam Jnanpith winners" is one card you will keep failing. Instead, make one card per winner ("Jnanpith: the first ever award, in 1965, went to which Malayalam poet? → G. Sankara Kurup"), use one cloze per item (next lesson), or put the list in a memory palace (Module 11).

### 4. Fight interference

Similar facts get mixed up: "longest river" and "second longest river"; Article 14 and Article 15. Make the difference obvious in the question: "Kerala rivers: the **second** longest? → Bharathapuzha (209 km)". When two facts keep colliding, make one card that contrasts them side by side.

### 5. Context cues, wording and sources

- Start each question with a short context word: "Constitution:", "Kerala rivers:", "Jnanpith:". It tells your brain where to search, and it keeps cards clear when your deck grows.
- Write the shortest question that has **one** correct answer.
- Add the source in brackets on the back (book and page, or paper and question number). When a card and an answer key disagree, you know where to check.

### 6. Both directions only when PSC asks both ways

**Basic (and reversed card)** makes two cards: "Article 17 is about...?" and "Abolition of untouchability is in which article?" That doubles the reviews, so use it only for pairs that exam questions really ask both ways: article and content, author and book, award and field.

### 7. Turn mistakes into cards

Every previous-year question you get wrong, or answer by recognition only, can become one to three cards. These are the most valuable cards in your deck, because they target exactly what you didn't know.

## Local example

**Sreeja** made her first 20 cards on the Kerala renaissance in a hurry, copying lines from her guide. Seven of them were lists, such as "Reformers from Travancore and their organisations". After a week she was pressing Again on those seven almost every time, and AnkiDroid felt like punishment.

She went through her cards with the card-writing checklist. The seven list cards became 19 one-fact cards, each starting with "Kerala renaissance:" and ending with the guide's page number. Two pairs she had mixed up for weeks got a contrast card each. She added Basic (and reversed) only for reformer and organisation pairs, because previous papers asked those both ways.

Her daily reviews now take her about 10 minutes, and she presses Again far less often. She also made 6 cards from her mistakes in a previous paper, and two of those exact facts came up in the next mock.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flashcards used for retrieval with spacing | **Strong** | Practice testing and distributed practice, the two high-utility techniques, in one tool. |
| One fact per card (minimum information principle) and avoiding lists | **Limited** | Practical rules from Wozniak's long experience, consistent with research on retrieval; not each tested separately. |
| Understanding before memorising | **Moderate** | Meaningful encoding lasts longer (Module 1); cards for things you don't understand are fragile. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Piotr Wozniak, "Effective learning: Twenty rules of formulating knowledge" (SuperMemo, 1999)](https://www.supermemo.com/en/blog/twenty-rules-of-formulating-knowledge) | Read rules 1 to 5, 9 to 12, 16 and 18 (understand first, minimum information, cloze, imagery, avoid sets and enumerations, interference, wording, context cues, sources) | 35 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki manual: Getting Started (cards, decks, notes, note types)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/getting-started.html) | Reread the part on note types, especially Basic (and reversed card) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Check your 15 cards from LRN-M04-L01 against the card-writing checklist. Rewrite every card that fails a line, and note what was wrong.
2. Write at least 30 new cards on your topic, so the deck has 45 or more. Follow the checklist for every card.
3. Use Basic (and reversed card) only for pairs that previous papers ask both ways; aim for at least 5 such pairs.
4. Make at least 5 cards from questions you got wrong in your pre-test or in a previous paper.
5. Ask a study partner or family member to read 10 random cards aloud. For each, ask: is the question clear, with only one correct answer? Fix any they find unclear.
6. Keep up your daily reviews: reviews first, then new cards.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of 5 cards before and after rewriting, and of the deck showing 45 or more cards.

## Template: card-writing checklist (core tool)

```
CARD-WRITING CHECKLIST (tick before you add a card)
[ ] I understand it: I could explain it in my own words
[ ] One fact per card (the minimum information principle)
[ ] The question has exactly one correct answer
[ ] The answer is short: a word, a number, a name or a phrase
[ ] Lists are split: one cloze per item, or a memory palace instead
[ ] A context cue starts the question when needed ("Constitution:", "Kerala rivers:")
[ ] Look-alike facts are made clearly different ("longest" vs "largest")
[ ] A picture, map or diagram is used where it helps (image occlusion)
[ ] The source is in the Source field (book and page, or PYQ paper and number)
[ ] It is worth knowing: it is on the syllabus or has appeared in PYQs
```

## Template: bad card to good card rewrite sheet

```
REWRITE SHEET
Old card (front -> back): ___________________________________________
Problem (tick): [ ] list or set  [ ] more than one fact  [ ] vague question
                [ ] no context cue  [ ] look-alike fact  [ ] no source  [ ] not understood
New card(s):
1. _______________: ________________ ? -> ________________ (source ______)
2. _______________: ________________ ? -> ________________ (source ______)
3. _______________: ________________ ? -> ________________ (source ______)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Putting a list on one card.** Split it: one card per item, one cloze per item, or a memory palace.
- **Copying whole textbook sentences as answers.** Shorten to the one fact you need: a word, number or name.
- **Making cards for facts outside your syllabus.** Check the syllabus and previous papers. Every card costs review time for months.
- **Reversing every card.** It doubles the work. Reverse only pairs that PSC asks both ways.
- **Leaving out the source.** When an answer key disagrees, the source tells you where to check.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which card follows the minimum information principle?
    - A) Kerala rivers? → all 44 rivers with lengths
    - B) Kerala rivers: the longest river? → Periyar (244 km)
    - C) Periyar → everything about it
    - D) Rivers and dams of Kerala? → a full table
2. What is the best way to learn the six Malayalam Jnanpith winners?
    - A) A reversed card with the whole list
    - B) One card asking for all six
    - C) One card or cloze per winner, or a memory palace for the list
    - D) Reading the list daily
3. Why start questions with a context word such as "Constitution:"?
    - A) AnkiDroid requires it
    - B) It makes cards longer
    - C) It is only for decoration
    - D) It tells your memory where to search and keeps cards clear as the deck grows
4. When should you use Basic (and reversed card)?
    - A) Never
    - B) Only for pairs that exam questions ask both ways
    - C) For every card
    - D) Only for maths
5. Which cards are often the most valuable in your deck?
    - A) Cards on facts you already know well
    - B) Cards made from questions you got wrong or only recognised
    - C) Cards on topics outside the syllabus
    - D) Cards copied from a friend's deck

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Wozniak's twenty rules (the rules listed in the resources) and the Anki note types
- **Action:** Rewrite your first cards with the checklist and grow your deck to 45 or more good cards. It is done when your proof is saved: screenshots of 5 cards before and after rewriting, and of the deck showing 45 or more cards.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** One short question with one short answer.
2. **C.** Sets and lists on one card are hard to recall and grade.
3. **D.** Context cues are one of Wozniak's rules and make short questions unambiguous.
4. **B.** Reversed cards double reviews, so use them only where both directions matter.
5. **B.** They target exactly the gaps that previous papers exposed.

Action: Rewrite your first cards with the checklist and grow your deck to 45 or more good cards

sections.title: LRN-M04-L03: Cloze deletions and image occlusion
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Make cloze cards from key sentences and image occlusion cards from maps and diagrams, and grow your deck to 70 or more cards. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 50 minutes making cards).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Cloze deletion: hide part of a sentence

A **cloze** card shows a sentence with a gap, and you recall what is missing. In Anki you choose the **Cloze** note type and wrap the hidden part in double braces ([Anki manual: Editing](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html)):

```
The Temple Entry Proclamation was issued in {{c1::1936}} in {{c2::Travancore}}.
Article {{c1::21A}} makes education a Fundamental Right for children aged {{c2::6 to 14}} years.
Kerala's longest river is the {{c1::Periyar::river}} ({{c2::244}} km).
```

- Each number (c1, c2, ...) makes **its own card**. The first line above makes two cards: one hides the year, the other hides the place.
- Text after a double colon inside a cloze, such as `::river`, is a **hint** shown in the gap.
- Giving two gaps the **same number** hides both on one card. Use that rarely; one gap per card is easier to grade.

Cloze is a quick way to make cards from good sentences in your textbook or notes. Wozniak calls it "easy and effective" (rule 5), with a warning: keep each sentence short and clear, and don't hide trivial words.

**Cloze works well for lists too**, because each card hides one item and shows the rest as context:

```
Kerala's three east-flowing rivers are {{c1::Kabani}}, {{c2::Bhavani}} and {{c3::Pambar}}.
```

### Image occlusion: hide part of a picture

**Image occlusion** works like cloze, but on a picture: you draw boxes over parts of a map or diagram, and each box becomes a card. It arrived in Anki 23.10 and is part of AnkiDroid from version 2.17 ([Anki forums](https://forums.ankiweb.net/t/image-occlusion-ankidroid-v2-17/43841)). Wozniak's rule 8 says graphic deletion is as good as cloze deletion.

To make one: add a note, choose the **Image Occlusion** note type, pick a photo or screenshot, draw boxes (or other shapes) over the labels you want to learn, and save. Each box makes a card. Two modes:

- **Hide all, guess one:** all boxes are hidden; one is marked as the question. Best for maps, where neighbouring labels would give the answer away.
- **Hide one, guess one:** only the asked box is hidden; the others are visible. Fine for diagrams where the other labels don't give clues.

If you delete a box later, its card stays until you run Tools → Empty Cards (in Anki for computers).

Good PSC uses: a map of Kerala's districts, national parks or rivers; a map of India's states; a diagram of the heart, the eye or the atmosphere; a chart of the Constitution's Parts; a timeline photo.

**If image occlusion doesn't work on your phone,** make these notes in Anki for computers on the laptop (if it runs Windows 10 or later or a recent Linux) and sync through AnkiWeb, or use a numbered hand-drawn map with Basic cards ("Kerala map: district number 4 from the north? → Kozhikode").

Take map photos from your SCERT textbook or draw your own. Check the map is correct and up to date; an old map can show old boundaries or names.

## Local example

**Anu** chose Kerala geography as her deck topic. Lists of districts and rivers were her weak spot.

She photographed the district map in her SCERT textbook, added an **Image Occlusion** note in AnkiDroid, drew a box over each of the 14 district names and chose **hide all, guess one**, so neighbouring names couldn't give the answer away. That one note made 14 cards.

For rivers she used cloze sentences from her notes, one fact per gap, with hints where two answers were possible: "Kerala's second longest river is the {{c1::Bharathapuzha}} ({{c2::209}} km)". In one evening her deck went from 46 to 78 cards. A week later she could fill a blank district map without errors, which she had never managed by reading.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloze cards and image occlusion as retrieval practice | **Strong** | Both make you produce the answer from memory, then check: retrieval with feedback. |
| Cloze or graphic deletion versus Basic cards | **Limited** | Wozniak calls them easy and effective; there is little research comparing card formats. Choose by the content. |
| Pictures that carry meaning (maps, diagrams) | **Moderate** | Dual coding (Module 3): the visual adds a second route to the memory. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Anki manual: Editing (cloze deletion and image occlusion)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html) | Read the sections on cloze deletion and image occlusion | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki forums (April 2024): image occlusion in AnkiDroid 2.17](https://forums.ankiweb.net/t/image-occlusion-ankidroid-v2-17/43841) | Read the thread on image occlusion in AnkiDroid 2.17 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Piotr Wozniak, "Effective learning: Twenty rules of formulating knowledge" (SuperMemo, 1999)](https://www.supermemo.com/en/blog/twenty-rules-of-formulating-knowledge) | Read rules 5 (cloze deletion) and 8 (graphic deletion) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Find 25 key sentences in your topic (from the textbook, your notes or answer explanations). Shorten each to one clear sentence.
2. Make 25 cloze cards: one key fact per gap, a hint where two answers could fit, and the source at the end.
3. Make at least one image occlusion note from a map, diagram, chart or timeline related to your topic, with 8 to 15 boxes. Choose hide all, guess one for maps.
4. If image occlusion doesn't work on your phone, make it on the laptop and sync, or use a numbered hand-drawn map with Basic cards.
5. Check that your deck now has 70 or more cards, and keep up the daily reviews.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of three cloze notes in the editor, the image occlusion screen with your boxes, and the deck count.

## Template: cloze patterns for PSC facts

```
FACT IN A SENTENCE   The {{c1::Vaikom Satyagraha}} began in {{c2::1924}}.
DEFINITION           {{c1::Federalism}} means power is divided between the centre and the states.
NUMBER WITH HINT     Kerala has {{c1::14::number}} districts.
LIST, ONE PER CARD   The three lists in the Seventh Schedule are the {{c1::Union}}, {{c2::State}} and {{c3::Concurrent}} lists.
CAUSE AND EFFECT     Rain is heavy on Kerala's side of the Western Ghats because {{c1::the moist winds rise and cool}}.
Rules: one key fact per gap; never hide small words (the, of, in); keep the sentence short; add the source.
```

## Template: image occlusion steps

```
1. Photo or screenshot: a clear map or diagram, cropped to what you need.
2. AnkiDroid: add a note -> note type "Image Occlusion" -> choose the image.
3. Draw a box over each label to learn (8 to 15 per image).
4. Choose: hide all, guess one (maps) or hide one, guess one (diagrams).
5. Add a header such as "Kerala districts" and the source.
6. Save, then study one card to check the masks look right.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Hiding several facts in one gap.** One key fact per cloze. Long gaps are hard to grade.
- **Clozing small words.** Hide the fact that matters (a name, a number, a term), not "the" or "of".
- **Forty boxes on one image.** Split big maps into regions; 8 to 15 boxes per image is easier to review.
- **Using hide one, guess one on a map.** The neighbours give the answer away. Use hide all, guess one.
- **Trusting an old or wrong map.** Check the map against your current textbook before making cards.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. How many cards does this cloze note make: "The {{c1::SNDP Yogam}} was founded in {{c2::1903}}"?
    - A) Three
    - B) None
    - C) One
    - D) Two
2. Which image occlusion mode suits a map of Kerala's districts?
    - A) No masks
    - B) Show all, guess none
    - C) Hide one, guess one
    - D) Hide all, guess one
3. What does the text after a double colon inside a cloze do, as in {{c1::Periyar::river}}?
    - A) It makes a second card
    - B) It adds a picture
    - C) It shows a hint in the gap
    - D) It hides the whole sentence
4. Image occlusion doesn't work on your phone. What is a good alternative?
    - A) Make the note in Anki on the laptop and sync, or use a numbered hand-drawn map with Basic cards
    - B) Copy the map ten times
    - C) Skip maps entirely
    - D) Buy a paid app

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Anki manual's sections on cloze deletion and image occlusion, and Wozniak's rules 5 and 8
- **Action:** Make 25 cloze cards and one image occlusion note, and bring your deck to 70 or more cards. It is done when your proof is saved: screenshots of three cloze notes in the editor, the image occlusion screen with your boxes, and the deck count.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Each cloze number makes its own card.
2. **D.** On a map, visible neighbouring labels would give the answer away.
3. **C.** The hint appears in the gap while you recall.
4. **A.** Both keep the map as a retrieval cue at no cost.

sections.title: LRN-M04-L04: The daily review habit and managing your workload
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Keep your daily AnkiDroid habit sustainable by budgeting new cards, rescuing a backlog and fixing cards you keep failing, and finish your deck at 100 or more cards. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus finishing the deck).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### New cards decide tomorrow's work

Every new card you add today will come back for reviews for weeks and months. So the number of **new cards a day** controls your future daily workload. The Anki manual gives a rule of thumb: if you consistently learn 20 new cards a day, you can expect roughly 200 reviews a day ([Anki manual: Deck Options](https://docs.ankiweb.net/deck-options.html)).

Scale that down to plan your own budget. Ten new cards a day leads, over time, to roughly 100 reviews a day. If a review takes you about 8 seconds (time yourself; it varies), 100 reviews take about 13 minutes. A sensible PSC budget is **10 to 15 new cards a day** and 15 to 25 minutes of reviews. When exam pressure rises, cut new cards first, never reviews.

### The daily routine

1. **Same time, same place, every day:** for example with your morning tea. Module 6 shows how to anchor a habit to something you already do.
2. **Reviews first, then new cards.** If time runs out, the new cards wait.
3. **Answer honestly and quickly.** Recall, reveal, judge, press. Don't think for minutes about one card.

### Desired retention

Newer versions of Anki can use a scheduler called **FSRS**, with a setting called **desired retention**: the share of cards you want to remember when they come up. The default is 90%. A higher number gives shorter gaps and more reviews, and the workload rises sharply as you approach 100%; the manual advises staying below 97%. If your AnkiDroid shows these options, the default is a good place to start; if not, the older scheduler works fine too.

### When you fall behind

Missed a few days? The reviews pile up, and the pile looks frightening. Don't delete the deck and don't try to do 500 reviews in one sitting.

1. Set **New cards/day to 0** until you are back on track.
2. Do a fixed amount every day, for example 150 reviews or 25 minutes.
3. When the daily due count is back to normal, turn new cards back on.

When you are behind, Anki shows the cards that have waited longest first ([Anki manual: Studying](https://docs.ankiweb.net/studying.html)), so the most forgotten cards get attention first.

### Leeches: cards you keep failing

Some cards you fail again and again. Anki calls them **leeches** and can tag them automatically. Repeating a bad card doesn't fix it; rewriting does:

- **Split it** if it holds more than one fact.
- **Add context or a contrast** if you confuse it with a similar fact (LRN-M04-L02).
- **Add a hook:** an example, a picture or a mnemonic (Module 11).
- **Check you understand it;** if not, relearn the idea first.
- **Suspend or delete it** if it is not worth the time.

### After the 30 days

Your 30 days prove the habit. Keep going: add decks for other PSC subjects one at a time, and keep the total review time within your budget. Export or sync your collection regularly as a backup.

## Local example

**Sreeja** was excited in her first week and set New cards/day to 30. By day 9 AnkiDroid showed 180 reviews due, she had a sick child and a busy week, and she didn't open the app for three days. When she did, it showed 400 due. She nearly gave up.

Her study partner showed her the backlog plan. She set new cards to 0 and did 25 minutes of reviews every day after dropping her children at school. After four days the due count was back below 80. She then set New cards/day to 12, which her timing showed would settle at about 15 minutes of reviews a day.

She also found four cards she had failed at least five times. Two were lists, which she split; one confused the Vaikom and Guruvayur satyagrahas, which got a contrast card; one she suspended because it was not in her syllabus. Her deck reached 112 cards on day 14, and she finished her 30 days without missing another day.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily spaced reviews (consistency) | **Strong** | Spacing works only if reviews happen near their due dates; daily review keeps the schedule intact. |
| New cards drive future workload (about ten reviews a day per daily new card) | **Moderate** | A rule of thumb from the Anki manual, based on how the scheduler works; your own timing gives your numbers. |
| Rewriting leeches instead of repeating them | **Limited** | Practical advice from Anki and Wozniak, consistent with research on interference and meaningful encoding. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Anki manual: Deck Options (daily limits, FSRS, desired retention)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/deck-options.html) | Read the parts on daily limits, FSRS and desired retention | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki manual: Studying (the four answer buttons)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/studying.html) | Read what happens when you fall behind | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AnkiDroid manual](https://docs.ankidroid.org/) | Find the statistics screen and the deck options in AnkiDroid | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Time 20 of your reviews to find your seconds per review. Fill in the workload calculator below and set New cards/day to match your daily minutes.
2. Finish your deck at 100 or more cards, adding cards from questions you got wrong in previous papers where you can.
3. Find three cards you have failed three or more times. Rewrite, split or suspend each, and note what was wrong.
4. Take a screenshot of the statistics screen showing your review days and the percentage of answers you got right.
5. Write your daily review rule in one line: when, where, and what comes just before it (for example: "After morning tea, at the kitchen table, before I open WhatsApp").

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your deck with 100 or more cards, your filled-in workload calculator, the three leech fixes, a statistics screenshot and your daily review rule.

## Template: AnkiDroid workload calculator

```
My seconds per review (timed over 20 reviews): ___ s
Minutes I can give to AnkiDroid each day: ___ min
Reviews that fit: minutes x 60 / seconds = ___ reviews a day
Long-run reviews are about 10 x new cards a day, so:
New cards a day = reviews that fit / 10 = ___   (cap at 15 while preparing for PSC)
Example: 8 s per review, 15 min a day -> 15 x 60 / 8 = 112 reviews -> about 11 new cards a day
```

## Template: backlog rescue plan

```
BACKLOG RESCUE      Start date: ______   Due count today: ___
1. New cards/day -> 0
2. Daily target: ___ reviews or ___ minutes (same time every day)
3. Track: day 1 ___ due | day 2 ___ | day 3 ___ | day 4 ___ | day 5 ___
4. When the due count is back near my normal (___), set new cards back to ___
Cause of the backlog: __________   My fix so it doesn't happen again: __________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Adding more new cards on good days.** Today's extra cards are next month's extra reviews. Keep new cards steady.
- **Skipping reviews to "catch up" on lessons.** Missed reviews pile up. Five minutes of reviews beats none.
- **Trying to clear a huge backlog in one sitting.** Set new cards to 0 and do a fixed amount daily; it clears in days.
- **Repeating a leech forever.** Rewrite, split, add a hook or suspend it.
- **Never backing up.** Sync to AnkiWeb or export your collection to your Learning Folder.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to the Anki manual, learning 20 new cards a day leads to roughly how many reviews a day?
    - A) None after a week
    - B) About 20
    - C) About 2,000
    - D) About 200
2. You missed five days and have 400 reviews due. What should you do?
    - A) Do all 400 tonight
    - B) Set new cards to 0 and do a fixed amount of reviews daily until the count is normal
    - C) Delete the deck and start again
    - D) Add more new cards to make up
3. What happens to your workload if you raise desired retention from 90% to 97%?
    - A) Reviews decrease
    - B) Reviews increase, sharply as you near 100%
    - C) Cards are deleted
    - D) Nothing changes
4. What is the best fix for a card you have failed six times?
    - A) Make five copies of it
    - B) Press Easy to get rid of it
    - C) Rewrite, split it, add a hook or contrast, or suspend it
    - D) Keep pressing Again until it sticks
5. Exam pressure rises and time is short. What do you cut first?
    - A) Sleep
    - B) Reviews
    - C) New cards
    - D) The weekly review

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Anki manual's Deck Options and the part of Studying on falling behind
- **Action:** Set a workload budget, fix three leeches and finish your deck at 100 or more cards. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your deck with 100 or more cards, your filled-in workload calculator, the three leech fixes, a statistics screenshot and your daily review rule.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** New cards keep coming back, so daily reviews grow to about ten times the daily new cards.
2. **B.** A steady daily amount clears the backlog without burning you out.
3. **B.** Higher retention means shorter gaps and more reviews.
4. **C.** Leeches usually have a problem in the card itself.
5. **C.** Reviews protect what you already learned; new cards can pause.

Action: Set a workload budget, fix three leeches and finish your deck at 100 or more cards

sections.title: Module 5: Focus and deep work
sections.summary: Protect your attention: understand why focus breaks, rebuild your study stamina with a focus ladder, plan your week in time blocks with Pomodoro-style breaks, and set up your Android phone so it helps instead of interrupting.
sections.content:
## Overview

Every method in this course needs attention first. A PSC aspirant who studies three focused hours learns more than one who sits for six with the phone buzzing. This module is practical: you measure your focus, change your setup, and measure again.

At the end you retake the week 0 focus test, so you can see how much your setup and practice have already changed.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain why focus breaks and what can and cannot "train" attention
- Run a focus ladder and keep a Focus log
- Plan a realistic week with the weekly study planner and Pomodoro-style blocks
- Set up Digital Wellbeing, notifications and physical rules on your phone
- Measure the change with your screen time and a repeat focus test

## Time

About 4 hours 45 minutes in total: 3 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 6–7, with the module project due in week 7.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M05-L01: Why focus breaks, and how to rebuild your attention span (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M05-L02: Pomodoro and time-blocking around real life (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M05-L03: Taming your Android phone (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **weekly study planner** (one of the six core tools)
- The **Focus** tab, the **focus ladder** and the **distraction pad**
- The **notification audit** and **phone setup checklist**

## Module project: My focus system and a repeat focus test

1. Make sure your Focus tab has at least 10 logged blocks and your phone setup checklist is complete.
2. Repeat the week 0 focus test (45 minutes, normal PSC study, tally marks), this time with your new setup.
3. Compare minutes to first distraction and tally marks with your week 0 average, and write two lines on what made the difference.
4. Write your three focus rules for the rest of the course (for example: phone in the kitchen, 35-minute blocks, maths at 7 a.m.).

**Proof to record:** Your Focus tab, the repeat focus test result next to your week 0 result, and your three focus rules.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Measurement | No Focus log | A few blocks logged | 10 or more blocks logged and a repeat focus test |
| Phone | Unchanged | Some settings changed | Full setup done and screen time compared after a week |
| Planning | Studying "when I get time" | A plan made but not followed | A weekly planner followed, with planned and done counted |
| Rules | None | General ideas | Three specific focus rules based on your own log |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do LRN-M05-L03 (phone setup) first: it gives the biggest change for the least time.
- Use one 25-minute Pomodoro a day with the phone in another room, and log it.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Three things that break focus | Outside interruptions, switching by choice, and mind-wandering. |
| The skill with mind-wandering | Notice it and come back; write urges on a distraction pad. |
| Focus ladder rule | Start 5 minutes above your baseline; add 5 minutes after five counted blocks; stop at 45 to 50. |
| The Pomodoro technique | 25 minutes on one task, a 5-minute break; a longer break after four rounds. |
| Biwer and others (2023) in one line | Fixed breaks gave less fatigue and more concentration, with the same work done in less time. |
| Digital Wellbeing tools | Dashboard, app timers, Focus mode and Bedtime mode. |
| Best physical rule for the phone | Out of reach (another room) during study blocks. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Changing everything at once and keeping nothing.** Make the phone changes this week and add one new habit at a time.
- **Judging focus by how you feel.** Use the numbers: minutes to first distraction, tallies and screen time.

sections.title: LRN-M05-L01: Why focus breaks, and how to rebuild your attention span
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain why focus breaks, measure your own focus with a Focus log, and start a focus ladder that lengthens your study blocks step by step. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 40 minutes action plus a week of logging).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Why focus breaks

Attention is the doorway to working memory (Module 1), and it is easily pulled away. Three things break it most often for PSC aspirants:

1. **Interruptions from outside:** notifications, calls, people, noise. Each one pulls attention away, and getting back into a hard topic takes time.
2. **Switching by choice:** "just checking" WhatsApp, a quick look at YouTube. In the Stanford multitasking study, heavy media multitaskers were worse at ignoring irrelevant information and at switching tasks ([Ophir and others, 2009](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/08/090825113133.htm)). That study shows a link, not proof that multitasking caused the problems, but the cost of switching is easy to feel.
3. **Mind-wandering from inside:** thoughts about family, money, the exam, food. This is normal for every human brain. The skill is not to stop it but to **notice it and come back**.

The phrase **deep work** comes from a popular book by the computer scientist Cal Newport. It means long, undistracted work on a demanding task. For you, a deep-work block is 25 to 50 minutes on one PSC topic, with nothing else competing for attention.

### Can you "train" your attention span?

Honestly: there is no proven quick training that enlarges attention in general. "Brain training" games make you better at those games, not at studying (Module 1; [Melby-Lervåg and others, 2016](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:daa9a729-f17b-4e45-97c0-cff5075ea404)). What reliably helps is practical:

- **Remove what pulls attention:** the phone out of reach, notifications off (LRN-M05-L03), a quiet place.
- **Practise focusing on real study,** in blocks that grow slowly, like building stamina for running. This is the **focus ladder** below.
- **Rest properly:** sleep (Module 19) and real breaks (LRN-M05-L02).
- **Handle urges:** when you feel the pull to check the phone, write the urge on a "distraction pad" and return to the task. The urge usually fades in a minute or two.

### The focus ladder

1. Take your baseline "minutes to first distraction" from week 0.
2. Set your study block **5 minutes longer** than that, with a minimum of 15 minutes.
3. A block **counts** when you stayed on the task the whole time, with any stray thoughts written on the pad instead of acted on.
4. After **five counted blocks** at one length, add 5 minutes.
5. Stop climbing at 45 to 50 minutes. Longer blocks rarely help; regular blocks do.

### The Focus log

Each block gets one row in a new **Focus** tab: task, planned minutes, minutes to first distraction, tally of distractions, where the phone was, and a focus rating. After two weeks, the log shows what helps your focus and what hurts it, which matters more than any general advice.

## Local example

**Ashiq** scored 9 minutes to first distraction in his week 0 focus test, with 11 tally marks in 45 minutes, nearly all of them phone checks. He did not believe he could ever sit for 45 minutes.

He started his focus ladder at 15-minute blocks, with the phone charging in the kitchen and a small notebook as his distraction pad. In the first week, the pad filled with lines like "reply to Faisal", "check the cricket score", "look up the meaning of 'concurrent'". He dealt with them in his breaks.

He logged every block in the Focus tab. By the end of week two he had moved to 25-minute blocks; by week four, 35. The log taught him two things he wouldn't have guessed: his worst blocks were straight after lunch, and blocks with earphones playing music had twice as many distractions as silent ones. He moved his maths practice to 7 a.m. and stopped the music.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heavy media multitasking goes with weaker attention control | **Moderate** | Ophir and others (2009) found the link; the study cannot show that multitasking caused it. |
| Brain-training games to build general attention | **No good evidence** | Training improves the trained task, with no convincing transfer (Melby-Lervåg and others, 2016). |
| Removing the phone and notifications during study | **Limited** | Plausible and widely used; studies of phones and attention have mixed results. Your Focus log shows whether it works for you. |
| A focus ladder of slowly longer blocks | **Limited** | A practical method with no direct research. Judge it by your log and your retest. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [ScienceDaily (26 August 2009): heavy media multitaskers pay a mental price (Ophir, Nass and Wagner, PNAS)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/08/090825113133.htm) | Reread the report on media multitaskers, noting the three findings | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Melby-Lervåg, Redick and Hulme (2016): working memory training does not improve far transfer](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:daa9a729-f17b-4e45-97c0-cff5075ea404) | Reread the abstract: why games don't build general attention | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.4 How to Manage Time, for ideas on where and when to study | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Add a Focus tab to your Learning Workbook with the headings below.
2. Look up your week 0 "minutes to first distraction". Set your first focus-ladder block length: 5 minutes more, and at least 15 minutes.
3. Keep a distraction pad (a small notebook or slip of paper) beside you in every study block. Write urges and stray thoughts on it instead of acting on them.
4. For one week, log every study block in the Focus tab, including where the phone was.
5. At the end of the week, write three lines: your most common distraction, the time of day you focus best, and one change for next week. Move up the ladder if you have five counted blocks.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Focus tab with a week of blocks, a photo of one page of your distraction pad, and your three lines.

## Template: Focus tab headings

```csv
Date,Task,Planned minutes,Minutes to first distraction,Distractions (tally),Phone where?,Focus (1-10),Note
```

## Template: focus ladder

```
FOCUS LADDER     Baseline minutes to first distraction: ___
Rung  Block length   Counted blocks (5 to climb)    Dates
1     ___ min        [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]            ______
2     ___ min        [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]            ______
3     ___ min        [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]            ______
4     ___ min        [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]            ______
5     45-50 min      [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]            ______
A block counts when I stayed on the task the whole time and wrote urges on the pad.
```

## Template: distraction pad

```
DISTRACTION PAD      Date: ______
Time   Urge or thought                          Deal with it when?
_____  ______________________________________   break / evening / never
_____  ______________________________________   break / evening / never
_____  ______________________________________   break / evening / never
```

## Common mistakes

- **Starting with 60-minute blocks.** Start just above your baseline and climb 5 minutes at a time.
- **Fighting every stray thought.** Write it on the pad and return. Noticing and returning is the skill.
- **Blaming yourself for poor focus.** Most poor focus comes from the setup. Change the setup first, then judge.
- **Not logging.** Without the Focus log you are guessing. Two weeks of rows show what really helps.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did the Stanford study find about heavy media multitaskers?
    - A) They had longer attention spans
    - B) They were better at focusing
    - C) Nothing at all
    - D) They were worse at ignoring irrelevant information and switching tasks, though the study shows a link, not cause
2. Your baseline minutes to first distraction is 12. What block length does the focus ladder start with?
    - A) 5 minutes
    - B) 17 minutes
    - C) 45 minutes
    - D) 60 minutes
3. An urge to check WhatsApp arrives mid-block. What does this lesson suggest?
    - A) Stop the block and start again tomorrow
    - B) Check quickly and come back
    - C) Write it on the distraction pad and return to the task
    - D) Keep the phone in your hand to resist it
4. What does research say about brain games for building attention?
    - A) They replace sleep
    - B) They improve the trained games, with no convincing transfer to studying
    - C) They double attention span
    - D) They work only for children

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The media multitasking report and College Success 3.4 How to Manage Time
- **Action:** Start the Focus tab, the focus ladder and a distraction pad, and log a week of blocks. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Focus tab with a week of blocks, a photo of one page of your distraction pad, and your three lines.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Ophir and others (2009) found weaker attention control in heavy multitaskers.
2. **B.** Start 5 minutes above your baseline, with a minimum of 15.
3. **C.** The pad takes the urge out of your head; it usually fades in a minute or two.
4. **B.** Gains stay narrow; practical changes to your setup help more.
