sections.title: LRN-M05-L02: Pomodoro and time-blocking around real life
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Plan a realistic week of focused study blocks around PSC, work and family, with Pomodoro-style breaks and the weekly study planner. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 40 minutes planning plus a week of blocks).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The Pomodoro technique

The **Pomodoro technique**, created by Francesco Cirillo, is simple: work on one task for 25 minutes, take a 5-minute break, and after four rounds take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. It is named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

How strong is the evidence? There is little direct research. One careful study with 87 university students compared fixed, Pomodoro-style breaks (24 minutes of study and 6 of rest, or 12 and 3) with breaks the students chose themselves. With fixed breaks, students reported less fatigue and distraction and more concentration and motivation, and they got as much work done in less time; students who chose their own breaks studied in longer stretches and took longer breaks ([Biwer and others, 2023](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/understanding-effort-regulation-comparing-pomodoro-breaks-and-sel)). One small study is a start, not proof. Treat Pomodoro as a useful tool, and judge it by your Focus log.

Useful adjustments:

- **25 and 5 is a starting point.** As your focus ladder climbs, 40 and 10 or 50 and 10 may suit you better.
- **A break is a real break:** stand up, drink water, look outside, stretch. Scrolling the phone is not a break; it tends to stretch to 20 minutes and drags your mind elsewhere.
- **One Pomodoro, one task, one method:** for example, "Kerala renaissance: two chunks with recall, then 10 MCQs".

### Time-blocking

**Time-blocking** means giving each study task a fixed slot in your week, written down in advance, instead of studying "whenever I get time". It turns vague intentions into appointments with yourself, and it links to the strongest habit research in Module 6 (if-then plans).

1. **Find your fixed commitments first:** work, family duties, travel, prayer times, meals.
2. **Protect your best hours** for your hardest PSC work. Many people focus best early in the morning; your Focus log tells you your own best time.
3. **Give every block a task and a method,** not just a subject. "Maths" is vague; "mixed set of 12: percentages, ratio, averages, time and work" is a block.
4. **Plan for real life in Kerala:** power cuts (keep offline PDFs and paper ready), monsoon days, functions and festivals, visitors. Leave one empty buffer block a week to catch up.
5. **Plan the week on Sunday** during your weekly review, and tick blocks as you finish them.

The **weekly study planner** below is one of the six core tools of your learning system. In Module 12 it becomes part of your 12-week PSC plan.

## Local example

**Sreeja** has two study windows a day: 10:00 to 10:45, after the children leave for school, and 21:30 to 22:15, after they sleep. She used to "study when the work is done", which often meant not at all.

On Sunday she filled in the weekly planner. Each morning window became one 25-minute Pomodoro of new learning and one 15-minute block of Revision-tab reviews, with a 5-minute break between them. Each evening window became AnkiDroid reviews and one 25-minute block of mixed MCQs. Saturday afternoon, when her husband takes the children to his mother's house, became her 90-minute block for the course's action task. Wednesday evening stayed empty as a buffer.

She ticked 11 of her 13 planned blocks in the first week. The two she missed were on the day of a family function, and the buffer block caught one of them. For the first time she could see exactly what she had studied in a week.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planned, fixed breaks (Pomodoro-style) | **Limited** | One study of 87 students (Biwer and others, 2023): less fatigue and distraction, more concentration, same work done in less time. Promising, not proven. |
| Time-blocking a week in advance | **Limited** | Little direct research; it applies if-then planning, which has strong evidence (Module 6). |
| Breaks spent scrolling the phone | **Limited** | Little research either way; the practical risk is that breaks stretch and attention leaves the topic. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Biwer et al. (2023), "Understanding effort regulation: Comparing Pomodoro breaks and self-regulated breaks"](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/understanding-effort-regulation-comparing-pomodoro-breaks-and-sel) | Read the abstract of the Pomodoro-breaks study | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.5 on prioritising and 3.7 on strategies for time and task management | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. List your fixed commitments for next week: work, family, travel, meals, prayer, and your best focus time from your Focus log.
2. Fill in the weekly study planner below for next week. Every block gets a subject, a topic and a method. Include daily AnkiDroid reviews, your Revision-tab reviews, one Saturday action-task block and one empty buffer block.
3. Use Pomodoro-style blocks (25 and 5, or your focus-ladder length) for every block, and log each one in the Focus tab.
4. Take real breaks, away from the phone.
5. At the end of the week, count planned versus done blocks, and note what got in the way. Plan the following week in your weekly review.

**Proof to record:** Your filled-in weekly planner with ticks, and a week of rows in the Focus tab.

## Template: weekly study planner (core tool)

```
WEEKLY STUDY PLANNER          Week of: ________
Exam: __________________ on ________   Weeks left: ___
Hours this week: course ___ + PSC study ___ = ___

DAY   BLOCK (time)   SUBJECT : TOPIC            METHOD                    DONE
Mon   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Tue   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Wed   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Thu   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Fri   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sat   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sun   20 minutes     Weekly learning review + plan next week               [ ]

METHOD words: retrieval (blank-page recall, practice questions), spaced review
(from the Revision tab), mixed practice (interleaving), Feynman, cards, mock test.

Every day:  [ ] AnkiDroid reviews (___ min)  [ ] one retrieval session
            [ ] phone in another room during blocks  [ ] sleep by ____
If-then plans: If ____________________, then I will ____________________.
```

## Template: one Pomodoro block card

```
BLOCK      Time: ______  Length: ___ min (break ___ min)
Task: ____________________________________________ (one task only)
Method: retrieval / mixed practice / Feynman / cards / reading + recall
Done when: _______________________________________ (e.g. 2 chunks + 10 MCQs)
Phone: in another room [ ]   Distraction pad ready [ ]
After: Focus log row added [ ]   Result: _____________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Planning ten hours a day.** Plan what you really did last week plus a little. A plan you keep beats a plan you admire.
- **Blocks without a task ("study GK").** Write the topic and method, so the block starts without decisions.
- **Spending breaks on the phone.** Stand up, drink water, look outside. Keep the phone for the long break or the evening.
- **No buffer.** Real life in Kerala includes power cuts, guests and functions. Keep one empty block a week.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Biwer and others (2023) find with fixed Pomodoro-style breaks?
    - A) Students felt more tired
    - B) Less fatigue and distraction and more concentration, with the same work done in less time
    - C) Students learned twice as much
    - D) No difference in anything
2. Which is a well-planned study block?
    - A) "Study GK"
    - B) "Read for a while"
    - C) "Revise everything"
    - D) "Kerala renaissance: two chunks with recall, then 10 MCQs, 25 minutes"
3. What is a good use of a 5-minute break?
    - A) Scroll Instagram
    - B) Start a new topic
    - C) Reply to every WhatsApp group
    - D) Stand up, drink water and look outside
4. Why keep one empty buffer block a week?
    - A) Because PSC exams are on that day
    - B) Because the brain needs one empty block
    - C) It is not needed
    - D) To catch up after power cuts, guests or functions

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Pomodoro-breaks study and College Success sections 3.5 and 3.7
- **Action:** Plan next week in the weekly study planner and run it with Pomodoro-style blocks. It is done when your proof is saved: your filled-in weekly planner with ticks, and a week of rows in the Focus tab.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** One study with 87 students; promising, not proof.
2. **D.** It names a topic, a method and when it is done.
3. **D.** A real break rests attention; phone breaks tend to stretch and pull you away.
4. **D.** Real life interrupts plans; a buffer keeps one bad day from ruining the week.

sections.title: LRN-M05-L03: Taming your Android phone
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Set up your Android phone to support study instead of interrupting it, using Digital Wellbeing, notification control and a few physical rules, and measure the change in screen time. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 40 minutes setup plus a check a week later).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

For most PSC aspirants, the phone is both the best study tool (PDFs, AnkiDroid, previous papers, classes) and the biggest distraction (WhatsApp groups, Reels, YouTube, games). This lesson keeps the first and tames the second.

### Step 1: see the truth

Android's **Digital Wellbeing** shows a dashboard of how long you used each app today and in the past days, how many notifications you got, and how many times you unlocked the phone ([Android Help: Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) (check current rules)). Most people underestimate their screen time. Take a screenshot before you change anything; that is your baseline.

Menus differ by phone brand and Android version. Samsung, Xiaomi, Realme and others may call these settings something slightly different; search your Settings for "Digital Wellbeing", "Focus mode" or "screen time".

### Step 2: silence the noise

- **Turn off notifications** for every app that isn't urgent: games, shopping, news, social media. Keep calls, SMS, your bank and the few people you must reach.
- **Mute WhatsApp groups** (open the group, tap its name, choose mute, then always). Read them once a day at a time you choose.
- **Turn off autoplay** in YouTube, so one PSC class doesn't become an hour of recommendations.

### Step 3: use the built-in tools

- **Focus mode** pauses the apps you choose (for example YouTube, Instagram, games) and can run on a schedule. Set it for your study blocks, and leave AnkiDroid and your PDF reader unpaused.
- **App timers** set a daily limit for an app; the limit resets at midnight. Try 30 minutes a day for your biggest time-taker.
- **Bedtime mode** can turn the screen grey and silence the phone at night. Greyscale makes scrolling much less attractive.

### Step 4: physical rules beat willpower

- **Out of reach during study blocks:** in another room, or in a drawer. Use a cheap timer or the clock app on a family member's phone if you need one.
- **Social apps off the home screen.** One extra tap to reach them is often enough to stop the automatic reach.
- **Charge the phone outside the bedroom** at night (Module 19).
- **Study offline when you can:** download PDFs and previous papers, then turn on airplane mode while reading them.

### Honest expectations

Research on phones and attention is mixed: some studies find that a nearby phone hurts focus, others don't. Nobody needs a study to know that a notification interrupts. Treat this lesson as an experiment: compare your Digital Wellbeing numbers and your Focus log before and after, and keep what works for you.

## Local example

**Ashiq** took his first Digital Wellbeing screenshot and was shocked: 6 hours 40 minutes of screen time on the day, more than 3 hours of it on Instagram and YouTube, and 92 unlocks.

He spent 40 minutes on setup. Notifications went off for all but calls, SMS, his bank and his family group. He muted 14 WhatsApp groups and decided to read them once at 8 p.m. Focus mode paused Instagram, YouTube and two games from 6 to 8 a.m. and 7 to 9 p.m., his study blocks. He set a 30-minute app timer on Instagram, turned on greyscale at 10:30 p.m., and moved every social app into a folder on the last screen.

A week later his screen time was 3 hours 50 minutes a day, with 41 unlocks. In his Focus log, minutes to first distraction rose from about 15 to 22. He had to switch Focus mode off twice for a class link sent on WhatsApp; he now asks for class links by SMS.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Notifications interrupt focus | **Moderate** | An interruption pulls attention away by definition; how long recovery takes varies by person and task. |
| Focus modes, app timers and greyscale reduce phone use | **Limited** | Little strong research; easy to test with your own Digital Wellbeing numbers. |
| A phone nearby (even silent) hurts focus | **Limited** | Studies have mixed results. Keeping it out of reach costs nothing, so test it with your Focus log. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Android Help: manage how you spend time with Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) | Read the parts on the dashboard, app timers, Focus mode and Bedtime mode, and find them on your phone | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [ScienceDaily (26 August 2009): heavy media multitaskers pay a mental price (Ophir, Nass and Wagner, PNAS)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/08/090825113133.htm) | Optional: reread why switching between media is costly | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Take a screenshot of your Digital Wellbeing dashboard (screen time per app, notifications and unlocks) before changing anything.
2. Do a notification audit with the template below: turn off every notification you don't need, and mute all WhatsApp groups except one or two.
3. Set Focus mode on a schedule for your study blocks, pausing your most distracting apps but not AnkiDroid or your PDF reader.
4. Set an app timer on your biggest time-taker, and turn on Bedtime mode with greyscale for your sleep time.
5. Move social apps off the home screen, and decide where the phone will be during study blocks and at night.
6. After 7 days, take a second dashboard screenshot and compare screen time, unlocks and your Focus log.

**Proof to record:** Your before and after dashboard screenshots, screenshots of Focus mode, the app timer and Bedtime settings, and your completed notification audit.

## Template: notification audit

```
NOTIFICATION AUDIT      Date: ______
App                 Keep notifications?   Why
Calls / SMS         yes                   family, emergencies
Bank app            yes                   fraud alerts
WhatsApp (chats)    yes / no              ______________
WhatsApp groups     muted (always)        read once a day at ____
YouTube             no                    ______________
Instagram / Reels   no                    ______________
Games               no                    ______________
Shopping            no                    ______________
Other: ________     yes / no              ______________
```

## Template: phone setup checklist

```
[ ] Baseline dashboard screenshot taken (screen time ___ h ___ min, unlocks ___)
[ ] Notifications off for everything not urgent
[ ] WhatsApp groups muted; reading time set: ____
[ ] YouTube autoplay off
[ ] Focus mode scheduled: ____ to ____ and ____ to ____ (AnkiDroid not paused)
[ ] App timer: __________ at ___ min a day
[ ] Bedtime mode with greyscale from ____
[ ] Social apps off the home screen
[ ] Study blocks: phone in ______________   Night: phone charges in ______________
[ ] After 7 days: screen time ___ h ___ min, unlocks ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Deleting every app in a burst of resolve.** All-or-nothing rarely lasts. Silence and limit them; keep the ones you need.
- **Relying on willpower with the phone on the desk.** Distance works better than willpower. Put it in another room.
- **Pausing your study apps in Focus mode.** Leave AnkiDroid and your PDF reader free; pause only the distractions.
- **Never checking the numbers again.** Look at the dashboard in your weekly review. Habits drift back.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does an Android app timer do?
    - A) Sets a daily limit for an app, which resets at midnight
    - B) Blocks calls
    - C) Deletes the app after a week
    - D) Speeds up the app
2. How should you set up Focus mode for study?
    - A) Pause every app including AnkiDroid
    - B) Use it only at night
    - C) Schedule it for study blocks, pausing distracting apps but not AnkiDroid or your PDF reader
    - D) Turn it on once a month
3. What is the honest summary of research on phones and attention?
    - A) Phones permanently damage attention
    - B) Mixed results, so test changes with your own screen time and Focus log
    - C) Phones have no effect at all
    - D) A silent phone on the desk always halves focus
4. Which physical rule tends to work better than willpower?
    - A) Keeping it face-down on the desk
    - B) Keeping it on silent beside the book
    - C) Holding it in your pocket
    - D) Keeping the phone in another room during study blocks

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Android Help page on Digital Wellbeing, with each setting found on your own phone
- **Action:** Audit notifications, set up Focus mode, an app timer and Bedtime mode, and compare screen time after a week. It is done when your proof is saved: your before and after dashboard screenshots, screenshots of Focus mode, the app timer and Bedtime settings, and your completed notification audit.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Digital Wellbeing app timers limit daily use and reset at midnight.
2. **C.** Keep the study tools; pause the distractions.
3. **B.** Studies disagree; your own before-and-after numbers decide.
4. **D.** Distance removes the automatic reach.

sections.title: Module 6: Motivation, procrastination and habits
sections.summary: Understand why you procrastinate, and build habits that run on days when motivation is low: if-then plans, tiny habits anchored to your routines, small rewards, and a restart protocol for bad weeks.
sections.content:
## Overview

PSC preparation is a long race, and most aspirants don't fail because of ability; they fail because study becomes irregular. This module treats procrastination as a feeling to manage, not a character flaw, and gives you the tool with some of the strongest evidence in behaviour research: the if-then plan.

The result is a small habit system, tracked in the free Loop app, with your reasons, rewards and a plan for restarting.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain procrastination as short-term mood repair and find your own triggers
- Use the five-minute start and shrink tasks you avoid
- Write if-then plans for habits and obstacles, and anchor tiny habits to routines
- Track habits in Loop and use rewards and streaks wisely
- Restart quickly after a bad week with a written protocol

## Time

About 4 hours 30 minutes in total: 3 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 7–8, with the module project due in week 8.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M06-L01: Why we procrastinate (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M06-L02: Implementation intentions and tiny habits (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M06-L03: Rewards, streaks and restarting after a bad week (about 1 hour)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **procrastination log** and **task shrinker**
- The **if-then planner** and **Loop Habit Tracker** with three habits
- Your **reason card**, **reward menu** and **restart protocol**

## Module project: My habit system

1. Show at least 14 days of Loop records for your three habits.
2. Review your if-then plans: keep those that worked, rewrite those that didn't, and add one for your weakest day.
3. Put your reason card, reward menu and restart protocol together on one page in your notebook.
4. Explain your habit system to your study partner or a family member, and ask them to check in with you once a week for the next month.

**Proof to record:** A Loop screenshot with 14 or more days, your updated if-then plans and your one-page habit system.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Understanding procrastination | Still "I'm lazy" | Know the triggers in general | Found my own triggers in a log and acted on them |
| If-then plans | None | Vague plans | Specific plans for habits and obstacles, revised after 14 days |
| Tracking | Not tracked | Tracked a few days | 14 or more days in Loop |
| Restarting | No plan | A plan in my head | A written protocol, used at least once if needed |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write three if-then plans and add one habit (daily AnkiDroid) to Loop.
- Keep the restart protocol in your notebook.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Procrastination in one line (Sirois and Pychyl) | Short-term mood repair: avoiding an unpleasant task to feel better now. |
| The five-minute start | Promise only five minutes; most people keep going. |
| Implementation intention | "If [situation], then I will [action]." |
| Effect of if-then plans (Gollwitzer and Sheeran) | Medium to large (d = 0.65) across 94 tests. |
| Average time to form a daily habit (Lally) | About 66 days, from 18 to 254. |
| Tiny habit with an anchor | "After I pour my morning tea, I will open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards." |
| Streak rule | Never miss twice. |
| First step after a bad week | Forgive yourself, then do the tiny version today. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Reading about habits without writing any if-then plans.** The plan is one sentence. Write it now.
- **Building a perfect system and abandoning it after one bad week.** The restart protocol is part of the system.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L01: Why we procrastinate
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain procrastination as short-term mood repair, find your own triggers with a procrastination log, and use the five-minute start on a task you have been avoiding. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus a 5-day log).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Procrastination is not laziness

**Procrastination** means delaying something you intended to do, even though you expect the delay to cost you. Almost everyone does it, and PSC preparation, with its long syllabus and distant exam dates, invites it.

Researchers Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl describe procrastination as a problem of **short-term mood repair**. When a task feels unpleasant (boring, confusing, frightening), avoiding it makes you feel better right now. The bill goes to your **future self**, who has less time and more stress ([Sirois and Pychyl, 2013](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/)). That is why "just be disciplined" rarely works: the problem is a feeling, so the fix has to deal with the feeling.

### What makes a PSC task feel bad

Notice which of these describe the tasks you put off:

- **Boring:** long lists of static GK facts
- **Hard or unclear:** a maths topic where you don't know the method
- **Big or vague:** "finish the Constitution", "start current affairs"
- **Frightening:** a full mock test that might show a low score
- **No reward now:** the exam is months away; Reels are right here
- **Unsure where to start:** a new subject with no plan

### Five ways to make starting easier

1. **Shrink the task.** Not "do maths" but "open the guide at page 34 and do five percentage questions". A small, specific task feels less threatening.
2. **The five-minute start.** Promise yourself only five minutes. Once started, most people continue; if you don't, you still did five minutes.
3. **Remove friction the night before.** Book open at the right page, phone charging in another room, pen on the table.
4. **Name the feeling.** "I feel bored" or "I'm afraid of this mock". Naming it makes it smaller, and you can start anyway.
5. **Talk to your future self.** Write one line from "exam-day me" to "today me": what you will be glad you did.

### Forgive yourself

One study followed 134 first-year university students through two sets of exams. Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before the first exams felt less negative afterwards and procrastinated less before the second exams ([BPS Research Digest on Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, 2010](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself)). Harsh self-criticism makes the next task feel even worse, which feeds the cycle. Forgiving yourself is not excusing the delay; it is clearing the way to start again.

## Local example

**Anu** kept postponing the mental ability section of her syllabus. Every evening she planned to start "time and work" and every evening she reorganised her notes, tidied her desk, or did another round of GK instead.

Her five-day procrastination log made the pattern clear. Every delay was on maths, the feeling was always the same ("I'll get them wrong and feel stupid"), and her escape was always a task that felt productive. The trigger was fear, not laziness.

She shrank the task to "two worked examples of time and work from the guide, then one problem of my own", and used the five-minute start. On the first evening she stopped after the five minutes. On the second she did 20 minutes. By the fourth she finished the chapter's first exercise. She also wrote a short note forgiving herself for the three weeks of delay, and kept it in the back of her maths notebook. "It was the feeling of failing I was avoiding," she wrote, "not the maths."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procrastination as short-term mood repair | **Moderate** | A well-supported view in procrastination research, set out by Sirois and Pychyl (2013). |
| Self-forgiveness reduces later procrastination | **Limited** | One study of 134 students (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, 2010); encouraging but not yet strong. |
| Shrinking tasks and the five-minute start | **Limited** | Practical methods consistent with research on task aversion and if-then plans (LRN-M06-L02). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sirois and Pychyl (2013), "Procrastination and the Priority of Short-Term Mood Regulation" (free author copy)](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/) | Read the abstract and introduction: why procrastination is about mood | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [BPS Research Digest (4 May 2010): to cure procrastination, forgive yourself (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett)](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself) | Read the summary of the self-forgiveness study | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.3 Procrastination: The Enemy Within | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional, later: Module 3 (Procrastination and Memory) of Learning How to Learn | About 3 hours | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For five days, keep a procrastination log: each time you delay a planned study block, note the task, the feeling, the trigger type, what you did instead, and for how long.
2. Pick the study task you avoided most. Shrink it to a first step of five minutes or less, written down exactly (book, page, number of questions).
3. Do the five-minute start three times on that task. After each, note whether you stopped at five minutes or kept going, and for how long.
4. The night before each start, remove friction: book open, pen out, phone charging in another room.
5. Write a short self-forgiveness note for one past delay, ending with what you will do next time.

**Proof to record:** Your 5-day procrastination log, notes from your three five-minute starts, and your self-forgiveness note.

## Template: procrastination log

```
PROCRASTINATION LOG
Day | Task I delayed        | Feeling (bored / confused / afraid / tired / other) | Trigger type | What I did instead | How long
1   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
2   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
3   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
4   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
5   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
Trigger types: boring, hard or unclear, big or vague, frightening, no reward now, unsure where to start
Pattern I see: ____________________________________________________________
```

## Template: task shrinker

```
BIG TASK: ______________________________________ (e.g. "start time and work")
First step of 5 minutes or less (book, page, exact action):
______________________________________________________________________
Friction removed the night before: [ ] book open  [ ] pen out  [ ] phone away
Five-minute starts:  1. date ___ kept going for ___ min
                     2. date ___ kept going for ___ min
                     3. date ___ kept going for ___ min
```

## Common mistakes

- **Calling yourself lazy.** Procrastination is usually avoiding a feeling. Find the feeling and shrink the task.
- **Waiting until you feel motivated.** Motivation often comes after starting. Start for five minutes.
- **Planning giant, vague tasks.** Write the first step so exactly that you could start without thinking.
- **Punishing yourself after a delay.** Forgive yourself and restart; harshness makes the next start harder.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to Sirois and Pychyl, what drives much procrastination?
    - A) A lack of intelligence
    - B) Too much sleep
    - C) Short-term mood repair: avoiding a task to feel better now
    - D) Knowing the subject too well
2. Which first step is best for a task you keep avoiding?
    - A) "Study maths properly this week"
    - B) "Master mental ability"
    - C) "Open the guide at page 34 and do five percentage questions"
    - D) "Be more disciplined"
3. What did the self-forgiveness study find?
    - A) Only harsh self-criticism helped
    - B) Self-forgiveness made students lazier
    - C) It had no effect on mood
    - D) Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating procrastinated less before their next exams
4. What is the five-minute start?
    - A) Taking a five-minute break before every task
    - B) Promising yourself only five minutes on the task, then deciding whether to continue
    - C) Studying for exactly five minutes a day
    - D) Reading for five hours

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Sirois and Pychyl's paper (abstract and introduction) and College Success 3.3 on procrastination
- **Action:** Keep a 5-day procrastination log and use the five-minute start on your most avoided task. It is done when your proof is saved: your 5-day procrastination log, notes from your three five-minute starts, and your self-forgiveness note.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Avoiding an unpleasant task improves mood now, while the cost falls on the future self.
2. **C.** A small, specific step makes the task less threatening and easier to start.
3. **D.** Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett (2010) followed 134 students through two sets of exams.
4. **B.** Starting is the hardest part; most people continue once they begin.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L02: Implementation intentions and tiny habits
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Write if-then plans for your key study habits and obstacles, shrink each habit to a tiny starter anchored to an existing routine, and track them in Loop Habit Tracker. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 25 minutes action plus 14 days of tracking).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Goals are not enough

"I will study more this month" is a **goal intention**. It names what you want, but not when, where or how. Most such goals fade within days.

An **implementation intention** is an if-then plan: **"If [situation], then I will [action]."** For example:

- "If it is 6 a.m. and I have poured my tea, then I will open AnkiDroid at the kitchen table."
- "If I sit down at the library after lunch, then I will start with a mixed set of 12 maths questions."

A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests found that forming implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals ([Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f)). That is one of the strongest findings in habit and motivation research, and it costs one sentence.

### If-then plans for obstacles

The same trick handles what usually derails you:

- "If a WhatsApp message arrives during a study block, then I will leave it until the break."
- "If there is a power cut at night, then I will switch to AnkiDroid and a paper recall of today's topic."
- "If I wake up late, then I will still do the 15-minute AnkiDroid review before anything else."

### Habits take time

A **habit** is an action that happens almost automatically in a familiar situation. Habits form by repeating the same action in the same context. Popular claims say a habit takes 21 days. In Dr Pippa Lally's research, forming a daily habit took **66 days on average**, with a very wide range, from 18 to 254 days ([University of Surrey, 2026](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally)). Expect weeks to months, and don't judge yourself at day 10.

### Tiny habits and anchors

Two ideas make new habits easier:

- **Make it tiny.** Start with a version so small it is hard to refuse: "open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards", "write three lines of recall", "solve one maths question". The tiny version builds the routine; on most days you will do more. This idea is popularised by B. J. Fogg's "Tiny Habits" method.
- **Anchor it to something you already do every day.** "After I pour my morning tea, I will open AnkiDroid." "After I return from the bus stop, I will do a five-minute recall." The existing routine becomes the "if".

### Track it with Loop

**Loop Habit Tracker** is a free, open-source Android app with reminders, charts and statistics ([Loop Habit Tracker](https://loophabits.org/)). Add only two or three habits at first: for example daily AnkiDroid, the morning study block, and the Sunday weekly review. Tick each day you do them. The chart makes progress visible and shows which days of the week are weak.

## Local example

**Sreeja** had tried to "study every day" many times. This time she wrote five if-then plans:

- If the children's school bus leaves, then I will sit at the dining table and open my Revision tab.
- If I have poured my evening tea, then I will do my AnkiDroid reviews before switching on the TV.
- If it is Sunday after lunch, then I will do my weekly review.
- If relatives visit during my morning slot, then I will do my reviews after they leave, before cooking.
- If I feel too tired at night, then I will do just 10 cards and sleep.

She installed Loop and added three habits with reminders. Her tiny versions were 10 cards, one Revision-tab review and three lines of weekly review. After 14 days Loop showed 13 out of 14 ticks for AnkiDroid, 11 for the morning slot and both Sunday reviews. The chart showed one weak day, Saturday, when her husband's family visits. She added an if-then plan for Saturdays.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If-then plans (implementation intentions) | **Strong** | Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006): a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment across 94 independent tests. |
| Habits take weeks to months to form | **Moderate** | Lally's research: an average of 66 days for a daily habit, ranging from 18 to 254. Based mainly on one well-known study. |
| Tiny habits anchored to existing routines | **Limited** | A popular method consistent with research on context cues and if-then plans; little direct testing. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), implementation intentions meta-analysis (free PDF)](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) | Read the abstract and the summary of results | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [University of Surrey (21 January 2026): does it really take 66 days to form a habit? (Dr Pippa Lally)](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally) | Read the whole article on how long habits take | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Install Loop Habit Tracker and add your first habit | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.6 Goal Setting and Motivation | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write three if-then plans for study habits, each with a time or cue, a place and an action.
2. Write two if-then plans for the obstacles that most often derail you (use your procrastination log).
3. For each of the three habits, write its tiny version (two minutes or less) and the existing routine it follows.
4. Install Loop Habit Tracker, add the three habits with reminders at the right times, and tick them each day.
5. Track for 14 days (and keep going). On day 14, look at the chart, find your weakest day, and add an if-then plan for it.

**Proof to record:** Your five if-then plans with tiny versions and anchors, and a Loop screenshot after 14 days.

## Template: if-then planner

```
IF-THEN PLANS (implementation intentions)
Habits
1. If ________________________________ (time / cue), then I will ________________ at ____________ (place).
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor (after I ...): ________________
2. If ________________________________, then I will ________________ at ____________.
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor: ________________
3. If ________________________________, then I will ________________ at ____________.
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor: ________________
Obstacles
4. If ________________________________ (obstacle), then I will ________________.
5. If ________________________________ (obstacle), then I will ________________.
```

## Template: Loop setup

```
[ ] Loop Habit Tracker installed
[ ] Habit 1: ______________  reminder at ____  days: every day
[ ] Habit 2: ______________  reminder at ____  days: ______
[ ] Habit 3: ______________  reminder at ____  days: Sunday
[ ] Ticked daily for 14 days
Day-14 check: weakest day ______  new if-then plan for it: _______________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Vague plans ("study in the morning").** Name the cue, place and action: "after tea, at the kitchen table, AnkiDroid".
- **Starting ten habits at once.** Two or three habits first. Add more when these feel automatic.
- **Expecting a habit in 21 days.** The average in Lally's research was 66 days. Keep going past the first month.
- **Only planning for good days.** Write if-then plans for your usual obstacles too.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is an implementation intention?
    - A) "I should use AnkiDroid more"
    - B) "I will study harder this month"
    - C) "I want to pass the PSC exam"
    - D) "If I have poured my morning tea, then I will open AnkiDroid at the kitchen table"
2. What did Gollwitzer and Sheeran's meta-analysis find?
    - A) They harm motivation
    - B) They work only for exercise
    - C) If-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals across 94 tests
    - D) If-then plans had no effect
3. In Lally's research, how long did forming a daily habit take on average?
    - A) One week
    - B) About 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254
    - C) Exactly 21 days
    - D) One year for everyone
4. What is a good tiny version of "do AnkiDroid reviews every day"?
    - A) Review only on Sundays
    - B) Make 50 new cards a day
    - C) Do 500 cards every morning
    - D) Open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards after morning tea

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Gollwitzer and Sheeran's abstract, the Surrey article on habits and College Success 3.6
- **Action:** Write five if-then plans, set up three tiny habits in Loop and track them for 14 days. It is done when your proof is saved: your five if-then plans with tiny versions and anchors, and a Loop screenshot after 14 days.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It names the situation, the place and the action.
2. **C.** The reported effect size was d = 0.65.
3. **B.** Habits take weeks to months, and people vary widely.
4. **D.** A tiny version anchored to a routine is easy to start every day.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L03: Rewards, streaks and restarting after a bad week
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use small rewards and streaks without letting them control you, connect daily study to your reasons, and restart quickly after a bad day or week. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 25 minutes action plus a week of rewards).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Motivation often follows action

Many people wait to feel motivated before they study. Often it works the other way round: you start, you make a little progress, and the progress makes you want to continue. The five-minute start (LRN-M06-L01) and tiny habits (LRN-M06-L02) use this. Motivation is helpful, but your system should work on days when you don't feel it.

### Rewards that help

The exam is months away; Reels are right here. A small, immediate reward after a study block gives your brain something now:

- A cup of tea or coffee, a short walk, a favourite song, a call with a friend, a sweet on Sundays
- **Pairing:** keep something you enjoy only for study-related moments, such as a favourite podcast only on the walk to the library

Two rules: the reward comes **after** the block, and it must not undo the work. An hour of Reels as a "reward" for a 25-minute block is a trap.

### Streaks: useful, with one rule

Loop and AnkiDroid show your streaks and calendars. A growing chain of ticks is motivating. The danger is **all-or-nothing thinking**: one missed day breaks the chain, you feel the streak is "ruined", and you stop for a week.

Use one rule: **never miss twice.** Missing one day is normal life. Missing two in a row starts a new habit: not studying. If you miss a day, the next day's tiny version is non-negotiable.

### Your reasons, and your process

Write down **why** you are doing this: a government job, security for your family, independence, pride, the subjects you enjoy. Read it on hard days. But don't rely only on the big outcome; it is far away and uncertain. Also take pride in the **process**: today's blocks done, this week's reviews done, this month's rising mock scores. Your Weekly tab and AnkiDroid statistics make the process visible.

### The restart protocol

Bad weeks will happen: illness, a wedding, exam stress, a family problem. What matters is how fast you restart.

1. **No guilt.** Forgive yourself (LRN-M06-L01); it makes restarting easier.
2. **Do the tiny version today,** not tomorrow and not "from Monday".
3. **Find what broke:** sleep, health, a family event, an unrealistic plan, stress.
4. **Adjust the plan:** fewer blocks, new cards to 0 in AnkiDroid until the backlog clears (LRN-M04-L04), one subject instead of three.
5. **Tell your study partner** or a family member, and agree on the next check-in.

If a bad week turns into weeks of low mood, exhaustion or dread, that is not a motivation problem; talk to someone you trust and see Module 19.

## Local example

**Ashiq** had a 23-day AnkiDroid streak when his cousin's wedding took over his family's life for five days. He didn't open the app once, and when he did, it showed 350 cards due. His first thought was, "The streak is gone, what's the point?"

His study partner Anu sent him the restart protocol from this lesson. He forgave himself (a wedding is a good reason), did the tiny version that same evening (10 cards), set new cards to 0, and did 20 minutes of reviews a day. He saw what had broken: no plan for family events. He added an if-then plan: "If there is a family function, then I will do 10 cards before leaving the house."

Within four days the backlog was gone. He started a new streak and wrote on the first page of his notebook: "Never miss twice." His reason card, taped inside the cover, says: "A permanent job, so Umma can stop working at the shop."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small immediate rewards after study | **Limited** | Consistent with basic research on reinforcement; little direct research with exam learners. |
| Forgiving yourself after a lapse | **Limited** | One study of 134 students (Wohl and others, 2010) found less later procrastination. |
| "Never miss twice" and restart protocols | **Limited** | Practical rules, consistent with Lally's finding that habit strength builds over many repetitions. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [BPS Research Digest (4 May 2010): to cure procrastination, forgive yourself (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett)](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself) | Reread the self-forgiveness study summary | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Reread 3.6 Goal Setting and Motivation, focusing on motivation | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Look at your Loop charts and statistics for the last two weeks | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write your reason card: three lines on why you are preparing and learning. Keep it inside your notebook cover or as your phone's lock-screen note.
2. Write a reward menu of five small rewards that don't undo your work.
3. For one week, take one reward from the menu after each completed study block, and tick it.
4. Write your restart protocol (use the template) and keep it in your notebook.
5. Look at your Loop and AnkiDroid records. Find the day of the week you are most likely to miss, and write an if-then plan for it.

**Proof to record:** Your reason card, your reward menu with a week of ticks, your restart protocol and your weak-day if-then plan.

## Template: reward menu

```
REWARD MENU (small, immediate, after the block, never undoing the work)
1. ____________________ (e.g. tea on the verandah)
2. ____________________ (e.g. a 10-minute walk)
3. ____________________ (e.g. one favourite song)
4. ____________________ (e.g. a call with a friend)
5. ____________________ (e.g. Sunday sweet after the weekly review)
Pairing: I only ____________________ when I ____________________.
Week: Mon [ ] Tue [ ] Wed [ ] Thu [ ] Fri [ ] Sat [ ] Sun [ ]
```

## Template: restart protocol

```
RESTART PROTOCOL (after a bad day or week)
1. Forgive: "I missed ____ because ____. That is human."
2. Tiny version TODAY: ______________________ (not "from Monday")
3. What broke? sleep / health / family event / unrealistic plan / stress / other: ____
4. Adjust: blocks ___ -> ___ ; AnkiDroid new cards -> 0 until due count < ___ ; subjects: ____
5. Tell: ______________ (study partner or family). Next check-in: ______
Rule: never miss twice.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Rewards that undo the work.** An hour of scrolling after 25 minutes of study is a trap. Keep rewards small and short.
- **Treating a broken streak as failure.** Never miss twice. One missed day is normal.
- **Restarting "from Monday".** Do the tiny version today.
- **Relying only on the big goal for motivation.** Track and celebrate the process: blocks, reviews, rising scores.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does the "never miss twice" rule mean?
    - A) You must never miss a single day
    - B) Miss two days, then restart on Monday
    - C) Study twice as much after missing a day
    - D) Missing one day is normal; the next day's tiny version is non-negotiable
2. Which is a good reward after a 25-minute study block?
    - A) An hour of Reels
    - B) Buying an expensive gadget
    - C) Skipping the next block
    - D) A cup of tea and a short walk
3. After a bad week, what is the first step of the restart protocol?
    - A) Forgive yourself
    - B) Plan a 12-hour study day
    - C) Wait for Monday
    - D) Delete your decks and start fresh
4. Why track the process (blocks, reviews, scores) and not only the exam goal?
    - A) Process tracking replaces studying
    - B) The exam goal doesn't matter
    - C) Goals reduce motivation
    - D) The goal is far away and uncertain; visible daily progress keeps you going

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The self-forgiveness summary, College Success 3.6 and your own Loop charts
- **Action:** Write your reason card, reward menu and restart protocol, and use rewards for a week. It is done when your proof is saved: your reason card, your reward menu with a week of ticks, your restart protocol and your weak-day if-then plan.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It keeps one lapse from becoming a new habit of not studying.
2. **D.** Small and immediate, and it doesn't undo the work.
3. **A.** Guilt makes restarting harder; forgiveness clears the way.
4. **D.** Seeing progress now supports motivation between now and the exam.

Action: Write your reason card, reward menu and restart protocol, and use rewards for a week

sections.title: Module 7: Metacognition: knowing what you really know
sections.summary: Learn to judge what you really know: spot the illusions of knowing, test yourself after a delay, measure your calibration with confidence ratings, and run a full weekly learning review that turns your data into decisions.
sections.content:
## Overview

Metacognition is often called the skill behind all other learning skills. Students waste the most time not by studying too little but by studying the wrong things: the topics that feel good instead of the ones they don't know. This module gives you three simple instruments (the traffic-light check, the calibration table and the weekly review) and the habit of trusting them over your feelings.

The weekly review you build here runs every Sunday for the rest of the course and after it.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Name five illusions of knowing and test topics after a delay
- Sort topics into green, amber and red and act on the result
- Rate confidence before checking answers and build a calibration table
- Fix confident errors first
- Run the full seven-part weekly review and track trends every four weeks

## Time

About 4 hours 45 minutes in total: 3 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 8–9, with the module project due in week 9.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M07-L01: Illusions of knowing, and how to judge your learning (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M07-L02: Self-testing and confidence ratings (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M07-L03: The weekly learning review (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **weekly review** (one of the six core tools) and the **Weekly** tab
- The **traffic-light topic check** and **five illusions checklist**
- The **calibration table** with S, U and G marks
- The **four-week look-back** and your **changes list**

## Module project: My metacognition dashboard

1. Extend your traffic-light check to at least 30 topics from your syllabus.
2. Keep your 50-question calibration table and your list of confident errors with fixes.
3. Complete two full weekly reviews, each recorded in the Weekly tab.
4. Write three decisions you made because of this data (for example: "relearn the 8 red topics before new ones", "underline NOT in every question", "maths in the morning").

**Proof to record:** Your 30-topic traffic-light sheet, the calibration table, two Weekly tab rows and your three data-based decisions.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Judging knowledge | By feeling | Some recall tests, done right after study | Delayed recall tests for 30 topics, colours assigned honestly |
| Calibration | Not measured | Measured but not acted on | Calibration table with confident errors fixed |
| Weekly review | Skipped | Short version only | Full seven-part review, twice, with Weekly tab rows |
| Decisions | None | Vague intentions | Three specific decisions based on the data |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do the traffic-light check on 10 topics.
- Do the full weekly review once, even if some numbers are missing.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Metacognition | Planning, checking and adjusting your own learning; knowing what you really know. |
| The fluency illusion | Smooth rereading feels like knowing, but recall shows the truth. |
| Best time to judge a topic | At least a day later, by recalling without help. |
| Green, amber, red | Green: recall plus a new question right. Amber: partial or recognition only. Red: neither. |
| Calibration | How well confidence matches accuracy. |
| S, U and G marks | Sure, unsure and guess, written before checking. |
| Fix first | Confident errors: sure but wrong. |
| The seven parts of the weekly review | Recall, numbers, cold self-test, calibration, error pattern, what worked, next week (with one change). |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Trusting the feeling of knowing.** Test it. The feeling is often wrong in both directions.
- **Collecting data and never acting on it.** Every check ends with a change to your Revision tab, cards or plan.

sections.title: LRN-M07-L01: Illusions of knowing, and how to judge your learning
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Recognise the main illusions of knowing, and judge what you really know with a delayed recall test and a traffic-light topic check. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Metacognition** means thinking about your own thinking: planning how to learn, checking how well it is going, and adjusting. Its most important part for an exam is simple to say and hard to do: **knowing what you really know**.

### Five illusions of knowing

1. **The fluency illusion.** A page you have read twice reads smoothly, so it feels learned. In Roediger and Karpicke's study, students who reread were more confident than those who tested themselves, yet remembered less a week later ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf)).
2. **Recognition passing for recall.** You see the four options, one looks familiar, and you feel you knew it. In the exam, with different options and no time, you don't.
3. **Hindsight from the answer key.** You check an answer and think "of course, I knew that". Knowing it after seeing it is not knowing it.
4. **The effort illusion.** Methods that feel hard (recall, mixed practice) feel less effective than easy ones. When Karpicke and Blunt compared retrieval practice with concept mapping, students predicted that concept mapping would work best; retrieval practice produced much better long-term retention ([Purdue University, 2011](https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2011/110120KarpickeScience.html)).
5. **The understanding illusion.** Following an explanation in a class or video is not the same as being able to recall it or use it on a new question.

There is also the **hours illusion**: time spent studying feels like progress, whatever happened in that time (Module 2).

### How to judge what you know

All five illusions have the same cure: **test yourself after a delay, without help**, and judge by the result, not the feeling.

- **Cover and recall:** close the book and write or say what you know about the topic. Two minutes is enough.
- **Apply it to a new question:** a PYQ or a question you haven't seen, with the options covered.
- **Wait first:** judge a topic a day or more after studying it, not right after. Right after reading, everything feels known.
- **Explain it** to someone, or aloud to yourself, without notes (Module 8).

### The traffic-light check

Use three colours for every topic you think you have "done":

- **Green:** after a gap, you can recall the main points and answer a new question.
- **Amber:** you recall part of it, or you only recognise answers when you see options.
- **Red:** you can't recall it or answer questions on it.

Most students find their list has far fewer greens than they expected. That isn't bad news; it is the most useful news you can get, because it tells you exactly where to spend your next hours.

## Local example

**Anu** had a list of 30 GK topics she had "finished": she had read each at least twice, and most were highlighted. Before the check, she rated her confidence for each from 1 to 5; she gave 22 topics a 4 or 5.

She did the traffic-light check over two evenings: for each topic, a two-minute recall on a blank page and one previous-year question with the options covered. The result: 12 green, 10 amber, 8 red. Six of the topics she had rated 5 came out amber or red; four were in the Kerala renaissance, where she knew the names but kept mixing up who did what.

She moved the 8 reds to the top of her Revision tab as "relearn", brought the ambers' next reviews forward to the next two days, and turned the renaissance mix-ups into contrast cards in AnkiDroid. "I had been revising the greens," she said, "because they felt good."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rereading creates false confidence (the fluency illusion) | **Strong** | Roediger and Karpicke (2006): rereaders were more confident and remembered less after a week. |
| Students misjudge which study methods work | **Moderate** | Students predicted concept mapping would beat retrieval practice; it didn't (Karpicke and Blunt, 2011). |
| Judging by delayed recall instead of feeling | **Moderate** | Follows from the findings above: judgements based on an actual recall attempt, after a gap, reflect real memory. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Purdue University (20 January 2011): retrieval practice beats concept mapping (Karpicke and Blunt, Science)](https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2011/110120KarpickeScience.html) | Read the press release, including what students predicted | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Roediger and Karpicke (2006), "Test-Enhanced Learning" (PDF)](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf) | Reread the part of the results on students' confidence | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional: the videos on illusions of competence in Module 2 of Learning How to Learn | About 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. List 20 PSC topics you consider "done". Next to each, rate your confidence from 1 to 5 before testing anything.
2. At least a day after you last studied them, test each topic: a two-minute blank-page recall, then one previous-year or new question with the options covered.
3. Mark each topic green, amber or red using the rules in this lesson.
4. Compare the colours with your confidence ratings. Count the topics you rated 4 or 5 that came out amber or red.
5. Update your Revision tab: reds become "relearn" at the top; ambers get their next review within two days. Turn any mix-ups into contrast cards.

**Proof to record:** Your 20-topic traffic-light sheet with confidence ratings and results, and a screenshot of the updated Revision tab.

## Template: traffic-light topic check

```
TRAFFIC-LIGHT CHECK      Date: ______   (test at least a day after studying)
Topic                 Confidence (1-5)  2-min recall (points)  New question right?  Colour
1. _________________  ___               ___                    Y / N                G / A / R
2. _________________  ___               ___                    Y / N                G / A / R
...
20. ________________  ___               ___                    Y / N                G / A / R
Greens ___  Ambers ___  Reds ___
Rated 4-5 but amber or red: ___ topics: ______________________________________
Green: recall the main points AND answer a new question.
Amber: partial recall, or recognition only.  Red: can't recall or answer.
```

## Template: five illusions checklist

```
Before I tick a topic as "done", I check:
[ ] Fluency: did I test myself, or did it just read smoothly?
[ ] Recognition: could I answer with the options covered?
[ ] Hindsight: did I know it before I saw the answer key?
[ ] Effort: am I choosing an easy method because it feels better?
[ ] Understanding: can I recall and use it, not just follow it?
```

## Common mistakes

- **Judging a topic right after reading it.** Everything feels known then. Test at least a day later.
- **Using the answer key to "confirm" you knew it.** Answer first, with the options covered, then check.
- **Revising the topics that feel good.** Spend your time on ambers and reds; greens need only short reviews.
- **Taking a red as a sign you're bad at the subject.** A red is a map, not a verdict. It shows where the next hour goes.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is an example of the fluency illusion?
    - A) A chapter feels learned because it reads smoothly the second time
    - B) You draw a map from memory
    - C) You fail a recall test and feel worried
    - D) You answer a PYQ with the options covered
2. What did students predict in Karpicke and Blunt's study?
    - A) That concept mapping would work best, although retrieval practice did better
    - B) That rereading would beat everything
    - C) That retrieval practice would work best, and it did
    - D) That nothing would work
3. When is the best time to judge whether you know a topic?
    - A) Immediately after reading it
    - B) At least a day after studying, by trying to recall it
    - C) Never; trust your feeling
    - D) While the book is open
4. A topic is "amber" when...
    - A) you have never studied it
    - B) you can recall it and answer new questions
    - C) you recall part of it, or only recognise answers when you see options
    - D) you have highlighted it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Karpicke and Blunt press release and the confidence results of Roediger and Karpicke
- **Action:** Run a traffic-light check on 20 "done" topics and update your Revision tab. It is done when your proof is saved: your 20-topic traffic-light sheet with confidence ratings and results, and a screenshot of the updated Revision tab.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Smooth reading feels like knowing, but memory is tested by recall.
2. **A.** Students misjudged which method would help them remember.
3. **B.** A delayed recall attempt shows what has really stayed.
4. **C.** Green needs recall plus answering a new question; red means neither.

sections.title: LRN-M07-L02: Self-testing and confidence ratings
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Rate your confidence before checking each answer, work out your calibration, and fix your confident errors first. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 55 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Calibration

**Calibration** is how well your confidence matches your accuracy. A well-calibrated student who feels "sure" is right almost every time, and one who feels "unsure" is right about half the time. Most of us are not well calibrated, and in an exam with negative marking, that costs marks in two ways:

- **Overconfidence:** you mark answers you are "sure" of, and some are wrong. Each wrong answer loses marks.
- **Underconfidence:** you skip questions you could have answered, because you feel unsure.

You can't fix what you don't measure. Confidence ratings measure it.

### How to rate confidence

While answering practice questions, write one letter beside each answer **before** you check it:

- **S (sure):** I would bet on this.
- **U (unsure):** I think so, but I could be wrong.
- **G (guess):** I am choosing between options without real knowledge.

After checking, count how many were right in each group:

| Group | What good calibration looks like | What it means if it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sure | Nearly all right (about 9 out of 10 or better) | Sure but wrong = confident errors: your most dangerous mistakes |
| Unsure | Roughly half right, or a bit more | If most are right, you know more than you think |
| Guess | Near chance (1 in 4 with four options) or a bit above | If well above chance, your partial knowledge is useful |

### What to do with the results

1. **Fix confident errors first.** A "sure" answer that was wrong is usually a mix-up of two similar facts, or a fact learned wrongly. Make a contrast card or correct the note at its source (Module 4). These are worth more than any new topic.
2. **Turn unsure-right into sure-right** with a few spaced reviews.
3. **Use your guess data for exam strategy.** If your guesses after ruling out one or two options are right well above chance, careful guessing can pay even with negative marking. Module 12 does the arithmetic for Kerala PSC's marking scheme.

### Self-testing at three time scales

- **Daily:** AnkiDroid reviews and the retrieval sandwich (Modules 3 and 4)
- **Weekly:** five cold questions in your weekly review (LRN-M07-L03)
- **Monthly:** a mock test with confidence marks (Module 12)

Each one is retrieval practice and a measurement at the same time.

## Local example

**Ashiq** took 50 questions from two previous papers and marked each S, U or G before checking. His calibration table: 30 sure, of which 24 right (80%); 12 unsure, of which 6 right (50%); 8 guesses, of which 3 right (38%).

His six confident errors told a clear story: four were mix-ups between similar facts (two Constitutional amendments, and two national parks), one was a fact he had learned from a wrong WhatsApp forward, and one was misreading "NOT" in a question. He made four contrast cards, fixed the wrong note, and started underlining NOT, EXCEPT and FIRST in every question.

His guesses were right more often than chance (38% against 25%), mostly where he had ruled out two options first. He saved that number for Module 12, where he would work out whether such guesses pay under negative marking.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-testing with practice questions | **Strong** | Practice testing is rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| Confidence ratings to measure calibration | **Limited** | A simple measuring tool; no single source was checked for this course. Your own table decides what to change. |
| Fixing confident errors first | **Limited** | A practical priority rule: confident errors are both likely to repeat and costly under negative marking. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dunlosky et al. (2013), "Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques", APS summary with the full paper](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/journals/pspi/learning-techniques.html) | Skim the summary of the ten techniques and their ratings | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, 6.3 Test Taking (including test anxiety)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking) | Read the part on multiple-choice questions and preparing for tests | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Take 50 previous-year questions on mixed topics from the papers you saved in week 0.
2. Answer them with the options covered first (Module 3). Before checking each, write S, U or G beside it.
3. Check all 50 against the answer key. Fill in the calibration table below.
4. List every sure-but-wrong question. For each, write the cause (mix-up, wrong source, misreading, other) and the fix: a contrast card, a corrected note or a reading rule.
5. Write two lines on what your unsure and guess rows suggest, and keep the numbers for Module 12.

**Proof to record:** Your 50-question sheet with S, U and G marks, the completed calibration table and your list of confident errors with fixes.

## Template: calibration table

```
CALIBRATION TABLE      Date: ______  Source: __________________  Questions: ___
Group    Answered   Right   % right   Target
Sure     ___        ___     ___%      90% or more
Unsure   ___        ___     ___%      about 50-70%
Guess    ___        ___     ___%      about 25% (4 options)
Confident errors (sure but wrong):
Q no   Cause (mix-up / wrong source / misread / other)   Fix (contrast card / note / rule)
____   ______________________________________________   ________________________________
____   ______________________________________________   ________________________________
```

## Template: confidence marks, quick key

```
Write BEFORE checking:
S = sure: I would bet on it
U = unsure: I think so
G = guess: no real knowledge, choosing between options
After checking, circle: sure-wrong (fix first), unsure-right (review more), guess-right (note how many options you ruled out)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Marking confidence after seeing the answer.** It must be written before you check, or it measures nothing.
- **Ignoring confident errors because the score was good.** Sure-wrong answers repeat in exams. Fix them first.
- **Marking everything "sure" to feel better.** Honest marks are the point. Nobody else sees them.
- **Treating calibration as a judgement of intelligence.** It is a skill that improves with practice and feedback.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is calibration?
    - A) How fast you answer questions
    - B) How neat your notes are
    - C) How many hours you study
    - D) How well your confidence matches your actual accuracy
2. Which mistakes should you fix first?
    - A) Guesses that were wrong
    - B) Answers you were sure of that turned out wrong
    - C) Questions you got right
    - D) Questions you skipped
3. When must you write your S, U or G mark?
    - A) Only for wrong answers
    - B) After checking the answer
    - C) At the end of the week
    - D) Before checking the answer
4. Your "unsure" answers are right 80% of the time. What does that suggest?
    - A) You know more than you think, and may be skipping questions you could answer
    - B) You should stop studying
    - C) Your calibration is perfect
    - D) You should guess everything

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The summary of Dunlosky and others' ratings and College Success 6.3 on test taking
- **Action:** Answer 50 PYQs with confidence marks, build your calibration table and fix your confident errors. It is done when your proof is saved: your 50-question sheet with S, U and G marks, the completed calibration table and your list of confident errors with fixes.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Good calibration means "sure" answers are nearly always right.
2. **B.** Confident errors repeat and cost marks under negative marking.
3. **D.** After seeing the answer, hindsight changes your feeling of confidence.
4. **A.** Underconfidence can cost marks; a few reviews turn unsure into sure.
