sections.title: LRN-M07-L03: The weekly learning review
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Run the full weekly learning review: recall, numbers, a cold self-test, calibration, errors and next week's if-then plans, and record it in the Weekly tab. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 10 minutes resources, 35 minutes for your first full review).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

You have done the short weekly review since week 1. Now it becomes the centre of your learning system: once a week, for 20 minutes, you **plan, check and adjust**, which is metacognition in practice.

### The seven parts

1. **Recall from memory.** Before looking at anything, write the three most important things you learned this week. If you can't, that itself is information.
2. **Numbers.** Copy this week's numbers from your tools: study hours (Study Log), AnkiDroid days and percentage correct (AnkiDroid statistics), Revision-tab scores, focus blocks (Focus tab), and any test or mock score.
3. **Cold self-test.** Five questions from this week's topics, answered without notes. Make them in the moment, or keep five margin questions from the week for this.
4. **Calibration.** What did you feel sure about but get wrong this week? Those go to the top of next week.
5. **Error pattern.** What kind of mistake happened most? From Module 12 on, your Errors tab answers this in seconds.
6. **What worked, what didn't.** One line each, based on the numbers, not on mood.
7. **Next week.** Three priorities, each with a day and time (if-then plans from Module 6), and **one change** to your system.

### One change at a time

Change one thing a week: a new block time, fewer new cards, a different place to study. If you change five things together, you won't know which one helped. Keep a short "changes" list at the back of your notebook with the date, the change and what happened.

### Every fourth week: look back

Every fourth review, put the last four weeks' numbers side by side in the **Weekly** tab. Trends tell you more than single weeks: Is the AnkiDroid percentage steady? Are mock scores rising? Are focus blocks growing? Which subject keeps slipping?

### Make it a ritual

Same day, same time, same place: for example Sunday after lunch at the dining table. Anchor it to something you already do (Module 6). The review is also where you fill in next week's study planner (Module 5), so the week starts on Monday with no decisions left to make.

## Local example

**Sreeja** does her review on Sunday after lunch, while the children watch a film. This week her recall came easily for the Kerala renaissance and not at all for the Lok Sabha topic she had studied on Thursday. Her numbers: 6 hours 10 minutes of study, AnkiDroid 7 out of 7 days at 88% correct, two focus blocks cut short by visitors, and 3 out of 5 on her cold test.

Calibration: she had been sure that the Rajya Sabha is dissolved like the Lok Sabha, and it is not (it is a permanent house). That became a contrast card. Her error pattern: both wrong questions in her mixed set were misreadings. What worked: morning reviews. What didn't: maths at night, when she was tired.

Her one change for next week: maths moves to the morning slot on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. She wrote three if-then plans, filled in next week's planner, and copied the numbers into the Weekly tab. It took 22 minutes.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A weekly cold self-test | **Strong** | It is spaced retrieval practice of the week's material (Dunlosky and others, 2013). |
| If-then plans for the coming week | **Strong** | Implementation intentions have a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006). |
| A regular weekly review routine | **Limited** | Planning, checking and adjusting is the core of self-regulated learning; this exact routine is a practical design, not a tested package. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), implementation intentions meta-analysis (free PDF)](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) | Reread the abstract: why the "next week" part uses if-then plans | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Reread 3.7 on strategies for time and task management | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose your fixed review time and anchor (for example, Sunday after lunch at the dining table) and add it to Loop as a weekly habit if it isn't there yet.
2. This Sunday, do the full seven-part review using the template below.
3. Copy the numbers into a new row of the Weekly tab.
4. Fill in next week's study planner, with your three priorities as if-then plans.
5. Start a "changes" list at the back of your notebook with this week's one change.

**Proof to record:** Your completed seven-part review, the new Weekly tab row, next week's planner and the first line of your changes list.

## Template: weekly learning review (core tool)

```
WEEKLY LEARNING REVIEW        Week ___ (dates ________)   20 minutes, Sunday
Numbers: study hours ___ | AnkiDroid days ___/7, % correct ___%
         self-test ___% | mock or PYQ score ___ | focus blocks ___
1. From memory, no notes: the three most important things I learned this week
   ______________________________________________________________________
2. Cold self-test: 5 questions from this week's topics. Score ___/5
3. Calibration: what did I feel sure about but get wrong? ________________
4. Error log: my most common error type this week ___ ; the fix ___________
5. What worked? ______________________  What didn't? ______________________
6. Next week's three priorities, each with a day and time (if-then plans)
   1. ________________ 2. ________________ 3. ________________
7. One change to my system: ______________________________________________
Copy the numbers into the Weekly tab of the Learning Workbook.
```

## Template: Weekly tab headings

```csv
Week,Dates,Study hours,AnkiDroid days (of 7),AnkiDroid % correct,Self-test score %,Mock or PYQ score,Focus blocks done,Top error type,One change for next week
```

## Template: every fourth week: look back

```
FOUR-WEEK LOOK-BACK      Weeks ___ to ___
                     Wk __   Wk __   Wk __   Wk __   Trend
Study hours          ____    ____    ____    ____    up / flat / down
AnkiDroid % correct  ____    ____    ____    ____    ______
Self-test %          ____    ____    ____    ____    ______
Mock / PYQ score     ____    ____    ____    ____    ______
Focus blocks         ____    ____    ____    ____    ______
Subject that keeps slipping: ______________  Plan for it: ______________________
Changes that worked (from my changes list): ___________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Listing hours and skipping the recall and self-test.** Hours measure effort, not learning. Recall and test first.
- **Changing five things at once.** One change a week, written down, so you can see what helped.
- **Ending the review without next week's plan.** The review finishes when the planner is filled in.
- **Reviewing only the good news.** The confident errors and slipping subjects are the reason to review.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the first part of the weekly review?
    - A) Copying hours from the Study Log
    - B) Recalling the week's three most important things from memory
    - C) Planning next week
    - D) Reading all the week's notes again
2. Why make only one change to your system each week?
    - A) So you can tell which change helped
    - B) To save paper
    - C) Because systems should never change
    - D) Because more changes are not allowed
3. What do you do every fourth weekly review?
    - A) Start a new deck
    - B) Skip the review
    - C) Compare the last four weeks' numbers to see trends
    - D) Take a full mock test
4. How should next week's priorities be written?
    - A) As a long wish list
    - B) As if-then plans with a day and time
    - C) They don't need writing
    - D) As "study more"

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Gollwitzer and Sheeran's abstract and College Success 3.7, with the seven-part review template
- **Action:** Do your first full seven-part weekly review and record it in the Weekly tab. It is done when your proof is saved: your completed seven-part review, the new Weekly tab row, next week's planner and the first line of your changes list.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Recall comes first, before any notes, because it shows what really stayed.
2. **A.** Several changes at once hide which one worked.
3. **C.** Trends over four weeks are more reliable than one week's numbers.
4. **B.** If-then plans are among the best-supported ways to follow through.

sections.title: Module 8: Deep understanding
sections.summary: Go beyond memorising: explain topics simply with the Feynman technique, ask deep questions, draw concept maps from memory and rebuild rules from first principles. Record five Feynman explanations of PSC topics and improve each one.
sections.content:
## Overview

Memorised facts answer simple questions; understanding answers the harder ones, such as statement questions, unfamiliar maths problems and "which of these is not" questions. This module gives you four ways to build understanding, each honest about its evidence and each combined with recall so it works for the exam too.

The module project is five recorded Feynman explanations, each with a first and an improved version. Listening to your own explanations is one of the fastest ways to find out what you really understand.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Use self-explanation and the Feynman technique, and record and improve explanations
- Ask six kinds of questions and write PSC-style statement questions
- Ask for help with a clear three-part question
- Draw and check concept maps from memory
- Rebuild arithmetic rules from first principles and test them

## Time

About 7 hours 15 minutes in total: 5 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 9–10, with the module project due in week 10.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M08-L01: Self-explanation and the Feynman technique (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. LRN-M08-L02: Asking good questions (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M08-L03: Concept maps, drawn from memory (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
4. LRN-M08-L04: First-principles thinking (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **Feynman template** (one of the six core tools) and **self-explanation prompts**
- The **question stems card**, **statement-question builder** and **three-part help question**
- The **concept map from memory** sheet and **linking words**
- The **first-principles sheet**

## Module project: Five Feynman explanations

1. Choose five PSC topics, including at least one maths or reasoning method and at least one Constitution topic. Your explanation from LRN-M08-L01 counts as the first.
2. For each, record v1 without notes, listen back with the Feynman template, fix the gaps from the source, and record v2.
3. Score every version (accuracy, clarity, completeness, without notes; out of 12) and work out your average for v1 and v2.
4. Turn the gaps from all five into flashcards (at least 10 in total).
5. Play one v2 to your study partner or a family member and ask: "What was unclear?" Note their answer.

**Proof to record:** Ten recordings (v1 and v2 for five topics), five filled-in Feynman templates with scores and averages, the new cards, and your listener's feedback.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recordings | Fewer than five topics | Five topics, some without v2 | Five topics, each with v1 and v2 |
| Gap finding | Listened without noting gaps | Some gaps noted | Every pause, vague phrase and error noted and fixed from the source |
| Improvement | No change from v1 to v2 | Small improvement | Clear improvement in scores and clarity |
| Follow-up | No cards | A few cards | At least 10 cards from the gaps and one listener's feedback |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do three Feynman explanations instead of five, each with v1 and v2.
- Skip the concept map lesson's redraw; keep the first-principles sheets for maths.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Self-explanation | Explaining to yourself why each statement or step is true while studying; moderate utility. |
| The six Feynman steps | Choose, explain simply without notes and record, find gaps, fix from source, simplify, record again. |
| Evidence position on the Feynman technique | Not tested by name; its parts (self-explanation, retrieval, explaining) are supported. |
| Six kinds of question | Fact, reason, process, comparison, application, what if. |
| Three-part help question | What I am trying to understand, what I know or tried, exactly where I am stuck. |
| Concept map versus retrieval (Karpicke and Blunt) | Mapping with the text open lost to retrieval practice; draw maps from memory instead. |
| A 20% rise then a 20% fall | A 4% fall overall (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96). |
| Facts with no first principles | Dates, names and article numbers: use cards and mnemonics. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Feeling that you understand because the explanation made sense in class.** Explain it yourself, without notes, and record it.
- **Spending hours on beautiful maps or notes.** Understanding shows in what you can explain and answer from memory.

sections.title: LRN-M08-L01: Self-explanation and the Feynman technique
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain a PSC topic aloud in simple words without notes, record it, find the gaps, and record an improved version: the first of your five Feynman explanations. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Self-explanation

**Self-explanation** means explaining to yourself, while you study, why each statement is true or why each step follows. Studying a solved maths problem, you ask: "Why do we divide by 100 here? Why add the rates?" Reading the Constitution, you ask: "Why would the makers put this in Part III and not Part IV?" Dunlosky and colleagues rated self-explanation **moderate utility**: it helps across many topics, although it takes time ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)).

### The Feynman technique

The **Feynman technique** is named after the physicist Richard Feynman, famous for explaining hard ideas in plain words. It turns self-explanation into a routine:

1. **Choose a topic** you have studied.
2. **Explain it simply, aloud, without notes,** as if to a 12-year-old or to someone at home. Record it on your phone.
3. **Listen back and find the gaps:** where you stopped, said "basically" or "something like", used a word you couldn't explain, or said something wrong.
4. **Go back to the source** and fix each gap.
5. **Simplify:** find an analogy or example from Kerala life.
6. **Explain it again** and record a second version. Compare.

Honesty about the evidence: Feynman didn't publish this as a method, and there are no studies of "the Feynman technique" under that name. Its parts are well supported. Explaining from memory is retrieval practice. Self-explanation is rated moderate utility. Research on learning by teaching finds that explaining to others helps learning, most of all when you explain **without notes**, which makes it a retrieval activity ([Fiorella, Learning by Teaching](https://www.unh.edu/teaching-learning-resource-hub/sites/default/files/media/2023-06/itow-learning-by-teaching-fiorella.pdf)).

### Why record it?

While you talk, you can't hear your own gaps. Playback shows them clearly: the long pause before a date, the vague "and then they made some changes". The recording is also your proof, and five of them become this module's project.

### What suits the technique

Use it for things that have reasons and connections: processes, causes and effects, how an institution works, a maths method, a science concept. For pure lists of facts (award winners, article numbers), cards and mnemonics work better (Modules 4 and 11).

### Simple is not careless

A simple explanation still has to be **correct**. Use the right terms, but explain each one the first time you use it. If you can't explain a term, that is a gap to fix, not a word to hide behind.

## Local example

**Ashiq** chose Article 32 and the writs for his first Feynman explanation. He explained it to his imaginary listener, his 12-year-old niece, and recorded 2 minutes 40 seconds.

When he listened back, the gaps were obvious. He said "the court can issue some orders called writs", then named only three of the five. He couldn't say clearly how mandamus differs from prohibition, and he called Article 32 "a fundamental right to go to court" without saying which court.

He went back to his textbook. The five writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto; Article 32 lets you go directly to the Supreme Court when a Fundamental Right is violated, and Article 226 gives High Courts their writ powers. For an analogy he used a school: habeas corpus is like asking "show me the student you are keeping in the staffroom"; mandamus is ordering a teacher to do a duty they are refusing to do.

His second recording was 2 minutes 15 seconds, named all five writs and had no long pauses. He scored v1 at 6 out of 12 and v2 at 11, and made three cards from the gaps.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-explanation | **Moderate** | Rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013): helps across topics, though it takes time. |
| Explaining to others without notes | **Moderate** | Fiorella (2023): explaining helps more than only preparing to teach, especially as a retrieval activity. |
| "The Feynman technique" as a named method | **Limited** | No direct studies; it packages self-explanation, retrieval and explaining, which are supported. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the section on self-explanation | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Fiorella (2023), "Learning by Teaching", in an APA Division 2 e-book (PDF)](https://www.unh.edu/teaching-learning-resource-hub/sites/default/files/media/2023-06/itow-learning-by-teaching-fiorella.pdf) | Read the parts on explaining to others and on teaching as retrieval | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a PSC topic you have studied that has reasons or steps in it (a Constitution provision, a history cause, a geography process or a maths method).
2. Without notes, explain it aloud for 2 to 3 minutes to an imaginary 12-year-old and record it (v1).
3. Listen back and fill in step 2 of the Feynman template: every pause, vague phrase, unexplained term and error.
4. Fix each gap from your textbook, and find one analogy or example from Kerala life.
5. Record a second version without notes (v2). Score both versions on the template.
6. Turn the gaps into 2 or 3 flashcards in AnkiDroid.

**Proof to record:** Your v1 and v2 recordings, the filled-in Feynman template with both scores, and the new cards. This is Feynman explanation 1 of 5.

## Template: Feynman explanation (core tool)

```
FEYNMAN EXPLANATION       Topic: ______________   Date: ________
Recording: v1 file ________  v2 file ________
1. Explain it aloud, without notes, to an imaginary 12-year-old (2-3 minutes).
   Record it on your phone (v1).
2. Listen back. Mark every gap: where I stopped, said "basically" or "something
   like", used a word I can't define, or got a fact wrong:
   ___________________________________________________________________
3. Go back to the source (book ______ page ___). Fix each gap:
   ___________________________________________________________________
4. Simplify: one analogy or example from Kerala life: ____________________
5. Record again without notes (v2). What is clearer now? __________________
6. Turn the gaps into 2-3 flashcards and 1 question for my Revision tab.
Score each 1-3:  Accuracy __  Clarity __  Complete __  Without notes __  Total __/12
```

## Template: self-explanation prompts (for worked examples and dense text)

```
For each step or sentence, ask and answer in a few words:
- Why is this step done? Why this operation and not another?
- What does this term mean, in my words?
- How does this connect to the line before it?
- What would change if this number or condition were different?
- Can I say this step without looking?
```

## Common mistakes

- **Glancing at notes while "explaining".** Notes turn it into reading aloud. Explain from memory, then check.
- **Explaining a list of facts.** Use the technique for reasons and processes; use cards for lists.
- **Skipping the listen-back.** The playback is where the gaps show. Listen with the template in hand.
- **Ten-minute recordings.** Two or three minutes per topic keeps it focused and easy to review.
- **Hiding behind jargon.** If you use a term, explain it. If you can't, it is a gap.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is self-explanation?
    - A) Asking a friend for the answer
    - B) Writing a summary at the end of the week
    - C) Reading your notes aloud
    - D) Explaining to yourself why each statement or step is true while you study
2. What is the honest evidence position on the Feynman technique?
    - A) No studies test it by name, but its parts (self-explanation, retrieval, explaining) are supported
    - B) It has been shown not to work
    - C) It has been proven in hundreds of studies
    - D) Feynman tested it himself
3. Why record your explanation?
    - A) Because PSC exams are oral
    - B) Playback reveals gaps you can't hear while talking, and it is your proof
    - C) To post it online
    - D) Recording makes you remember automatically
4. Which topic suits the Feynman technique best?
    - A) Telephone codes of districts
    - B) The list of Jnanpith winners
    - C) How Article 32 protects Fundamental Rights through writs
    - D) Kerala's 14 district names

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Dunlosky's section on self-explanation and Fiorella on explaining and teaching
- **Action:** Record, review and improve your first Feynman explanation of a PSC topic. It is done when your proof is saved: your v1 and v2 recordings, the filled-in Feynman template with both scores, and the new cards. This is Feynman explanation 1 of 5.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It is rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others.
2. **A.** It is a popular package of well-supported principles.
3. **B.** You can't listen critically while you are explaining.
4. **C.** It has reasons and connections to explain; lists suit cards and mnemonics.

sections.title: LRN-M08-L02: Asking good questions
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn any PSC text into deep questions with question stems, write exam-style statement questions, and ask for help in a way that gets useful answers. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 45 minutes action over two days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Understanding grows from questions. Most students ask only "what" questions (what is it, when was it, who did it). Those matter for PSC, but deeper questions build the connections that hold the facts (Module 3) and help with the trickier question types in modern papers.

### Six kinds of question

| Kind | Question stems | PSC example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fact | What? When? Who? Where? | When was the 73rd Amendment passed? |
| Reason | Why? What caused...? | Why was a constitutional amendment needed for panchayats? |
| Process | How does... work? What are the steps? | How does a money bill pass Parliament? |
| Comparison | How is X different from Y? What do they share? | How is a writ of mandamus different from prohibition? |
| Application | What is an example of...? How would this apply to...? | Which Fundamental Right applies when a child is denied school admission? |
| What if | What would happen if...? What would change if...? | What would happen if the Rajya Sabha did not return a money bill in 14 days? |

Write questions of every kind, then **answer them from memory a day later**. Writing questions is useful; answering them is retrieval practice, which is where most of the benefit comes from.

### Think like the examiner

Kerala PSC papers include more than simple recall. Common forms include:

- **Statement questions:** "Consider the following statements. Which is/are correct?"
- **Match the following**
- **Chronological order:** arrange events in the order they happened
- **Odd one out**

Writing your own questions in these forms trains you to notice the details examiners test: the exact year, the difference between similar bodies, the word "not". For example: *"Consider the statements: (1) The 73rd Amendment added Part IX to the Constitution. (2) It deals with municipalities. Which is correct?"* (Only 1: municipalities are in Part IXA, added by the 74th Amendment.)

### Asking for help well

When you are stuck, a good question gets a good answer from a teacher, a study partner or an AI tutor (Module 17). A good help question has three parts:

1. **What I am trying to understand:** "how the writ of certiorari works"
2. **What I already know or tried:** "I know it is issued by a higher court to a lower court"
3. **Exactly where I am stuck:** "I don't see how it differs from prohibition"

"Explain the writs" gets a lecture. The three-part question gets the one explanation you need.

## Local example

**Joseph sir**'s study group took the chapter on Panchayati Raj. Each member wrote twelve questions using at least six different stems, two of each kind, and three statement questions in PSC style.

Vinod's best question was a "what if": "What would happen to local planning if panchayats had no fixed term?" Answering it, the group worked out for themselves why the 73rd Amendment fixed a five-year term and required elections, which made the facts easier to remember. Sreeja's statement question caught the whole group: two of five members wrongly said the 73rd Amendment covered municipalities.

The next day, each member answered their own questions without the book, then swapped sheets. Joseph sir asked everyone to write one three-part help question about what was still unclear. Three members were stuck on the same point, the Eleventh Schedule, and he explained it once for all of them.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asking and answering why-questions (elaborative interrogation) | **Moderate** | Rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| Writing your own questions | **Limited** | Studied less than retrieval; the benefit grows when you also answer them from memory later. |
| Answering your own questions from memory | **Strong** | This is retrieval practice, rated high utility. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: elaboration materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/elaboration) | Use the elaboration bookmark prompts as extra question stems | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 5: Reading and Notetaking (SQ3R, Cornell method)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking) | Read 5.2 Effective Reading Strategies, noting where questions come in | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Take one chapter or section of your PSC material.
2. Write 12 questions on it using at least six different kinds from the table (two of each), and mark each question's kind.
3. Write 3 PSC-style statement questions with their answers and the reason each statement is right or wrong.
4. The next day, answer all 15 from memory, then check against the source and correct in another colour.
5. Write two three-part help questions about what is still unclear, and ask one of them to your study partner, teacher or an AI tutor.

**Proof to record:** Your question sheet with kinds marked, the three statement questions, your next-day answers with corrections, and the help questions with the answer you got.

## Template: question stems card

```
FACT         What...? When...? Who...? Where...?
REASON       Why...? What caused...? Why was it needed?
PROCESS      How does... work? What are the steps of...?
COMPARISON   How is ___ different from ___? What do ___ and ___ share?
APPLICATION  What is an example of...? Which rule applies when...?
WHAT IF      What would happen if...? What would change if...?
Rule: write them today, answer from memory tomorrow, then check.
```

## Template: PSC-style statement question builder

```
Topic: ______________
Consider the following statements:
1. ______________________________________ (true / false: ____________)
2. ______________________________________ (true / false: ____________)
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(A) 1 only  (B) 2 only  (C) Both 1 and 2  (D) Neither 1 nor 2
Answer: ___   Why each statement is right or wrong: ______________________
Source: ______________ page ___
```

## Template: three-part help question

```
I am trying to understand: ___________________________________________
What I already know or tried: _________________________________________
Exactly where I am stuck: ____________________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Writing only "what" questions.** Use all six kinds; reason and comparison questions build understanding.
- **Writing questions and never answering them.** Answer them from memory the next day. That is where the benefit is.
- **Making statement questions you can't check.** Every statement needs a source, so the answer is certain.
- **Asking vague help questions.** Use the three-part form: goal, what you know, where you are stuck.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is a comparison question?
    - A) Who was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
    - B) When was the 73rd Amendment passed?
    - C) Where is the Supreme Court?
    - D) How is a writ of mandamus different from prohibition?
2. Consider: (1) The 73rd Amendment added Part IX to the Constitution. (2) It deals with municipalities. Which is correct?
    - A) 2 only
    - B) 1 only
    - C) Both 1 and 2
    - D) Neither 1 nor 2
3. Where does most of the benefit of writing your own questions come from?
    - A) Sharing them online
    - B) Answering them from memory later
    - C) Writing them neatly
    - D) Copying them into a notebook
4. Which is the best help question?
    - A) "I don't understand anything."
    - B) "I'm trying to understand certiorari. I know a higher court issues it to a lower court. I don't see how it differs from prohibition."
    - C) "Is this important?"
    - D) "Explain the writs."

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The elaboration bookmark prompts and College Success 5.2
- **Action:** Write and answer 12 deep questions and 3 statement questions, and ask a three-part help question. It is done when your proof is saved: your question sheet with kinds marked, the three statement questions, your next-day answers with corrections, and the help questions with the answer you got.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It asks how two similar things differ.
2. **B.** Municipalities are in Part IXA, added by the 74th Amendment.
3. **B.** Answering from memory is retrieval practice.
4. **B.** It states the goal, what you know and exactly where you are stuck.

sections.title: LRN-M08-L03: Concept maps, drawn from memory
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Draw concept maps of connected PSC ideas from memory, check and correct them, and use them as retrieval practice rather than decoration. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 45 minutes action plus a 15-minute redraw two days later).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What a concept map is

A **concept map** shows ideas (concepts) in boxes, joined by **labelled arrows** that say how they are related. Each box-arrow-box reads as a sentence: "Lok Sabha → elected directly by → the people"; "Vice-President → is the chairman of → Rajya Sabha". The labels are the point: they force you to say exactly how ideas connect.

It differs from a mind map (Module 9), which branches out from one central topic, usually without labelled links.

### What the research found, honestly

In a well-known study, Karpicke and Blunt compared students who studied a science text by making concept maps with the text available against students who practised retrieval (reading, then recalling on paper). Retrieval practice produced much better long-term retention, and students had predicted the opposite ([Purdue University, 2011](https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2011/110120KarpickeScience.html)).

So concept mapping **with the book open** is not the best use of your time. But you don't have to choose. Draw the map **from memory**, then check it against the source. That makes the map a form of retrieval practice, and it adds what retrieval alone doesn't show: whether you understand how the ideas fit together.

### How to draw one from memory

1. **List 10 to 15 key concepts** from the topic, from memory.
2. **Place the most general one at the top** (for example "Parliament") and more specific ones below.
3. **Join them with arrows and write a short label** on each: "consists of", "elected by", "appoints", "can delay", "causes", "is part of".
4. **Add cross-links** between distant parts of the map; these show deep understanding.
5. **Check against the source** and fix wrong or missing links in another colour.
6. **Redraw it from memory** two days later and count the correct links.

### Topics that suit concept maps

Topics with many connected parts: the structure of Parliament, the Indian monsoon, the Kerala renaissance (leaders, organisations, movements and places), inflation and the RBI, the structure of local government. Simple lists don't need maps.

## Local example

**Anu** drew a concept map of Parliament from memory, with 12 concepts: President, Parliament, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Speaker, Vice-President, money bill, ordinary bill, members, people, state legislatures, joint sitting.

She drew arrows such as "Parliament → consists of → President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha", "Vice-President → is the chairman of → Rajya Sabha", "Rajya Sabha members → elected by → elected members of state legislative assemblies", and "money bill → can be introduced only in → Lok Sabha".

When she checked with her textbook, she found two wrong links: she had drawn the President presiding over joint sittings (it is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha), and she had forgotten that the Rajya Sabha must return a money bill within 14 days. She fixed both in red. Two days later she redrew the map from memory with 17 of 18 links right. The joint-sitting fact became a contrast card.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concept mapping with the text open | **Limited** | Karpicke and Blunt (2011): less effective for long-term retention than retrieval practice. |
| Drawing concept maps from memory, then checking | **Moderate** | It turns mapping into retrieval with feedback, and shows how well you understand the connections. |
| Labelled links between concepts | **Limited** | A practical feature of concept maps that forces precise thinking; little direct research on labels alone. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Purdue University (20 January 2011): retrieval practice beats concept mapping (Karpicke and Blunt, Science)](https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2011/110120KarpickeScience.html) | Reread the press release: what concept mapping was compared with | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding) | Revisit the dual coding poster: maps and diagrams as a second route to memory | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: retrieval practice materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/retrieval-practice) | Revisit the retrieval practice poster: drawing from memory counts | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a PSC topic with many connected ideas that you have already studied.
2. Without the book, list 10 to 15 key concepts, then draw the map with labelled arrows and at least two cross-links (about 15 minutes).
3. Open the source. Add missing concepts and links, and fix wrong ones, in another colour. Count your correct links.
4. Turn every wrong link into a contrast card or a margin question.
5. Two days later, redraw the map from memory without looking, and count the correct links again.

**Proof to record:** Your first map with corrections and link count, and the two-day redraw with its link count.

## Template: concept map from memory

```
CONCEPT MAP FROM MEMORY     Topic: ______________  Date: ______
1. Concepts I can recall (10-15): ____________________________________________
2. Most general concept (top): ______________
3. Draw boxes and LABELLED arrows. Each arrow must read as a sentence.
4. Cross-links (at least 2): __________________ ; __________________
5. Checked against: ______________ page ___
   Correct links ___ / total ___   Wrong links fixed ___   Missing links added ___
6. Two-day redraw: correct links ___ / ___
```

## Template: linking words

```
consists of | is part of | is elected by | is appointed by | is the head of
presides over | can delay | must approve | causes | leads to | prevents
depends on | is an example of | is different from | replaced | was founded by
```

## Common mistakes

- **Lines without labels.** Every arrow needs a label; otherwise you can't tell if the link is right.
- **Copying a map from the book.** Draw from memory first, then check. Copying is not retrieval.
- **Thirty concepts on one page.** Ten to fifteen is enough. Split big topics into two maps.
- **Using maps instead of recall practice.** A map drawn from memory is recall practice; one drawn with the book open mostly isn't.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Karpicke and Blunt find about concept mapping with the text available?
    - A) It was never tested
    - B) It beat every other method
    - C) It gave worse long-term retention than retrieval practice
    - D) It was the same as rereading
2. How do you turn a concept map into retrieval practice?
    - A) Draw it from memory, then check against the source
    - B) Copy it neatly from the book
    - C) Colour it carefully
    - D) Print one from the internet
3. Which is a properly labelled link?
    - A) "Vice-President → ?"
    - B) "Vice-President → is the chairman of → Rajya Sabha"
    - C) "Vice-President — Rajya Sabha"
    - D) "Vice-President, Rajya Sabha, Lok Sabha"
4. Who presides over a joint sitting of the two houses of Parliament?
    - A) The Prime Minister
    - B) The President
    - C) The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
    - D) The Chief Justice of India

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Karpicke and Blunt press release, revisited with the dual coding and retrieval posters
- **Action:** Draw a concept map from memory, check it, and redraw it two days later. It is done when your proof is saved: your first map with corrections and link count, and the two-day redraw with its link count.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Retrieval practice produced much better long-term retention.
2. **A.** Producing it from memory is retrieval; checking gives feedback.
3. **B.** The label turns the link into a checkable sentence.
4. **C.** This was one of the errors Anu found and fixed by checking her map.

sections.title: LRN-M08-L04: First-principles thinking
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Rebuild formulas and rules from a few basic truths so you can work them out instead of memorising them, starting with PSC arithmetic. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What first principles are

**First principles** are the basic truths from which other things follow. A student who knows only the shortcut formula is stuck when a question is phrased differently. A student who knows **why** the formula works can rebuild it, check it and adapt it under pressure.

### Six PSC examples

1. **Per cent means "per hundred".** So x% of y = x × y ÷ 100, and percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A classic trap: a price rises 20% and then falls 20%. From first principles, the price becomes 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 of the original: a **4% fall**, not "no change".
2. **Profit and loss** are percentages of the **cost price**. Selling price = cost price × (1 + profit% ÷ 100).
3. **Speed:** distance = speed × time. Two people moving towards each other close the gap at the **sum** of their speeds; moving the same way, at the **difference**. Every "relative speed" formula follows.
4. **Time and work:** if A finishes a job in 10 days, A does 1/10 of it each day. Rates add. A (1/10 a day) and B (1/15 a day) together do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 a day, so they finish in **6 days**.
5. **Simple interest:** R% of the principal P each year for T years gives P × R × T ÷ 100. Compound interest applies the same R% to a growing amount each year.
6. **Calendars:** a 365-day year is 52 weeks and **1 extra day**, so the same date moves one weekday later the next year (two if a 29 February comes between). "Odd days" questions are all built on this.

### The method

1. **Ask: what must be true for this rule to work?**
2. **Go down to the definition:** per cent, rate, distance, a week.
3. **Rebuild the rule** step by step in your own words.
4. **Test it with small, easy numbers:** a price of ₹100, a job of 1, a distance of 60 km.
5. **Keep the principle,** and make a card only for the principle plus one example.

Then practise until applying the principle is fast. In the exam you won't have time to derive slowly; first principles make the method reliable, and practice makes it quick (Module 14).

### Beyond maths

The same habit helps in GK when there is a reason behind a rule: why the Rajya Sabha is permanent (continuity), why Directive Principles can't be enforced in court (they depend on resources and policy), why the monsoon rains on the windward side of the Ghats (Module 3). **Dates, names and article numbers have no first principles.** Learn those with cards and mnemonics (Modules 4 and 11).

## Local example

**Ashiq**'s maths guide had a page of 42 shortcut formulas, and he had tried to learn them all. In mocks he kept using the wrong one, especially for successive percentage changes and time-and-work questions.

He picked five formulas and rebuilt each from its definition, testing with small numbers. For successive changes he wrote: "Each change multiplies: 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, so two 10% rises make 21%." For time and work: "Turn days into a daily rate, add the rates, turn back into days." For pipes and cisterns he noticed it was the same principle with one rate negative, which removed four formulas from his list.

He solved two previous-year questions for each principle without the shortcut page. All ten were right, and for the first time he could explain why. His list of 42 shortcuts became 6 principles and a few cards.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Understanding why a method works (self-explanation of worked examples) | **Moderate** | Self-explanation is rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013); worked examples help beginners (CESE review). |
| Rebuilding rules from first principles | **Limited** | A practical approach consistent with research on self-explanation and schemas; little direct research by this name. |
| Memorising many shortcut formulas without understanding | **Limited** | Little direct research; shortcuts are fragile when a question is phrased differently. Keep principles, practise speed. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, 6.1 Understand Percent](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/6-1-understand-percent) | Read the definition of percent and do the first exercises, rebuilding each conversion from the definition | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e (free, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/preface) | Look at the table of contents and note the chapters that match your PSC maths syllabus | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NSW Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation (2017), "Cognitive load theory: Research that teachers really need to understand" (PDF)](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory.pdf) | Reread the part on worked examples and expertise reversal | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Pick five formulas or shortcuts from your PSC maths or reasoning guide that you often confuse.
2. For each, fill in the first-principles sheet: the basic truth, the rule rebuilt step by step, and a test with small numbers.
3. Solve two previous-year questions for each principle without looking at the shortcut page.
4. Pick one non-maths rule (for example why the Rajya Sabha is permanent) and explain its reason from first principles in five lines; check it in your textbook.
5. Make one AnkiDroid card per principle: the principle on the back, with one worked example.

**Proof to record:** Five first-principles sheets with tests and PYQ solutions, your five-line non-maths explanation, and a screenshot of the new cards.

## Template: first-principles sheet

```
FIRST PRINCIPLES      Formula or rule: ______________________________
The basic truth (definition): ________________________________________
Rebuilt step by step:
1. ______________________________________________________________
2. ______________________________________________________________
3. ______________________________________________________________
Small-number test (e.g. ₹100, a job of 1, 60 km): ___________________ works? Y / N
PYQ 1: ______ solved with the principle: right? Y / N
PYQ 2: ______ solved with the principle: right? Y / N
Card: front "____________ (principle)?"  back "____________ + one example"
```

## Template: principle or memorise?

```
Has a reason or a definition behind it?  -> rebuild it from first principles
  (percentages, rates, interest, speed, calendars, why a rule exists)
Pure fact with no reason to derive?       -> card or mnemonic
  (dates, names, article numbers, places, awards)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Memorising pages of shortcuts.** Keep the few principles they come from, and practise applying them.
- **Deriving slowly in the exam.** Understand first, then practise until the method is fast.
- **Trying to "derive" dates and names.** Facts have no first principles. Use cards and mnemonics.
- **Skipping the small-number test.** Testing with ₹100 or a job of 1 catches mistakes in your rebuilt rule.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the overall change?
    - A) A 4% rise
    - B) A 40% fall
    - C) No change
    - D) A 4% fall
2. A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. How long do they take together?
    - A) 5 days
    - B) 6 days
    - C) 12.5 days
    - D) 25 days
3. Why does a date move one weekday later in the next ordinary year?
    - A) Because the calendar was changed
    - B) Because of leap seconds
    - C) 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 extra day
    - D) It moves two weekdays every year
4. Which of these should you learn with cards rather than first principles?
    - A) Successive percentage change
    - B) Relative speed
    - C) Simple interest
    - D) The year the Vaikom Satyagraha began

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Prealgebra 6.1 on percent, and the CESE review on worked examples
- **Action:** Rebuild five PSC formulas from first principles and solve two PYQs with each. It is done when your proof is saved: five first-principles sheets with tests and PYQ solutions, your five-line non-maths explanation, and a screenshot of the new cards.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 of the original price.
2. **B.** 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the job per day.
3. **C.** The one odd day shifts the weekday; a 29 February makes it two.
4. **D.** Dates have no principle to derive; the others follow from definitions.

sections.title: Module 9: Note-making that leads to recall
sections.summary: Make notes that lead to recall: Cornell notes and outlines, mind maps and sketchnotes, and a daily routine that turns every note page into questions, flashcards and revision entries within 24 hours.
sections.content:
## Overview

Most PSC aspirants have notebooks full of copied text. This module changes notes from a record into a tool: short, in your own words, with questions you answer later. It is honest that the famous formats (Cornell, mind maps, sketchnotes) have little direct research; they work when they lead to retrieval, and the lessons make sure they do.

The result is a note-to-recall pipeline: what you write today becomes tomorrow's practice.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Make Cornell notes and outlines in your own words, with cue questions
- Draw mind maps and sketchnotes from memory and check them
- Choose a note format that suits the content
- Process each day's notes into cards, questions and Revision-tab entries within 24 hours
- Measure your notes by what you can recall from them

## Time

About 4 hours 45 minutes in total: 3 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 10–11, with the module project due in week 11.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M09-L01: Cornell notes and outlines (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M09-L02: Mind maps and sketchnotes (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M09-L03: Turning notes into questions and flashcards (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **Cornell page checklist** and **outline with question headings**
- The **mind map from memory** steps and your **visual vocabulary**
- The **daily note-processing routine** and the **what becomes what** table

## Module project: My note-to-recall pipeline

1. For one week, make all your PSC notes as Cornell pages or question outlines.
2. Process each day's notes within 24 hours, logging what each day produced.
3. Draw one chapter mind map from memory and check it.
4. At the end of the week, take a 20-question test on the week's notes without looking, and compare with a similar test on old, unprocessed notes.

**Proof to record:** Photos of a week of processed notes, the processing log, your mind map and both test scores.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Own words | Mostly copied | Mixed | Short phrases in my own words throughout |
| Questions | No cue questions | Some pages with questions | Every key point has a question, answered the next day |
| Processing | Notes left as they are | Processed sometimes | Processed within 24 hours every day, cards within budget |
| Measured result | No test | Tested once | Tested and compared with unprocessed notes |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use only the cue column: add questions to your existing notes and answer them the next day.
- Process notes on three days of the week instead of every day.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Note-taking versus note-making | Copying versus processing: choosing, own words, questions for recall. |
| The three parts of a Cornell page | Notes column, cue column (questions), summary at the bottom. |
| The step of Cornell notes that matters most | Covering the notes and answering the cue questions from memory. |
| Mind map versus concept map | Mind map: branches from one centre. Concept map: labelled links between ideas. |
| Rule for mind maps and sketchnotes | Draw from memory, then check. |
| The 24-hour rule | Process today's notes into cards, questions and revision entries within a day. |
| What a list in your notes becomes | One cloze per item, or a memory palace. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Judging notes by length or neatness.** Judge them by what you can recall a week later.
- **Keeping notes and cards in separate worlds.** The processing routine connects them every day.

sections.title: LRN-M09-L01: Cornell notes and outlines
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Make Cornell notes and outlines from PSC sources in your own words, and use the cue column as a recall test. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 40 minutes action plus a 10-minute check the next day).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Note-taking versus note-making

**Note-taking** often means copying: lines from the textbook, everything the teacher says, whole paragraphs from a PDF. It feels productive and keeps you busy, but copying needs little thinking. **Note-making** means processing: choosing what matters, putting it in your own words, and preparing it for recall later.

The test of good notes is simple: **can you use them to recall and answer questions?** Not: are they long, neat or colourful?

### The Cornell method

The Cornell method was developed by Walter Pauk, an education professor at Cornell University, and described in his book *How to Study in College* ([Cornell Learning Strategies Center](https://lsc.cornell.edu/how-to-study/taking-notes/cornell-note-taking-system/)). OpenStax's *College Success* explains it in its note-taking section ([chapter 5](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking)). Divide each page into three parts:

```
+-----------+-------------------------------------+
| CUE       | NOTES                               |
| column    | (about two-thirds of the width)     |
| (about    |                                     |
| 6 cm)     | Key points in your own words,       |
| questions | short phrases, abbreviations,       |
| and       | small diagrams                      |
| keywords  |                                     |
+-----------+-------------------------------------+
| SUMMARY (bottom 5 cm): 2-3 sentences in your    |
| own words, written after the notes              |
+-------------------------------------------------+
```

The method is often summarised in five steps:

1. **Record:** while reading or listening, write key points in the notes column, in your own words.
2. **Reduce:** soon after, write questions or keywords in the cue column for each key point.
3. **Recite:** cover the notes column and answer the cue questions from memory. This is the step that matters most: it is retrieval practice.
4. **Reflect:** write the summary at the bottom and link the page to what you already know.
5. **Review:** come back to the cue column on your revision days (Module 3).

### Outlines

An **outline** arranges notes as headings and sub-points, like the structure of a textbook. It suits subjects with a clear hierarchy, such as the Constitution (Parts, Articles, clauses) or a geography chapter (physical features, climate, soils, forests). Write outline headings as questions where you can, so the outline doubles as a recall test.

### Paper or phone?

The famous claim that handwritten notes beat typed ones did not hold up when the study was repeated; what you write matters more than how ([The Learning Scientists, 2019](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2019/2/21-1)). Use paper for Cornell pages and diagrams if you prefer, or Joplin on the phone or laptop (Module 18). Either way: your own words, few words, and questions you will answer later.

### Notes from video classes

Pause the video every 5 to 10 minutes and write the key points from memory, then rewind to check. Never try to write everything the teacher says.

## Local example

**Sreeja** used to copy her guide's page on Fundamental Duties into a notebook, word for word: two pages, neat handwriting, nothing remembered a week later.

This time she made one Cornell page. In the notes column she wrote short phrases in her own words: "Article 51A, Part IVA. Added by 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. 10 duties at first; 11th added by 86th Amendment, 2002: parents or guardians to give children aged 6 to 14 opportunities for education. Not enforceable in court." In the cue column she wrote questions: "Which article? Which amendment added them? Which committee? How many at first? What did the 86th add?"

The next morning she covered the notes column and answered the cue questions aloud: 6 out of 7. At the bottom she had written her summary: "Duties were added in 1976 and expanded in 2002; they guide citizens but can't be enforced like rights." The page took 25 minutes instead of 50.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answering cue-column questions with the notes covered | **Strong** | This is retrieval practice, rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| The Cornell layout itself | **Limited** | Widely taught, with little direct research; its value comes mostly from the questions and the recall step. |
| Handwritten notes always beat typed notes | **Limited** | The well-known result did not replicate (Learning Scientists, 2019). Content matters more than the tool. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [College Success, chapter 5: Reading and Notetaking (SQ3R, Cornell method)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking) | Read 5.3 on taking notes, including the Cornell method | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Cornell University Learning Strategies Center: the Cornell note-taking system](https://lsc.cornell.edu/how-to-study/taking-notes/cornell-note-taking-system/) | Look at the Cornell Learning Strategies Center page on the method (it claims handwriting is better; see the next link) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists blog (21 February 2019): laptop versus longhand notes, a failed replication](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2019/2/21-1) | Reread why the handwriting-versus-laptop claim is doubtful | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose one PSC chapter or section you haven't made notes on yet.
2. Make 2 or 3 Cornell pages on it: key points in your own words in the notes column (no copying of whole sentences).
3. Within the same day, write a question or keyword in the cue column for every key point, and write a 2 to 3 sentence summary at the bottom of each page.
4. The next day, cover the notes column and answer every cue question aloud from memory. Score yourself and mark misses.
5. Make a short outline of a different section, with headings written as questions, and compare which format suited that content better.

**Proof to record:** Photos of your Cornell pages and outline, and your next-day cue-column score.

## Template: Cornell page checklist

```
[ ] Line drawn: cue column about 6 cm on the left; summary space 5 cm at the bottom
[ ] Notes column: key points in MY words, short phrases, small diagrams
[ ] Cue column: one question or keyword per key point (written the same day)
[ ] Summary: 2-3 sentences, written without looking at the source
[ ] Next day: notes covered, cue questions answered aloud. Score ___/___
[ ] Misses added to: AnkiDroid / Revision tab / margin questions
```

## Template: outline with question headings

```
TOPIC: ________________________ (source ______ page ___)
1. What is ______________?
   a. ______________________
   b. ______________________
2. Why / how ______________?
   a. ______________________
3. How is ______ different from ______?
   a. ______________________
Recall test: cover everything except the headings and answer them.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Copying the textbook into a notebook.** Write key points in your own words, in short phrases.
- **An empty cue column.** The questions are the point. Write them the same day.
- **Never covering the notes to recall.** Without the recall step, Cornell notes are just tidy copying.
- **Spending time on colours and neatness.** Judge notes by what you can recall from them, not by how they look.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which step of the Cornell method matters most for memory?
    - A) Using three colours
    - B) Drawing the lines neatly
    - C) Covering the notes and answering the cue questions from memory
    - D) Copying the textbook exactly
2. What goes in the cue column?
    - A) Questions or keywords for each key point
    - B) The page numbers only
    - C) The full text of the chapter
    - D) Nothing; it stays empty
3. What happened when the handwriting-beats-laptop study was repeated?
    - A) Laptops won clearly
    - B) It was never repeated
    - C) The advantage did not hold up; content matters more
    - D) Handwriting won by more
4. How should you take notes from a video class?
    - A) Take no notes at all
    - B) Write everything the teacher says
    - C) Pause every 5 to 10 minutes, write key points from memory, then check
    - D) Watch at double speed and note the slides

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** College Success 5.3 on the Cornell method and the Learning Scientists post on handwriting and laptops
- **Action:** Make Cornell notes on a PSC chapter, test yourself from the cue column the next day, and try an outline. It is done when your proof is saved: photos of your Cornell pages and outline, and your next-day cue-column score.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Reciting from the cues is retrieval practice.
2. **A.** They turn the page into a recall test.
3. **C.** Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019) did not find a reliable advantage.
4. **C.** Recalling at pauses turns watching into retrieval.

sections.title: LRN-M09-L02: Mind maps and sketchnotes
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Make mind maps and simple sketchnotes for PSC topics where structure and pictures help, drawing them from memory and checking them. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action plus a 10-minute redraw the next day).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Mind maps

A **mind map** puts the main topic in the centre of a page, with branches for its subtopics and smaller branches for details: keywords, not sentences, and small pictures where they help. It shows the **shape of a whole chapter** on one page.

Mind maps and concept maps look similar but do different jobs. A mind map is a tree that branches out from one centre; a concept map (LRN-M08-L03) is a network with labelled links between any ideas. Use mind maps for overview and revision; use concept maps when the relationships themselves are what you must understand.

Good uses for PSC:

- **A one-page overview of a chapter** before you study it in detail, and again before the exam
- **Revision:** one mind map per chapter, drawn from memory, is a fast way to check what you remember
- **Linking subtopics:** seeing that rivers, soils and crops all depend on the same three regions of Kerala

### Sketchnotes

**Sketchnotes** mix words with simple drawings: boxes, arrows, icons and small figures. They apply dual coding (Module 3) to your own notes. You don't need drawing skills. A stick figure, a box, an arrow and a dozen simple icons are enough. Build a small "visual vocabulary" of icons you reuse: a person, a building, a rupee sign, a scale for law, a calendar, a map pin, a factory, a book, a water drop, a flag.

### What the evidence says

Mind maps and sketchnotes have **little direct research**, and the claims made for them online are often exaggerated. They rest on two principles that are well supported: combining words with meaningful pictures (dual coding) and, when you draw them from memory, retrieval. So the rule from Module 8 applies again: **draw from memory, then check**. A beautiful mind map copied from a book is decoration.

### When not to use them

- **Detailed facts** (articles, dates, award winners): cards and mnemonics are better.
- **Maths and reasoning:** practise problems instead.
- **When drawing takes longer than learning.** If you spend 40 minutes colouring, switch to Cornell notes.

## Local example

**Ashiq** drew a mind map of Kerala geography from memory, with "Kerala" in the centre and six branches: physical divisions, rivers, climate, soils, forests and wildlife, and minerals. Under physical divisions he drew the three regions taught in his SCERT textbook: highland, midland and lowland, each with a tiny icon (a mountain, gentle hills, waves).

When he checked against the textbook, he had left out an entire branch for agriculture and put two facts under the wrong region. He fixed them in red. The next morning he redrew the map from memory in 8 minutes, with all seven branches and no misplaced facts.

He also tried a sketchnote of a 25-minute video class on the Indian economy: boxes for sectors, a rupee icon for income, arrows for flows. Watching his own sketchnote the next day brought back the class better than his old line-by-line notes, but it took him longer to make, so he uses sketchnotes only for classes with lots of processes.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mind maps and sketchnotes as such | **Limited** | Little direct research, and online claims are often exaggerated. |
| Meaningful pictures combined with words (dual coding) | **Moderate** | One of the six strategies in Module 3. |
| Drawing a map from memory, then checking | **Moderate** | It turns the map into retrieval with feedback. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding) | Read the dual coding blog post and keep the poster beside your notebook | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Purdue University (20 January 2011): retrieval practice beats concept mapping (Karpicke and Blunt, Science)](https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/research/2011/110120KarpickeScience.html) | Reminder: maps made with the book open lost to retrieval practice | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a whole PSC chapter you have studied. Draw a one-page mind map of it from memory, with the topic in the centre and keywords on the branches (15 minutes).
2. Check against the source. Add missing branches and fix misplaced facts in another colour.
3. Draw your visual vocabulary: 10 simple icons you will reuse in notes.
4. Make a sketchnote of one PSC class, video or chapter section (20 to 30 minutes of material), using at least five of your icons.
5. The next day, redraw the mind map from memory and compare with your corrected version.

**Proof to record:** Your corrected mind map, the next-day redraw, your 10-icon visual vocabulary and the sketchnote.

## Template: mind map from memory, steps

```
1. Centre: the chapter's topic, with a small picture.
2. Main branches: the chapter's 4-7 subtopics, from memory.
3. Smaller branches: keywords only (no sentences), small icons where they help.
4. Check against the source; fix and add in another colour.
5. Next day: redraw from memory. Branches right ___/___  details right ___/___
```

## Template: visual vocabulary (draw your own version of each)

```
person (stick figure)   building (institution)   rupee sign (money, economy)
scale (law, courts)     calendar (date, year)    map pin (place)
factory (industry)      book (literature)        water drop (rivers, rain)
flag (nation, state)    arrow (cause, flow)      box (group, category)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Spending more time on art than on content.** Simple icons, few colours. If it takes longer than learning, switch methods.
- **Copying a mind map from a book or the internet.** Draw from memory, then check; copying is decoration.
- **Sentences on branches.** Keywords only. Sentences turn a map into crowded notes.
- **Using mind maps for lists of dates and articles.** Use cards and mnemonics for detailed facts.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. How does a mind map differ from a concept map?
    - A) They are exactly the same
    - B) A mind map has no keywords
    - C) A concept map has no boxes
    - D) A mind map branches out from one centre; a concept map links ideas with labelled arrows
2. What is the honest evidence position on mind maps?
    - A) Little direct research; they work through dual coding and retrieval when drawn from memory
    - B) Proven harmful
    - C) Proven to double memory
    - D) Only for visual learners
3. Which PSC content is least suited to a mind map?
    - A) A list of article numbers and their exact contents
    - B) Linking subtopics of a chapter
    - C) An overview of a geography chapter
    - D) Revision of a history chapter's main themes
4. What is a visual vocabulary?
    - A) A collection of photos
    - B) A list of colours
    - C) A small set of simple icons you reuse in your notes
    - D) A dictionary of English words

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Learning Scientists' dual coding post, with the Karpicke and Blunt reminder
- **Action:** Draw a chapter mind map from memory, make a sketchnote, and redraw the map the next day. It is done when your proof is saved: your corrected mind map, the next-day redraw, your 10-icon visual vocabulary and the sketchnote.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Use mind maps for overview and concept maps for relationships.
2. **A.** The principles behind them are supported; the method itself is less tested.
3. **A.** Detailed facts suit cards and mnemonics.
4. **C.** Reusable icons make sketchnotes fast without drawing skills.
