sections.title: LRN-M09-L03: Turning notes into questions and flashcards
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn every page of notes into questions, flashcards and Revision-tab entries within 24 hours, so your notes become recall practice. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 15 minutes a day for 5 days plus a 20-minute test on day 6).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Notes are a means, not the product. A notebook full of good notes that you never test yourself on is a slow way to forget. This lesson connects your notes to the rest of your system.

### The 24-hour rule

Process today's notes **within 24 hours**, before the forgetting curve (Module 1) takes most of them. Processing takes about 15 minutes a day:

1. **Mark the key points** on today's pages.
2. **Write a question** for each in the cue column or margin.
3. **Facts become AnkiDroid cards,** following the card-writing checklist (Module 4).
4. **Reasons and processes become why-questions** or go on your Feynman list (Module 8).
5. **The topic goes into the Revision tab** with today's date (Module 3).
6. **Mistakes go into the error log** (Module 12).

### What becomes what

| In your notes | Becomes | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A single fact (date, name, article, place) | A Basic or cloze card | AnkiDroid |
| A list (rivers, awards, duties) | One cloze per item, or a memory palace | AnkiDroid or Module 11 |
| A map or diagram | An image occlusion note | AnkiDroid |
| A cause, reason or process | A why or how question; a Feynman topic | Cue column; Feynman list |
| Two similar things | A comparison table and a contrast card | Notes and AnkiDroid |
| A whole topic | A row with review dates | Revision tab |
| A maths method | A worked example plus a first-principles card | Notes and AnkiDroid |

### Don't drown in cards

Only facts that are on your syllabus or in previous papers become cards, and new cards stay within your daily budget (LRN-M04-L04). If processing produces 40 new cards a day, you are carding too much: keep the facts that matter and let the rest live in your notes and the Revision tab.

### Notes in your knowledge base later

From Module 18, processed notes can live in Joplin or Logseq, linked to each other. The processing routine stays the same.

## Local example

**Anu** attends a PSC coaching class two evenings a week and studies her guide on the other days. She used to fill a notebook and look at it again only before exams.

For five days she processed each day's notes before her morning AnkiDroid reviews, using the 24-hour rule. A typical day: three pages of notes became 9 new cards (within her budget of 12), 6 margin questions, 1 Revision-tab entry and 1 topic for her Feynman list. It took 12 to 18 minutes.

On day 6 she tested herself with 20 questions drawn from all five days, without looking: 16 right. On an older, unprocessed set of notes from the previous month, the same kind of test gave 7. She now writes "P" at the top of each page once it is processed, and a page without a P is her first job the next morning.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Turning notes into questions and cards you answer later | **Strong** | It turns notes into retrieval practice, rated high utility. |
| Processing notes within 24 hours | **Limited** | A practical rule consistent with the forgetting curve; no direct study of the 24-hour cut-off. |
| Keeping new cards within a daily budget | **Moderate** | The Anki manual's workload rule: new cards drive future reviews. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Anki manual: Editing (cloze deletion and image occlusion)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html) | Refresh the cloze and image occlusion steps you will use when processing | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Piotr Wozniak, "Effective learning: Twenty rules of formulating knowledge" (SuperMemo, 1999)](https://www.supermemo.com/en/blog/twenty-rules-of-formulating-knowledge) | Reread rules 4, 9 and 10 (minimum information, avoid sets, avoid enumerations) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 6: Studying, Memory, and Test Taking](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking) | Read 6.2 Studying, with an eye to how notes are used after class | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For the next five study days, process each day's notes within 24 hours using the six steps, in about 15 minutes.
2. Each day, log what the processing produced: cards, questions, Revision-tab entries, Feynman topics.
3. Keep new cards within your daily budget; let extra facts stay in your notes.
4. Mark each processed page with a P at the top.
5. On day 6, test yourself with 20 questions drawn from all five days, without looking. Score it.

**Proof to record:** Photos of two processed note pages, your five-day processing log, your AnkiDroid card count before and after, and the day-6 score.

## Template: daily note-processing routine (15 minutes)

```
NOTE PROCESSING      Date: ______   Pages: ___
[ ] 1. Key points marked
[ ] 2. A question for each key point (cue column or margin)
[ ] 3. Facts -> cards (checklist!)      new cards today: ___ (budget ___)
[ ] 4. Reasons and processes -> why-questions / Feynman list: _____________
[ ] 5. Topic -> Revision tab (first-studied date = today)
[ ] 6. Mistakes -> error log
[ ] Page marked P
```

## Template: five-day processing log

```
Day | Pages | Cards | Questions | Revision entries | Feynman topics | Minutes
1   | ___   | ___   | ___       | ___              | ___            | ___
2   | ___   | ___   | ___       | ___              | ___            | ___
3   | ___   | ___   | ___       | ___              | ___            | ___
4   | ___   | ___   | ___       | ___              | ___            | ___
5   | ___   | ___   | ___       | ___              | ___            | ___
Day-6 test (20 questions from all five days): ___/20
```

## Common mistakes

- **Processing notes weeks later.** By then most of it is forgotten. Process within 24 hours.
- **Making a card of every line.** Card only syllabus facts, within your budget; the rest stays in notes.
- **Writing questions without answers in your notes.** Every question must be answerable from your notes or source, so you can check.
- **Never reopening processed pages.** The Revision tab brings each topic back; follow it.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the 24-hour rule?
    - A) Rewrite notes every 24 hours
    - B) Study for 24 hours before an exam
    - C) Process today's notes into questions, cards and revision entries within a day
    - D) Wait 24 hours before taking notes
2. Your notes contain a list of Kerala's east-flowing rivers. What should it become?
    - A) Nothing
    - B) A long paragraph
    - C) One card asking for the whole list
    - D) One cloze per river, or a memory palace
3. Processing produces 40 new cards a day. What should you do?
    - A) Card only syllabus facts within your budget and leave the rest in notes
    - B) Double the budget
    - C) Add all 40 every day
    - D) Stop using AnkiDroid
4. A cause-and-effect explanation in your notes should become...
    - A) An image occlusion note
    - B) A highlight
    - C) A single fact card
    - D) A why-question or a Feynman topic

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Anki cloze refresher, Wozniak's rules on lists and College Success 6.2
- **Action:** Process five days of notes within 24 hours each and test yourself on day 6. It is done when your proof is saved: photos of two processed note pages, your five-day processing log, your AnkiDroid card count before and after, and the day-6 score.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Processing before most is forgotten turns notes into recall practice.
2. **D.** Lists are split so each item is recalled on its own.
3. **A.** New cards drive future reviews; too many leads to backlog.
4. **D.** Reasons are best tested by explaining them.

sections.title: Module 10: Reading
sections.summary: Read for learning, not just for covering pages: active reading with SQ3R, skimming and scanning when they fit, the honest truth about speed and comprehension, and a short, reliable current-affairs routine from official free sources.
sections.content:
## Overview

Reading is where most PSC study time goes, and where most of it leaks away. This module gives you three reading gears and the judgement to choose between them, measures your effective reading rate (speed multiplied by understanding), and replaces hours of news watching with 20 minutes that you can test yourself on.

The result is a reading system: textbooks with SQ3R, facts found by scanning, a four-week reading practice and a dated current-affairs note with monthly reviews.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Read a textbook chapter with SQ3R and recite after every section
- Choose close reading, skimming or scanning to fit the job
- Explain why speed reading doesn't work and measure your effective reading rate
- Use vocabulary and practice to read better over time
- Run a daily current-affairs routine from official sources with monthly self-tests

## Time

About 5 hours 45 minutes in total: 4 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 11–12, with the module project due in week 12.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M10-L01: Active reading with SQ3R (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M10-L02: Skimming and scanning (about 1 hour)
3. LRN-M10-L03: Speed and comprehension: the honest truth (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
4. LRN-M10-L04: Newspapers and current affairs for PSC (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **SQ3R sheet** and **heading-to-question patterns**
- The **which gear?** guide and the **PSC notification scan checklist**
- The **reading log** with effective reading rate
- The **daily current-affairs note** and **monthly current-affairs review**

## Module project: My reading system

1. Read one more full chapter with SQ3R and test yourself on it the next day.
2. Keep the reading log for two weeks, with at least two timed readings and their effective rates.
3. Keep 14 days of current-affairs notes with dates, sources and links, and do a 20-question self-test on them.
4. Write your reading rules on one card: which gear for which job, your daily reading practice, and your current-affairs routine.

**Proof to record:** The SQ3R sheet and score, two weeks of the reading log, 14 days of current-affairs notes with the self-test, and your reading rules card.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Active reading | Read and close the book | SQ3R with some steps skipped | SQ3R with recite after every section, tested next day |
| Gears | Everything read the same way | Skimming or scanning used sometimes | Gear chosen for each job; scanning with PDF search |
| Speed and comprehension | Not measured | Speed measured only | Effective reading rate logged and practice running |
| Current affairs | Hours of videos, no notes | Notes without sources | Dated, sourced notes with links and a self-test |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use only the Recite step: close the book after each section and answer from memory.
- Do the current-affairs routine on three days a week, with the monthly review.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| SQ3R | Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. |
| The strongest steps of SQ3R | Recite and Review: retrieval and spaced retrieval. |
| Three reading gears | Close reading to learn, skimming for gist, scanning for one fact. |
| Speed-reading verdict (Rayner and others, 2016) | A speed-accuracy trade-off; eye movements are not the bottleneck. |
| Effective reading rate | Words per minute × comprehension % ÷ 100. |
| Official current-affairs sources | PIB, All India Radio News, PRD Kerala. |
| The 20-minute current-affairs routine | Scan headlines 5, read 2-3 items closely 10, write dated, sourced facts 5. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Measuring reading by pages covered.** Measure by what you can recall and answer the next day.
- **Chasing speed tricks.** Build vocabulary and background knowledge; speed follows slowly.

sections.title: LRN-M10-L01: Active reading with SQ3R
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Read a PSC textbook chapter with SQ3R (survey, question, read, recite, review), and compare the result with ordinary reading. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 45 minutes action plus a 10-minute test the next day).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Reading to learn is different

Reading a story and reading a textbook chapter for an exam are different jobs. For a story, you read once, front to back. For a chapter you must remember, reading once and closing the book loses most of it within days (Module 1). **Active reading** means doing something with the text while you read, so that you remember it.

### SQ3R

**SQ3R** is a classic active-reading method, popular since the 1940s and explained in OpenStax *College Success* ([chapter 5, section 5.2](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking)). The name stands for five steps:

1. **Survey (2 to 3 minutes):** before reading, look over the chapter: title, headings, pictures, maps, tables, the summary and the questions at the end. You are building a frame for what is coming.
2. **Question:** turn each heading into a question. "Climate of India" becomes "What controls India's climate, and how does it vary?"
3. **Read:** read **one section** at a time, looking for the answer to its question. Slow down for dense paragraphs.
4. **Recite:** close the book and answer the question aloud or on paper, in your own words. Then check.
5. **Review:** at the end of the chapter, recall all the questions without looking; then again on your revision days (Module 3).

### Why it works, honestly

SQ3R as a whole package has been studied less than you might expect, and the research on it is limited. But two of its steps are exactly the strongest methods in this course: **Recite** is retrieval practice and **Review** is spaced retrieval. The Survey and Question steps help you read with a purpose. If you only have time for one step, keep Recite.

### Reading SCERT textbooks for PSC

Many Kerala PSC aspirants build their GK on school textbooks from **SCERT Kerala**, because they are official, written for Kerala, and cover history, geography, economics, the Constitution and science step by step ([SCERT Kerala](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/)). NCERT textbooks are another free official source ([NCERT](https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php)). Read them with SQ3R, one chapter per session, and add margin questions instead of highlights (Module 2).

### Reading speed for textbooks

Dense textbook pages should be read slowly. Going back to reread a sentence you didn't understand is normal and useful. Fast reading belongs to skimming and scanning (next lesson), not to learning.

## Local example

**Sreeja** wanted to compare SQ3R with her usual reading. She took two SCERT social science chapters of similar length.

The first she read her usual way: start to finish, with a pencil, in 35 minutes. The second she read with SQ3R: a 3-minute survey of headings, maps and the end-of-chapter questions; six headings turned into questions on a sheet; then one section at a time, closing the book after each section to answer its question aloud before checking. It took 45 minutes.

The next day she answered ten questions on each chapter without looking. Ordinary reading: 4 out of 10. SQ3R: 8 out of 10. She noticed that the recite step was the uncomfortable part, and that it was also the step that showed her, section by section, what she hadn't understood.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQ3R as a complete method | **Limited** | Widely taught since the 1940s, with limited rigorous research on the whole package. |
| The Recite and Review steps | **Strong** | These are retrieval practice and spaced retrieval, both rated high utility. |
| Surveying a chapter and turning headings into questions | **Limited** | Sensible preparation that gives reading a purpose; little direct evidence on its own. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [College Success, chapter 5: Reading and Notetaking (SQ3R, Cornell method)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking) | Read 5.2 Effective Reading Strategies, including SQ3R | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SCERT Kerala: school textbooks](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/) | Find the textbook chapter you need for your PSC syllabus and download it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCERT: free textbooks (PDF)](https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php) | Optional: NCERT textbooks as a second official source | As needed | unverified: the site blocks automated checks |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose two textbook chapters of similar length and difficulty from your PSC syllabus (SCERT or NCERT).
2. Read the first in your usual way, and note the time taken.
3. Read the second with SQ3R, using the sheet below: survey, questions from headings, one section at a time, recite after each section, review at the end.
4. The next day, answer ten questions on each chapter without looking (from the end-of-chapter questions, previous papers or your own). Score both.
5. Add the SQ3R chapter to your Revision tab and its key facts to AnkiDroid.

**Proof to record:** Your SQ3R sheet, the times for both chapters and the two next-day scores.

## Template: SQ3R sheet

```
SQ3R     Chapter: ______________________  Source: ______  Date: ______
SURVEY (2-3 min): headings ___ | maps/tables ___ | summary read [ ] | end questions read [ ]
Section | Heading -> my question                       | Recite: my answer (book closed)   | Checked
1       | ____________________________________________ | _________________________________ | [ ]
2       | ____________________________________________ | _________________________________ | [ ]
3       | ____________________________________________ | _________________________________ | [ ]
4       | ____________________________________________ | _________________________________ | [ ]
5       | ____________________________________________ | _________________________________ | [ ]
REVIEW (end of chapter): questions answered from memory ___/___
Added to: Revision tab [ ]  AnkiDroid ___ cards
```

## Template: heading to question patterns

```
"Climate of India"           -> What controls India's climate, and how does it vary?
"Causes of the revolt"       -> What caused the revolt, and which cause mattered most?
"Powers of the Governor"     -> What can the Governor do, and what can't they do?
"Types of soil"              -> Which soils are found where, and why there?
Pattern: WHAT + WHY/HOW + a comparison or limit
```

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping the Recite step.** It is the step with the strongest evidence. Close the book after each section.
- **Turning the survey into full reading.** Two to three minutes: headings, pictures, summary, end questions. Then stop.
- **Reading several sections before reciting.** One section, one recite. Long stretches overload working memory.
- **Highlighting instead of questioning.** Write a margin question; it becomes tomorrow's recall.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does SQ3R stand for?
    - A) Survey, Quote, Read, Rewrite, Remember
    - B) Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review
    - C) Study, Quiz, Read, Repeat, Rest
    - D) Skim, Question, Reread, Recall, Rewrite
2. Which steps of SQ3R have the strongest research support?
    - A) None of them
    - B) Survey and Question
    - C) Read only
    - D) Recite and Review, because they are retrieval and spaced retrieval
3. How should you turn the heading "Powers of the Governor" into a question?
    - A) "Highlight the powers"
    - B) "What can the Governor do, and what can't they do?"
    - C) "Read about the Governor"
    - D) "Governor?"
4. When should you recite?
    - A) Never; reading is enough
    - B) After each section, with the book closed
    - C) While reading, with the book open
    - D) Only once at the end of the book

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** College Success 5.2 on reading strategies and SQ3R
- **Action:** Read one textbook chapter with SQ3R, one the usual way, and compare next-day scores. It is done when your proof is saved: your SQ3R sheet, the times for both chapters and the two next-day scores.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Five steps that make reading active.
2. **D.** The package has limited research, but retrieval and spacing are rated high utility.
3. **B.** A real question gives you something to answer while reading and reciting.
4. **B.** One section, then recall, keeps the load small and shows gaps early.

sections.title: LRN-M10-L02: Skimming and scanning
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Choose between close reading, skimming and scanning, and use skimming and scanning to find PSC information fast in long sources. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 35 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Three reading gears

Good readers change gear depending on the job:

| Gear | What you do | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Close reading | Read every sentence, slow down, recite (SQ3R) | Learning a chapter for the exam |
| Skimming | Read headings, first sentences of paragraphs, summaries, bold words and pictures | Getting the gist; deciding what to read closely; previewing |
| Scanning | Search for one item (a date, name, number or keyword) without reading the rest | Finding a specific fact: checking an answer, reading a notification |

OpenStax *College Success* describes these different kinds of reading ([chapter 5, section 5.1](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking)).

### Skimming, honestly

Skimming is fast because it skips most of the text, so it **loses detail**. The reading research reviewed by Rayner and others found exactly this: skimming can give you the gist, but understanding drops ([APS, 2016](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html)). Use skimming to decide what to read and to preview, never as a way of learning a chapter.

### Scanning: find it fast

When you scan, you hold the target in mind (a year, a name, a keyword) and let your eyes run down the page looking for its shape. On a phone or laptop, **use the search function** in your PDF reader: it is scanning done by the computer. Search for the rarest word in your question: "Vaikom" finds more than "satyagraha".

### PSC uses for each gear

- **Checking PYQ answers:** scan your textbook or guide for the keyword, then close-read the paragraph you find.
- **Previewing a chapter:** skim it for 3 minutes before SQ3R.
- **Current affairs:** skim headlines, then close-read only the PSC-relevant items (LRN-M10-L04).
- **Reading a Kerala PSC notification:** scan for the details that matter to you (below). Getting one of them wrong can cost you an exam, so close-read those lines once you find them.

### Scanning a PSC notification

Kerala PSC notifications are long, but you need a few details. Scan for: the **post name and category number**, **qualifications**, **age limit**, **last date** to apply, the **mode of selection** (for example an OMR test), and the link to the **syllabus**. The official website lists notifications and syllabuses ([Kerala PSC](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/) (check current rules)). Always check details on the official notification, not in a forwarded message.

## Local example

**Ashiq** had 30 previous-year questions he had answered wrongly, and he wanted to find each answer in his 300-page guide PDF and in his SCERT textbooks. The first time he tried it, he paged through looking for each one, and it took nearly two hours.

This time he scanned. For each question he picked the rarest keyword ("Aruvippuram", "quo warranto", "Eravikulam") and used the PDF reader's search on his phone. When the search found the word, he close-read the paragraph around it and wrote the answer with the page number. All 30 took 40 minutes.

He also skimmed a new economics chapter for three minutes before reading it with SQ3R, writing down the five main points he expected. After reading closely, four of his five were right, and the skim had shown him that the chapter's hardest part was a table on sectors, so he gave it extra time.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skimming loses detail and understanding | **Strong** | A clear finding of the reading research reviewed by Rayner and others (2016). |
| Scanning and search for specific facts | **Limited** | A practical skill with little formal research; it saves time when you know exactly what you need. |
| Choosing the reading gear to fit the purpose | **Limited** | Standard advice in study-skills books such as College Success; judge it by time saved and scores kept. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [College Success, chapter 5: Reading and Notetaking (SQ3R, Cornell method)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/05%3A_Reading_and_Notetaking) | Read 5.1 on the nature and types of reading | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [APS (14 January 2016): speed-reading promises are too good to be true (Rayner et al.)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html) | Reread the part on skimming | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala Public Service Commission (official website)](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/) | Open a current notification relevant to you and practise scanning it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Skim a new chapter for 3 minutes and write the 5 main points you expect. Then read it closely (SQ3R) and mark how many of your 5 were right.
2. Take 10 previous-year questions whose answers you need to check. For each, scan your textbook or guide (use PDF search) with the rarest keyword, then close-read the paragraph. Time the whole job.
3. Scan one current Kerala PSC notification for a post you might apply for, and fill in the notification checklist below.
4. Write two lines on which gear you overuse and which you will use more.

**Proof to record:** Your skim prediction compared with the close reading, the timed scan log for 10 questions, and the completed notification checklist.

## Template: which gear?

```
I need to LEARN this for the exam             -> close reading (SQ3R)
I need the GIST, or to decide what to read   -> skim: headings, first lines, summary, pictures
I need ONE FACT (date, name, number)         -> scan: rarest keyword, PDF search, then close-read that paragraph
```

## Template: PSC notification scan checklist

```
Post name: ______________________   Category number: ______
Department: _____________________
Qualifications: _______________________________________________
Age limit (and relaxations that apply to me): __________________
Last date to apply: ______   Mode of selection: ______________
Syllabus link found: [ ]   Saved in 12 Exam: [ ]
I close-read each of these lines on the official notification: [ ]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Skimming a chapter and calling it studied.** Skimming gives the gist only. Learn with close reading and recall.
- **Scanning without a clear target.** Choose the rarest keyword first, then search.
- **Reading every line of every source closely.** Switch gears: preview by skimming, find facts by scanning.
- **Trusting notification details from a forward.** Check the official notification on the Kerala PSC website.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. You need to check one date in a 300-page guide. Which gear?
    - A) Close reading of the whole guide
    - B) Skimming the whole guide
    - C) Scanning, with the PDF search and the rarest keyword
    - D) Reading the guide twice
2. What does research say about skimming?
    - A) It improves comprehension
    - B) It is the best way to learn
    - C) It doubles memory
    - D) It gives the gist but loses detail and understanding
3. Which keyword should you search to find a question about the Aruvippuram consecration?
    - A) "temple"
    - B) "Kerala"
    - C) "Aruvippuram"
    - D) "reform"
4. Where should you confirm the last date to apply for a PSC post?
    - A) On any coaching website
    - B) From a friend
    - C) In a WhatsApp forward
    - D) On the official notification on the Kerala PSC website

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** College Success 5.1 on types of reading and the APS summary on skimming
- **Action:** Skim and predict a chapter, scan for 10 PYQ answers, and scan a PSC notification. It is done when your proof is saved: your skim prediction compared with the close reading, the timed scan log for 10 questions, and the completed notification checklist.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Scanning finds one specific item fast.
2. **D.** Rayner and others (2016) found understanding drops with skimming.
3. **C.** The rarest word finds the right page fastest.
4. **D.** Only the official notification is authoritative.

sections.title: LRN-M10-L03: Speed and comprehension: the honest truth
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Measure your reading rate and comprehension honestly, understand what limits reading speed, and start the practice that makes you a faster reader without losing understanding. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus 15 minutes a day for four weeks).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The honest truth about speed reading

You will see apps and courses that promise reading at 1,000 words a minute or more with full understanding. A major review of reading research, led by Keith Rayner and published by the Association for Psychological Science, examined such claims ([APS, 2016](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html)). Its main findings:

- **There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy.** When you read much faster than normal, you understand and remember less.
- **Eye movements are not the bottleneck.** The limit is how fast your mind can recognise words and build meaning, not how fast your eyes move.
- **Skimming loses detail** (LRN-M10-L02).
- **The best way to read faster is to become a better reader:** read a lot, and grow your vocabulary.

So no trick will let you read a SCERT chapter in two minutes and remember it. But you **can** become a faster, better reader over months.

### What actually makes reading faster

1. **Vocabulary.** Each unknown word slows you down and breaks understanding. A vocabulary deck in AnkiDroid (Module 15) is one of the best investments for PSC English and Malayalam.
2. **Background knowledge.** The more you know about a topic, the faster you read about it, because familiar ideas take little working memory (Module 1). Your GK study makes your GK reading faster.
3. **Lots of reading practice,** in both English and Malayalam, on varied texts slightly above your comfort level.
4. **Familiarity with question language.** Reading many PSC questions makes you faster at reading new ones.

### Measure effective reading, not just speed

In week 0 you measured your **effective reading rate**: words per minute multiplied by comprehension. That number matters more than speed alone, because reading fast and understanding half gets you nothing in an exam.

```
Reading speed (wpm)     = words in the passage ÷ minutes taken
Comprehension (%)       = correct answers ÷ questions × 100
Effective reading rate  = wpm × comprehension % ÷ 100
Example: 540 words in 2.5 minutes = 216 wpm; 6 of 8 right = 75%; effective rate = 162
```

### A four-week reading practice

Fifteen minutes a day: alternate English and Malayalam. For English, the British Council's free LearnEnglish site has graded reading texts with tasks from beginner to advanced levels ([LearnEnglish](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/)). For Malayalam, read a newspaper editorial or a chapter of a Malayalam book. Once a week, time yourself on a new text and answer its questions, and log your effective reading rate.

## Local example

**Anu** had once paid for a "speed reading" video course from an advertisement. After a week of flashing words on the screen, she could "read" a page in a minute and remember almost nothing, so she stopped.

In week 0 her baseline was 190 words a minute with 6 of 8 questions right: an effective rate of about 143. She started this lesson's practice: 15 minutes a day, English texts from LearnEnglish at her level on odd days and Malayalam editorials on even days, plus five new English words a day in her vocabulary deck.

After four weeks, her timed reading on a new LearnEnglish text was about 215 words a minute with 7 of 8 right: an effective rate of about 188. Her speed rose modestly; her comprehension rose more, and the combination rose by almost a third. She stopped looking for tricks.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Speed reading several times faster with full comprehension | **No good evidence** | Rayner and others (2016): a speed-accuracy trade-off; eye movements are not the bottleneck. |
| Vocabulary and wide reading make you a better, faster reader | **Moderate** | The route recommended by the same review; improvement is gradual. |
| Tracking effective reading rate (speed × comprehension) | **Limited** | A practical measure for your own progress, not a research standard. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [APS (14 January 2016): speed-reading promises are too good to be true (Rayner et al.)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html) | Read the whole news release on the speed-reading review | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [British Council LearnEnglish (free)](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/) | Open the reading section, choose your level, and do one text with its tasks | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a new reading text with questions: a LearnEnglish text at your level is ideal. Count its words (or count the words in five lines, divide by five, and multiply by the number of lines).
2. Time yourself reading it once at normal study pace, then answer its questions without looking back. Work out wpm, comprehension and effective reading rate.
3. Plan four weeks of 15-minute daily reading practice, alternating English and Malayalam, and write it into your study planner.
4. Start a vocabulary list: five new words a day from your reading, added to AnkiDroid (Module 15 builds this into a full deck).
5. Once a week, time yourself on a new text and log the results in the reading log.

**Proof to record:** Your first timed reading with all three numbers, your four-week plan, and the reading log after the first week.

## Template: reading log

```
READING LOG
Date   | Text (title, language, level) | Words | Minutes | wpm | Questions right | Comprehension % | Effective rate
______ | _____________________________ | ____  | ____    | ___ | ___/___         | ___%            | ___
______ | _____________________________ | ____  | ____    | ___ | ___/___         | ___%            | ___
Week 0 baseline effective rate: ___   Target in 4 weeks: ___
```

## Template: counting words quickly

```
1. Count the words in 5 full lines.
2. Divide by 5 = average words per line.
3. Count the lines in the passage.
4. Words ≈ average words per line × number of lines.
Example: 5 lines = 60 words -> 12 per line; 42 lines -> about 504 words.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Paying for speed-reading courses or apps.** The research finds a speed-accuracy trade-off. Read more and build vocabulary instead.
- **Measuring speed without comprehension.** Always answer questions and use the effective reading rate.
- **Reading only easy texts.** Practise slightly above your comfort level, where new words appear.
- **Never measuring.** Time yourself once a week; small gains are invisible without numbers.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to Rayner and others (2016), what limits reading speed?
    - A) The colour of the paper
    - B) How fast the mind recognises words and builds meaning, not eye movements
    - C) How fast the eyes move
    - D) The size of the font
2. You read 600 words in 3 minutes and answer 6 of 8 questions correctly. What is your effective reading rate?
    - A) 150
    - B) 75
    - C) 200
    - D) 600
3. Which is the best route to faster reading, according to the review?
    - A) Reading a lot and growing vocabulary
    - B) Flashing one word at a time
    - C) Moving your eyes faster
    - D) Reading only headings
4. Why does GK study make GK reading faster?
    - A) It doesn't; reading speed is fixed
    - B) Background knowledge makes familiar ideas take less working memory
    - C) Because GK texts are shorter
    - D) It trains eye muscles

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The APS release on the speed-reading review and one LearnEnglish reading text
- **Action:** Measure your effective reading rate and start a four-week reading practice with a vocabulary list. It is done when your proof is saved: your first timed reading with all three numbers, your four-week plan, and the reading log after the first week.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Eye movements are not the bottleneck; understanding is.
2. **A.** 600 ÷ 3 = 200 wpm; 6 of 8 = 75%; 200 × 0.75 = 150.
3. **A.** Becoming a better reader is the reliable path.
4. **B.** What you already know frees working memory for new information.

Action: Measure your effective reading rate and start a four-week reading practice with a vocabulary list

sections.title: LRN-M10-L04: Newspapers and current affairs for PSC
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a 20-minute daily current-affairs routine from free, reliable sources, and turn the news into dated notes, cards and monthly self-tests. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 20 minutes a day for a week plus a 30-minute review).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Current affairs questions appear in most Kerala PSC general papers: national and Kerala news, appointments, awards, sports, science, government schemes and international events. The trap is spending two hours a day on news and remembering little. This lesson builds a short, reliable routine.

### Reliable free sources

| Source | What it gives you | Language |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Press Information Bureau (PIB)](https://www.pib.gov.in/) | Official press releases of central government ministries: schemes, appointments, events | English and Hindi, with regional offices |
| [All India Radio News](https://newsonair.gov.in/) | National and regional news bulletins, including audio bulletins you can listen to | English, Hindi and others |
| [Kerala I&PRD](https://www.prd.kerala.gov.in/) | Kerala government press releases, and the monthly e-magazines Janapadham and Kerala Calling | Malayalam (and some English) |
| A daily newspaper | Wider coverage; read the family copy, the library copy, or a free e-paper where one is offered | English or Malayalam |

Official sources are slower and drier than YouTube channels, but they are correct. "Current affairs PDFs" and forwards are often full of errors; if you use them, check every fact against an official or reliable source.

### Find your time window

How far back do current affairs questions go in your exam? Check your saved previous papers: find the current affairs questions and see how old the events were at the time of the exam. Plan your coverage from that, not from a coaching centre's guess.

### The 20-minute daily routine

1. **Scan headlines (5 minutes):** PIB, PRD Kerala and your newspaper. Pick 2 or 3 items that PSC could ask about.
2. **Read closely (10 minutes):** only those items. Find who, what, where, when, and why it matters.
3. **Write (5 minutes):** 3 to 5 one-line facts in your current-affairs note for the month, each with the **date and source**.

### Link news to the syllabus

Each news item connects to a static topic: a new national park links to geography; a constitutional amendment to the Constitution; an award to your awards list. Write the link next to the fact ("links to: Part IX, panchayats"). This is elaboration (Module 3), and it makes both the news and the static topic easier to remember.

### Monthly review

On the last Sunday of each month: reread the month's note once, then cover it and answer 20 questions you write from it. Make cards for what you missed (within your AnkiDroid budget), and add the month to your Revision tab.

## Local example

**Anu** used to watch PSC current-affairs videos for an hour every night and still struggle with current-affairs questions in mocks.

She started the 20-minute routine at 7:30 each evening. She scanned PIB's releases and the PRD Kerala press releases, picked two or three items, and wrote facts in a note called "CA 2026-11" with the date and source for each. Next to each fact she wrote its static link, such as "links to: Kerala rivers" or "links to: awards (literature)".

At the end of the first week she covered her notes and answered 15 questions she had written from them: 11 right. The four misses became cards. When she checked two recent PSC papers, she counted their current-affairs questions and found the events they asked about mostly from the previous year, so she planned her monthly reviews to cover the last 12 months.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly self-tests and spaced cards for current affairs | **Strong** | Retrieval and spacing, rated high utility, applied to news facts. |
| Linking news to static syllabus topics | **Moderate** | A form of elaboration: connected facts are easier to remember. |
| A short daily routine instead of long news sessions | **Limited** | A practical design; judge it by your monthly self-test scores. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Press Information Bureau (PIB), Government of India](https://www.pib.gov.in/) | Explore the latest releases and find two that PSC could ask about | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [All India Radio News (News Services Division)](https://newsonair.gov.in/) | Listen to one news bulletin and note three facts | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Information and Public Relations Department, Government of Kerala](https://www.prd.kerala.gov.in/) | Find the latest Kerala press releases and the Kerala Calling e-magazine | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Count the current-affairs questions in two recent papers and note how old the events were | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Start a current-affairs note for this month (paper notebook or phone) using the template below.
2. For 7 days, do the 20-minute routine: scan, read 2 or 3 items closely, write 3 to 5 facts with date, source and static link.
3. On day 7, cover your notes and answer 15 questions you write from them. Make cards for the misses.
4. Check two recent PSC papers: count the current-affairs questions and estimate their time window.
5. Put the monthly review (last Sunday of the month) into your calendar and Loop.

**Proof to record:** Seven days of current-affairs notes with dates, sources and links, your day-7 self-test score, and your PYQ count with the time window.

## Template: daily current-affairs note

```
CURRENT AFFAIRS     Month: ______
Date   | Fact (one line: who / what / where / when)            | Source        | Links to (syllabus)
______ | _____________________________________________________ | PIB / PRD / __ | __________________
______ | _____________________________________________________ | ____________  | __________________
______ | _____________________________________________________ | ____________  | __________________
```

## Template: monthly current-affairs review

```
MONTHLY REVIEW     Month: ______   Date: ______ (last Sunday)
1. Reread the month's note once (10 min).
2. Cover it. Answer 20 questions written from it. Score ___/20
3. Misses -> cards (within budget): ___ cards
4. Month added to the Revision tab [ ]
5. Time window check: my exam asks about roughly the last ___ months
```

## Common mistakes

- **Two hours of news a day.** Twenty focused minutes with notes and monthly tests beat hours of watching.
- **Notes without dates and sources.** Every fact needs its date and source, so you can check it later.
- **Collecting PDFs you never read.** A thin note you test yourself on beats a folder of unread PDFs.
- **Ignoring Kerala news.** PRD Kerala covers state schemes and events that PSC asks about.
- **Trusting forwards.** Check every fact against an official or reliable source.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which source gives official press releases of central government ministries?
    - A) A WhatsApp group
    - B) The Press Information Bureau (PIB)
    - C) A coaching centre poster
    - D) A random YouTube channel
2. Where can you find Kerala government press releases and the Kerala Calling e-magazine?
    - A) The Information and Public Relations Department (PRD) website
    - B) Only in paid magazines
    - C) Nowhere online
    - D) The PIB website only
3. How should you decide how far back to study current affairs?
    - A) Study only today's news
    - B) Check how old the events were in your exam's previous papers
    - C) Study ten years of news
    - D) Follow any coaching centre's guess
4. Why write the "links to" syllabus topic next to each fact?
    - A) Linking it to a static topic is elaboration, making both easier to remember
    - B) PSC requires it
    - C) It looks neat
    - D) It replaces revision

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** PIB, All India Radio News, PRD Kerala and two recent PSC papers
- **Action:** Run the 20-minute current-affairs routine for 7 days and test yourself on day 7. It is done when your proof is saved: seven days of current-affairs notes with dates, sources and links, your day-7 self-test score, and your PYQ count with the time window.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** PIB publishes the ministries' releases.
2. **A.** PRD Kerala publishes state releases and e-magazines.
3. **B.** Your own exam's papers show the real window.
4. **A.** Connected facts have more routes back in memory.

Action: Run the 20-minute current-affairs routine for 7 days and test yourself on day 7

sections.title: Module 11: Memory techniques
sections.summary: Learn the memory techniques that work for PSC lists, orders and numbers: chunking, acronyms, acrostics and stories; the memory palace, with real training evidence; and pegs and the major system for article numbers and dates. Build a memory palace for the Fundamental Rights or another real PSC topic.
sections.content:
## Overview

PSC rewards memory for many arbitrary facts. Memory techniques can make that much easier, but they are often oversold. This module is honest: the memory palace has strong training evidence, other techniques have less, and all of them need rehearsal with spaced retrieval to last.

The module project brings the techniques together into your PSC memory toolkit, with a palace tested after a week.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Use chunking, acronyms, acrostics and stories for PSC lists, after checking the facts
- Build a memory palace with vivid images and recall it forwards and backwards
- Use a peg list and the major system for ordered items and numbers
- Say honestly which techniques have strong evidence and which don't
- Combine every mnemonic with spaced retrieval

## Time

About 5 hours 45 minutes in total: 4 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 12–13, with the module project due in week 13.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M11-L01: Chunking, acronyms and stories for GK lists (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M11-L02: The memory palace (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
3. LRN-M11-L03: Pegs and the major system for numbers, dates and articles (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **mnemonic builder** and **should I use a mnemonic?** check
- The **memory palace planner** and **making images stick** rules
- The **major system table**, **word builder** and **peg list**

## Module project: My PSC memory toolkit

1. Keep your memory palace from LRN-M11-L02 alive: recall it once more two weeks after building it, and score it.
2. Make sure your three list mnemonics and your ten number images are on AnkiDroid cards.
3. Write one page: which technique worked best for which kind of PSC content (lists, orders, numbers), with your scores as evidence.
4. Teach one of your mnemonics or your palace to your study partner or a family member, and test them the next day.

**Proof to record:** Your palace plan with all recall scores including the two-week one, your one-page technique summary, and your partner's next-day result.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Palace | Not built | Built but not reviewed | Built, reviewed at 10 minutes, 1, 3, 7 and 14 days |
| Lists and numbers | No mnemonics | Mnemonics made but not tested | Checked mnemonics tested after 3 days and put on cards |
| Honesty about evidence | Believes every claim | Knows some limits | Can say which techniques have strong, limited or low evidence |
| Use | Techniques kept separate from study | Used sometimes | Each technique matched to the content it suits |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Build only the memory palace (LRN-M11-L02) and review it on schedule.
- Make one acrostic for a list that keeps appearing in previous papers.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| What mnemonics are for | Arbitrary lists, orders and numbers, not understanding. |
| Dunlosky's rating of the keyword mnemonic | Low utility. |
| Acrostic for the five writs | "Hari's Mother Prepared Chakka Quickly": habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. |
| Method of loci | Vivid images placed along a familiar route, recalled by walking it in your mind. |
| Dresler and others (2017) | Six weeks of loci training gave ordinary adults large memory gains, still there after four months. |
| Major system: digits 1 to 5 | 1 t/d, 2 n, 3 m, 4 r, 5 l. |
| Major system: digits 6 to 0 | 6 j/sh/ch, 7 k/hard g, 8 f/v, 9 p/b, 0 s/z. |
| Why Article 31 is missing from Part III | The right to property was removed in 1978. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Collecting techniques without rehearsing them.** Every mnemonic needs spaced recall to last.
- **Using mnemonics instead of understanding.** Explain reasons (Module 8); use mnemonics for arbitrary facts.

sections.title: LRN-M11-L01: Chunking, acronyms and stories for GK lists
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use chunking, acronyms, acrostics and stories to remember PSC lists, and know honestly when mnemonics help and when they don't. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 40 minutes action plus short recalls over three days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What mnemonics are for

A **mnemonic** is a trick that gives information without its own structure (a list, an order, a number) something to hold on to. PSC is full of such information: the five writs, the order of Kerala's districts, the three east-flowing rivers, the Malayalam Jnanpith winners.

Be honest about what they can and can't do:

- They are good for **arbitrary lists and orders**, where there is nothing to understand.
- They are **not** a substitute for understanding. Use Module 8 for reasons and processes.
- They need **practice**. A mnemonic you made once and never rehearsed is forgotten like anything else. Combine every mnemonic with spaced retrieval (cards or the Revision tab).
- The evidence varies by technique. Dunlosky and colleagues rated the **keyword mnemonic** (linking a word to a sound-alike image, mostly studied for vocabulary) as **low utility**: it can work, but it takes time and the benefit may not last ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). The memory palace (next lesson) has much stronger training evidence.

### Chunking

Working memory holds about four chunks (Module 1). **Chunking** groups items into a few meaningful units. Kerala's 14 districts from north to south are hard as one list, easier as four chunks:

| Chunk | Districts |
| --- | --- |
| North (4) | Kasaragod, Kannur, Wayanad, Kozhikode |
| North-central (3) | Malappuram, Palakkad, Thrissur |
| Central (4) | Ernakulam, Idukki, Kottayam, Alappuzha |
| South (3) | Pathanamthitta, Kollam, Thiruvananthapuram |

Four chunks of three or four are easy to hold; then you learn each chunk on its own.

### Acronyms and acrostics

An **acronym** makes a word from first letters; an **acrostic** makes a sentence. Silly, local sentences are easier to remember:

- **The five writs:** Habeas corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo warranto. Acrostic: **"Hari's Mother Prepared Chakka Quickly."**
- **Kerala's three east-flowing rivers:** Kabani, Bhavani, Pambar. Acrostic: **"Kerala's Big Payasam."**

Malayalam acrostics work just as well, often better for Malayalam speakers. Make your own.

### Stories

A **story** links items in order through a vivid chain of events. The order of four landmarks of the Kerala renaissance (1888, 1903, 1924, 1936): *A guru places a sacred stone by a river (the Aruvippuram consecration); his followers form a club to spread his message (the SNDP Yogam); a crowd walks the roads around a temple demanding the right to use them (the Vaikom Satyagraha); and finally the temple doors are thrown open to all (the Temple Entry Proclamation).* The story holds the order; your cards hold the years.

### Rules for good mnemonics

1. **Vivid, personal, a little absurd:** you remember the strange and the funny.
2. **Check the facts** before you build the mnemonic; a mnemonic for a wrong fact is worse than none.
3. **Rehearse it:** recall the list from the mnemonic three times on the first day, then on your review days.
4. **Put it on a card:** the mnemonic on the back of the card that asks for the list.

## Local example

**Joseph sir**'s study group spent one evening making mnemonics for lists that kept appearing in previous papers. Each member made one, and the group voted for the most memorable.

Vinod's acrostic for the writs, "Hari's Mother Prepared Chakka Quickly", won because everyone in the group could picture the jackfruit. Sreeja chunked the districts and drew the four chunks as four colours on a hand-drawn map. Joseph sir, the Malayalam teacher, made a Malayalam acrostic for a list of literary works, which the group found easiest of all.

They tested themselves three days later without warning. Lists with a mnemonic: 9 out of 10 recalled on average. Lists they had only read: 5 out of 10. One member's mnemonic turned out to be built on a wrong fact from a forward; the group fixed the fact and rebuilt it, and Joseph sir made "check before you build" the group rule.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chunking items into a few meaningful groups | **Strong** | Working memory holds about four chunks (OpenStax 8.1; CESE review); grouping makes lists manageable. |
| The keyword mnemonic | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013): it can work, but takes time and the benefit may not last. |
| Acronyms, acrostics and stories for lists | **Limited** | Widely used, with mixed research; they help most when rehearsed with spaced retrieval. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the section on the keyword mnemonic and why it was rated low | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1 How Memory Functions](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions) | Reread the part on short-term memory capacity | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional: the memory videos in Module 3 of Learning How to Learn | About 1 hour | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose three lists from your PSC syllabus or previous papers, each with 3 to 15 items. Check every item against your textbook first.
2. Make one mnemonic of each kind: a chunking scheme for one list, an acronym or acrostic for another, and a story for a list with an order.
3. Recall each list from its mnemonic three times today, with gaps of at least 10 minutes, and once tomorrow.
4. On day 3, test yourself on all three lists without looking. Score each.
5. Add a card for each list in AnkiDroid, with the mnemonic on the back.

**Proof to record:** Your three checked lists with their mnemonics, the day-3 scores, and a screenshot of the three cards.

## Template: mnemonic builder

```
LIST: ______________________  Items (checked in ______ page ___):
1. ________ 2. ________ 3. ________ 4. ________ 5. ________ 6. ________
Does it have an order I must keep?  yes / no
Technique:  chunking / acronym / acrostic / story / memory palace (LRN-M11-L02)
My mnemonic: _______________________________________________________
Recall from the mnemonic: day 1 x3 [ ][ ][ ]  day 2 [ ]  day 3 test ___/___
Card added (mnemonic on the back): [ ]
```

## Template: should I use a mnemonic?

```
Is there something to understand (a reason, a process)?  -> no mnemonic: explain it (Module 8)
Is it an arbitrary list, order or number?                -> yes, use a mnemonic
Have I checked the facts?                                -> if not, check first
Will I rehearse it on spaced review days?                -> if not, it will fade
```

## Common mistakes

- **Making mnemonics for things you could understand.** Reasons and processes need explaining, not tricks.
- **Dull, forgettable mnemonics.** Make them vivid, local and a little absurd.
- **Making a mnemonic once and never rehearsing it.** Recall from it three times on day 1 and on your review days.
- **Building a mnemonic on a wrong fact.** Check the list against your textbook before you build.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which list from the PSC syllabus suits a mnemonic best?
    - A) The five writs in order
    - B) How a money bill passes Parliament
    - C) Why Directive Principles are not enforceable
    - D) Why the monsoon reaches Kerala first
2. How did Dunlosky and colleagues rate the keyword mnemonic?
    - A) Moderate utility for maths
    - B) High utility for everything
    - C) Low utility: it can work but takes time and may not last
    - D) They did not review it
3. What does "Hari's Mother Prepared Chakka Quickly" help you remember?
    - A) Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto
    - B) The Fundamental Duties
    - C) The east-flowing rivers
    - D) Kerala's districts
4. What must you do after making a mnemonic?
    - A) Never look at it again
    - B) Rehearse it with spaced recall and put it on a card
    - C) Share it and forget it
    - D) Make a second mnemonic for the same list

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Dunlosky's section on the keyword mnemonic and OpenStax 8.1 on short-term memory capacity
- **Action:** Build and test three checked mnemonics (chunking, acrostic and story) for PSC lists. It is done when your proof is saved: your three checked lists with their mnemonics, the day-3 scores, and a screenshot of the three cards.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** An arbitrary list suits a mnemonic; the others need understanding.
2. **C.** The memory palace has stronger training evidence (next lesson).
3. **A.** Each first letter stands for one writ.
4. **B.** Mnemonics are forgotten like anything else unless rehearsed.

sections.title: LRN-M11-L02: The memory palace
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a memory palace in your own home that holds a real PSC topic, the Fundamental Rights from Article 14 to Article 32, and recall it forwards and backwards after a week. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes building plus short recalls over a week).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The method of loci

The **memory palace**, or **method of loci** ("places"), is more than two thousand years old. You take a route you know perfectly, such as the way through your own house, pick a series of places (**loci**) along it, and leave a vivid image of one item at each place. To recall, you walk the route in your mind and "see" each image.

It is the main method of memory champions, and it has unusually good training evidence. In a study published in *Neuron*, ordinary adults trained the method of loci in 40 sessions of 30 minutes over six weeks. Their memory improved substantially, the gain was still there four months later, and their brain networks shifted towards those of memory champions ([Dresler and others, 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5439266/)).

Be clear about what it is for: **ordered lists and sets of separate items**. It doesn't create understanding, and it takes practice to become fast.

### Building your palace

1. **Choose a route** you know with your eyes closed: your house from the gate to the backyard works well. Pick **10 to 20 loci** in a fixed order: gate, courtyard, verandah, front door, sitting room, TV, dining table, kitchen, and so on.
2. **Walk it in your mind** forwards and backwards until you know the order without thinking.
3. **Make a vivid image for each item and put it at its locus,** interacting with it. Exaggerate it, make it move, make noise, add smell or humour.
4. **Walk the route to recall** the items, forwards and backwards.
5. **Review on a spaced schedule:** after 10 minutes, 1 day, 3 days and 7 days.

### A worked example: the Fundamental Rights

Here are the first twelve loci of a palace built in a typical house:

| Locus | Article | Content | Image |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Gate | 14 | Equality before law | A huge weighing scale at the gate: the rich man and the fish seller weigh exactly the same |
| 2. Courtyard | 15 | No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth | One tea kettle in the courtyard pouring for everyone in the queue |
| 3. Verandah | 16 | Equal opportunity in public employment | A PSC notification pinned to the verandah pillar: "all may apply" |
| 4. Front door | 17 | Abolition of untouchability | The door wide open, an old "keep out" board smashed on the floor |
| 5. Sitting room | 18 | Abolition of titles | A crown and a title badge thrown into the dustbin |
| 6. TV | 19 | Six freedoms: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession | Six people climbing out of the TV, one shouting into a microphone |
| 7. Dining table | 20 | Protection in respect of conviction for offences | A man punished once refusing a second plate of punishment |
| 8. Kitchen | 21 | Protection of life and personal liberty | A bird flying free from a cage on the kitchen window |
| 9. Store room | 21A | Education for children aged 6 to 14 | A small school bag hanging on the store-room door |
| 10. Bedroom | 22 | Protection against arrest and detention | A policeman at the bed showing an arrest memo, a lawyer beside him |
| 11. Bathroom | 23 | No traffic in human beings or forced labour | Chains broken on the bathroom floor |
| 12. Backyard | 24 | No employment of children in factories | A child flying a kite instead of working in a factory |

You continue in the garden or a second "floor" for Articles 25 to 28 (freedom of religion), 29 and 30 (cultural and educational rights) and 32 (constitutional remedies). Article 31 is missing because the right to property was removed from this Part in 1978; a locus with an empty chair can mark that.

### Tips

- **One palace per topic** at first. Using the same route for two lists at once causes interference.
- **Numbers** (such as article numbers) can come from the order, as above, or from number images (next lesson).
- **Keep a written plan** of the palace, but recall from your head.

## Local example

**Anu** built her first palace in her family's house in Kakkattil for the Fundamental Rights. She walked the real route once with a notebook: gate, the courtyard with the mango tree, the verandah, the front door, the sitting room, the TV, the dining table, the kitchen, the store room, her bedroom, the bathroom, the backyard well, the coconut tree, the cowshed, the compost pit, the back gate and the lane. Seventeen loci.

She used the images in this lesson for the first twelve and made her own for the rest: a temple, a church and a mosque sharing one cowshed for freedom of religion, and the moon shining over the back gate for Article 32 (she remembered it as "go straight to the top"). She recalled the route after 10 minutes, the next morning, after 3 days and after 7 days.

On day 7 she recalled all 17 loci forwards and 16 backwards. In a 20-question test on Fundamental Rights from previous papers, she scored 17; her pre-module score on similar questions had been 10. She added "Article → locus" cards to AnkiDroid only for the three she had once confused.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The memory palace (method of loci) for ordered lists | **Strong** | One of the best-studied mnemonics; Dresler and others (2017) showed large, lasting gains in trained adults. |
| The memory palace for understanding complex topics | **Limited** | It holds items and their order, not reasons. Combine it with explanation (Module 8). |
| Spaced recall walks of the palace | **Strong** | Spaced retrieval, rated high utility, applied to the palace. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dresler et al. (2017), "Mnemonic Training Reshapes Brain Networks to Support Superior Memory", Neuron](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5439266/) | Read the abstract and the description of the training | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional: the memory palace videos in Module 3 of Learning How to Learn | About 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a route you know perfectly (your house is best) and write down 15 to 20 loci in order.
2. Walk it in your mind forwards and backwards until the order is automatic.
3. Place the Fundamental Rights (Articles 14 to 32), or another PSC list of 15 or more items that you have checked, along the route: one vivid image per locus. Use the worked example for the first twelve if you choose the Fundamental Rights.
4. Recall the whole palace forwards and backwards after 10 minutes, 1 day, 3 days and 7 days, without the plan. Score each recall.
5. On day 7, answer 15 to 20 previous-year questions on the topic and compare with your earlier score, if you have one.

**Proof to record:** Your palace plan (route, loci and images), the four recall scores forwards and backwards, and the day-7 question score.

## Template: memory palace planner

```
MEMORY PALACE     Topic: ______________________  Route: ______________________
Locus (in order)     Item (checked)                   Image (vivid, moving, funny)
1. ______________    _______________________________  _________________________
2. ______________    _______________________________  _________________________
3. ______________    _______________________________  _________________________
...
20. _____________    _______________________________  _________________________
Recall      10 min   day 1   day 3   day 7
Forwards    ___      ___     ___     ___
Backwards   ___      ___     ___     ___
```

## Template: making images stick

```
Make it BIG, MOVING, NOISY, SMELLY or FUNNY.
Make it INTERACT with the locus (on, in, through, crashing into it).
Use PEOPLE and ANIMALS doing things.
For abstract ideas, use a symbol: scale = equality, cage = liberty, chains = slavery, crown = titles.
```

## Common mistakes

- **A route you don't know perfectly.** If you hesitate over the order of rooms, the palace fails. Use your own home.
- **Dull images ("a picture of equality").** Make every image vivid and interacting with its place.
- **Several items on one locus.** One item per locus keeps the order clear.
- **Building it and never walking it again.** Recall after 10 minutes, 1, 3 and 7 days, then on review days.
- **Two lists in one palace at the same time.** Use a different route for each topic to avoid interference.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Dresler and others (2017) show?
    - A) Brain-training apps beat the memory palace
    - B) The memory palace works only for champions
    - C) Memory cannot be trained
    - D) Six weeks of method-of-loci training gave ordinary adults large, lasting memory gains
2. What is the memory palace best for?
    - A) Ordered lists and sets of separate items
    - B) Solving maths problems
    - C) Speed reading
    - D) Understanding why a law was passed
3. In the worked example, what is at the kitchen locus?
    - A) A weighing scale: Article 14
    - B) A school bag: Article 21A
    - C) A bird flying free from a cage: Article 21, life and personal liberty
    - D) Broken chains: Article 23
4. Why is Article 31 missing from the Fundamental Rights list?
    - A) The right to property was removed from Part III in 1978
    - B) It is a Directive Principle
    - C) It is in Part IV
    - D) It was never written

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The abstract and training description of Dresler and others (2017)
- **Action:** Build a 15 to 20 locus memory palace for a PSC topic and recall it over a week. It is done when your proof is saved: your palace plan (route, loci and images), the four recall scores forwards and backwards, and the day-7 question score.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** The gain lasted four months, and brain networks changed.
2. **A.** It holds items and order; understanding needs explanation.
3. **C.** The cage image stands for liberty.
4. **A.** The 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from the Fundamental Rights.
