sections.title: LRN-M11-L03: Pegs and the major system for numbers, dates and articles
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn numbers into words with the major system, use a simple peg list, and fix article numbers and dates to their PSC facts with vivid images. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 55 minutes action plus short recalls over three days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Why numbers are hard

PSC asks for many numbers: article numbers, amendment numbers, years, lengths, ranks. Numbers are abstract, so they have no meaning to hook onto (Module 1). Two classic systems turn numbers into pictures.

### A simple peg list

A **peg list** gives each number from 1 to 10 a fixed image that rhymes with it. Learn it once, then "hang" the items of any ordered list on the pegs:

```
1 bun    2 shoe    3 tree    4 door    5 hive
6 sticks 7 heaven  8 gate    9 wine    10 hen
```

To remember the first five items of a list in order, picture item 1 squashed in a bun, item 2 stuffed in a shoe, item 3 hanging from a tree, and so on. You can make a Malayalam peg list too, from rhymes or shapes that are natural for you.

### The major system

The **major system** turns digits into consonant sounds, then into words. Vowels and the sounds w, h and y are free fillers ([Wikipedia: Mnemonic major system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic_major_system)):

| Digit | Sounds | Memory hook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | s, z | "z" for zero |
| 1 | t, d | one downstroke |
| 2 | n | two downstrokes |
| 3 | m | three downstrokes |
| 4 | r | the last sound of "four" |
| 5 | l | L is the Roman numeral for 50 |
| 6 | j, sh, ch, soft g | a reversed J looks like 6 |
| 7 | k, hard g | a K can be drawn from two 7s |
| 8 | f, v | a handwritten f has two loops, like 8 |
| 9 | p, b | P is a mirrored 9 |

It works by **sound, not spelling**: "knee" is just n (2), because the k is silent; a double letter that makes one sound counts once, so "shell" is sh-l, 65.

### PSC examples

| Number | Fact | Word (sounds) | Image |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14 | Article 14: equality before law | DooR (d-r) | Everyone, rich or poor, enters through one door |
| 17 | Article 17: abolition of untouchability | DuCK (d-k) | A duck that every child is allowed to touch |
| 19 | Article 19: the six freedoms | TuB (t-b) | Six people singing freely in a bathtub |
| 21 | Article 21: life and personal liberty | NeT (n-t) | A safety net catching a falling person |
| 32 | Article 32: constitutional remedies | MooN (m-n) | Appealing all the way to the moon, the highest court |
| 51 | Article 51A: Fundamental Duties | LighT (l-t) | A lamp that every citizen must keep burning |
| 1956 | Kerala state formed | TaPe LaSH (t-p, l-sh) | A giant tape measure lashing Travancore-Cochin and Malabar together |
| 1965 | First Jnanpith Award, to G. Sankara Kurup | TuB SHeLL (t-b, sh-l) | The poet in a tub, blowing a conch shell |

### Honest evidence and cost

The peg and major systems have **little modern research**, and Dunlosky and colleagues rated the related keyword mnemonic low utility. Learning the major system takes a few hours of practice before it becomes quick. It is worth it only if you have many numbers to learn, which, for PSC, you do. If you try it for a week and it stays slow, keep the numbers on cards instead; cards with spaced repetition always work.

## Local example

**Ashiq** always confused article numbers in Part III: was it Article 16 or 15 for public employment? Was Article 22 arrest or education? He spent two evenings learning the major system with ten AnkiDroid cards, one per digit, until he could convert any two-digit number in a few seconds.

Then he made words for the ten article numbers he confused most, each tied to an image: DiSH (16) became a government canteen dish served to every job applicant; TiLe (15) a floor tile laid the same for every caste and religion. He recalled the ten images after 1 day and after 3 days: 10 out of 10 both times.

In his next previous-year paper, he got every Part III article number right for the first time. He found the system too slow for four-digit years at first, so for years he kept using cards and the stories from LRN-M11-L01, and he plans to try the major system for years again after more practice.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The major system and peg lists for numbers | **Limited** | Little modern research; they need practice to become quick and help most when you have many numbers to learn. |
| The keyword mnemonic (a related technique) | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| Spaced-repetition cards for numbers | **Strong** | Retrieval with spacing works whether or not you add a mnemonic. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Wikipedia: Mnemonic major system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic_major_system) | Read the introduction and the digit-to-sound table | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Reread the keyword mnemonic section, for the honest limits | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Learn the major system: make 10 AnkiDroid cards (digit → sounds) and study them until you can convert any two-digit number in about 5 seconds.
2. Learn the 10-word peg list and use it once, for an ordered list of up to 10 items from your syllabus that you have checked.
3. Choose 10 PSC numbers you often confuse (article numbers, amendments or years). For each, make a major-system word and a vivid image tied to the fact.
4. Recall all 10 number facts after 1 day and after 3 days, without looking. Score both.
5. Add the images to the backs of the matching AnkiDroid cards.

**Proof to record:** Your digit cards, the peg-list use, your 10 number images with facts, and the day-1 and day-3 scores.

## Template: major system word builder

```
NUMBER: ______  FACT: ______________________________  (checked in ______)
Digits -> sounds:  __ = ___   __ = ___   __ = ___   __ = ___
Word(s) (sounds only; vowels, w, h, y are free): __________________
Image tying the word to the fact: _________________________________
Recall: day 1 [ ]  day 3 [ ]   Added to the card's back: [ ]
```

## Template: peg list (learn once, reuse forever)

```
1 bun    2 shoe    3 tree    4 door    5 hive
6 sticks 7 heaven  8 gate    9 wine    10 hen
My list: 1 ________ 2 ________ 3 ________ 4 ________ 5 ________
         6 ________ 7 ________ 8 ________ 9 ________ 10 _______
Picture each item interacting with its peg. Recall in order, then backwards.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Encoding by spelling instead of sound.** "Knee" is 2, not 72. Silent letters don't count; double letters making one sound count once.
- **Building words without fixing them to the fact.** The word must appear in an image together with the fact it stands for.
- **Giving up after one slow evening.** The system takes a few hours to become quick. If it stays slow after a week, use cards.
- **Using the major system for everything.** It is for numbers. Lists suit the palace; reasons suit explanation.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In the major system, which word encodes 21?
    - A) MooN
    - B) DooR
    - C) TeN
    - D) NeT
2. Which number does "moon" encode?
    - A) 22
    - B) 32
    - C) 23
    - D) 33
3. What number is "shell"?
    - A) 655
    - B) 65
    - C) 6
    - D) 56
4. What is the honest position on the major system?
    - A) Works instantly without practice
    - B) Proven useless
    - C) Little modern research; it needs practice and helps most with many numbers
    - D) Proven to double memory for everyone

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Wikipedia article on the major system and Dunlosky's note on the keyword mnemonic
- **Action:** Learn the major system and a peg list, and fix 10 PSC numbers to images. It is done when your proof is saved: your digit cards, the peg-list use, your 10 number images with facts, and the day-1 and day-3 scores.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** n = 2 and t = 1, so "net" is 21.
2. **B.** m = 3 and n = 2.
3. **B.** sh = 6 and the double l makes one sound, l = 5.
4. **C.** Cards with spaced repetition remain the reliable fallback.

Action: Learn the major system and a peg list, and fix 10 PSC numbers to images

sections.title: Module 12: Exam mastery for Kerala PSC
sections.summary: Master the Kerala PSC exam itself: map the official syllabus, analyse previous-year questions, take mock tests and keep an error log, use the arithmetic of negative marking, build a complete 12-week study and revision plan, and manage exam anxiety and exam day.
sections.content:
## Overview

Everything so far has made you a better learner. This module points that learning at the exam. It uses only official sources for the rules (the syllabus, previous papers, answer keys and OMR instructions on the Kerala PSC website) and marks every rule with "check current rules", because schemes can change.

By the end you have an exam system: a Syllabus tab with priorities, a PYQ analysis, an Errors tab, a guessing rule based on your own data, a 12-week plan and an exam-day checklist.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Turn the official syllabus into a prioritised Syllabus tab
- Analyse 200 or more previous-year questions and act on the patterns
- Take mocks under real conditions and fix every error by type
- Decide when to answer using expected value and your own calibration
- Build and run a 12-week study and revision plan
- Manage exam anxiety and prepare for exam day

## Time

About 11 hours in total: 9 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 13–15, with the module project due in week 15.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M12-L01: Map the syllabus (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. LRN-M12-L02: Analyse previous-year questions (about 2 hours)
3. LRN-M12-L03: Mock tests and the error log (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
4. LRN-M12-L04: Time management and negative marking (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
5. LRN-M12-L05: Your 12-week study and revision plan (about 2 hours)
6. LRN-M12-L06: Exam anxiety and exam day (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **error log** (one of the six core tools) and the **Errors** tab
- The **study planner** (core tool) used inside the **12-week plan**
- The **Syllabus** and **PYQ** tabs with the priority and COUNTIF formulas
- The **guessing calculator**, **two-pass time plan** and **mock test conditions** checklist
- The **exam-day checklist** and **in-hall reset**

## Module project: My exam system

1. Make sure your Syllabus tab is complete, with PYQ counts and priorities from at least 200 tagged questions.
2. Take a second full mock, log every error and compare both mocks: score, error types, timing.
3. Finalise your 12-week plan with the results of both mocks.
4. Put your guessing rule, two-pass plan and exam-day checklist on one card.
5. Write a one-page summary: your three biggest gaps, your plan for them, and your target score.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of your Syllabus, PYQ and Errors tabs, both mock scores with the comparison, your 12-week plan, your exam card and the one-page summary.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Syllabus map | No map | Topics listed without priorities | All topics with confidence, PYQ counts and priorities |
| PYQ analysis | Fewer than 100 questions | 100 to 199 tagged | 200 or more tagged, patterns written, misses turned into cards |
| Mocks and errors | No mock | One mock, errors noted loosely | Two mocks, every error typed, fixed and retested |
| Exam strategy | Guessing by feeling | Rule known but not tested | Guessing rule from my data and two-pass plan used in a mock |
| 12-week plan | None | A plan without mocks or revision cycles | Complete plan with capacity check, mocks, cycles and taper |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do LRN-M12-L02 with one paper of 100 questions, and LRN-M12-L03 with one mock.
- Write a simple 12-week plan: weeks 1-8 learn and revise, 9-11 cycles and weekly mocks, 12 taper.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Kerala PSC OMR marking | +1 for a correct answer, −1/3 for a wrong one, 0 for unanswered (check your exam's instructions). |
| Break-even chance for answering under −1/3 marking | 1 in 4; answer when your chance is higher. |
| Expected value with two options ruled out | +1/3 of a mark. |
| Mock score formula | Correct − wrong ÷ 3. |
| The seven error types | K didn't know, F forgot, I interference, M misread, C careless, G bad guess, T time. |
| Priority score | (PYQ count + 1) × (6 − confidence). |
| The 12-week structure | Weeks 1-8 learn and revise, 9-11 revision cycles and weekly mocks, 12 taper. |
| Expressive writing before exams | 10 minutes writing about worries just before; helped anxious students (Ramirez and Beilock, 2011). |
| Free mental health helpline | Tele-MANAS: 14416 or 1-800-891-4416. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Studying hard without looking at the exam itself.** The syllabus, PYQs and mocks tell you where your hours earn marks.
- **Trusting forwarded rules about marking or dates.** Check the official instructions, notification and admission ticket.

sections.title: LRN-M12-L01: Map the syllabus
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn your exam's official syllabus into a Syllabus tab of topics with weights, previous-paper counts and confidence ratings, and pick your top priorities with a simple formula. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 45 minutes building the tab).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The syllabus is the contract

Everything in your exam comes from the official syllabus, and everything outside it is optional. Many aspirants study from a coaching centre's list or a guide's chapters and never read the official syllabus closely. Kerala PSC publishes a syllabus for each post ([post-wise syllabus page](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/syllabus1) (check current rules)). You downloaded yours in week 0; now you turn it into a working tool.

Notices often state the total marks and the duration. For example, the 2022 notice for the Degree Level Common Preliminary Examination gave 100 marks and 1 hour 15 minutes, with questions in English and in Malayalam, Tamil or Kannada ([Kerala PSC notice, 2022](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/2022-07/degree_level_cpe__for_confirmation_.pdf) (check current rules)). Many syllabuses also list marks for each part, such as general knowledge, current affairs, simple arithmetic and mental ability, English and Malayalam. Check exactly what yours says; schemes differ between exams and change over time.

### Building the Syllabus tab

1. **List every part** of the syllabus with its marks, if given.
2. **Break each part into topics** small enough to study in one to three sessions: not "History" but "Kerala renaissance: reformers and organisations", "Freedom struggle: 1885–1919" and so on. Aim for 10 to 40 topics per part.
3. **Add the marks share** of each part (if given) and, after LRN-M12-L02, the **number of previous-year questions** on each topic.
4. **Rate your confidence** from 1 to 5 using a delayed recall test, not a feeling (Module 7).
5. **Add status, source and next review** for each topic.

### Choosing priorities

A simple priority score combines how often a topic is asked with how weak you are in it:

```
Priority = (PYQ count + 1) × (6 − confidence)
```

A topic asked 6 times with confidence 2 scores 7 × 4 = 28. A topic asked twice with confidence 4 scores 3 × 2 = 6. Sort by priority and you have your study order. The "+ 1" keeps topics that haven't been asked yet from scoring zero; they can still appear.

Use the score as a guide, not a law. A low-priority topic that takes 20 minutes to learn may be worth doing early, and topics that support others (basic arithmetic, the structure of the Constitution) come first whatever their score.

## Local example

**Anu** mapped the syllabus for the Degree Level preliminary she was preparing for. Her syllabus PDF listed its parts with marks; she broke them into 64 topics, from "Kerala renaissance" to "Ratio and proportion" to "Malayalam: synonyms (പര്യായപദങ്ങൾ)".

She rated confidence with two-minute recall tests over three evenings (Module 7) instead of guessing. Twelve topics she had thought were strong got a 2 or 3. After counting previous-year questions in LRN-M12-L02, she filled in the priority formula and sorted.

Her top ten surprised her: three were in mental ability, which she had been avoiding, and two in English grammar, which she had assumed was easy. Kerala history, which she had studied most, ranked eleventh. She printed the top ten and taped it inside her notebook cover.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Studying from the official syllabus | **Limited** | Common sense rather than research: the exam is set from it. It prevents wasted time. |
| Prioritising by question frequency and weakness | **Limited** | A practical planning rule; past patterns guide but do not guarantee future papers. |
| Rating confidence with delayed recall instead of feeling | **Moderate** | Feelings of knowing are often wrong (Module 7); recall tests are more accurate. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: post-wise syllabus](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/syllabus1) | Download the syllabus for your post again if needed, and read it line by line | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala PSC: Degree Level Common Preliminary Examination notice, 2022 (PDF)](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/2022-07/degree_level_cpe__for_confirmation_.pdf) | See how a notice states marks, duration and the language of questions | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.5 on prioritisation | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Add a Syllabus tab to your Learning Workbook with the headings below, plus a "Priority" column.
2. Enter every part of your exam's official syllabus, broken into topics of one to three sessions each.
3. Enter the marks for each part, if your syllabus gives them.
4. Rate your confidence in each topic from 1 to 5 using a two-minute recall test (spread over several days if needed).
5. Add the priority formula, sort by priority, and write your top ten topics. (You will add the PYQ counts in the next lesson and re-sort.)

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Syllabus tab with every topic, and your top-ten priority list.

## Template: Syllabus tab headings

```csv
Subject,Topic (from the official syllabus),Marks or share,PYQ count,Confidence (1-5),Status (not started / learning / revising / solid),Source I use,Next review,Priority
```

## Template: priority formula

```
With PYQ count in D2 and confidence (1-5) in E2, in the Priority column (I2):
=(D2+1)*(6-E2)
Copy down. Then sort the tab by Priority, largest first (Data -> Sort range).
```

## Template: syllabus breakdown sheet

```
EXAM: ______________________  Syllabus file: ______________  Date: ______
Part (as in the syllabus)       Marks   Topics (1-3 sessions each)
1. ___________________________  ___     ______________________________________
2. ___________________________  ___     ______________________________________
3. ___________________________  ___     ______________________________________
...
Total topics: ___   Topics rated by recall test: ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using a coaching centre's list instead of the official syllabus.** Start from the official PDF; use guides only as sources for each topic.
- **Topics that are too big.** "History" can't be scheduled. Break it into topics of one to three sessions.
- **Rating confidence by feeling.** Use a two-minute recall test; feelings of knowing mislead.
- **Never updating the tab.** Update confidence after every review and re-sort every four weeks.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Topic A was asked 6 times and your confidence is 2. Topic B was asked twice and your confidence is 4. Which has the higher priority score?
    - A) A (28 against 6)
    - B) They are equal
    - C) B (6 against 28)
    - D) Neither has a score
2. Where should your list of topics come from?
    - A) A WhatsApp forward
    - B) A coaching centre's advertisement
    - C) The official syllabus for your post on the Kerala PSC website
    - D) The chapters of any guide
3. What did the 2022 Degree Level preliminary notice state?
    - A) 200 marks and 3 hours
    - B) 100 marks and 1 hour 15 minutes
    - C) 50 marks and 30 minutes
    - D) No time limit
4. Why add 1 to the PYQ count in the priority formula?
    - A) To make the numbers bigger
    - B) Because PSC adds one mark
    - C) It is a mistake
    - D) So topics not yet asked don't score zero

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Your exam's official syllabus, the 2022 preliminary notice and College Success 3.5
- **Action:** Build your Syllabus tab with confidence ratings and a priority list. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Syllabus tab with every topic, and your top-ten priority list.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** (6 + 1) × (6 − 2) = 28; (2 + 1) × (6 − 4) = 6.
2. **C.** The exam is set from the official syllabus.
3. **B.** Check your own exam's notice; schemes differ.
4. **D.** Unasked syllabus topics can still appear.

sections.title: LRN-M12-L02: Analyse previous-year questions
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Tag at least 200 previous-year questions by subject and topic, count the patterns into your Syllabus tab, and turn your misses into cards. **Time:** about 2 hours (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 75 minutes tagging (it can be split over several days)).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Why previous-year questions matter

Previous-year questions (PYQs) are the best free study material you have. They show:

- **What is asked:** which topics, and which details within them
- **How deeply:** a name, a reason, a calculation, a statement to judge
- **In what form:** direct questions, statement questions, match the following, odd one out
- **What repeats:** facts and topics asked again and again across years

Kerala PSC publishes previous question papers by year, post, paper code and test date ([previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers)), and answer keys for OMR exams ([answer keys](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) (check current rules)). Use the **final** answer key, not the provisional one, when you check answers.

### Choosing papers

Pick papers for **your post or the same level** (for example, all degree-level preliminaries, or several LDC papers) from the last three to five years. Two or three papers of 100 questions give you a solid first picture.

### Tagging

Add a **PYQ** tab and give each question one row: the paper, question number, subject, topic (copied **exactly** from your Syllabus tab, so formulas can count it), subtopic, type (fact, concept, calculation, statement), whether it repeats an earlier question, whether it was in your study material, and whether you got it right when you first tried it.

Then count. In your Syllabus tab, a formula counts how many PYQs match each topic:

```
In the Syllabus tab, PYQ count for the topic in B2 (D2):
=COUNTIF(PYQ!D:D,B2)
LibreOffice may need: =COUNTIF($PYQ.D:D;B2)
```

A pivot table (Insert → Pivot table in Google Sheets; Data → Pivot Table in LibreOffice) shows counts by subject and by type in seconds.

### What to look for

1. **Which topics are asked most** for your exam
2. **Repeated facts:** the same fact asked in different years. These are among the highest-value facts you can learn.
3. **Question types:** if a third of the questions are statement questions, practise them (LRN-M08-L02).
4. **Gaps:** questions on things that weren't in your material at all. Find a source for them.

### Two cautions

- **Patterns guide, they don't guarantee.** Syllabuses change, and examiners ask new things. Don't drop syllabus topics that haven't been asked yet; just give them lower priority.
- **Tagging is not studying.** Its value comes from what you do next: every question you got wrong, guessed or didn't know becomes a card, a note or a Revision-tab entry.

## Local example

**Ashiq** downloaded three degree-level preliminary papers from the last three years and their final answer keys. Tagging 300 questions took him four evenings of about an hour each.

His counts showed things he hadn't seen while simply solving papers. In his three papers, mental ability and arithmetic together made up a large and steady share. In GK, the Constitution and Kerala history were asked every year, while some topics in his guide had never appeared. He found 14 facts asked in two or more of the three papers; they became a special AnkiDroid sub-deck called "Repeated".

He also counted how many questions came from facts he had never seen in his material: 23 of 300. Most were current affairs or recent government schemes, which sent him back to the routine in LRN-M10-L04. He turned his 61 wrong or unknown questions into cards over the next week, within his daily budget.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Practising with previous-year questions | **Strong** | Practice testing is rated high utility; PYQs are the closest practice to the real exam. |
| Using question frequency to set priorities | **Limited** | Sensible, but patterns can change between years and exams. |
| Turning missed questions into cards and notes | **Strong** | Retrieval with feedback, targeted at your real gaps. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Download two or three papers for your post or level from recent years | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: answer keys for OMR exams](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) | Find the final answer keys for the same papers | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Add a PYQ tab to your Learning Workbook with the headings below.
2. Choose two or three recent papers for your post or level (at least 200 questions) with their final answer keys.
3. Answer each question first (options covered, confidence marked, as in Module 7), then check, and tag it in the PYQ tab. Copy topic names exactly from the Syllabus tab.
4. Add the COUNTIF formula to the Syllabus tab, re-sort by priority, and write your top 15 topics.
5. List the repeated facts and make them cards. Then, over the next week, turn every wrong, guessed or unknown question into cards or Revision-tab entries within your daily budget.

**Proof to record:** Your PYQ tab with at least 200 tagged rows, the Syllabus tab with PYQ counts and the new top 15, and your list of repeated facts.

## Template: PYQ tab headings

```csv
Paper (post and year),Question no,Subject,Topic,Subtopic,Type (fact / concept / calculation / statement),Repeated? (Y/N),Seen in my material? (Y/N),Right at first try? (Y/N),Notes
```

## Template: PYQ pattern summary

```
PYQ PATTERN SUMMARY     Papers: ___________________________  Questions: ___
Most-asked topics (top 5): 1. ______ 2. ______ 3. ______ 4. ______ 5. ______
Question types: fact ___%  concept ___%  calculation ___%  statement ___%
Repeated facts (asked 2+ times): ___  -> "Repeated" sub-deck made [ ]
Questions on things not in my material: ___  -> new source needed for: ______
Right at first try: ___%   Wrong or unknown -> cards / Revision tab: ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Solving PYQs without tagging them.** Tagging shows patterns that solving alone hides.
- **Topic names that don't match the Syllabus tab.** Copy them exactly, or COUNTIF won't count them.
- **Treating patterns as guarantees.** Lower the priority of unasked topics; don't delete them.
- **Checking with the provisional key.** Use the final answer key; provisional keys can change after complaints.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which answer key should you use to check previous papers?
    - A) The provisional key only
    - B) A coaching centre's key
    - C) The final answer key
    - D) Your own guess
2. Why must topic names in the PYQ tab match the Syllabus tab exactly?
    - A) To make the sheet look neat
    - B) So the COUNTIF formula can count them
    - C) Because PSC requires it
    - D) It doesn't matter
3. What are "repeated facts"?
    - A) Facts you got wrong twice
    - B) Facts that appear in two textbooks
    - C) Facts asked in two or more different years' papers
    - D) Facts you studied twice
4. A syllabus topic hasn't appeared in your three papers. What should you do?
    - A) Study it first
    - B) Delete it from your plan
    - C) Give it lower priority but keep it on the plan
    - D) Complain to PSC

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Two or three previous papers and their final answer keys from the Kerala PSC website
- **Action:** Tag at least 200 PYQs, count them into your Syllabus tab and turn the misses into cards. It is done when your proof is saved: your PYQ tab with at least 200 tagged rows, the Syllabus tab with PYQ counts and the new top 15, and your list of repeated facts.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Provisional keys can be revised after complaints.
2. **B.** COUNTIF matches text exactly.
3. **C.** They are among the highest-value facts to learn.
4. **C.** Patterns guide but don't guarantee; it can still be asked.

Action: Tag at least 200 PYQs, count them into your Syllabus tab and turn the misses into cards

sections.title: LRN-M12-L03: Mock tests and the error log
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Take a full mock test under real conditions, record every wrong or guessed answer in the Errors tab, and fix each error by its type. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (10 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, a full mock (about 75 minutes) plus 60 minutes of analysis).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### A mock is a rehearsal

A **mock test** is a full paper taken under exam conditions: the same number of questions, the same time limit, an answer sheet like the real one, no phone, no breaks, and ideally at the same time of day as your exam. The best free mocks are **previous papers you haven't seen yet**. Keep a few unseen papers aside for this.

A mock does three jobs: it is retrieval practice on the whole syllabus, it trains your timing, and it makes the exam hall feel familiar.

### Answer sheets and marking

Kerala PSC's instructions for OMR exams say that each correct answer gets 1 mark and each wrong answer loses one-third of a mark, and that marking more than one answer, or altering an answer, also counts against you ([OMR instructions](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) (check current rules)). Practise on an OMR-style sheet (print one, or draw rows of four bubbles) so that shading carefully becomes a habit.

Score your mock the same way:

```
Score = correct answers − (wrong answers ÷ 3)        unanswered = 0
Example: 60 correct, 15 wrong, 25 unanswered -> 60 − 5 = 55
```

### The analysis is where you learn

The mock takes 75 minutes; the analysis should take about as long. Go through **every question you got wrong, and every one you got right by guessing** (your S, U and G marks from Module 7 show these). Add each to the **Errors** tab with its error type:

| Code | Error type | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| K | Didn't know: never learned it, or not on my cards | 1 to 3 cards, or add the topic to the Revision tab |
| F | Forgot: learned it once, could not recall it in time | 1 to 3 cards; check the topic's review dates |
| I | Interference: mixed it up with a similar fact | One card contrasting the two facts side by side |
| M | Misread: missed a word such as NOT, first, largest, except | Underline NOT, EXCEPT, FIRST, LARGEST in every question for a week |
| C | Careless: a slip in calculation or in marking the OMR bubble | Slow down on the last step; check the bubble number |
| G | Bad guess: guessed when I could not rule anything out | Guess only after ruling out at least one option (LRN-M12-L04) |
| T | Time: rushed, or never reached the question | Use the two-pass method and time checkpoints (LRN-M12-L04) |

### Retest your errors

Seven days later, answer each logged question again from memory. Clear an error only when you get it right **twice** in separate retests. Errors that keep coming back go to your weekly review.

### How often?

Start with a mock every two weeks while you are still learning topics. In the last weeks before the exam, one a week (LRN-M12-L05). More mocks without analysis teach little; fewer mocks with careful analysis teach a lot.

## Local example

**Sreeja** took her first full mock with a 2021 paper she had kept unseen. She set a 75-minute timer at the dining table at 10 a.m., the usual start time of her exam, used a hand-drawn OMR sheet, and marked S, U or G beside each answer.

Her result: 52 correct, 20 wrong, 28 unanswered: 52 − 20 ÷ 3 = 45.33. The analysis took an hour. Of her 20 wrong answers and 7 guessed-right ones, she logged 8 as K (didn't know), 6 as F (forgot), 4 as I (mixed up two facts), 5 as M (misread) and 4 as C (careless). Five misreadings shocked her: three questions had "NOT" in them.

Her fixes: 14 new cards, 4 contrast cards, a week of underlining NOT and EXCEPT in every question she practised, and a rule to recheck the bubble number every tenth question. A week later her retest cleared 19 of the 27 errors on the first try.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full practice tests | **Strong** | Practice testing is rated high utility; full mocks also train timing. |
| Reviewing errors with the correct answers (feedback) | **Strong** | Feedback after testing corrects errors so they don't repeat. |
| Sorting errors by type | **Limited** | A practical way to choose the right fix; little direct research on the categories. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: instructions to candidates for OMR examinations (PDF)](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) | Read the instructions for OMR exams, especially marking and shading rules | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [College Success, 6.3 Test Taking (including test anxiety)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking) | Read the parts on test day and after the test | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Choose an unseen recent paper for your post or level as your mock | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Take a full mock: an unseen previous paper, the real time limit, an OMR-style sheet, no phone, ideally at your exam's time of day. Mark S, U or G beside each answer.
2. Score it: correct − wrong ÷ 3. Record the score in your Weekly tab.
3. Add an Errors tab with the headings below. Log every wrong answer and every guessed-right answer, with its type, why it happened and the fix.
4. Apply the fixes: cards, contrast cards, notes and reading rules.
5. Put a retest date seven days later in the Errors tab, and do the retest.

**Proof to record:** A photo of your answer sheet, your score calculation, your Errors tab with types and fixes, and the retest results.

## Template: Errors tab headings

```csv
Date,Source (mock / PYQ / practice),Question no,Subject,Topic,My answer,Correct answer,Error type,Why it happened,Fix (card / note / rule),Retest date,Retest result
```

## Template: error log rules (core tool)

```
ERROR LOG (one row per wrong or guessed question; Errors tab)
Date | Source | Q no | Subject | Topic | My answer | Correct | Type | Why | Fix | Retest date | Retest result
Error types:
K = didn't know      F = forgot         I = interference (mixed up two facts)
M = misread          C = careless slip  G = bad guess      T = ran out of time
Fix rules:
K or F -> make 1-3 cards, or add the topic to the Revision tab
I      -> one card that contrasts the two facts side by side
M      -> underline NOT / EXCEPT / FIRST / LARGEST in every question for a week
C      -> slow down on the last step; check the OMR bubble number
G      -> guess only after ruling out at least one option
T      -> two-pass method in the next mock
Retest every error 7 days later, from memory. Clear it only when it is right twice.
```

## Template: mock test conditions

```
MOCK TEST     Paper: ______________ (unseen [ ])   Date: ______   Start: ____
[ ] Real time limit: ___ minutes    [ ] Real number of questions: ___
[ ] OMR-style sheet (printed or drawn)  [ ] Blue or black ball-point pen
[ ] Phone in another room           [ ] No breaks, no notes
[ ] S / U / G marked beside every answer
Score: correct ___ − wrong ___ ÷ 3 = ___   Unanswered: ___
Analysis done (all wrong + guessed-right logged): [ ]   Time spent: ___ min
```

## Common mistakes

- **Taking mocks without analysing them.** The analysis is where the learning happens. Spend as long on it as on the mock.
- **Logging only wrong answers.** Guessed-right answers are also gaps. Log them.
- **Vague reasons ("silly mistake").** Use the error types; each type has a different fix.
- **Never retesting errors.** Retest after seven days; clear an error only when it is right twice.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Under Kerala PSC's OMR marking, what is the score for 60 correct, 15 wrong and 25 unanswered?
    - A) 45
    - B) 55
    - C) 50
    - D) 60
2. Which questions go into the Errors tab after a mock?
    - A) Every wrong answer and every guessed-right answer
    - B) Only maths questions
    - C) Only wrong answers
    - D) Only questions you skipped
3. You answered a question wrongly because you missed the word NOT. Which error type is it?
    - A) K: didn't know
    - B) C: careless calculation
    - C) M: misread
    - D) T: time
4. When can you clear an error from the log?
    - A) After one week whatever happens
    - B) When you get it right in two separate retests
    - C) As soon as you read the right answer
    - D) Never

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Kerala PSC's OMR instructions and College Success 6.3 on test day
- **Action:** Take a full mock under real conditions, log and fix every error, and retest after a week. It is done when your proof is saved: a photo of your answer sheet, your score calculation, your Errors tab with types and fixes, and the retest results.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** 60 − 15 ÷ 3 = 55; unanswered questions score 0.
2. **A.** A lucky guess hides a real gap.
3. **C.** The fix is to underline NOT and EXCEPT in every question for a while.
4. **B.** Two correct retests show the fix has stuck.

sections.title: LRN-M12-L04: Time management and negative marking
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Plan your time in the exam hall with a two-pass method and checkpoints, and decide when to guess using the arithmetic of negative marking and your own calibration data. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 30 minutes calculation plus your next mock).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The arithmetic of negative marking

Kerala PSC's OMR instructions give **+1 for a correct answer and −1/3 for a wrong one**; unanswered questions score 0 ([OMR instructions](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) (check current rules)). With four options, the **expected value** of answering depends on your chance of being right, p:

```
Expected marks from answering = p × 1 − (1 − p) × 1/3

Blind guess among 4 options (p = 1/4):   1/4 − 3/4 × 1/3 = 0        (no gain on average)
One option ruled out (p = 1/3):          1/3 − 2/3 × 1/3 = 1/9      (about +0.11)
Two options ruled out (p = 1/2):         1/2 − 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/3      (about +0.33)
"Unsure" answers that are right 60%:     0.6 − 0.4 × 1/3 ≈ 0.47

Break-even: p − (1 − p)/3 = 0  ->  p = 1/4
```

So, under this scheme, **answering pays on average whenever your chance of being right is above 1 in 4**. A blind guess gains nothing on average and only adds risk. But as soon as you can rule out even one option, answering is worth it on average.

Your calibration table from Module 7 tells you your real chances. If your "unsure" answers are right 55% of the time, you should almost always answer them. If your guesses after ruling out two options are right about half the time, answer those too.

This is arithmetic, not a guarantee: on a single question you can still lose a third of a mark. Over a whole paper, following the rule raises your expected score. Check the marking scheme in your own exam's instructions; if it differs, redo the calculation.

### Time: the two-pass method

Work out your time per question first. In the 2022 Degree Level preliminary (100 marks at one mark a question, in 1 hour 15 minutes), that is 45 seconds a question ([2022 notice](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/2022-07/degree_level_cpe__for_confirmation_.pdf) (check current rules)).

1. **Pass 1 (about 60% of the time):** go through every question. Answer the ones you know (S) immediately and shade them. Mark the doubtful ones (U, G) in the way your exam allows, and skip long calculations.
2. **Pass 2 (about 30%):** return to the marked questions. Rule out options, use the break-even rule, and do the skipped calculations.
3. **Last 10% of the time:** check that every shaded bubble matches its question number. Don't change answers without a clear reason.

OpenStax *College Success* gives the same core advice: answer the questions you are confident about first, skip very difficult ones and return, and keep time at the end to review ([College Success 6.3](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking)).

### Time checkpoints

Before the exam, write your checkpoints: for 100 questions in 75 minutes, you want to be at about question 25 by minute 12, question 50 by minute 23 and question 100 by minute 45 in pass 1. Practise them in every mock and record where you actually were.

## Local example

**Ashiq** used to skip every question he wasn't sure of, about 25 per mock, because he feared negative marks. His calibration table from Module 7 said his guesses after ruling out two options were right about half the time.

He did the arithmetic: at p = 1/2, each such answer is worth +1/3 of a mark on average. In his next mock he used the two-pass method and answered the doubtful questions where he could rule out at least one option. He answered 12 more questions than usual; 6 were right and 6 wrong, which gave him 6 − 2 = +4 marks compared with skipping them.

His timing checkpoints showed something else: he reached question 50 at minute 31, eight minutes behind plan, because he solved every calculation in pass 1. In the following mock he skipped long calculations in pass 1 and finished pass 1 at minute 46, with time to check every bubble.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The expected value of answering under +1 and −1/3 marking | **Strong** | This is arithmetic, not research: it holds whenever the scheme is +1 and −1/3 with four options. |
| Using your own calibration data to decide when to answer | **Limited** | A practical use of Module 7's data; your calibration can change, so update it after each mock. |
| The two-pass method and time checkpoints | **Limited** | Standard test-taking advice (College Success 6.3); judge it by your mock timing and scores. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: instructions to candidates for OMR examinations (PDF)](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) | Read the marking rules in the OMR instructions | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala PSC: Degree Level Common Preliminary Examination notice, 2022 (PDF)](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/2022-07/degree_level_cpe__for_confirmation_.pdf) | Note the marks and duration in the 2022 notice as an example | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [College Success, 6.3 Test Taking (including test anxiety)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking) | Reread the multiple-choice advice | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Read your own exam's marking instructions and write down the scheme. If it isn't +1 and −1/3 with four options, redo the break-even calculation.
2. Fill in the guessing calculator below with your calibration data from Module 7 and your latest mock.
3. Work out your time per question and your three pass-1 checkpoints.
4. In your next mock, use the two-pass method, the checkpoints and the break-even rule. Note where you were at each checkpoint.
5. Compare with your previous mock: questions answered, accuracy, net score and time left at the end.

**Proof to record:** Your filled-in guessing calculator, your timing plan, the next mock's checkpoint times and the comparison with your previous mock.

## Template: guessing calculator

```
MARKING SCHEME (from my exam's instructions): +___ correct, −___ wrong, options ___
Break-even chance: p where p × (right mark) = (1 − p) × (wrong mark) -> p = ___
My data (from calibration and mocks):
  "Unsure" answers right: ___%   -> answer them?  yes / no
  Guesses after ruling out 1 option right: ___%   -> answer?  yes / no
  Guesses after ruling out 2 options right: ___%  -> answer?  yes / no
  Blind guesses right: ___%  (expected value about 0: skip unless I want the risk)
My rule: I answer when ______________________________________________
```

## Template: two-pass time plan

```
Questions ___   Minutes ___   Seconds per question = minutes × 60 ÷ questions = ___
PASS 1 (about 60% of time = ___ min): answer S, mark U and G, skip long calculations
  Checkpoints: Q25 by min ___   Q50 by min ___   Q100 by min ___
PASS 2 (about 30% = ___ min): marked questions, rule out options, calculations
CHECK (last 10% = ___ min): every bubble matches its question number
Actual in this mock: Q25 at ___  Q50 at ___  end of pass 1 at ___  time left ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Blind guessing on every question.** A blind guess gains nothing on average and adds risk. Rule out options first.
- **Skipping everything you are unsure of.** If your unsure answers are right more than 1 time in 4, answering pays on average.
- **Spending minutes on one hard question in pass 1.** Mark it and move on; come back in pass 2.
- **Not checking the bubbles.** One shifted row can cost many marks. Keep the last minutes for checking.
- **Assuming the marking scheme.** Read your own exam's instructions; schemes can differ.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Under +1 and −1/3 marking with four options, what is the expected value of a blind guess?
    - A) 0
    - B) +1/2
    - C) +1/4
    - D) −1/3
2. You can rule out two of the four options. What is the expected value of answering?
    - A) +1/3
    - B) +1
    - C) −1/6
    - D) 0
3. Above what chance of being right does answering pay on average under this scheme?
    - A) 1 in 4
    - B) 3 in 4
    - C) 1 in 2
    - D) 1 in 10
4. An exam has 100 questions in 75 minutes. How many seconds per question is that?
    - A) 60
    - B) 45
    - C) 30
    - D) 75
5. What happens in pass 1 of the two-pass method?
    - A) Solve every question in order, however long it takes
    - B) Check all the bubbles
    - C) Answer the questions you know, mark doubtful ones and skip long calculations
    - D) Guess every question

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The marking rules in the OMR instructions, the 2022 notice and College Success 6.3
- **Action:** Calculate your guessing rule from your own data and use the two-pass method in your next mock. It is done when your proof is saved: your filled-in guessing calculator, your timing plan, the next mock's checkpoint times and the comparison with your previous mock.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** 1/4 × 1 − 3/4 × 1/3 = 0.
2. **A.** 1/2 − 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/3.
3. **A.** Break-even: p − (1 − p)/3 = 0 gives p = 1/4.
4. **B.** 75 × 60 ÷ 100 = 45 seconds.
5. **C.** Secure the sure marks first; return to the rest in pass 2.

Action: Calculate your guessing rule from your own data and use the two-pass method in your next mock

sections.title: LRN-M12-L05: Your 12-week study and revision plan
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a complete 12-week PSC study and revision plan from your syllabus map, PYQ analysis and real weekly hours, with revision cycles and mocks built in. **Time:** about 2 hours (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 90 minutes building the plan).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What goes into the plan

A good plan starts from facts, not hopes:

- **The exam date,** or a target date 12 weeks away if your exam date isn't announced yet. Kerala PSC lists exam programmes under its exam schedule ([Kerala PSC website](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/) (check current rules)).
- **Your real weekly hours** for PSC study, from your Study Log, not the hours you wish you had.
- **Your priorities** from the Syllabus tab (LRN-M12-L01) and PYQ analysis (LRN-M12-L02).
- **Your current mock score** (LRN-M12-L03), so you can track progress.
- **Your daily routines:** AnkiDroid, Revision-tab reviews and the Sunday weekly review.

### A default 12-week structure

| Weeks | Phase | How the time splits (a sensible default) | Mocks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–8 | Learn and revise | About 60% new topics in priority order, 25% spaced reviews (Revision tab and AnkiDroid), 15% mixed practice and PYQs | One every two weeks (weeks 2, 4, 6, 8) |
| 9–11 | Revision cycles and mocks | A full revision cycle through every topic by recall, weak-topic sprints, few new topics | One a week, with full analysis |
| 12 | Taper | Short reviews, error-log retests, sleep, logistics; nothing new in the last three days | One early in the week |

The percentages are a starting point, not research. Adjust them in your weekly reviews.

### Revision cycles

A **revision cycle** goes through every topic once, by recall, in priority order. Cycle 1 runs through weeks 9 and 10; cycle 2 through week 11, faster, focusing on ambers and reds from your traffic-light check; a light cycle 3 in week 12 uses only cue questions, cards and the error log. Every review starts with recall, never with rereading (Module 3).

### The capacity check

Multiply your weekly hours by the weeks for each phase and compare with the number of topics. If the topics don't fit, don't pretend: cut or shorten the lowest-priority topics, or plan them for a lighter depth (key facts on cards only). A realistic plan you follow beats an ideal plan you abandon in week 3.

### Each week

Every week of the plan becomes a filled-in **weekly study planner** (LRN-M05-L02), written on Sunday in your weekly review, with if-then plans for your three priorities (Module 6). Each day has the same skeleton: AnkiDroid reviews, DUE Revision-tab reviews, one or two new-topic blocks and a mixed-practice block.

### Keep it alive

- **Every 4 weeks:** re-sort the Syllabus tab, compare mock scores, and adjust the remaining weeks.
- **If the exam date moves:** stretch the learning phase and keep the last four weeks as they are.
- **After the exam:** start the next 12-week cycle for your next exam, with what you learned from this one.

## Local example

**Anu**'s LDC exam was about 12 weeks away when she reached this lesson. Her Study Log showed about 18 hours of PSC study a week, on top of 6 hours for this course; she tutors on weekday evenings.

Her capacity check: weeks 1 to 8 gave her about 144 hours, of which 60%, about 86 hours, could go to new topics. Her Syllabus tab had 64 topics, of which 41 were amber or red. At about 2 hours per topic, 41 topics needed about 82 hours: just enough, with the 23 green topics left to reviews and cards.

She wrote the 12-week plan with mocks in weeks 2, 4, 6 and 8, then weekly. Each Sunday she fills in the week's planner from the plan. Week 1 included three priority topics from mental ability, two from English grammar and her daily routines. She put all mock dates and the taper week into her calendar, and showed the plan to her study partner, who promised to ask every Sunday whether she had followed it.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced reviews, retrieval and practice tests built into the plan | **Strong** | The plan schedules the two high-utility techniques every week. |
| Written if-then plans for each week's priorities | **Strong** | Implementation intentions have a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. |
| This exact 12-week structure and time split | **Limited** | A practical design, not tested research. Adjust it with your weekly review data. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala Public Service Commission (official website)](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/) | Check the exam schedule for your exam's date, if announced | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Reread 3.4 How to Manage Time | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write down your exam date (or a target date 12 weeks away), your real weekly PSC hours from the Study Log, and your latest mock score.
2. Do the capacity check below for weeks 1 to 8 against your amber and red topics.
3. Fill in the 12-week plan template: topics for each week in priority order, mock weeks, the revision cycles in weeks 9 to 11 and the taper week.
4. Fill in the weekly study planner for week 1 from the plan, with if-then plans for its three priorities.
5. Put all mock dates and the taper week in your calendar. Show the plan to your study partner or a family member and agree on a Sunday check-in.

**Proof to record:** Your complete 12-week plan, the capacity check, the week-1 planner and a screenshot of the mock dates in your calendar.

## Template: 12-week PSC plan

```
12-WEEK PLAN     Exam: ______________  Date: ______ (or target)  Start: ______
Weekly PSC hours (real, from the Study Log): ___   Course hours: ___
Starting mock score: ___   Target score: ___
Week | Phase        | New topics (priority order)        | Mock?  | Notes
1    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | -      | ______
2    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | Mock 1 | ______
3    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | -      | ______
4    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | Mock 2 | ______
5    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | -      | ______
6    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | Mock 3 | ______
7    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | -      | ______
8    | Learn+revise | __________________________________ | Mock 4 | re-sort Syllabus tab
9    | Cycle 1      | all topics by recall (part 1)      | Mock 5 | ______
10   | Cycle 1      | all topics by recall (part 2)      | Mock 6 | ______
11   | Cycle 2      | ambers and reds, error log         | Mock 7 | ______
12   | Taper        | cards, cue questions, error retests | Mock 8 early | nothing new in last 3 days
Daily skeleton: AnkiDroid ___ min | DUE reviews | new-topic block(s) | mixed practice | sleep by ____
```

## Template: capacity check

```
Hours in weeks 1-8 = weekly PSC hours ___ × 8 = ___
Hours for new topics (about 60%) = ___
Amber and red topics: ___ × about ___ hours each = ___ hours needed
Fits?  yes / no.  If no: cut or shorten these lowest-priority topics: ___________
```

## Template: weekly study planner (core tool)

```
WEEKLY STUDY PLANNER          Week of: ________
Exam: __________________ on ________   Weeks left: ___
Hours this week: course ___ + PSC study ___ = ___

DAY   BLOCK (time)   SUBJECT : TOPIC            METHOD                    DONE
Mon   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Tue   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Wed   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Thu   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Fri   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sat   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sun   20 minutes     Weekly learning review + plan next week               [ ]

METHOD words: retrieval (blank-page recall, practice questions), spaced review
(from the Revision tab), mixed practice (interleaving), Feynman, cards, mock test.

Every day:  [ ] AnkiDroid reviews (___ min)  [ ] one retrieval session
            [ ] phone in another room during blocks  [ ] sleep by ____
If-then plans: If ____________________, then I will ____________________.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Twelve weeks of new topics and no revision.** Weeks 9 to 12 are for revision cycles and mocks; plan them now.
- **Leaving all mocks to the end.** A mock every two weeks from week 2 shows progress and gaps early.
- **Planning with the hours you wish you had.** Use your Study Log hours, and cut topics if they don't fit.
- **No buffer.** Keep one empty block a week (Module 5) for illness, functions and power cuts.
- **Never revisiting the plan.** Re-sort the Syllabus tab and adjust every four weeks.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In the default plan, what happens in weeks 9 to 11?
    - A) No study at all
    - B) Only new topics
    - C) Only current affairs
    - D) Revision cycles through all topics by recall, and a mock every week
2. Your capacity check shows the topics don't fit. What should you do?
    - A) Ignore it and hope
    - B) Drop all reviews
    - C) Cut or shorten the lowest-priority topics
    - D) Plan to sleep less
3. Where do your weekly hours for the plan come from?
    - A) Your coaching centre
    - B) The hours you hope to study
    - C) A topper's timetable
    - D) Your Study Log: the hours you really studied
4. What should the last three days before the exam contain?
    - A) All-night study
    - B) Short reviews, error-log retests and sleep, but no new topics
    - C) Three full mocks a day
    - D) Several new chapters

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Kerala PSC exam schedule for your exam and College Success 3.4
- **Action:** Build your complete 12-week PSC study and revision plan and fill in week 1. It is done when your proof is saved: your complete 12-week plan, the capacity check, the week-1 planner and a screenshot of the mock dates in your calendar.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** The final weeks consolidate everything and train exam conditions.
2. **C.** A realistic plan you follow beats an ideal plan you abandon.
3. **D.** Plans built on real hours survive.
4. **B.** New topics at the end add stress and little marks; sleep consolidates.

Action: Build your complete 12-week PSC study and revision plan and fill in week 1

sections.title: LRN-M12-L06: Exam anxiety and exam day
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Manage exam anxiety with techniques that have evidence behind them, prepare an exam-day checklist, and know what to do after the exam and when anxiety needs more help. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus your next mock).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Some nerves are normal

Feeling nervous before a PSC exam is normal; it shows the exam matters to you. Strong anxiety is different: worry thoughts take up working memory (Module 1), so there is less room for thinking. The goal is not zero nerves, but nerves that don't take over.

### Techniques, with honest evidence

1. **Prepare well, and practise under exam conditions.** OpenStax *College Success* puts preparation first among ways to manage test anxiety: it is the part you control ([College Success 6.3](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking)). Mocks (LRN-M12-L03) make the hall, the timing and the answer sheet familiar.
2. **Write about your worries for 10 minutes just before the exam.** In studies published in *Science* in 2011, students who wrote about their worries for 10 minutes right before an exam did better than those who didn't; anxious ninth-grade students who wrote averaged a B+ on their final, against a B− for anxious students who didn't ([University of Chicago on Ramirez and Beilock](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/writing-about-worries-eases-anxiety-and-improves-test-performance)). One well-known paper with two studies: promising, not settled.
3. **Slow breathing and relaxation.** College Success recommends controlled breathing, visualisation and positive self-talk. Research support in exam settings is limited, but slow breathing is free and calming for many people.
4. **Keep perspective.** One exam is not your whole future; Kerala PSC holds many exams every year, and the system you are building works for all of them.

### In the hall: the reset

If panic rises during the exam: put the pen down, take three slow breaths, and go to a question you know. Getting one right brings the thinking part of your mind back.

### Exam-day checklist

Kerala PSC's OMR instructions include being in your seat 30 minutes before the exam and using a blue or black ball-point pen ([OMR instructions](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) (check current rules)). Your admission ticket gives the rules for your exam, including what identity proof to carry. Read it the day you download it, not on exam morning.

### After the exam

Kerala PSC publishes **provisional** answer keys for OMR exams, then **final** keys. If you find an error in a provisional key, complaints are made online through your One Time Registration profile within five days ([answer keys page](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) (check current rules)). Check your answers calmly against the provisional key, file a complaint only with a solid source, then start your next cycle.

### When it is more than exam nerves

If anxiety stays high for weeks, affects your sleep or eating, or comes with panic attacks or hopeless thoughts, it is more than exam nerves. Talk to someone you trust and to a doctor. **Tele-MANAS** is a free government mental health helpline, open 24 hours, in your language of choice: call **14416** or **1-800-891-4416** ([Tele-MANAS](https://ehrc.iiitb.ac.in/project/tele-manas)).

## Local example

**Sreeja** always felt her mind go blank in the first ten minutes of an exam. In her last real exam she had left several easy questions unanswered, and only remembered the answers on the bus home.

Before her next mock she tried the 10-minute worry writing. At the dining table, with the timer set, she wrote everything she was afraid of: her children, the cost of another year without a job, what relatives would say. She rated her anxiety 8 out of 10 before writing and 5 after. Then she took three slow breaths and started.

She did the same before the next two mocks and her first ten minutes went smoothly each time; her scores rose too, though her practice was also improving, so she can't be sure how much was the writing. She wrote her exam-day checklist and her in-hall reset on one card, and saved the Tele-MANAS number in her phone, "just in case, for me or for someone else".

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expressive writing about worries just before an exam | **Moderate** | Ramirez and Beilock (2011), in Science: two studies, with gains for anxious students. Promising, not settled. |
| Preparation and practice under exam conditions | **Limited** | Standard advice (College Success 6.3) and very plausible; little direct research on anxiety itself. |
| Slow breathing and relaxation | **Limited** | Recommended by College Success; research in exam settings is limited, but it is free and harmless. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [University of Chicago (2011): writing about worries eases anxiety and improves test performance (Ramirez and Beilock, Science)](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/writing-about-worries-eases-anxiety-and-improves-test-performance) | Read the news article on the expressive-writing studies | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, 6.3 Test Taking (including test anxiety)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking/6.03%3A_Test_Taking) | Read the sections on test anxiety and test day | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: instructions to candidates for OMR examinations (PDF)](https://keralapsc.gov.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/new-omr-instructionsENGLISH.pdf) | Read the rules for candidates on exam day | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala PSC: answer keys for OMR exams](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) | Read how provisional and final keys and complaints work | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Tele-MANAS: free 24x7 mental health helpline, 14416 or 1-800-891-4416](https://ehrc.iiitb.ac.in/project/tele-manas) | Save the helpline number in your phone | 2 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write your exam-day checklist with the template below, using your own admission ticket and exam instructions.
2. Before your next mock, rate your anxiety from 1 to 10, do the 10-minute worry writing, and rate it again. Keep the writing private; you can tear it up afterwards.
3. Take the mock and note your score and how the first ten minutes felt.
4. Write your in-hall reset on the same card as your checklist.
5. Save the Tele-MANAS number in your phone.

**Proof to record:** Your exam-day checklist and in-hall reset card, and your before-and-after anxiety ratings with the mock score (not the private writing itself).

## Template: exam-day checklist

```
THE WEEK BEFORE
[ ] Admission ticket downloaded and read: date ____ time ____ centre ____________
[ ] ID proof required: ______________   Other items allowed / not allowed: ________
[ ] Route to the centre checked; travel time ___ (visit it if possible)
THE DAY BEFORE
[ ] Light review only: cue questions, cards, error-log retests. Nothing new.
[ ] Pens (blue or black ball-point, two), ticket, ID, water, watch if allowed
[ ] Sleep by ____
EXAM DAY
[ ] Leave by ____ to be seated 30 minutes before the start
[ ] 10-minute worry writing while waiting, then three slow breaths
[ ] Two-pass plan and checkpoints (LRN-M12-L04)
AFTER
[ ] Check against the provisional key; complaint within the deadline only with a solid source
```

## Template: 10-minute worry writing and the in-hall reset

```
WORRY WRITING (10 minutes, just before the exam or mock)
Anxiety before (1-10): ___
Write freely about what you are worried about in this exam. Nobody will read it.
Anxiety after (1-10): ___

IN-HALL RESET (if panic rises)
1. Pen down.  2. Three slow breaths, longer out than in.
3. Go to a question you know and answer it.  4. Continue the two-pass plan.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Cramming new topics the night before.** Review lightly and sleep; consolidation needs the night.
- **Reading the admission ticket on exam morning.** Read it the day you download it, so there are no surprises.
- **Reading "expected questions" forums on exam morning.** They raise anxiety and add nothing. Use your checklist instead.
- **Ignoring anxiety that lasts for weeks.** Talk to someone you trust and a doctor; Tele-MANAS is free at 14416.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Ramirez and Beilock (2011) test?
    - A) Writing about worries for 10 minutes just before an exam
    - B) Listening to music during the exam
    - C) Studying for 10 hours the night before
    - D) Skipping breakfast
2. According to Kerala PSC's OMR instructions, when should you be in your seat?
    - A) Two hours before
    - B) 30 minutes before the exam
    - C) At the exact start time
    - D) 5 minutes after the start
3. You find an error in a provisional answer key. What can you do?
    - A) Nothing at all
    - B) Phone the exam centre
    - C) Complain online through your One Time Registration profile within five days, with a solid source
    - D) Wait for the final key and complain then
4. What is Tele-MANAS?
    - A) A PSC coaching app
    - B) A free 24-hour government mental health helpline: 14416
    - C) A paid counselling service only
    - D) An exam scheduling site

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The expressive-writing studies, College Success 6.3 on test anxiety, and the PSC rules for exam day and answer keys
- **Action:** Write your exam-day checklist and reset, and try the 10-minute worry writing before a mock. It is done when your proof is saved: your exam-day checklist and in-hall reset card, and your before-and-after anxiety ratings with the mock score (not the private writing itself).
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Anxious students who wrote did better; promising evidence from two studies.
2. **B.** Check your admission ticket for your exam's exact rules.
3. **C.** Complaints are made through the OTR profile within the deadline.
4. **B.** It offers support in your language of choice, free of charge.

sections.title: Module 13: Deliberate practice and skill acquisition
sections.summary: Turn practice into improvement: target your weakest skills with immediate feedback in a practice loop, and plan self-directed learning projects for any skill you want after PSC.
sections.content:
## Overview

Hours of practice are not equal. Practice that targets a weakness, gives immediate feedback and repeats with changes improves skills far faster than repeating what you can already do. This module is also honest about the limits: practice explains only part of why some people become experts, which is a reason to practise well, not a reason to stop.

The second lesson turns everything in this course into a plan for learning without a syllabus: the skill of learning anything you choose, for the rest of your life.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain deliberate practice and the honest evidence about it
- Run a practice loop with immediate feedback on your weakest PSC skill
- Find the edge of your ability and adjust practice to it
- Plan a self-directed learning project with a clear outcome and baseline
- Avoid tutorial traps with the watch-to-do rule

## Time

About 3 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 15–16, with the module project due in week 16.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M13-L01: Deliberate practice and feedback loops (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M13-L02: Self-directed learning projects (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **practice loop sheet** and **finding the edge** guide
- The **learning project canvas** and **watch-to-do rule**

## Module project: My practice loop and learning project

1. Show the accuracy trend from your three practice-loop sessions, and start a loop on the next weakest skill.
2. Keep your learning project going for two more weeks with at least two sessions a week, each producing something.
3. At the end of the two weeks, write a short review: what you can do now that you couldn't at the baseline.

**Proof to record:** Your practice-loop accuracy trend for two skills, and your learning project canvas with logged sessions and the two-week review.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Practice loop | Practising strengths | Weak skill chosen, feedback at the end | Weak skill, immediate feedback, specific fixes, rising accuracy |
| Evidence | Believes "practice is everything" or "practice doesn't matter" | Knows the 12% figure | Can explain what the numbers do and don't mean |
| Project plan | Vague goal | Outcome without baseline or plan | Complete canvas with baseline, 10-hour plan and feedback source |
| Doing | Only watching | Some sessions with output | Every session produced something; watch-to-do rule kept |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Run one practice-loop session a week on your weakest skill.
- Fill in the learning project canvas and save the project for after your exam.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Four features of deliberate practice | Targets a weakness, just beyond your level, immediate feedback, repeats with changes. |
| Macnamara and others (2014) | Deliberate practice explained about 12% of performance differences overall; 4% in education. |
| What the 12% does not mean | It doesn't mean practice fails to help you; it describes differences between people. |
| The five steps of a feedback loop | Attempt, check immediately, find the exact error, fix it, attempt two more. |
| The edge of ability | Some items wrong, most right. |
| A good project outcome | Something someone could watch you do. |
| Watch-to-do rule | For every hour of watching or reading, at least an hour of doing. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Counting practice hours instead of fixing errors.** Track accuracy and the fixes you made.
- **Waiting for the perfect course before starting a project.** Start with one resource and make something in the first session.
