sections.title: LRN-M13-L01: Deliberate practice and feedback loops
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Design practice that targets your weakest PSC skill with immediate feedback, and run a practice loop that you can see improving session by session. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 60 minutes action over three sessions).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Practice is not the same as repetition

Two aspirants each do maths for an hour a day. One solves the types she is already good at, checks the answers at the end, and feels productive. The other picks the type she gets wrong most, checks each answer immediately, works out exactly why it went wrong, and does two more of the same kind. After a month, the second one has improved far more. The difference is not the hours; it is the **kind** of practice.

The psychologist K. Anders Ericsson called the second kind **deliberate practice**: practice that

- **targets a specific weakness,** not the whole subject
- is **just beyond** what you can already do
- gives **immediate, specific feedback**
- **repeats with changes** until the weakness is fixed

### Honest evidence: practice matters, but it isn't everything

A popular idea says that practice is all it takes to become an expert ("10,000 hours"). In 2014, Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald combined many studies and found that the amount of deliberate practice explained about **12%** of the differences in performance between people overall: about 26% in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions ([APS, 2014](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/becoming-an-expert-takes-more-than-practice.html)).

Read those numbers carefully. They describe **differences between people**: other things matter too, such as starting age, prior knowledge, teaching quality and individual ability. They do **not** mean that practice doesn't help **you** improve. For an exam, how you practise (retrieval, spacing, mixing, feedback) matters a great deal, as the research in Module 3 shows.

### Feedback loops

A **feedback loop** is the core of good practice:

1. **Attempt** one item: a problem, a sentence, a question.
2. **Check it immediately,** not after fifty items.
3. **Find the exact error:** which step, which rule, which fact.
4. **Fix it:** a rule card, a worked example, a contrast card.
5. **Attempt two more** of the same kind, to confirm the fix.

The faster and more specific the feedback, the faster you improve. Checking 100 answers at the end of a session tells you your score, but not much about what to change.

### Finding the edge

Practise where you get **some** items wrong but **most** right. If you get everything right, it is too easy; move on. If you get almost everything wrong, go back to worked examples (Module 1). Your Errors tab and Syllabus tab (Module 12) show you where the edge is.

### PSC feedback loops

| Skill | Attempt | Immediate feedback | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic (e.g. time and work) | One problem at a time | Answer key after each problem | Rebuild the principle (LRN-M08-L04); two more of the same type |
| English grammar (e.g. articles, prepositions) | Ten sentences | Check each against the key | A rule card with your wrong sentence corrected |
| Malayalam grammar (e.g. sandhi, samasam) | Ten examples | Check with the textbook | A rule card with two examples |
| Statement questions | One question | Check each statement's source | Note why each statement is true or false |

## Local example

**Ashiq**'s Errors tab showed time-and-work problems as his weakest type. He used to practise them in sets of 25 and check at the end; his accuracy hovered around 55%.

He set up a practice loop: one problem, check immediately, name the exact error, fix it, and two more of the same kind. In session 1 he found that most of his errors came from one step: converting "A can do it in 12 days" into a daily rate. He made a rule card ("days → rate: 1/days") and a worked example.

Over three 20-minute sessions his accuracy went from 55% to 70% to 85%. By session 3 he was getting pipes-and-cisterns problems right too, because they use the same principle with one rate negative. He moved on to the next weak type in his Errors tab and set a review of time and work in his Revision tab for a week later.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Practice on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback | **Moderate** | Consistent with research on practice testing and feedback; the most useful form of practice for exam skills. |
| Practice alone explains who becomes an expert ("10,000 hours") | **No good evidence** | Macnamara and others (2014): deliberate practice explained about 12% of performance differences overall, 4% in education. |
| Practising at the edge: some wrong, most right | **Limited** | A practical rule from skill learning; judge it by your accuracy trend. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [APS (2 July 2014): becoming an expert takes more than practice (Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/becoming-an-expert-takes-more-than-practice.html) | Read the whole news release, including the numbers by field | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Reread the part on practice testing and feedback | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Use your Errors tab and Syllabus tab to choose your weakest PSC skill (a maths type, a grammar area or a question type).
2. Prepare at least 40 items of that skill with answers: from previous papers, your guide or your textbook.
3. Run three practice-loop sessions of about 20 minutes on different days: attempt one item, check it immediately, name the exact error, fix it, then attempt two more of the same kind.
4. Record your accuracy in each session and the rule cards or worked examples you made.
5. When accuracy passes about 80%, add the skill to your Revision tab and choose the next weakest skill.

**Proof to record:** Your three practice-loop sheets with accuracy for each session, and the rule cards or worked examples you made.

## Template: practice loop sheet

```
PRACTICE LOOP     Skill: ______________________  Session ___  Date: ______
Item | Right? | Exact error (step / rule / fact)        | Fix (card / example / rule) | 2 more right?
1    | Y / N  | _______________________________________ | ___________________________ | __ / 2
2    | Y / N  | _______________________________________ | ___________________________ | __ / 2
...
Accuracy this session: ___ / ___ = ___%   (session 1 ___%  session 2 ___%  session 3 ___%)
Next: stay on this skill / move on (over 80%) / back to worked examples (under 40%)
```

## Template: finding the edge

```
Almost all right (over 90%)   -> too easy: move to a harder type or mix it with others
Some wrong, most right        -> the edge: practise here with the loop
Almost all wrong (under 40%)  -> too hard: study worked examples first, then return
```

## Common mistakes

- **Practising what you are already good at.** It feels good and teaches little. Practise your weakest skill.
- **Checking answers only at the end.** Check each item immediately, so you can fix the error before repeating it.
- **Repeating without changing anything.** Every error needs a specific fix: a rule, an example or a contrast.
- **Reading the 12% figure as "practice doesn't work".** It describes differences between people; good practice still improves you.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is deliberate practice?
    - A) Rereading the formula page
    - B) Watching a solved-problem video at 2x speed
    - C) Solving 50 problems you already find easy
    - D) Picking your weakest maths type, checking each problem immediately and fixing the exact error
2. What did Macnamara and others (2014) find?
    - A) Practice has no effect on anything
    - B) Deliberate practice explained about 12% of performance differences overall, 4% in education
    - C) Practice explains 100% of expertise
    - D) Only music needs practice
3. Your accuracy on a skill is under 40%. What should you do?
    - A) Skip the skill for good
    - B) Go back to worked examples, then return to practice
    - C) Do 200 more problems the same way
    - D) Practise faster
4. What makes feedback most useful?
    - A) It is immediate and specific
    - B) It comes once a month
    - C) It comes from a stranger
    - D) It only gives the total score

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The APS release on Macnamara and others (2014) and Dunlosky on practice testing
- **Action:** Run three practice-loop sessions on your weakest PSC skill and track your accuracy. It is done when your proof is saved: your three practice-loop sheets with accuracy for each session, and the rule cards or worked examples you made.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It targets a weakness with immediate, specific feedback.
2. **B.** Practice matters, but other factors also explain differences between people.
3. **B.** It is beyond your edge; worked examples build the base first.
4. **A.** Immediate, specific feedback lets you fix the exact error before repeating it.

sections.title: LRN-M13-L02: Self-directed learning projects
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Plan and start a self-directed learning project for a new skill (AI tools, business, a language or anything else), with a clear outcome, a baseline test, free resources, a practice loop and a measure of progress. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes planning plus the first two hours of the project).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Your system works beyond PSC

The methods in this course work for anything you learn: AI tools, running a business, marketing, a new language, accounts, a craft. After PSC, or alongside it if your time allows, you will learn without a syllabus or an exam. That needs a plan you make yourself: a **self-directed learning project**.

### The learning project canvas

1. **Outcome:** what you will be able to **do**, so that someone could watch you do it. Not "learn AI", but "use an AI chat tool to draft and check a one-page letter in English and Malayalam". Not "learn Excel", but "build a monthly report with SUMIF and a chart".
2. **Why:** your reason (Module 6), in one line.
3. **Baseline:** a small test of the outcome now: try it and record the result, as you did in week 0.
4. **Skill map:** break the outcome into 4 to 8 sub-skills.
5. **Resources:** free, current and reliable: official guides, open textbooks, the other courses in this app. Choose one main resource per sub-skill; collecting twenty is a way to avoid starting.
6. **First 10 hours:** a concrete plan for the first 10 hours, with what you will **make or do** in each session.
7. **Practice loop:** how you will attempt, get feedback and fix (LRN-M13-L01).
8. **Feedback source:** an answer key, a test, a person who knows the skill, a community, or an AI tool whose answers you check (Module 17).
9. **Memory:** which facts or terms go into AnkiDroid.
10. **Measure and review:** repeat the baseline test at the end, with weekly reviews in between.

### Learn by making things

Projects work best when you **make something real** early: a spreadsheet, a short video, a one-page business plan, a conversation in a new language. You learn what you need, when you need it, and the thing you make shows your progress. Combine it with retrieval and spacing for the facts and terms that come up.

### Avoid tutorial traps

Watching course after course without making anything feels like learning but builds little skill: it is the fluency illusion again (Module 7). A good rule: for every hour of watching or reading, spend at least an hour doing.

### Where to start in this app

| If you want to learn | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| AI tools for work, freelancing or business | The Free AI Generalist Course in this app |
| Starting a small business | Practical Entrepreneurship in this app |
| Marketing and freelancing with social media | Practical Social Media Marketing in this app |
| Managing money | Practical Personal Finance in this app |
| A new language | LRN-M15-L04 and [Language Transfer](https://www.languagetransfer.org/) |

If your PSC exam is close, keep the project small (an hour or two a week) or plan it for after the exam. Your capstone (Module 21) can also be a 30-day sprint on a new skill instead of a PSC subject.

## Local example

**Joseph sir** wanted his study group to be able to revise Malayalam grammar at home, so he decided to learn to make short explainer videos on his phone. At 61, he had never edited a video.

His canvas: the outcome was "a 3-minute video explaining one grammar rule, with clear sound, simple text on screen and one example". His baseline attempt took two hours and had echoing sound and no text. His skill map had five sub-skills: planning a script, recording clear audio, filming steady shots, simple editing with captions, and sharing. For feedback he asked the group to answer three questions after each video: Was it clear? Could you hear it? What would you change?

His first 10 hours each produced something: a script, an audio test in three rooms (a bedroom with curtains was best), a 30-second test video, and so on. After four weeks he made a 3-minute video on sandhi in 50 minutes, with clear sound and captions. The group now asks for one every week.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Learning skills through practice with feedback | **Moderate** | Consistent with research on practice testing and feedback. |
| Self-directed, project-based learning | **Limited** | Research on project-based learning is mixed; it works best with clear outcomes, feedback and retrieval of key knowledge. |
| A baseline test repeated at the end | **Limited** | A measuring tool rather than a technique; it makes progress visible. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dunlosky et al. (2013), "Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques", APS summary with the full paper](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/journals/pspi/learning-techniques.html) | Skim the ten techniques again and choose which you will use in your project | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional: Module 4 of Learning How to Learn on learning throughout life | About 3 hours | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Language Transfer: free audio courses](https://www.languagetransfer.org/) | If your project is a language: look at the free courses | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose one new skill you want for after PSC (or alongside it) and fill in the learning project canvas below.
2. Do the baseline test of your outcome and record the result.
3. Choose one main free resource for each sub-skill, from this app's other courses or official and open sources.
4. Plan your first 10 hours session by session, each producing something you make or do.
5. Do the first two hours, log them in your Study Log, and put weekly project sessions and a review date in your calendar.

**Proof to record:** Your completed learning project canvas, the baseline result and your log of the first two hours.

## Template: learning project canvas

```
LEARNING PROJECT CANVAS        Start: ______   Review date: ______
1. Outcome (what I will be able to DO): ______________________________________
2. Why: _____________________________________________________________________
3. Baseline test (try it now): _____________________  Result: _______________
4. Skill map (4-8 sub-skills): a. ______ b. ______ c. ______ d. ______ e. ______
5. Main resource per sub-skill (free): a. ______ b. ______ c. ______ d. ______
6. First 10 hours (what I make or do each session):
   1. ________ 2. ________ 3. ________ 4. ________ 5. ________
   6. ________ 7. ________ 8. ________ 9. ________ 10. _______
7. Practice loop: attempt ______ -> feedback from ______ -> fix -> repeat
8. Feedback source: ________________________________________________________
9. Facts and terms for AnkiDroid: deck name ______________
10. End test (repeat the baseline) on ______  Result: ______
```

## Template: watch-to-do rule

```
For every hour of watching or reading, at least one hour of doing.
Doing = making something, solving something, saying something, or testing yourself.
Weekly check: watching/reading ___ h   doing ___ h   ratio OK?  yes / no
```

## Common mistakes

- **A vague outcome ("learn AI").** Write an outcome someone could watch you do.
- **Collecting resources instead of starting.** One main resource per sub-skill. Start the first session today.
- **Skipping the baseline.** Without it, you can't see your progress.
- **Running five projects at once.** One project at a time, especially while preparing for PSC.
- **Watching tutorials without making anything.** Follow the watch-to-do rule.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is a well-written project outcome?
    - A) "Watch an Excel course"
    - B) "Learn spreadsheets"
    - C) "Build a monthly report with SUMIF and a chart in Google Sheets"
    - D) "Get better at computers"
2. Why do a baseline test at the start of a project?
    - A) It isn't useful
    - B) To decide whether to give up
    - C) Because it is required by law
    - D) So you can measure your progress at the end
3. What is the watch-to-do rule?
    - A) Do first, never watch
    - B) For every hour of watching or reading, at least an hour of doing
    - C) Watch three courses before doing anything
    - D) Never watch videos
4. Your PSC exam is six weeks away. What does the lesson suggest for a new project?
    - A) Keep it very small, or plan it for after the exam
    - B) Drop PSC study for the project
    - C) Never start projects
    - D) Start three projects now

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Dunlosky's technique summary for choosing methods, and (optionally) Learning How to Learn Module 4
- **Action:** Fill in a learning project canvas for a new skill, take its baseline and do the first two hours. It is done when your proof is saved: your completed learning project canvas, the baseline result and your log of the first two hours.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** It is something someone could watch you do.
2. **D.** Repeating it at the end shows what changed.
3. **B.** Doing builds skill; watching alone creates the fluency illusion.
4. **A.** The exam is the priority; the system will still work afterwards.

sections.title: Module 14: Numerical ability and reasoning
sections.summary: Build speed and accuracy in PSC numerical ability and mental ability: mental-maths tricks made automatic, the core arithmetic topics solved from principles, a method for each reasoning type, and a weekly practice system.
sections.content:
## Overview

For many aspirants, the mental ability section decides the rank. The good news is that it rewards method and practice more than talent. This module applies the course's strongest tools (worked examples, first principles, interleaving, immediate feedback and spaced cards) to the maths and reasoning in your syllabus.

The result is a maths and reasoning practice system that runs every week until your exam, with a monthly retest to measure progress.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Use a dozen mental-maths tricks and check answers in seconds
- Make basic facts automatic with AnkiDroid and a daily warm-up
- Solve the core arithmetic topics from principles with a five-step method
- Solve eight common reasoning types with a method for each, drawing where it helps
- Run a weekly maths and reasoning system and measure it monthly

## Time

About 6 hours in total: 4 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 16–17, with the module project due in week 17.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M14-L01: Mental maths tricks (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. LRN-M14-L02: PSC arithmetic: the core topics (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
3. LRN-M14-L03: Reasoning practice and a maths practice system (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **mental maths warm-up log** and **checking an answer in seconds** list
- **Topic principle cards** and the **five-step solving sheet**
- The **reasoning methods card set** and the **weekly maths and reasoning system**

## Module project: My maths and reasoning system

1. Run the weekly system for two weeks in full.
2. At the end, take a fresh mixed set of 30 (arithmetic and reasoning) under time and compare with the first mixed sets you did in this module.
3. Choose the next two weakest types from your Errors tab and plan practice loops for them.

**Proof to record:** Two weeks of the system log, the 30-question retest score and time compared with your first mixed sets, and your next two practice loops.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basics | Slow, error-prone calculations | Some tricks used | Daily warm-up with rising speed and accuracy |
| Arithmetic topics | Formula hunting | Principles known for some topics | Principle cards for all core topics, PYQs solved with five steps |
| Reasoning | Solved in the head, often wrong | Methods known | A method and a diagram where needed, for every type |
| System | Practice when there is time | Some weekly practice | The weekly system run for two weeks with a measured retest |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Keep only the 10-minute daily warm-up and one mixed set of 15 a week.
- Draw every blood-relation and direction question.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Multiply by 25 | × 100, then divide by 4. |
| Squares ending in 5 | First digit × (first digit + 1), then 25. |
| Successive percentage changes | a + b + (a × b) ÷ 100. |
| Profit percentage is on... | The cost price. |
| km/h to m/s | Multiply by 5/18. |
| Average speed for a round trip | Total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the speeds. |
| Angle between clock hands | The difference between 30 × hours and 5.5 × minutes. |
| Odd days | An ordinary year moves the weekday by 1, a leap year by 2. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Thinking you are "not a maths person".** Method and practice decide most of this section. Measure your progress.
- **Practising only the types you like.** Your Errors tab chooses next week's practice.

sections.title: LRN-M14-L01: Mental maths tricks
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use a dozen reliable mental-maths tricks for PSC arithmetic, check answers in seconds, and practise until the basics are automatic. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 45 minutes action plus a 10-minute daily warm-up for a week).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Why mental maths matters

In a PSC paper you may have about 45 seconds a question (LRN-M12-L04). If "17 × 6" or "15% of 640" takes you 30 seconds, you have no time left to think about the problem itself. When basic calculations are **automatic**, they take almost no working memory, and the reasoning gets the space it needs. The CESE review of cognitive load theory describes exactly this: extensive practice makes knowledge automatic, which frees working memory for new problems ([CESE, 2017](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory.pdf)).

### A dozen tricks that always work

These are arithmetic facts, so they are always correct; the only question is practice.

| Trick | How | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| × 5 | × 10, then halve | 48 × 5 = 480 ÷ 2 = 240 |
| × 25 | × 100, then divide by 4 | 36 × 25 = 3,600 ÷ 4 = 900 |
| × 9 | × 10, then subtract the number | 47 × 9 = 470 − 47 = 423 |
| × 11 (two digits) | Write the two digits apart and put their sum between (carry if 10 or more) | 53 × 11 = 583; 78 × 11 = 858 |
| Squares ending in 5 | First digit × (first digit + 1), then write 25 | 65² = (6 × 7) then 25 = 4,225 |
| Near a round number | (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b² | 47 × 53 = 50² − 3² = 2,500 − 9 = 2,491 |
| Percentages | 10% is a decimal shift; 5% is half of that; build the rest | 15% of 640 = 64 + 32 = 96 |
| Swap a percentage | x% of y = y% of x | 8% of 25 = 25% of 8 = 2 |
| Successive changes | Net % = a + b + (a × b) ÷ 100 | +20% then −20%: 20 − 20 − 4 = −4% |
| Averages with a base | Pick a base, average the differences | 46, 48, 52, 54: base 50, differences sum to 0, average 50 |
| BODMAS | Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction | 8 + 4 × 3 = 20, not 36 |
| Last-digit check | The last digit of a product is the last digit of the product of last digits | 47 × 23 must end in 1 (7 × 3 = 21); it is 1,081 |

### Facts worth making automatic

Put these in AnkiDroid (Module 4) and they will become instant within weeks:

- **Fractions and percentages:** 1/2 = 50%, 1/3 = 33.33%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 = 16.67%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/12 = 8.33%, 1/16 = 6.25%, 1/20 = 5%
- **Squares from 11 to 30** and **cubes from 1 to 15**
- **Multiplication tables to 20,** if you don't know them already
- **Divisibility rules:** by 3 or 9, the sum of the digits is divisible by 3 or 9; by 4, the last two digits; by 8, the last three; by 11, the difference between the sums of alternate digits is 0 or a multiple of 11

### Checking in seconds

With four options, a quick check often picks the answer without full working: the last digit, a rough estimate (is it about 400 or about 4,000?), or divisibility. Always check before marking the bubble.

### How speed really comes

Tricks help only after practice. Ten minutes of mixed mental arithmetic a day, timed, with immediate checking (the practice loop from Module 13), builds speed far better than learning fifty tricks once.

## Local example

**Sreeja** lost a lot of time in the arithmetic section, mainly on the calculations rather than the problems. She learned six tricks from this lesson (× 5, × 25, × 11, squares ending in 5, percentages and successive changes) and made AnkiDroid cards for the fraction-percentage table and squares from 11 to 30.

Each morning, before her first study block, she did a 20-problem mental maths warm-up from a sheet she wrote by mixing problems from her guide, timed on the phone's stopwatch and checked straight away. Day 1 took 9 minutes with 14 right. By day 7 it took 6 minutes with 18 right, and after three weeks under 5 minutes with 19 or 20 right.

In her next mock she finished the arithmetic questions with time to spare, and for the first time she used the last-digit check to choose between two options that looked close.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic basic facts free working memory for problem solving | **Strong** | The CESE review describes automation through extensive practice; it follows from working-memory limits (Module 1). |
| The mental-maths tricks in this lesson | **Strong** | They are arithmetic identities, always correct. What varies is how well you have practised them. |
| Short daily timed practice with immediate checking | **Moderate** | It combines spacing, retrieval and feedback; speed grows with practice. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NSW Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation (2017), "Cognitive load theory: Research that teachers really need to understand" (PDF)](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory.pdf) | Reread the part on automation and long-term memory | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e (free, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/preface) | Do a few exercises from the chapters on whole numbers, fractions, decimals and percents, using the tricks | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, 6.1 Understand Percent](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/6-1-understand-percent) | Practise converting between fractions, decimals and percents | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Learn six of the tricks in the table, one at a time: for each, do five examples from your guide and check them.
2. Make AnkiDroid cards for the fraction-percentage table and for squares from 11 to 30.
3. Write a sheet of 20 mixed mental-maths problems (or use one from your guide). Each day for 7 days, do a fresh 20 under a stopwatch and check each answer straight away.
4. Log time and accuracy each day.
5. In your next practice set, use the last-digit check or an estimate on at least five questions before marking an answer.

**Proof to record:** Your 7-day warm-up log with times and scores, and a screenshot of your new cards.

## Template: mental maths warm-up log

```
WARM-UP LOG (20 mixed problems, timed, checked straight away)
Day | Date   | Time (min:sec) | Right /20 | Trick I used most | Error I made
1   | ______ | ____           | ___       | ____________      | ____________
2   | ______ | ____           | ___       | ____________      | ____________
...
7   | ______ | ____           | ___       | ____________      | ____________
```

## Template: checking an answer in seconds

```
1. Last digit: does the option's last digit match?
2. Estimate: round the numbers; is the option about the right size?
3. Divisibility: should the answer be even, a multiple of 3, 5, 9 or 11?
4. Reverse: put the answer back into the question.
5. Units: rupees, km/h or m/s, days, percent?
```

## Common mistakes

- **Learning fifty tricks and practising none.** Six tricks, practised daily, beat fifty read once.
- **Speed without checking.** A fast wrong answer loses a third of a mark. Check before you mark.
- **Ignoring BODMAS.** Many PSC simplification questions test the order of operations.
- **Doing calculations on paper that tricks could do mentally.** Use the warm-up to make the basics automatic.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is 36 × 25?
    - A) 1,000
    - B) 850
    - C) 960
    - D) 900
2. What is 65²?
    - A) 4,225
    - B) 4,025
    - C) 4,125
    - D) 3,625
3. What is 15% of 640?
    - A) 90
    - B) 96
    - C) 64
    - D) 106
4. A price rises 10% and then another 10%. What is the total rise?
    - A) 11%
    - B) 19%
    - C) 21%
    - D) 20%
5. What is 47 × 53?
    - A) 2,491
    - B) 2,509
    - C) 2,500
    - D) 2,481

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The CESE review on automation and OpenStax Prealgebra exercises on whole numbers, fractions, decimals and percents
- **Action:** Learn six tricks, make cards for the key facts and do a timed mental-maths warm-up for 7 days. It is done when your proof is saved: your 7-day warm-up log with times and scores, and a screenshot of your new cards.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** 36 × 100 = 3,600, and 3,600 ÷ 4 = 900.
2. **A.** 6 × 7 = 42, then 25: 4,225.
3. **B.** 10% is 64 and 5% is 32; 64 + 32 = 96.
4. **C.** 10 + 10 + (10 × 10) ÷ 100 = 21%.
5. **A.** 50² − 3² = 2,500 − 9.

sections.title: LRN-M14-L02: PSC arithmetic: the core topics
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Solve the core PSC arithmetic topics (percentages, profit and loss, ratio, averages, interest, time and work, speed and distance) from a few principles, and check every answer. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Most PSC arithmetic questions come from a small set of topics, and each topic rests on one or two principles (LRN-M08-L04). Learn the principle, see one worked example, then practise with previous papers.

### The core topics

| Topic | Principle | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Percentages | Change ÷ original × 100 | Salary rises from ₹20,000 to ₹23,000: 3,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 15% |
| Profit and loss | Profit % is on the cost price | Bought for ₹800, sold for ₹1,000: profit 200 ÷ 800 × 100 = 25% |
| Discount | Discount is on the marked price | Marked ₹1,200, 15% discount: 1,200 × 0.85 = ₹1,020 |
| Ratio and proportion | Add the parts, find one part, multiply | ₹1,800 in the ratio 2:3:4: 9 parts of ₹200, so ₹400, ₹600, ₹800 |
| Averages | Total = average × count | Average of 5 numbers is 42; without one of them, the average of 4 is 40: removed = 210 − 160 = 50 |
| Simple interest | SI = P × R × T ÷ 100 | ₹5,000 at 8% for 3 years: 5,000 × 8 × 3 ÷ 100 = ₹1,200 |
| Compound interest | Amount = P × (1 + R/100)^T | ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years: 10,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹12,100, so CI = ₹2,100 |
| Time and work | Daily rates add: rate = 1 ÷ days | A in 12 days, B in 18: 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 a day, so 36/5 = 7.2 days together |
| Speed and distance | Distance = speed × time; km/h × 5/18 = m/s | A 200 m train at 72 km/h (20 m/s) passes a pole in 10 s and a 300 m platform in 500 ÷ 20 = 25 s |
| Relative speed | Towards each other: add speeds; same direction: subtract | Trains 180 km apart at 50 and 40 km/h towards each other meet in 180 ÷ 90 = 2 hours |

A useful extra: for two years, the difference between compound and simple interest is P × (R/100)². For ₹10,000 at 10%, that is ₹100 (CI ₹2,100 against SI ₹2,000).

### A five-step method for every question

1. **Name the type** (Module 3): "this is time and work".
2. **Write the principle** in a few words: "rates add".
3. **Set up** the numbers with units.
4. **Calculate,** using mental tricks where they fit (LRN-M14-L01).
5. **Check:** estimate, last digit, units, or put the answer back into the question.

### Common traps

- **Profit on selling price** instead of cost price
- **Mixing units:** km/h with metres, months with years in interest
- **Averaging speeds:** going at 40 km/h and returning at 60 km/h does **not** average 50 km/h; work it out from total distance ÷ total time
- **Percentage of what?** "A is 25% more than B" is not the same as "B is 25% less than A"
- **Forgetting the train's own length** when it crosses a platform or bridge

### Practise from previous papers

Your PYQ tab (Module 12) shows which topics your exam asks most. Collect three previous-year questions per topic, solve them with the five steps, then mix them into timed sets (Module 3).

## Local example

**Anu** knew most formulas but kept losing marks to traps. She went through ten topics with this lesson's table: for each, she wrote the principle on a card in her own words, studied the worked example, and then solved three previous-year questions with the five-step method.

Her Errors tab told her which traps she fell into: profit calculated on the selling price twice, and the "average speed" trap once. She made a contrast card for each ("Profit % is on COST price"; "Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the speeds").

Then she built a mixed set of 20 (two per topic), shuffled, timed. First attempt: 14 right in 22 minutes. A week later, a new mixed set: 18 right in 16 minutes. The five steps felt slow at first; by the second week, naming the type and the principle took her a few seconds.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Worked examples first, then practice | **Strong** | The worked example effect (CESE review): beginners learn more from studied solutions before solving alone. |
| Mixed sets of different arithmetic types | **Moderate** | Interleaving is rated moderate utility, with its strongest evidence in maths (Dunlosky and others, 2013). |
| Solving from principles instead of many formulas | **Limited** | A practical approach consistent with research on self-explanation (Module 8). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, 6.1 Understand Percent](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/6-1-understand-percent) | Review percent conversions and do the end-of-section practice | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e (free, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/preface) | Do a few exercises from the chapters on fractions and decimals, using the five steps | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Collect three previous-year arithmetic questions for each core topic | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For each of the ten topics in the table, write the principle on an AnkiDroid card in your own words, with the worked example on the back.
2. Solve three previous-year questions per topic (or as many as you can find) using the five-step method, writing the type and principle first.
3. Log every error in your Errors tab, and make a contrast card for any trap you fall into.
4. Build a mixed, shuffled set of 20 (two per topic) and solve it timed. Record time and score.
5. A week later, solve a new mixed set of 20 and compare.

**Proof to record:** Your ten principle cards, your worked PYQ solutions with types and principles written, and both mixed-set scores and times.

## Template: topic principle card

```
FRONT: Time and work: the principle?
BACK:  Daily rates add. Rate = 1 / days.
       Example: A 12 days, B 18 days -> 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 a day -> 36/5 = 7.2 days.
(Make one card like this for each topic.)
```

## Template: five-step solving sheet

```
Q ___  Type: ______________  Principle: ____________________________
Set up (with units): ______________________________________________
Calculate: ________________________________________________________
Check (estimate / last digit / units / reverse): ____________________
Answer: ___   Right? Y / N   If wrong, error type (K F I M C G T): ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Hunting for a formula for each question.** Name the type and use its principle; most topics need one or two.
- **Mixing units.** Write units at every step; convert km/h to m/s with × 5/18.
- **Averaging two speeds directly.** Use total distance ÷ total time.
- **Not checking when options are close.** Use the last digit, an estimate or reverse substitution.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. An item is bought for ₹800 and sold for ₹1,000. What is the profit percentage?
    - A) 20%
    - B) 12.5%
    - C) 200%
    - D) 25%
2. What is 72 km/h in metres per second?
    - A) 25
    - B) 18
    - C) 72
    - D) 20
3. A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. How long together?
    - A) 15 days
    - B) 6 days
    - C) 7.2 days
    - D) 30 days
4. What is the compound interest on ₹10,000 at 10% a year for 2 years?
    - A) ₹12,100
    - B) ₹1,100
    - C) ₹2,100
    - D) ₹2,000
5. Divide ₹1,800 in the ratio 2:3:4. What is the largest share?
    - A) ₹900
    - B) ₹720
    - C) ₹800
    - D) ₹600

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Prealgebra on percent, fractions and decimals, and three PYQs per topic
- **Action:** Write principle cards for ten arithmetic topics, solve PYQs with the five steps and compare two mixed sets. It is done when your proof is saved: your ten principle cards, your worked PYQ solutions with types and principles written, and both mixed-set scores and times.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Profit 200 ÷ cost 800 × 100 = 25%.
2. **D.** 72 × 5/18 = 20.
3. **C.** 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 a day, so 36/5 = 7.2 days.
4. **C.** Amount is ₹12,100, so the interest is ₹2,100.
5. **C.** 9 parts of ₹200; the largest is 4 parts.

sections.title: LRN-M14-L03: Reasoning practice and a maths practice system
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Solve the common PSC reasoning types (series, coding, analogies, odd one out, blood relations, directions, clocks and calendars) with a method for each, and run a weekly maths and reasoning practice system. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 55 minutes action plus the first week of the system).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Mental ability questions look varied, but each type has a reliable method. Learn the method, practise it with previous papers, then mix the types (Module 3).

### Reasoning types and their methods

| Type | Method | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number series | Check differences, then ratios, then squares or cubes, then alternate terms | 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?: differences 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next is 30 + 12 = 42 |
| Coding | Write letter positions (A = 1 ... Z = 26) and find the shift | If CAT is written DBU (each letter + 1), DOG is EPH |
| Analogy | State the relationship in a sentence first | Doctor : hospital :: teacher : school (where each works) |
| Odd one out | Find the rule that three share | 9, 25, 49, 50: the first three are squares of odd numbers, so 50 |
| Blood relations | Draw a family tree: generations in rows, + male, − female, = married | "He is the son of my father's only brother": he is my cousin |
| Directions | Draw it, with north at the top | 5 km north, right 3 km, right 5 km: you are 3 km east of the start, facing south |
| Clocks | Angle between the hands = the difference between 30 × hours and 5.5 × minutes (ignore the sign) | At 3:20: 30 × 3 = 90 and 5.5 × 20 = 110, so 20° |
| Calendars | Count odd days: an ordinary year adds 1 weekday, a leap year adds 2 | 1 January 2025 was a Wednesday, so 1 January 2026 is a Thursday |

### Draw it

Blood relations, directions and seating arrangements are hard to hold in working memory (Module 1). **Draw them** on paper: a family tree, a compass sketch, a row of seats. It takes a few seconds and prevents most errors. This is dual coding (Module 3) used as a thinking tool.

### Check against every term

In series questions, a rule that fits two terms may not fit the third. Check your rule against **every** term before choosing an answer.

### A weekly maths and reasoning system

Combine everything in this module into a routine:

| When | What | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every day | Mental-maths warm-up (LRN-M14-L01) | 10 minutes |
| Every day | AnkiDroid: principle cards, squares, fraction-percentages, formulas | Part of your reviews |
| Three days a week | Mixed set of 15 (arithmetic and reasoning), timed, each answer checked straight away | 20 to 25 minutes |
| One day a week | The mental-ability section of a previous paper under exam timing | 20 to 30 minutes |
| Every week | Errors tab updated; next week's weakest type chosen for a practice loop (Module 13) | 10 minutes |
| Every month | Retest on a fresh mixed set; compare with last month | 30 minutes |

## Local example

**Ashiq** was strong in arithmetic but lost marks in reasoning, especially blood relations and directions, which he tried to solve in his head. He started drawing every one: a family tree with + and − signs, a compass sketch for directions. His accuracy on those two types went from about half to almost all within a week.

He then set up the weekly system. Every morning: the 10-minute warm-up. Monday, Wednesday and Friday: a shuffled set of 15 mixed questions, checked one by one. Saturday: the mental-ability section of an unseen previous paper, under the real time limit. Sunday: the Errors tab, and the weakest type chosen for next week's practice loop.

His first month's retest showed his accuracy on mixed sets rising from 70% to 87%, and his time per question falling. Calendar questions became his favourite after he made one card for the odd-days rule and checked it against a calendar.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drawing diagrams for relations, directions and arrangements | **Moderate** | Dual coding (Module 3) and lower working-memory load (Module 1); widely recommended for reasoning. |
| Mixed sets of reasoning and arithmetic types | **Moderate** | Interleaving: moderate utility, strongest in maths and category learning. |
| A weekly practice system with timed sections | **Limited** | A practical combination of spacing, retrieval, interleaving and feedback; judge it by your monthly retests. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Collect two previous-year questions for each reasoning type from the mental-ability sections | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: interleaving materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/interleaving) | Revisit the interleaving poster before building mixed sets | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, chapter 5: Logic and Reasoning](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/5-introduction) | Optional: read 5.4 Types of Inferences for the logic behind patterns | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For each of the eight reasoning types, write the method on an AnkiDroid card with one example.
2. Solve two previous-year questions per type with the method, drawing a diagram for blood relations and directions.
3. Set up the weekly maths and reasoning system in your study planner for next week.
4. Run the first week: daily warm-ups, three mixed sets, one timed previous-paper section, and the Sunday Errors-tab review.
5. Choose your weakest reasoning type for a practice loop next week.

**Proof to record:** Your eight method cards, the solved PYQs with diagrams, and your first week's system log with scores.

## Template: reasoning methods card set

```
SERIES      differences -> ratios -> squares/cubes -> alternate terms; check EVERY term
CODING      A=1 ... Z=26; find the shift or pattern; apply it to the new word
ANALOGY     say the relationship in a sentence first
ODD ONE OUT find the rule three items share
RELATIONS   family tree: rows = generations, + male, - female, = married
DIRECTIONS  sketch with north at the top; track turns (right = clockwise)
CLOCKS      angle = difference between 30H and 5.5M (ignore the sign)
CALENDARS   ordinary year +1 weekday, leap year +2; count odd days
```

## Template: weekly maths and reasoning system log

```
WEEK ___
Mon  warm-up ___/20 in ___ | mixed set ___/15 in ___ min
Tue  warm-up ___/20 in ___
Wed  warm-up ___/20 in ___ | mixed set ___/15 in ___ min
Thu  warm-up ___/20 in ___
Fri  warm-up ___/20 in ___ | mixed set ___/15 in ___ min
Sat  previous-paper mental ability section: ___/___ in ___ min
Sun  Errors tab updated [ ]  weakest type for next week: ______________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Solving relations and directions in your head.** Draw them. A few seconds of sketching prevents most errors.
- **Accepting a series rule that fits only two terms.** Check the rule against every term.
- **Practising each reasoning type only in blocks.** Mix types in timed sets, as the exam does.
- **Skipping clock and calendar rules because they seem hard.** Each is one formula or one rule, and questions on them are often quick marks.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the next number in 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
    - A) 40
    - B) 36
    - C) 42
    - D) 44
2. What is the angle between the clock hands at 3:20?
    - A) 0°
    - B) 40°
    - C) 20°
    - D) 30°
3. You walk 5 km north, turn right and walk 3 km, then turn right and walk 5 km. Where are you?
    - A) 3 km east of the start
    - B) Back at the start
    - C) 3 km west of the start
    - D) 10 km south of the start
4. If CAT is written DBU, how is DOG written?
    - A) CNF
    - B) DPH
    - C) EPH
    - D) EPG
5. 1 January 2025 was a Wednesday. What day is 1 January 2026?
    - A) Friday
    - B) Tuesday
    - C) Thursday
    - D) Wednesday

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Two previous-year questions per reasoning type, and the interleaving poster
- **Action:** Learn a method for eight reasoning types and run the first week of the maths and reasoning system. It is done when your proof is saved: your eight method cards, the solved PYQs with diagrams, and your first week's system log with scores.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12.
2. **C.** 30 × 3 = 90 and 5.5 × 20 = 110; they differ by 20°.
3. **A.** North, then east, then south: you end 3 km east, facing south.
4. **C.** Each letter moves forward by one.
5. **C.** 2025 is not a leap year, so the weekday moves on by one.

sections.title: Module 15: Language learning
sections.summary: Learn languages the way the research suggests: lots of understandable input, regular output with feedback, and vocabulary with spaced repetition. Apply it to PSC English and Malayalam, improve listening and pronunciation with shadowing, and plan any new language for after PSC.
sections.content:
## Overview

Language questions are some of the most learnable marks in a PSC paper, and English and Malayalam skills keep paying off long after the exam. This module uses the tools you already have (AnkiDroid, practice loops, previous-paper analysis and recordings) and adds the two habits that matter most for language: daily input and daily vocabulary.

The result is a language routine: a vocabulary deck, rule cards from your own mistakes, a listening and shadowing habit, and a plan for your next language.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain the roles of input, output and vocabulary
- Build a vocabulary deck with meaning, production, cloze and phrase cards
- Find and fix your weakest PSC English areas with rule cards and practice loops
- Improve listening and pronunciation with daily input and shadowing, measured by recordings
- Apply the same methods to PSC Malayalam and plan a new language

## Time

About 7 hours in total: 5 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 17–18, with the module project due in week 18.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M15-L01: How languages are learned: input, output and vocabulary (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M15-L02: English for PSC (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
3. LRN-M15-L03: Listening, speaking and shadowing (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
4. LRN-M15-L04: PSC Malayalam, and a plan for any new language (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **vocabulary card formats** and **word-capture list**
- The **English syllabus map** and **rule card format**
- The **shadowing steps** and **listening and speaking log**
- The **PSC Malayalam map** and **new-language plan**

## Module project: My language routine

1. Grow your English (or Malayalam) vocabulary deck to at least 100 notes, all from words you have met.
2. Show the accuracy trend from your English grammar practice loops and one Malayalam loop.
3. Keep your day-1 and day-14 listening and speaking recordings with your comparison.
4. Write your daily and weekly language routine on one card, and your new-language plan for after PSC.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your vocabulary deck with 100 or more notes, your practice-loop sheets, the two recordings with comparison, and your routine card and plan.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vocabulary | Word lists only | A deck with meaning cards only | 100 or more notes from real reading, with production and cloze cards |
| Grammar | Studying the whole grammar book | Weak areas known | Weak areas fixed with rule cards and loops, accuracy rising |
| Listening and speaking | None | Some listening | Daily listening, shadowing and recorded talks compared over two weeks |
| Malayalam and new language | Malayalam ignored | Malayalam cards made | Malayalam loops and cards, and a new-language plan written |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Add five words a day from your reading to a vocabulary deck.
- Run one practice loop a week on your weakest English or Malayalam area.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| The three things every language is learned through | Input, output and vocabulary. |
| Production card | Meaning on the front, the word on the back: it trains using the word. |
| Why example sentences on vocabulary cards | Words live in phrases; the sentence shows how they are used. |
| Question tag for a positive statement | A negative tag: "He is a doctor, isn't he?" |
| Shadowing | Speaking along with a recording, just behind the speaker. |
| Evidence for shadowing | Small studies with promising results; not proven. |
| First Jnanpith Award | G. Sankara Kurup, in 1965. |
| A free source of audio language courses | Language Transfer. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Collecting word lists instead of meeting words in reading.** Learn words from your reading and papers, with their sentences.
- **Practising only the language skills you enjoy.** Your error data chooses your next practice loop.

sections.title: LRN-M15-L01: How languages are learned: input, output and vocabulary
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain the roles of input, output and vocabulary in learning a language, and start an AnkiDroid vocabulary deck with card formats that build real use, not just recognition. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Whether it is English for PSC, Malayalam grammar, or Hindi or Arabic for a future job, every language is learned through the same three things.

### 1. Input: lots of understandable listening and reading

You learn a language mostly by understanding it: hearing and reading a lot of it, at a level where you understand most of what you meet. Language researchers broadly agree that large amounts of such input are essential. The stronger claim, that input alone is enough and practice in speaking adds nothing, is disputed. (No single source was checked for this course on this point; treat it as the general picture.) For you, input means daily reading (Module 10) and listening (LRN-M15-L03).

### 2. Output: speaking and writing

When you try to say or write something, you notice what you can't yet say: a missing word, a tense you're unsure of. That gap is where learning happens, if you get feedback. Output includes your Feynman explanations in English (Module 8), writing answers, and speaking with a partner (Module 20).

### 3. Vocabulary: the words that carry meaning

Without enough words, input is incomprehensible and output is impossible. Vocabulary is also tested directly in PSC: synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutes, idioms, spelling. And vocabulary is exactly where spaced repetition shines: thousands of small items, each needing retrieval at growing gaps (Module 4).

### Learn phrases, not lonely words

Words live in company. "Decision" is used with "make" (make a decision), "exam" with "take" or "write" (take an exam), "interested" with "in". Learning these chunks (collocations and phrases) helps both understanding and correct use. So every vocabulary card should include an **example sentence**, ideally one from your reading.

### Four card formats for vocabulary

| Format | Front | Back | What it trains |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meaning | diligent (word, with an example sentence) | hard-working, careful; Malayalam: ഉത്സാഹമുള്ള | Understanding |
| Production | hard-working and careful (one word): "a ___ student" | diligent | Using the word: harder and more useful |
| Cloze sentence | She was {{c1::diligent}} about her daily reviews. | diligent | The word in context |
| Phrase | to stop working for the day (idiom) | to call it a day | Idioms and set phrases |

Use **production** and **cloze** cards for words you want to use; **meaning** cards for words you only need to recognise. Avoid the keyword mnemonic as your main method: Dunlosky and colleagues rated it low utility, partly because its benefits for vocabulary may not last ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)).

### Which words first?

Common words first: the words you meet again and again in your reading, in previous papers and in the news. A word from three PSC papers is worth more than a rare word from a vocabulary list.

## Local example

**Sreeja** had a notebook of English words copied from a "1,000 words for competitive exams" list, but she couldn't use them and kept forgetting them.

She started a deck called `Lang::English::Vocabulary` and filled it only with words and phrases she had met: in the English sections of previous papers, in LearnEnglish texts and in the newspaper. For each she wrote an example sentence from where she had found it. She used production cards for words she wanted to use ("hard-working and careful (one word)") and meaning cards for rarer ones, with a Malayalam gloss.

She added 8 new cards a day. After four weeks she had about 220 cards and noticed the difference in two places: English passages in mocks were easier to follow, and she got synonym and antonym questions right that she would once have guessed.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced retrieval for vocabulary | **Strong** | Practice testing and spacing (both high utility) suit vocabulary well. |
| Large amounts of understandable input | **Moderate** | Widely accepted in language research; the claim that input alone is enough is disputed. |
| Learning words with example sentences and phrases | **Limited** | Sensible and widely recommended; no specific source was checked for this course. |
| The keyword mnemonic for vocabulary | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [British Council LearnEnglish (free)](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/) | Open the vocabulary section and do one exercise at your level | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Anki manual: Editing (cloze deletion and image occlusion)](https://docs.ankiweb.net/editing.html) | Refresh cloze syntax for sentence cards | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Reread the keyword mnemonic section on vocabulary | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Create a deck named Lang::English::Vocabulary (or a Malayalam or other language deck if English is not your priority).
2. Collect 30 words and phrases you have actually met: from the English sections of your previous papers, your reading log (Module 10) and the news.
3. Make cards in at least three of the four formats, each with an example sentence and a Malayalam gloss where it helps.
4. Set the deck to 5 to 10 new cards a day, within your total AnkiDroid budget.
5. Keep a word-capture list on your phone or in your notebook, and add to it during reading and listening.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your vocabulary deck with at least 30 notes, and one example of each card format you used.

## Template: vocabulary card formats

```
MEANING      Front: diligent  ("She was diligent about her reviews.")
             Back:  hard-working and careful | ഉത്സാഹമുള്ള
PRODUCTION   Front: hard-working and careful (one word): "a ___ student"
             Back:  diligent
CLOZE        She was {{c1::diligent}} about her daily reviews.
PHRASE       Front: to stop working for the day (idiom)
             Back:  to call it a day  ("It was late, so we called it a day.")
```

## Template: word-capture list

```
WORD CAPTURE     (add during reading and listening; make cards within 24 hours)
Date   | Word or phrase | Sentence where I met it                 | Source        | Card made?
______ | ______________ | _______________________________________ | ____________ | [ ]
______ | ______________ | _______________________________________ | ____________ | [ ]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Learning lonely words from long lists.** Learn words you meet, with the sentence you met them in.
- **Only meaning cards.** Add production and cloze cards for words you want to use.
- **Fifty new words a day.** Five to ten a day, within your AnkiDroid budget, lasts.
- **Rare words first.** Common words from your papers and reading first.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which card trains you to use a word, not just recognise it?
    - A) A highlighted word in a book
    - B) "Hard-working and careful (one word)" → diligent
    - C) A list of 50 words
    - D) "Diligent" → hard-working and careful
2. Why include an example sentence on vocabulary cards?
    - A) Words are used in phrases and contexts; the sentence shows how
    - B) It makes cards longer
    - C) AnkiDroid requires it
    - D) It isn't useful
3. Which words should you learn first?
    - A) The rarest words you can find
    - B) Words starting with A
    - C) Words from a random list
    - D) Common words you meet in your reading and previous papers
4. What is the honest position on "input alone is enough to learn a language"?
    - A) Input is essential, but the claim that it alone is enough is disputed
    - B) Proven false: input doesn't matter
    - C) Proven true
    - D) Only children need input

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The LearnEnglish vocabulary section and the Anki cloze refresher
- **Action:** Start a vocabulary deck with 30 words and phrases you have met, in at least three card formats. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your vocabulary deck with at least 30 notes, and one example of each card format you used.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Production cards make you recall the word itself.
2. **A.** Context and collocations help understanding and correct use.
3. **D.** Frequent words pay off most in understanding and in exams.
4. **A.** Most agree input is essential; output and feedback also help.

sections.title: LRN-M15-L02: English for PSC
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Map the English part of your PSC syllabus, find your weakest areas from previous papers, and fix them with rule cards and practice loops. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What PSC English usually tests

English sections in general Kerala PSC papers commonly cover areas like these. **Check your own syllabus**, because the exact list differs between exams:

| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Grammar | Articles, prepositions, tenses, subject-verb agreement, active and passive voice, direct and indirect speech, question tags, degrees of comparison |
| Vocabulary | Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, phrasal verbs, foreign words and phrases |
| Spelling and correction | Correctly spelt words, spotting the error in a sentence |
| Comprehension | Short passages with questions, in some exams |

### Find your weak areas from data

Tag the English questions from your saved previous papers by area in your PYQ tab (Module 12). Your errors will cluster in two or three areas. Those are your practice-loop targets (Module 13), not the whole grammar book.

### Rule cards with your own mistakes

For each weak area, learn the rule with examples (the LearnEnglish grammar pages explain each area simply, by level: [LearnEnglish](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/)), then make **rule cards** that include a sentence you got wrong and its correction:

| Area | Rule card front | Back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question tags | He is a doctor, ___ ? (tag) | isn't he? A positive statement takes a negative tag. |
| Subject-verb agreement | Each of the students ___ (have / has) a book. | has: "each" takes a singular verb. |
| Articles | ___ honest man (a / an) | an: the choice follows the sound, and "honest" starts with a vowel sound. |
| Articles | ___ university (a / an) | a: "university" starts with a "yoo" sound. |
| Prepositions | good ___, interested ___, afraid ___ | good at, interested in, afraid of |
| Reported speech | He said, "I am tired." (indirect) | He said that he was tired. |
| Passive voice | The PSC conducts the exam. (passive) | The exam is conducted by the PSC. |
| One-word substitution | Fear of heights (one word) | acrophobia |
| Idioms | a piece of cake | something very easy |

### Practice loops for grammar

For a weak area, take 10 sentences at a time from previous papers or LearnEnglish exercises. Do one, check it immediately, and if it is wrong, say which rule you broke and make or update a rule card. Then do two more of the same kind. Track accuracy over three sessions (Module 13).

### Spelling

Spelling questions often use the same troublesome words: accommodation, committee, necessary, separate, occurrence, embarrass. Put misspellings you meet into cloze cards, with the tricky letters as the gap ("acco{c1::mm}odation").

### A daily English habit

Ten minutes of English reading (Module 10), five new words or phrases (LRN-M15-L01), and one grammar loop a week is enough to move steadily, alongside the rest of your PSC study.

## Local example

**Ashiq** believed his English was "fine" because he read English news easily. Tagging 50 English questions from three previous papers told a different story: 9 of his 14 errors were in prepositions and question tags.

He made 20 rule cards, each with a sentence he had got wrong and its correction, for example "afraid ___ the dark: afraid of" and "You haven't finished, ___? : have you?". Then he ran three practice loops of 10 sentences each on prepositions and question tags, checking each sentence as he went.

His accuracy on those two areas rose from 45% to 70% to 90% across the three sessions. In a mixed set of 20 English questions a week later he scored 18, and the two misses were spelling, which became his next loop.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Practice on weak grammar areas with immediate feedback | **Moderate** | Consistent with research on practice testing and feedback (Modules 3 and 13). |
| Rule cards built from your own mistakes | **Limited** | A practical method combining feedback and spaced retrieval; no direct study of this format. |
| Spaced retrieval of rules, idioms and spellings | **Strong** | Practice testing and spacing, rated high utility. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [British Council LearnEnglish (free)](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/) | Open the grammar section and study your two weakest areas at your level, with their exercises | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Collect the English questions from your saved papers for tagging | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SCERT Kerala: school textbooks](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/) | Optional: the grammar sections of SCERT English textbooks for your level | As needed | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. List the English areas in your exam's syllabus.
2. Tag at least 50 English questions from previous papers by area in your PYQ tab, and mark which you got wrong.
3. Choose your two weakest areas. Learn each rule with examples, and make at least 20 rule cards that include your own wrong sentences, corrected.
4. Run three practice loops of 10 sentences on each weak area, checking each sentence immediately. Record accuracy.
5. A week later, do a mixed set of 20 English questions and score it.

**Proof to record:** Your tagged English questions with the weak areas marked, your rule cards, the practice-loop sheets with accuracy, and the mixed-set score.

## Template: English syllabus map

```
ENGLISH MAP     Exam: ______________
Area                 In my syllabus?   PYQs tagged   My errors   Priority
Articles             Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Prepositions         Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Tenses               Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Agreement            Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Voice                Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Reported speech      Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Question tags        Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Synonyms/antonyms    Y / N             ___           ___         ___
One-word substitutes Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Idioms and phrases   Y / N             ___           ___         ___
Spelling/correction  Y / N             ___           ___         ___
```

## Template: rule card format

```
FRONT: [area]: [your wrong sentence with a gap or choice]
BACK:  [correct form] + the rule in one line + one more example
Example:
FRONT: Question tags: You haven't finished, ___ ?
BACK:  have you? A negative statement takes a positive tag. ("She can't swim, can she?")
```

## Common mistakes

- **Learning grammar terms without practising.** Rules stick through practice loops with immediate checking.
- **Studying the whole grammar book.** Your errors show the two or three areas that matter; start there.
- **Idioms without example sentences.** Put each idiom in a sentence on its card.
- **Ignoring spelling.** Spelling questions repeat the same tricky words; card them.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Choose the correct tag: "He is a doctor, ___?"
    - A) wasn't he
    - B) doesn't he
    - C) isn't he
    - D) is he
2. Choose the correct verb: "Each of the students ___ a book."
    - A) has
    - B) are having
    - C) were having
    - D) have
3. Which is correct?
    - A) the honest a man
    - B) a honest man
    - C) an honest man
    - D) honest an man
4. What is one word for "fear of heights"?
    - A) acrophobia
    - B) xenophobia
    - C) hydrophobia
    - D) claustrophobia
5. Change to indirect speech: He said, "I am tired."
    - A) He said that I am tired.
    - B) He says he is tired.
    - C) He said that he is being tired.
    - D) He said that he was tired.

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The LearnEnglish grammar pages for your two weakest areas, and the English questions in your saved papers
- **Action:** Tag 50 English PYQs, make rule cards for your two weakest areas and run three practice loops on each. It is done when your proof is saved: your tagged English questions with the weak areas marked, your rule cards, the practice-loop sheets with accuracy, and the mixed-set score.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** A positive statement takes a negative tag with the same auxiliary.
2. **A.** "Each" takes a singular verb.
3. **C.** The article follows the sound; "honest" starts with a vowel sound.
4. **A.** Claustrophobia is fear of closed spaces; hydrophobia, of water; xenophobia, of foreigners.
5. **D.** The pronoun changes and the present tense moves back to the past.
