sections.title: LRN-M15-L03: Listening, speaking and shadowing
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Improve listening and pronunciation with daily input and shadowing, and practise speaking every week with a simple routine, even without a partner. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 15 minutes a day for two weeks).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Listening every day

Listening is input (LRN-M15-L01), and it helps reading, speaking and comprehension questions. Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough to make progress, if the audio is at the right level: you should understand most of it.

Two free sources do double duty:

- **All India Radio News** in English: national and regional bulletins with audio ([newsonair.gov.in](https://newsonair.gov.in/)). Listening to a bulletin is English practice and current affairs at the same time (Module 10).
- **British Council LearnEnglish:** listening practice at levels from beginner to advanced, with tasks and transcripts, and a speaking section ([LearnEnglish](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/)).

### Shadowing

**Shadowing** means speaking along with a recording, a fraction of a second behind the speaker, copying their words, rhythm and intonation, like a shadow. It trains pronunciation, rhythm and listening together.

1. **Choose a clip** of 30 to 60 seconds with a transcript (LearnEnglish has many).
2. **Listen twice** without speaking.
3. **Read the transcript** and check any words you didn't catch.
4. **Shadow with the transcript:** speak along with the audio, three times.
5. **Shadow without the transcript,** three times.
6. **Record yourself** once and compare it with the original.

Honest evidence: shadowing has been studied mostly in small studies, many with learners of English in Japan, with promising results for listening and pronunciation. It is not proven, but it is free, quick and easy to measure with recordings.

### Speaking without a partner

You can practise speaking alone:

- **Talk to yourself** in English while walking or cooking: describe what you are doing.
- **One-minute talks:** pick a PSC topic, speak about it for one minute without notes, and record it. This is also retrieval practice; your Feynman explanations (Module 8) can be in English.
- **Read aloud** a paragraph from your reading practice each day.

With a partner or study group (Module 20), add a weekly 15-minute English conversation on a PSC topic. For posts that include an interview, speaking practice also helps you feel at ease.

### Measure it

Record a one-minute talk and a shadowed clip on day 1. Record the same clip and a new talk on day 14. Listen to both: is your speech smoother, are there fewer long pauses, are hard words clearer?

## Local example

**Anu** could read English well but froze when she had to speak, and she found fast English news hard to follow. She started 15 minutes a day: on most days a 10-minute English bulletin from All India Radio News while she prepared tea, then 5 minutes of shadowing a 45-second LearnEnglish clip.

On day 1 she recorded herself shadowing the clip and giving a one-minute talk on the Kerala renaissance in English. Listening back was uncomfortable: long pauses, and "renaissance" pronounced three different ways.

She kept going for two weeks, with three one-minute talks a week on PSC topics. On day 14 she recorded the same clip and a new talk. Her shadowing kept up with the speaker almost all the way, and her talk had two pauses instead of nine. The news bulletins were easier to follow too, and she started noting their facts for current affairs.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily listening at an understandable level | **Moderate** | Input is widely accepted as essential for language learning. |
| Shadowing for pronunciation and listening | **Limited** | Small studies, many with Japanese learners of English; promising, not proven. |
| Recording yourself and comparing over time | **Limited** | A practical feedback tool; it makes progress audible. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [All India Radio News (News Services Division)](https://newsonair.gov.in/) | Listen to one English news bulletin and note three facts | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [British Council LearnEnglish (free)](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/) | Open the listening and speaking sections; choose a clip at your level with a transcript | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a 30 to 60 second clip with a transcript at your level. On day 1, record yourself shadowing it and giving a one-minute talk on a PSC topic.
2. For 14 days, listen for 10 minutes a day (a news bulletin or a LearnEnglish track) and shadow your clip for 5 minutes on at least five days a week.
3. Give and record three one-minute talks a week on PSC topics, without notes.
4. Log each day in the listening and speaking log.
5. On day 14, record the same clip and a new talk. Compare with day 1 and write three lines on what changed.

**Proof to record:** Your day-1 and day-14 recordings, the two-week log, and your three lines of comparison.

## Template: shadowing steps

```
SHADOWING      Clip: ______________ (30-60 s, with transcript)
[ ] Listen twice, no speaking
[ ] Read the transcript; check words I didn't catch: ____________________
[ ] Shadow with the transcript x3
[ ] Shadow without the transcript x3
[ ] Record once; compare with the original. Hardest words: ______________
```

## Template: listening and speaking log

```
Day | Listened (source, minutes) | Shadowed? | One-minute talk (topic) | Note
1   | ________________________   | Y / N     | ______________________  | recorded [ ]
2   | ________________________   | Y / N     | ______________________  | ______
...
14  | ________________________   | Y / N     | ______________________  | recorded [ ]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Listening to audio far above your level.** You should understand most of it; otherwise choose an easier level.
- **Shadowing without ever checking the transcript.** Check the words you didn't catch, or you will copy mistakes.
- **Never recording yourself.** Day-1 and day-14 recordings show progress you can't feel.
- **Waiting for a partner before speaking.** Self-talk, one-minute talks and reading aloud work alone.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is shadowing?
    - A) Speaking along with a recording just behind the speaker, copying rhythm and intonation
    - B) Reading silently in a dark room
    - C) Writing a summary of a podcast
    - D) Translating every word
2. What is the honest evidence position on shadowing?
    - A) Shown to harm pronunciation
    - B) Proven in hundreds of large trials
    - C) Small studies with promising results; not proven
    - D) Never studied
3. Which free source gives English practice and current affairs at once?
    - A) A random music channel
    - B) A paid language app
    - C) All India Radio News English bulletins
    - D) None
4. How can you practise speaking without a partner?
    - A) One-minute recorded talks on PSC topics, self-talk and reading aloud
    - B) Only by writing
    - C) Only by listening
    - D) You can't

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** One All India Radio English bulletin and the LearnEnglish listening and speaking sections
- **Action:** Listen daily, shadow a clip and record one-minute talks for two weeks, comparing day 1 with day 14. It is done when your proof is saved: your day-1 and day-14 recordings, the two-week log, and your three lines of comparison.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** It trains pronunciation, rhythm and listening together.
2. **C.** Many studies are small, often with learners in Japan.
3. **C.** News bulletins are listening practice and PSC current affairs together.
4. **A.** Speaking alone still gives output practice, and recordings give feedback.

sections.title: LRN-M15-L04: PSC Malayalam, and a plan for any new language
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Apply the course's methods to the Malayalam part of your PSC syllabus, and write a plan for learning a new language with free resources. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Part A: PSC Malayalam

Many aspirants neglect Malayalam because it is their own language, then lose easy marks to grammar and vocabulary questions. Malayalam sections in general PSC papers commonly include areas like these; **check your own syllabus**:

| Area | Examples (Malayalam terms) |
| --- | --- |
| Vocabulary | പര്യായപദങ്ങൾ (synonyms), വിപരീതപദങ്ങൾ (antonyms), ഒറ്റപ്പദം (one-word substitution) |
| Grammar | സന്ധി (sandhi), സമാസം (samasam), ശരിയായ പ്രയോഗം and വാക്യശുദ്ധി (correct usage, sentence correction) |
| Idioms and proverbs | ശൈലികൾ, പഴഞ്ചൊല്ലുകൾ |
| Literature | Authors, works, pen names, awards |
| Translation | English sentences or phrases into Malayalam |

The same tools work here:

- **Vocabulary deck:** synonyms and antonyms are perfect for cards, for example the synonyms of സൂര്യൻ (sun) such as ആദിത്യൻ, ഭാനു, രവി and ദിവാകരൻ. Use one card per word, or a cloze per synonym, rather than a list on one card (Module 4).
- **Grammar rule cards** with examples and your own mistakes, plus practice loops (LRN-M15-L02 and Module 13).
- **Literature facts:** cards, acrostics and memory palaces (Module 11). For example, the Malayalam Jnanpith winners in order: G. Sankara Kurup (1965, the first Jnanpith of all), S. K. Pottekkatt (1980), Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai (1984), M. T. Vasudevan Nair (1995), O. N. V. Kurup (2007) and Akkitham Achuthan Namboothiri (2019) ([Jnanpith Award list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award)).
- **Translation:** practise with previous-year questions and check against the answer keys.

Use your SCERT Malayalam textbooks and previous papers as the main sources ([SCERT Kerala](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/); [previous papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers)).

### Part B: any new language

After PSC, you may want Hindi for central government work, Arabic for a job in the Gulf, or German, French or Spanish for interest or study. The system is the same:

1. **A functional goal:** "introduce myself and talk about my work for five minutes", "read a simple notice", not "learn Arabic".
2. **A main free course:** Language Transfer offers free audio courses with no fees, adverts or sign-up, in languages including Arabic, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Greek, Turkish and Swahili ([Language Transfer](https://www.languagetransfer.org/)).
3. **Daily input:** a little listening and reading you mostly understand.
4. **A vocabulary deck** in AnkiDroid with the formats from LRN-M15-L01.
5. **Output:** self-talk, one-minute talks, and later a conversation partner.
6. **Shadowing** short clips for pronunciation (LRN-M15-L03).
7. **A baseline and monthly checks:** a recorded self-introduction now, and every month.

If your PSC exam is near, write the plan now and start after the exam.

## Local example

**Joseph sir** was surprised when his study group's previous-paper analysis showed that several members, all native Malayalam speakers, were losing marks in the Malayalam section. Synonyms, sandhi and pen names were the main problems.

The group built a shared list of Malayalam vocabulary from previous papers and SCERT textbooks; each member made their own cards from it, one synonym per card. Joseph sir taught one sandhi rule each week with examples, and members ran practice loops on it. For literature, Sreeja made a memory palace of the six Malayalam Jnanpith winners in order along the road from her house to the bus stop.

Vinod, who drives an autorickshaw and hopes to work in the Gulf, wrote a new-language plan for Arabic: a goal of a five-minute self-introduction and talk about driving work, Language Transfer's free Arabic course for 20 minutes a day after his PSC exam, and an AnkiDroid deck for words from the course. He recorded his baseline self-introduction: "Marhaba." That was all, and that was fine.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced retrieval for Malayalam vocabulary and literature facts | **Strong** | Practice testing and spacing, rated high utility, suit these facts well. |
| Practice loops with rule cards for grammar | **Moderate** | Immediate feedback on specific weaknesses (Module 13). |
| Free audio courses such as Language Transfer | **Limited** | No research on this particular course was checked for this course; judge it by your monthly recordings. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Collect the Malayalam questions from your saved papers | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SCERT Kerala: school textbooks](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/) | Find the Malayalam textbook for your level for grammar and vocabulary | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Wikipedia: Jnanpith Award (list of recipients)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award) | Check the Malayalam Jnanpith winners and years before making cards | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Language Transfer: free audio courses](https://www.languagetransfer.org/) | Look through the free courses and choose one if you plan a new language | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. List the Malayalam areas in your exam's syllabus, and tag at least 30 Malayalam questions from previous papers by area. Find your two weakest areas.
2. Make at least 30 Malayalam cards from your weak areas (synonyms, antonyms, idioms, grammar rules or literature facts), checked against your textbook.
3. Run one practice loop of 10 items on your weakest grammar area, checking each immediately.
4. Write a new-language plan for one language you want after PSC, using the template.
5. If your exam is not close, do the first lesson of your chosen free course and record a baseline self-introduction.

**Proof to record:** Your tagged Malayalam questions, the 30 cards, the practice-loop sheet, and your new-language plan (with a baseline recording if you started).

## Template: PSC Malayalam map

```
MALAYALAM MAP     Exam: ______________
Area                                  In syllabus?   PYQs   My errors   Plan
പര്യായപദങ്ങൾ (synonyms)                Y / N          ___    ___         cards
വിപരീതപദങ്ങൾ (antonyms)                Y / N          ___    ___         cards
ഒറ്റപ്പദം (one-word substitution)        Y / N          ___    ___         cards
സന്ധി / സമാസം (sandhi / samasam)        Y / N          ___    ___         rule cards + loops
ശരിയായ പ്രയോഗം (correct usage)          Y / N          ___    ___         rule cards + loops
ശൈലികൾ / പഴഞ്ചൊല്ലുകൾ (idioms/proverbs) Y / N          ___    ___         cards with examples
Literature (authors, works, awards)    Y / N          ___    ___         cards / palace
Translation                            Y / N          ___    ___         PYQ practice
```

## Template: new-language plan

```
NEW LANGUAGE PLAN      Language: __________   Start date: ______
Goal (what I will be able to DO): ___________________________________
Main free course: ______________________   Minutes a day: ___
Daily input (listening/reading): ______________________________
Vocabulary deck: Lang::__________::Vocabulary   new cards a day: ___
Output: self-talk [ ]  one-minute talks [ ]  partner (later): ______
Shadowing clips from: ______________________
Baseline (recorded self-introduction) on ______; monthly checks on ______
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring Malayalam because it is your own language.** PSC Malayalam tests grammar and vocabulary you may not use every day. Check your error data.
- **Literature lists without hooks.** Use cards, acrostics or a memory palace, after checking the facts.
- **Putting all synonyms of a word on one card.** One card or one cloze per synonym.
- **Starting a new language just before the exam.** Write the plan now; start when the exam is over.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is a synonym (പര്യായം) of സൂര്യൻ?
    - A) പർവതം
    - B) ആദിത്യൻ
    - C) സമുദ്രം
    - D) ചന്ദ്രൻ
2. Who received the first Jnanpith Award, in 1965?
    - A) O. N. V. Kurup
    - B) M. T. Vasudevan Nair
    - C) Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai
    - D) G. Sankara Kurup
3. Which is a well-written goal for a new language?
    - A) "Learn Arabic"
    - B) "Be fluent soon"
    - C) "Introduce myself and talk about my work for five minutes"
    - D) "Watch Arabic films"
4. What does Language Transfer offer?
    - A) Paid coaching only
    - B) Free audio language courses, run on donations
    - C) Malayalam grammar notes
    - D) PSC mock tests

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Malayalam questions in your saved papers, your SCERT Malayalam textbook and (optionally) Language Transfer
- **Action:** Map PSC Malayalam, make 30 cards from your weak areas, run one loop and write a new-language plan. It is done when your proof is saved: your tagged Malayalam questions, the 30 cards, the practice-loop sheet, and your new-language plan (with a baseline recording if you started).
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** ആദിത്യൻ, ഭാനു, രവി and ദിവാകരൻ are synonyms of സൂര്യൻ.
2. **D.** He was the first recipient of the award in any language.
3. **C.** A functional goal can be tested and measured.
4. **B.** Its courses have no fees, adverts or sign-up.

sections.title: Module 16: Thinking skills
sections.summary: Think more clearly: judge claims by evidence and sources, test arguments with logic and Venn diagrams, solve unfamiliar problems with a four-step process and a few mental models, and catch the cognitive biases that distort study decisions.
sections.content:
## Overview

Thinking skills appear in PSC papers directly (statements and conclusions, assumptions, syllogisms) and indirectly in every decision about how to prepare. This module uses free OpenStax books on philosophy and psychology, applies them to PSC questions and to forwards, guides and coaching claims, and is honest that knowing about thinking errors is not the same as avoiding them.

The result is a thinking toolkit: the five-minute claim check, the Venn method, the four-step sheet, the inversion list and the debiasing checklist.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Judge claims by evidence and rank your PSC sources
- Tell deductive from inductive reasoning and test validity
- Solve syllogisms with Venn diagrams and spot common fallacies
- Use Pólya's four steps and a few mental models on unfamiliar problems
- Audit your own biases and use a debiasing checklist for decisions

## Time

About 6 hours in total: 5 hours of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 18–19, with the module project due in week 19.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M16-L01: Critical thinking: claims, evidence and sources (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M16-L02: Logical reasoning (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M16-L03: Mental models and problem solving (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
4. LRN-M16-L04: Cognitive biases (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **five-minute claim check** and **PSC source ranking**
- The **Venn diagram method** and **fallacy spotting card**
- The **four-step problem sheet** and **inversion list**
- The **bias audit** and **debiasing checklist**

## Module project: My thinking toolkit

1. Check five more claims you meet this week with the five-minute check.
2. Solve a mixed set of 15 reasoning questions from previous papers (syllogisms, assumptions, statements and conclusions), with diagrams where needed.
3. Review the decision you made with the debiasing checklist: was it right, given what happened?
4. Put your five tools on one page: your thinking checklist for study and exams.

**Proof to record:** Your five new claim checks, the 15-question mixed set with score, your decision review and your one-page thinking checklist.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claims and sources | Believes forwards | Checks sometimes | Checks claims with the routine and ranks sources |
| Logic | Answers syllogisms from real-world knowledge | Draws one diagram | Draws every diagram and knows valid forms |
| Problem solving | Calculates before understanding | Uses some steps | Uses all four steps and working backwards |
| Biases | Sees biases only in others | Knows the names | Audited own biases and used the checklist on a real decision |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use the five-minute claim check on every forward about PSC.
- Draw Venn diagrams for every syllogism question.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Critical thinking | Judging claims by evidence and reasoning, not by who says them or how confident they sound. |
| The five-minute check | Stop, find the original source, check sideways, check the date, decide. |
| Valid versus sound | Valid: the conclusion follows. Sound: valid and the premises are true. |
| Affirming the result (invalid) | If P then Q; Q; so P. |
| When a syllogism conclusion follows | Only if it is true in every possible diagram. |
| Pólya's four steps | Understand, plan, carry out, look back. |
| Inversion | Ask "what would make me fail?" and prevent each cause. |
| Sunk cost bias | Continuing something because of what you already spent on it. |
| Planning fallacy | Underestimating how long things take; plan from your real data. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Treating thinking skills as theory.** Use them on today's forwards, questions and decisions.
- **Judging other people's thinking more harshly than your own.** Audit your own decisions first.

sections.title: LRN-M16-L01: Critical thinking: claims, evidence and sources
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Judge claims by their evidence and sources, check a forward or video claim in five minutes, and rank your PSC sources by reliability. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What critical thinking means

**Critical thinking** means judging a claim by its evidence and reasoning, not by who says it, how confident they sound or how many people share it. OpenStax's free *Introduction to Philosophy* explains how to gather information, evaluate sources and understand evidence ([chapter 2, section 2.4](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/2-introduction)).

For a PSC aspirant, this is practical every day: forwarded "notifications", coaching PDFs with wrong facts, guides that disagree with textbooks, and videos that promise secrets.

### Three kinds of claim

- **Facts:** can be checked ("The Temple Entry Proclamation was issued in 1936").
- **Opinions and values:** can be argued but not proved ("this is the best guide").
- **Predictions:** about the future ("these ten questions will come this year").

Facts need sources. Opinions need reasons. Predictions about exam questions deserve suspicion.

### Weighing evidence

Not all evidence is equal. From strongest to weakest, roughly:

1. **Official documents and data:** Kerala PSC notifications and syllabuses, Acts and government orders, PIB and PRD releases, official textbooks
2. **Reviews of research and expert consensus**
3. **Single studies and expert opinions**
4. **Personal stories and testimonials** ("I cleared PSC with this trick")
5. **Anonymous forwards and rumours**

### The five-minute check

Before you believe, save or share a claim:

1. **Stop.** Urgent tone, "forward to everyone", and claims that are too good or too bad to be true are warning signs.
2. **Find the original source.** Who first said it? Is there a link to an official page?
3. **Check it sideways.** Open the official website or a reliable source directly and search for the claim, instead of reading more of the same forward.
4. **Check the date.** Old notifications and old news are often recirculated as new.
5. **Decide:** believe, doubt or reject, and note the source you used.

### Ranking your PSC sources

When two sources disagree on a fact, the more official one usually wins. Final answer keys show what Kerala PSC accepted for a question (Module 12). Keep a short source ranking for your subjects, so you know where to check.

One warning: knowing a lot doesn't protect you automatically. In the neuromyths survey, teachers who knew more general facts about the brain believed **more** myths, probably because they read more popular material ([Dekker and others, 2012](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00429/full)). Use the five-minute check, not your confidence.

## Local example

**Joseph sir**'s study group WhatsApp group received a forward one evening: "URGENT: PSC changes negative marking to half a mark from next month. Share with all aspirants!" Three members had already shared it in other groups.

Joseph sir made it the evening's exercise. Stop: urgent tone, no link, "share with all". Original source: none given. Check sideways: the group opened the Kerala PSC website and found no such notification, and the OMR instructions on the site still showed the one-third rule. Date: the forward's image had an old-style logo. Verdict: reject.

Then each member checked one fact in their guide that disagreed with their SCERT textbook. Two of the five guide facts turned out to be wrong. The group agreed a rule: official source first, textbook second, guide third, forwards never without a check.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Knowing more doesn't automatically protect against false beliefs | **Moderate** | Dekker and others (2012): teachers with more general brain knowledge believed more neuromyths. |
| Checking claims against original and official sources | **Limited** | Standard advice in critical-thinking texts such as OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy; little research was checked for this course. |
| A quick routine before believing or sharing | **Limited** | A practical habit; judge it by how many errors it catches in your own sources. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, chapter 2: Critical Thinking, Research, Reading, and Writing](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/2-introduction) | Read 2.4 Gathering Information, Evaluating Sources, and Understanding Evidence | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dekker et al. (2012), "Neuromyths in Education", Frontiers in Psychology](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00429/full) | Reread the finding that more knowledge went with more myths | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala Public Service Commission (official website)](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/) | Practise checking a claim about PSC rules against the official website | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Collect five claims: two from WhatsApp, YouTube or social media about PSC or current affairs, two facts where your guide and your textbook disagree, and one claim about learning or memory.
2. Check each with the five-minute check. Write down the original source (if any), the official or reliable source you checked, the date, and your verdict.
3. Write your source ranking for each PSC subject: what you check first, second and third.
4. For one claim you rejected, write two lines on which warning signs you could have spotted earlier.

**Proof to record:** Your five-claim check log with sources and verdicts, and your source ranking.

## Template: five-minute claim check

```
CLAIM CHECK      Date: ______
Claim: _______________________________________________________________
Where I saw it: _______________   Kind: fact / opinion / prediction
1. Stop: warning signs? urgent [ ] no source [ ] "share with all" [ ] too good/bad [ ]
2. Original source: _____________________________________ (none found [ ])
3. Checked sideways at: _________________________________
4. Date of the original: ______   Recirculated old item? yes / no
5. Verdict: believe / doubt / reject.   Source I will cite: ______________
```

## Template: PSC source ranking

```
SUBJECT              1st check (official)          2nd (textbook)     3rd (guide/notes)
Constitution         ____________________          ______________     ______________
Kerala history       ____________________          ______________     ______________
Current affairs      PIB / PRD / ____________      ______________     ______________
Exam rules           Kerala PSC website            admission ticket   (never forwards)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Believing claims because they sound confident.** Confidence is not evidence. Check the source.
- **Sharing before checking.** Five minutes first. A wrong forward wastes many people's time.
- **Trusting one source.** Check sideways against an official or reliable source.
- **Checking only the claims you dislike.** Check claims you agree with too; that is where bias hides (LRN-M16-L04).

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is the strongest evidence for a rule about PSC marking?
    - A) The instructions on the official Kerala PSC website
    - B) A forward with many shares
    - C) A friend's memory
    - D) A coaching centre's poster
2. What does "check it sideways" mean?
    - A) Open an official or reliable source directly and search for the claim
    - B) Share it to see what people say
    - C) Read the forward again more slowly
    - D) Ask the person who forwarded it
3. "These ten questions will come in this year's exam." What kind of claim is it?
    - A) An opinion about books
    - B) An official rule
    - C) A checkable fact
    - D) A prediction, which deserves suspicion
4. What did the neuromyths survey find about knowledge and myths?
    - A) Nobody believed the myths
    - B) More knowledge always protects you
    - C) Teachers with more general brain knowledge believed more myths
    - D) Only students believed myths

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy 2.4 on sources and evidence
- **Action:** Check five claims with the five-minute routine and write your PSC source ranking. It is done when your proof is saved: your five-claim check log with sources and verdicts, and your source ranking.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Official documents come first.
2. **A.** Going outside the claim itself is how you test it.
3. **D.** Predictions about exam questions can't be checked in advance.
4. **C.** Knowing more is not enough; use a checking routine.

sections.title: LRN-M16-L02: Logical reasoning
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Tell deductive from inductive reasoning, test arguments for validity, solve syllogism and statement-conclusion questions with diagrams, and spot common fallacies. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes resources, 35 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Arguments

An **argument** gives reasons (premises) for a conclusion. OpenStax's *Introduction to Philosophy* covers arguments, types of inference and informal fallacies in its logic chapter ([chapter 5](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/5-introduction)).

### Deductive and inductive reasoning

- **Deductive:** if the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion **must** be true. "All rivers in this list flow west. The Periyar is in this list. So the Periyar flows west."
- **Inductive:** the premises make the conclusion **likely**, not certain. "Kerala history questions appeared in every one of my five previous papers, so they will probably appear this year."

**Validity is about form, not truth.** "All fish can fly; a shark is a fish; so a shark can fly" is valid (the conclusion follows) but unsound (a premise is false). In PSC reasoning questions, you are told to **accept the statements as true** even if they seem odd, and judge only whether the conclusion follows.

### Valid and invalid forms

| Form | Pattern | Valid? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Affirming the condition (modus ponens) | If P, then Q. P. So Q. | Valid |
| Denying the result (modus tollens) | If P, then Q. Not Q. So not P. | Valid |
| Affirming the result | If P, then Q. Q. So P. | Invalid: Q could have other causes |
| Denying the condition | If P, then Q. Not P. So not Q. | Invalid: Q could still happen |

Example: "If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was cancelled. So it rained." Invalid: the match could have been cancelled for another reason.

### Syllogisms with Venn diagrams

PSC "statements and conclusions" questions are often **syllogisms**. Draw circles (Venn diagrams) and test every possible arrangement:

| Statements | Conclusion | Follows? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All A are B. All B are C. | All A are C. | Yes |
| Some A are B. All B are C. | Some A are C. | Yes |
| All A are B. Some B are C. | Some A are C. | No: the C part of B may not include any A |
| No A is B. All C are B. | No C is A. | Yes |

A conclusion **follows** only if it is true in **every** diagram you can draw from the statements. If you can draw even one diagram where it fails, it does not follow.

### Statements and assumptions

An **assumption** is something the statement takes for granted without saying it. "Use AnkiDroid daily to remember facts" assumes that AnkiDroid helps memory and that you want to remember facts. Ask: "What must be true for the speaker to say this?"

### Informal fallacies

Some arguments fail not in form but in content. Common ones:

- **Attacking the person** instead of the argument (ad hominem)
- **Straw man:** arguing against a weaker version of what someone said
- **False dilemma:** "either you join this coaching centre or you will fail"
- **Appeal to popularity:** "everyone uses this method, so it must work"
- **Hasty generalisation:** "my cousin passed using this book, so it is the best book"
- **Slippery slope:** "if you miss one day, you will never finish"

## Local example

**Ashiq** lost marks in statements-and-conclusions questions because he answered from what he knew of the real world. For "All pens are birds; some birds are trees", he rejected every conclusion because "pens aren't birds".

He started drawing Venn diagrams for every syllogism and reminding himself: accept the statements, test every diagram. For "All A are B; some B are C; so some A are C", he drew two diagrams: one where the C part of B overlapped A and one where it didn't. Since the conclusion failed in the second, it didn't follow.

On ten previous-year syllogism questions he went from 5 right to 9 right. He also kept a fallacy log for a week from advertisements and forwards: a coaching centre ad that said "join us or stay unemployed" (false dilemma) and an app that boasted "a million downloads" as proof it works (appeal to popularity).

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drawing Venn diagrams for syllogisms | **Moderate** | Turns a working-memory task into a visual check (Modules 1 and 3); a standard method in logic teaching. |
| Learning valid and invalid forms | **Limited** | Helps with exam reasoning questions; evidence that logic training improves everyday reasoning is limited. |
| Spotting informal fallacies | **Limited** | A useful critical-thinking habit described in OpenStax; little research was checked for this course. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, chapter 5: Logic and Reasoning](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/5-introduction) | Read 5.3 Arguments, 5.4 Types of Inferences and 5.5 Informal Fallacies | 40 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Kerala PSC: previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers) | Collect 10 statements-and-conclusions or syllogism questions from previous papers | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Solve 10 syllogism or statements-and-conclusions questions from previous papers, drawing every possible Venn diagram before answering.
2. Write three valid arguments and three invalid ones of your own on PSC topics, and name the form of each.
3. Keep a fallacy log for a week: find five fallacies in advertisements, forwards or arguments you hear, and name each.
4. Write two "statement and assumption" examples of your own and check them with a study partner.

**Proof to record:** Your 10 diagram solutions with scores, your six arguments with their forms, and your fallacy log.

## Template: Venn diagram method for syllogisms

```
1. Accept every statement as true, even if it sounds strange.
2. Draw the circles for the statements. If more than one arrangement fits, draw each one.
3. A conclusion FOLLOWS only if it is true in EVERY diagram.
4. "Some A are B" means at least one A is B (it may be all).
5. Check: did I use real-world knowledge? If yes, start again.
```

## Template: fallacy spotting card

```
FALLACY LOG      Week of ______
Where I met it            Claim                                  Fallacy
_______________________   ____________________________________   attacking the person / straw man /
_______________________   ____________________________________   false dilemma / popularity /
_______________________   ____________________________________   hasty generalisation / slippery slope
```

## Common mistakes

- **Answering syllogisms with real-world knowledge.** Accept the statements as true; judge only the logic.
- **Confusing valid with true.** Valid means the conclusion follows; true depends on the premises too.
- **Drawing only one Venn diagram.** Draw every arrangement the statements allow.
- **Treating "some" as "only some".** In logic, "some" means at least one, possibly all.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. "If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was cancelled. So it rained." Is this valid?
    - A) No: affirming the result is invalid
    - B) Yes: it is modus ponens
    - C) No: denying the condition
    - D) Yes: the premises are true
2. All A are B. Some B are C. Does "Some A are C" follow?
    - A) No
    - B) Only on Sundays
    - C) Only if A is large
    - D) Yes
3. All A are B. All B are C. Does "All A are C" follow?
    - A) No
    - B) Only sometimes
    - C) Yes
    - D) Cannot be decided
4. "Either you join our coaching centre or you will fail the exam." Which fallacy is it?
    - A) False dilemma
    - B) Attacking the person
    - C) Slippery slope
    - D) Straw man
5. What is the difference between deductive and inductive reasoning?
    - A) They are the same
    - B) Inductive is always wrong
    - C) Deductive conclusions must follow from true premises; inductive ones are only likely
    - D) Deductive needs numbers

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5
- **Action:** Solve 10 syllogism questions with Venn diagrams, write six arguments and keep a fallacy log. It is done when your proof is saved: your 10 diagram solutions with scores, your six arguments with their forms, and your fallacy log.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** The match could have been cancelled for another reason.
2. **A.** You can draw a diagram where the C part of B doesn't touch A.
3. **C.** A sits inside B, which sits inside C.
4. **A.** It pretends there are only two options.
5. **C.** Deduction gives certainty from valid form; induction gives probability.

sections.title: LRN-M16-L03: Mental models and problem solving
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use a four-step problem-solving process and a handful of mental models to handle unfamiliar PSC questions and everyday study decisions. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 35 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Problem-solving strategies

OpenStax *Psychology 2e* describes several strategies people use to solve problems: **trial and error**, **algorithms** (step-by-step procedures that always work, like a formula), **heuristics** (rules of thumb that usually work) and **working backwards** from the goal. It also names common obstacles: **functional fixedness** (seeing an object only in its usual role) and a **mental set** (sticking with a method that worked before, even when it doesn't fit) ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.3](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-3-problem-solving)).

### Four steps for any problem

The mathematician George Pólya, in his classic book *How to Solve It*, set out four steps that suit almost any problem:

1. **Understand the problem.** What is being asked? What is given? What are the units? Is there a NOT or EXCEPT?
2. **Make a plan.** Which type is it? Which principle or method fits (Modules 8 and 14)?
3. **Carry out the plan,** step by step.
4. **Look back.** Does the answer make sense? Can you check it another way?

Most PSC errors happen in step 1 (misreading) or step 4 (no check), not in the calculation.

### A small set of mental models

A **mental model** is a simple idea that explains or guides many situations. A few are worth keeping:

| Model | The idea | PSC use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First principles | Rebuild from basic truths | Arithmetic rules (LRN-M08-L04) |
| Working backwards | Start from the goal or the options | Test MCQ options in the question; plan backwards from the exam date |
| Elimination | Rule out what can't be true | Improve your odds before answering (LRN-M12-L04) |
| Opportunity cost | Every hour on one thing is an hour not spent on another | Choosing topics by priority; an hour of Reels costs an hour of review |
| Inversion | Ask "what would make me fail?" and avoid it | Exam planning: list the ways to fail, then prevent each |
| Second-order thinking | Ask "and then what?" | Adding 50 new cards today means 500 reviews later (Module 4) |
| The 80/20 rule of thumb | A few causes often produce most of the effect | A few topics may carry many marks; check with your PYQ data, as it is not a law |

Use models as **questions to ask**, not as fancy words. Their value is in making you look at a problem from another side.

### Getting unstuck

When you are stuck: reread the question (step 1 again), try a simpler version with small numbers, draw it, work backwards from the options, or take a short break. A break works partly because it lets you drop a mental set and see the problem fresh.

## Local example

**Anu** used inversion on her 12-week plan. She asked: "How could I fail the next exam?" Her list: sleeping late before mocks, skipping AnkiDroid when tutoring ran late, leaving maths to the end, misreading NOT questions, and losing a week to a family function without a plan.

Next to each she wrote a countermeasure: a fixed bedtime the night before mocks, a 10-card minimum on tutoring days, maths blocks in the morning, underlining NOT, and a buffer week in the plan. She put the list inside her notebook cover.

She also used Pólya's four steps on five unfamiliar previous-year questions she would usually have skipped. Writing "what is being asked?" first made her notice that two of them asked for the difference, not the total. She got four of the five right, and for the fifth, working backwards from the options found the answer.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem-solving strategies and obstacles | **Limited** | Described in OpenStax Psychology 2e; useful structure, but teaching them alone has limited evidence of wide transfer. |
| Pólya's four steps | **Limited** | A classic, widely taught framework; little direct research was checked for this course. |
| Mental models such as inversion and opportunity cost | **Limited** | Practical thinking tools; judge them by the decisions and plans they improve. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.3 Problem Solving](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-3-problem-solving) | Read the section on problem-solving strategies and the obstacles to problem solving | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, chapter 2: Critical Thinking, Research, Reading, and Writing](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/2-introduction) | Read 2.3 Developing Good Habits of Mind | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose five unfamiliar previous-year questions (maths, reasoning or GK). Solve each on paper using the four steps, writing a line for each step.
2. Solve five MCQs by working backwards from the options, and note when it is faster than solving forwards.
3. Use inversion on your exam plan: list at least five ways you could fail, and a countermeasure for each.
4. Use opportunity cost and second-order thinking on one real decision this week (for example, whether to add a new subject deck, or how to spend Saturday), and write your reasoning in five lines.

**Proof to record:** Your five four-step solutions, the five working-backwards solutions, your inversion list with countermeasures and your decision note.

## Template: four-step problem sheet

```
Q ___
1. UNDERSTAND: asked for ______________ | given ______________ | units ______ | NOT/EXCEPT? ___
2. PLAN: type ______________ | method or principle ______________________________
3. CARRY OUT: _________________________________________________________________
4. LOOK BACK: does it make sense? ___ | checked by ______________ | answer ______
```

## Template: inversion list

```
GOAL: ______________________________________
How could I fail?                         Countermeasure
1. _____________________________________  _________________________________
2. _____________________________________  _________________________________
3. _____________________________________  _________________________________
4. _____________________________________  _________________________________
5. _____________________________________  _________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Calculating before understanding the question.** Step 1 first: what is asked, what is given, any NOT or EXCEPT?
- **Sticking with a method that isn't working.** That is a mental set. Try another approach, or work backwards.
- **Using mental models as jargon.** Use them as questions that make you look at the problem another way.
- **Treating 80/20 as an exact law.** It is a rule of thumb. Check your own PYQ data.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What are Pólya's four steps?
    - A) Survey, question, read, review
    - B) Understand, plan, carry out, look back
    - C) Plan, practise, perform, praise
    - D) Read, guess, mark, move on
2. What is a mental set?
    - A) A set of flashcards
    - B) Sticking with a method that worked before even when it doesn't fit
    - C) A type of syllogism
    - D) A group of study partners
3. Which question uses inversion?
    - A) "Which book is the best?"
    - B) "What did I study yesterday?"
    - C) "How could I fail the next exam, and how do I prevent each cause?"
    - D) "How do I get full marks?"
4. You add 50 new AnkiDroid cards today. What does second-order thinking ask?
    - A) "And then what?": about ten times as many reviews later
    - B) "How do I add 50 more?"
    - C) "Who made this app?"
    - D) "Why not 100?"

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Psychology 2e 7.3 on problem solving and Introduction to Philosophy 2.3
- **Action:** Solve unfamiliar PYQs with the four steps and working backwards, and apply inversion to your exam plan. It is done when your proof is saved: your five four-step solutions, the five working-backwards solutions, your inversion list with countermeasures and your decision note.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** They come from his classic book How to Solve It.
2. **B.** OpenStax lists it as an obstacle to problem solving.
3. **C.** Inversion looks at the goal from the opposite side.
4. **A.** It looks at the consequences of the consequences (Module 4).

sections.title: LRN-M16-L04: Cognitive biases
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Recognise the cognitive biases that most affect study and exams, audit them in your own recent decisions, and use a debiasing checklist. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 35 minutes resources, 35 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What a bias is

A **cognitive bias** is a systematic error in thinking: not a random slip, but a predictable way in which human minds go wrong. OpenStax *Psychology 2e* describes several, including anchoring, confirmation bias, hindsight bias, the representative bias and the availability heuristic ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.3](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-3-problem-solving)), and OpenStax *Introduction to Philosophy* discusses how to overcome them ([section 2.2](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/2-introduction)).

### Seven biases in a PSC aspirant's life

| Bias | What it is | How it shows up in study | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Confirmation bias | Noticing only evidence that supports what you already believe | "My method works": you remember the good mocks and forget the bad ones | Look at all your scores in the Weekly tab |
| Anchoring | Being pulled by the first number or option you see | The first option looks right, so you stop thinking | Cover the options and answer first (Module 3) |
| Availability | Judging by what comes to mind easily | A vivid question from last year feels "important" | Use your PYQ counts, not memorable questions |
| Hindsight | "I knew it all along" after seeing the answer | Marking a topic green after reading the key | Answer before checking (Module 7) |
| Overconfidence | Feeling surer than your accuracy justifies | Sure-but-wrong answers under negative marking | Your calibration table (LRN-M07-L02) |
| Sunk cost | Continuing something because of what you already spent | Using a poor guide or coaching material because you paid for it | Judge by what helps from now on, not by past cost |
| Planning fallacy | Underestimating how long things take | A plan that needs 40 hours a week when you have 20 | Plan from your Study Log hours (LRN-M12-L05) |

### Knowing isn't enough

Learning the names of biases doesn't make you immune to them. Remember the neuromyths survey: more knowledge went with more myths (LRN-M16-L01). What helps is **outside structure**: data, checklists and other people.

### A debiasing checklist for decisions

Before a decision that matters (a study plan, a coaching course, a change of method, whether to apply for a post):

1. **What would change my mind?** If nothing could, you are not deciding; you are defending.
2. **What does my data say?** Study Log, Weekly tab, Errors tab, mock scores.
3. **What is the outside view?** How long did similar plans take before? How did similar people do?
4. **What would I advise a friend?** Distance reduces bias.
5. **Sleep on it,** if it involves money or a big commitment.
6. **Ask someone** who will disagree with you honestly.

### Don't overcorrect

The goal is not to doubt everything until you can't act. Use the checklist for decisions that matter, trust your data, decide, and review the decision in a few weeks.

## Local example

**Sreeja** did a bias audit of her last month. Sunk cost: she had kept working through a set of coaching PDFs she had paid ₹1,500 for, though her error log showed they had several wrong answers; she switched to previous papers and textbooks. Planning fallacy: her first 12-week plan assumed 25 hours a week, while her Study Log showed 14; she rebuilt the plan.

Confirmation bias was harder to see. She was sure evening study suited her, and she remembered her good evening sessions. Her Focus tab showed that her evening blocks had twice as many distractions as her morning ones.

She used the debiasing checklist on one decision: whether to join a new paid crash course. What would change her mind? Evidence that it covered her weak topics better than her free sources. Her data: her weakest areas were mental ability and English grammar, which the course barely covered. She decided not to join, and wrote a note to review the decision after her next mock.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cognitive biases exist and affect judgement | **Strong** | A well-established area of psychology, described in OpenStax Psychology 2e. |
| Learning about biases protects you from them | **Limited** | Awareness alone helps little; outside structure (data, checklists, other people) helps more. |
| Using data and checklists for decisions | **Limited** | Practical debiasing tools; judge them by the decisions you review later. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.3 Problem Solving](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-3-problem-solving) | Read the part on biases and heuristics, with its table of biases | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, chapter 2: Critical Thinking, Research, Reading, and Writing](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/2-introduction) | Read 2.2 Overcoming Cognitive Biases and Engaging in Critical Reflection | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For each of the seven biases in the table, write one example from your own study or decisions in the last month, and a fix.
2. Check each example against your data where you can (Study Log, Weekly, Focus and Errors tabs).
3. Choose one real decision you face this week and go through the debiasing checklist in writing.
4. Put a review date for that decision in your calendar, two to four weeks away.

**Proof to record:** Your seven-bias audit with examples and fixes, and your written checklist for one decision with its review date.

## Template: bias audit

```
BIAS AUDIT      Month: ______
Bias                My example (last month)                    Data that shows it      Fix
Confirmation        ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Anchoring           ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Availability        ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Hindsight           ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Overconfidence      ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Sunk cost           ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
Planning fallacy    ________________________________________   ____________________    ______________
```

## Template: debiasing checklist

```
DECISION: _____________________________________________   Date: ______
[ ] What would change my mind? ________________________________________
[ ] What does my data say? ____________________________________________
[ ] Outside view (similar cases before): ________________________________
[ ] What would I advise a friend? _____________________________________
[ ] Slept on it (if money or a big commitment) [ ]
[ ] Asked someone who will disagree honestly: ______________ said ______
Decision: ______________________   Review on: ______
```

## Common mistakes

- **Seeing biases only in other people.** Audit your own decisions with your own data.
- **Thinking "I know about biases, so I'm safe".** Knowledge alone protects little. Use checklists and data.
- **Doubting everything until you can't act.** Use the checklist for decisions that matter, then decide and review.
- **Keeping a bad resource because you paid for it.** Past cost is gone. Judge by what helps from now on.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. You keep using coaching notes you paid for, though your error log shows they have wrong answers. Which bias?
    - A) Sunk cost
    - B) Availability
    - C) Anchoring
    - D) Hindsight
2. How do you reduce anchoring in MCQs?
    - A) Cover the options and answer first
    - B) Always pick the first option
    - C) Read the options twice before the question
    - D) Guess quickly
3. Your plan needs 40 hours a week; your Study Log shows 20. Which bias?
    - A) Confirmation bias
    - B) Planning fallacy
    - C) Hindsight bias
    - D) Sunk cost
4. What does the research suggest about learning the names of biases?
    - A) It makes you immune
    - B) It makes bias worse every time
    - C) It replaces all decisions
    - D) It alone protects little; data, checklists and other people help more

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Psychology 2e 7.3 on biases and Introduction to Philosophy 2.2
- **Action:** Audit seven biases in your own recent decisions and use the debiasing checklist on one real decision. It is done when your proof is saved: your seven-bias audit with examples and fixes, and your written checklist for one decision with its review date.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Past spending shouldn't decide future use.
2. **A.** The first option you see shouldn't pull your answer.
3. **B.** People underestimate how long things take; plan from real data.
4. **D.** Outside structure is what changes decisions.

sections.title: Module 17: Learning with AI
sections.summary: Use AI tools to learn more, not less: as a Socratic tutor that questions you, as a question machine built on your own notes, and as a source of explanations you always check. Write clear rules so AI never does the thinking that builds your memory and skill.
sections.content:
## Overview

Free AI chat tools can be excellent study partners or very effective crutches. Research is still young, but one large study already shows the difference: an AI that gave answers improved practice and harmed exam results, while a hint-based tutor did not cause that harm. This module turns that warning into a practical setup, consistent with everything else in the course: retrieval, explanation and checking.

For using AI as a work skill, the Free AI Generalist Course in this app goes much further. Here the goal is learning.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Set up an AI tool as a Socratic tutor and run good tutoring sessions
- Generate practice questions from your own notes and answer before seeing answers
- Check every AI fact against a textbook or official source
- Explain why answer-giving AI can harm learning
- Write and follow your own rules for learning with AI

## Time

About 4 hours 30 minutes in total: 3 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 19–20, with the module project due in week 20.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M17-L01: AI as a Socratic tutor (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M17-L02: Quizzes, explanations and checking AI answers (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M17-L03: Avoiding over-reliance (about 1 hour)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **Socratic tutor prompt** and **tutoring session log**
- The **quiz-from-my-notes prompt** and **AI fact-check log**
- Your **AI rules for learning** and **AI use log**

## Module project: My AI study setup

1. Save your tutor prompt, quiz prompt, fact-check log template and AI rules together in one note on your phone.
2. Run one more tutoring session and one more quiz from your notes, following your rules.
3. Count the AI errors you found across all your quizzes and sessions, and write your rule for which facts you will never take from AI unchecked.
4. In your weekly review, record your AI minutes against your own practice minutes for two weeks.

**Proof to record:** Your saved AI setup note, the new session and quiz logs, your total AI error count with your checking rule, and two weeks of AI minutes in your weekly reviews.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tutoring | AI used to get answers | Some questioning sessions | Socratic sessions with my own summaries |
| Questions | AI quizzes with answers shown at once | Answered first sometimes | Quizzes from my notes, answered one at a time |
| Checking | AI facts learned unchecked | Some facts checked | Every fact checked, errors logged and reported |
| Reliance | AI first for everything | Some rules | Written rules followed and AI minutes tracked weekly |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use AI only for quizzes from your own notes, answered before seeing answers, with every fact checked.
- Never use AI during practice sets or mocks.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Good AI tutor behaviour | Asks first, one idea at a time, hints before answers, quiz at the end. |
| ChatGPT study mode, per OpenAI | Socratic questions, hints and knowledge checks; tools menu, "Study and learn". |
| The quiz prompt's two key settings | "Use only the text below" and "don't show the answers yet". |
| When AI and the textbook disagree | The textbook or official source wins; for PSC questions, the final answer key. |
| The Wharton study in one line | Answer-giving AI: practice up, exam score 17% lower; hint-based tutor: no harm. |
| Try-first rule | Attempt it yourself before asking AI. |
| Where AI should never be used while learning | Retrieval practice, practice sets, mocks and tests. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Treating AI as an answer key.** Treat it as a questioner whose facts you check.
- **Judging AI help by how smooth practice feels.** Judge it by your scores days later without AI.

sections.title: LRN-M17-L01: AI as a Socratic tutor
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Set up an AI chat tool as a Socratic tutor that questions you instead of answering for you, and run three tutoring sessions on PSC topics. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 60 minutes for three sessions).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Two ways to use an AI tutor

AI chat tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude have free plans that can explain ideas, answer questions and quiz you. Used one way, they make you think: they ask questions, give hints and check your understanding. Used the other way, they think for you: they give you finished answers and notes, which feels efficient and teaches little. This module is about using them the first way.

If you want to understand how these tools work and why they sometimes make things up, the **Free AI Generalist Course** in this app covers it in Level 0, and prompting in Level 1.

### Built-in learning modes

Some tools now have modes designed for learning:

- **ChatGPT study mode** combines Socratic questioning, hints and self-reflection prompts with quizzes and knowledge checks. OpenAI says it is available to logged-in users on the Free plan; you turn it on from the tools menu by choosing "Study and learn" ([OpenAI, July 2025](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-study-mode/) (check current rules)).
- **Gemini Guided Learning** breaks problems down step by step, asks probing questions and can add diagrams and quizzes ([Google, August 2025](https://blog.google/outreach-initiatives/education/guided-learning/) (check current rules)).

Features, names and free limits change often, so check what your app offers today. Any good chat tool can behave like a Socratic tutor if you ask it to, with a prompt like the one below.

### What a good tutoring session looks like

1. **You set the goal:** the topic, your source, what you want to be able to do.
2. **The tutor asks first:** two or three questions to find what you know and where you are wrong.
3. **One idea at a time:** after each, you explain it back or answer a question.
4. **Hints before answers:** you do the thinking; the tutor nudges.
5. **A quiz at the end,** answered one question at a time.
6. **You write the summary yourself:** what you learned, what to review, any fact to check.

This turns the AI into a partner for retrieval practice and self-explanation (Modules 3 and 8), the two things that build memory and understanding.

### Language

You can ask for a hard idea to be explained in simple Malayalam, then answer in English, which practises both. You can also ask the tutor to correct your English answers.

### Privacy

Don't paste personal details (Aadhaar, phone numbers, addresses, passwords) into AI chats. Your study notes and questions are fine.

## Local example

**Sreeja** opened ChatGPT on her phone, chose "Study and learn" from the tools menu, and pasted the Socratic tutor prompt below with the topic "Panchayati Raj after the 73rd Amendment".

Instead of a long explanation, it asked her three questions. Her answer to the second showed a misconception: she thought the State Election Commission and the Election Commission of India were the same body. The tutor pointed it out, gave her a hint, and asked her to explain the difference back. Twenty minutes later she answered five PSC-style questions, one at a time, and got four right.

She wrote her own summary in her notebook: the misconception, the corrected idea, and two facts to check. Checking them in her textbook, one was right and one was slightly off in the tutor's wording, which she corrected on her card. She did two more sessions that week, on the Directive Principles and on time-and-work problems, and found the questions more useful than any explanation.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI tutoring that gives hints, not answers | **Limited** | In a large school study, a hint-based GPT tutor did not harm exam results, unlike an answer-giving one (Bastani and others, reported by Wharton); benefits for adults are not yet proven. |
| Retrieval and self-explanation inside tutoring | **Strong** | The session design uses practice testing (high utility) and self-explanation (moderate). |
| Built-in study modes in AI apps | **Limited** | New features with little independent research yet; judge them by your own delayed test scores. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenAI (29 July 2025): Introducing study mode in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-study-mode/) | Read what ChatGPT study mode does and how to turn it on | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Google (6 August 2025): Guided Learning in Gemini](https://blog.google/outreach-initiatives/education/guided-learning/) | Read what Gemini Guided Learning does | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Knowledge at Wharton (27 August 2024): without guardrails, generative AI can harm education (Bastani et al.)](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/without-guardrails-generative-ai-can-harm-education) | Read how a hint-based tutor differed from an answer-giving one | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose one AI chat tool with a free plan. If it has a study or guided-learning mode, turn it on; either way, paste the Socratic tutor prompt below.
2. Run three sessions of 20 to 30 minutes on PSC topics you have already studied (one GK, one Constitution or history, one maths or English).
3. In each session, answer every question yourself before asking for hints, and answer the final quiz one question at a time.
4. After each session, write your own summary: misconceptions found, the corrected ideas, what to review.
5. Check at least one fact from each session against your textbook or an official source, and correct your notes or cards if needed.

**Proof to record:** Your three session summaries (written by you, not the AI) with the facts you checked and what you found.

## Template: Socratic tutor prompt (version 2)

```
You are my Socratic tutor for the Kerala PSC exam. Topic: [topic]. I have
already studied it from [source]. My goal today: [goal].
Rules for you:
1. Do NOT start by explaining. First ask me 2-3 questions to find out what I
   already know and what I get wrong.
2. Teach one small idea at a time. After each, ask me to explain it back in my
   own words or answer a question about it.
3. When I am wrong, give a hint first. Give the answer only if I am still
   stuck after two hints.
4. Point out any misconception you notice, clearly.
5. At the end, give me 5 PSC-style questions one at a time and wait for my
   answer to each before telling me if it is right.
6. Then list what I should review. If you are unsure about any fact, say so
   and tell me which official source or textbook to check.
You may explain a hard idea in simple Malayalam if I ask, but ask me to answer
in English.
```

## Template: tutoring session log

```
AI TUTOR SESSION     Date: ______  Tool: ______________  Topic: ______________
Questions it asked me first: ____________________________________________
Misconceptions it found: _______________________________________________
Corrected idea, in MY words: ___________________________________________
Quiz: ___/5 (answered one at a time)
Facts checked in: ______________  Right? Y / N   Fixed: __________________
To review / cards to make: ______________________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for notes or answers instead of questions.** Ask the AI to question you; you do the explaining.
- **Reading long AI explanations passively.** One idea at a time, then explain it back.
- **Trusting every fact the AI states.** Check facts against your textbook or an official source (LRN-M17-L02).
- **Pasting personal details into the chat.** Share study material only.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What should a good AI tutor do first in a session?
    - A) Show all the answers
    - B) Write your notes for you
    - C) Ask you questions to find what you know and where you are wrong
    - D) Give a long explanation
2. According to OpenAI, how do you turn on ChatGPT study mode?
    - A) By paying for a special plan only
    - B) From the tools menu, by choosing "Study and learn"
    - C) By typing "exam" three times
    - D) It can't be turned on
3. Who should write the summary at the end of a tutoring session?
    - A) A friend
    - B) You, in your own words
    - C) Nobody
    - D) The AI
4. What did the school study find about a hint-based AI tutor?
    - A) It did not harm exam results, unlike an answer-giving version
    - B) It was not tested
    - C) It harmed results more than the answer-giving version
    - D) It doubled exam scores

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The ChatGPT study mode and Gemini Guided Learning announcements, and the Wharton summary of the tutoring study
- **Action:** Run three Socratic AI tutoring sessions on PSC topics and write your own summaries with fact checks. It is done when your proof is saved: your three session summaries (written by you, not the AI) with the facts you checked and what you found.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Diagnosing first, then teaching one idea at a time, keeps you thinking.
2. **B.** OpenAI says it is open to logged-in Free users; features can change.
3. **B.** Writing it yourself is retrieval and self-explanation.
4. **A.** Students with answer-giving AI did worse in exams without AI; the hint-based tutor avoided that harm.
