sections.title: LRN-M17-L02: Quizzes, explanations and checking AI answers
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use AI to generate practice questions and explanations at the right level, and check every AI fact against your textbook or an official source before you learn it. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 60 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### AI as a question machine

One of the best uses of AI for PSC study is turning your own notes into practice questions. Give it your notes, ask for PSC-style questions, and answer them one at a time. That is retrieval practice (Module 3) on exactly the material you studied.

Two settings make the questions much better:

1. **"Use only the text below."** Questions built from your own notes are tied to your source, so they are easier to check, and the AI is less likely to invent facts.
2. **"Don't show the answers yet."** Answer each question before you see whether you were right, ideally with the options covered first (Module 3).

### AI makes things up

AI chat tools can state false facts in a fluent, confident voice: a wrong year, a wrong article number, an invented scheme, a mixed-up name. This is widely documented, and the Free AI Generalist Course in this app explains why it happens (Level 0). It matters especially for PSC, where one wrong year costs a third of a mark.

### Five checking rules

1. **Check any fact before you learn it.** Before a fact becomes a card or a note, confirm it in your textbook or an official source. If it can't be confirmed, don't learn it.
2. **Prefer questions from your own notes.** "Use only the text below" keeps the AI close to a source you trust.
3. **Never rely on AI for current affairs.** Many tools have a knowledge cutoff and may not know recent events, or may get them wrong. Use PIB, PRD Kerala and All India Radio News (Module 10).
4. **When AI and your textbook disagree, the textbook or official source wins.** For PSC questions, the final answer key shows what PSC accepted ([Kerala PSC answer keys](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) (check current rules)).
5. **Ask for the supporting sentence.** Ask the AI to quote the line from your notes that supports each answer; if it can't, be suspicious.

### Explanations at the right level

When you don't understand something, ask for the explanation you need, not a lecture:

- "Explain this as if I were 12, with one example from Kerala life."
- "Explain the difference between X and Y in a two-column table."
- "Give me one worked example, then a similar problem for me to solve."
- "Explain it in simple Malayalam, in five lines."

Then close the chat and explain it back in your own words (Module 8). If you can't, the explanation didn't land; ask again differently.

## Local example

**Ashiq** pasted his notes on the Fundamental Rights into an AI chat with the quiz prompt from this lesson. He answered the ten questions one at a time and got seven right.

Then he checked every question and explanation against his textbook. Eight were fine. Two had problems: one explanation said Article 21A was added to the Constitution in 1976, when his textbook says it came with the 86th Amendment in 2002; another question gave the right answer but a wrong year for the 44th Amendment, which removed the right to property in 1978. He reported both errors back to the AI and logged them.

Over three quizzes, he found 4 errors in 30 questions. "That is too many to trust," he wrote, "but few enough that checking is worth it." He made cards only from his three missed questions whose facts he had confirmed.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Practice questions from your own notes (retrieval practice) | **Strong** | Practice testing is rated high utility; AI is a new way to produce the questions. |
| AI tools can state false facts confidently | **Moderate** | Widely documented and explained in the AI Generalist course; no single source was checked for this course. Checking is essential. |
| Asking AI for tailored explanations | **Limited** | Little research yet on learning gains; useful when followed by explaining it back yourself. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenAI (29 July 2025): Introducing study mode in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-study-mode/) | Note the "knowledge checks" feature: quizzes with feedback | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala PSC: answer keys for OMR exams](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams) | Remember that final answer keys show what PSC accepted | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [SCERT Kerala: school textbooks](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/) | Have your textbook ready as the checking source | As needed | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose three sets of your own notes on PSC topics (for example from Module 9).
2. For each, use the quiz prompt below to get 10 questions. Answer each before seeing whether you were right.
3. Check every question, answer and explanation against your textbook or an official source, and log each AI error you find.
4. Ask for one explanation at the right level on something you found hard, then close the chat and explain it back in your own words.
5. Make cards only from missed questions whose facts you have confirmed.

**Proof to record:** Your three quizzes with your answers, the fact-check log with the number of AI errors, your explain-back, and the confirmed cards.

## Template: quiz-from-my-notes prompt

```
Use ONLY the text below (my notes) to write 10 Kerala PSC-style multiple-choice
questions, with 4 options each. Include 3 statement-type questions ("Which of
the statements is/are correct?"). Do not show the answers yet. Ask me the
questions one at a time, wait for my answer, then tell me if I am right and
explain in two lines, quoting the sentence from my notes that supports the
answer. If a question can't be answered from my notes alone, don't ask it.
NOTES:
[paste your notes here]
```

## Template: AI fact-check log

```
AI FACT CHECK      Date: ______  Tool: ______________  Topic: ______________
Q  | AI's fact or answer               | Checked in (book/page or official) | Correct?
1  | _________________________________ | __________________________________ | Y / N
2  | _________________________________ | __________________________________ | Y / N
...
AI errors found: ___ of ___   Errors reported back to the AI [ ]
Cards made only from confirmed facts [ ]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Learning facts from AI without checking.** Confirm every fact in a textbook or official source before it becomes a card.
- **Using AI for current affairs.** Use PIB, PRD Kerala and All India Radio News instead.
- **Letting the AI show answers at once.** Answer first; that is where the learning happens.
- **Vague prompts ("give me questions on history").** Paste your notes and say "use only the text below".

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why ask the AI to "use only the text below" when making a quiz?
    - A) Questions tied to your notes are easier to check and less likely to include invented facts
    - B) It is required by PSC
    - C) It makes the AI faster
    - D) It avoids all errors for certain
2. The AI says Article 21A was added in 1976; your textbook says 2002. Which do you trust?
    - A) Neither; skip the topic
    - B) Whichever you read first
    - C) The AI, because it sounds confident
    - D) The textbook (it came with the 86th Amendment, 2002)
3. Where should you get current-affairs facts?
    - A) Random forwards
    - B) PIB, PRD Kerala and All India Radio News
    - C) Old guides
    - D) An AI chat tool
4. After an AI explains an idea, what should you do?
    - A) Close the chat and explain it back in your own words
    - B) Ask for a longer explanation
    - C) Move on immediately
    - D) Copy the explanation into your notes

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The study-mode description of knowledge checks, with your textbook ready for checking
- **Action:** Generate three quizzes from your own notes, check every AI fact, and make cards only from confirmed facts. It is done when your proof is saved: your three quizzes with your answers, the fact-check log with the number of AI errors, your explain-back, and the confirmed cards.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** It keeps the AI close to a source you trust; you still check.
2. **D.** Textbooks and official sources win over AI.
3. **B.** AI tools may have a knowledge cutoff and can get recent events wrong.
4. **A.** Explaining back shows whether you understood, and builds memory.

sections.title: LRN-M17-L03: Avoiding over-reliance
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use AI in ways that build your own skill instead of replacing it, test the difference on yourself, and write clear rules for when to use it and when not to. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 60 minutes action over three days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The crutch problem

In a large field study reported by Knowledge at Wharton, nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey practised with one of two AI tools. One, like an ordinary chatbot, gave answers ("GPT Base"). The other gave hints, with safeguards designed with teachers ("GPT Tutor"). During practice, both groups did better than students without AI: 48% better with GPT Base and 127% better with GPT Tutor. But in the exam, taken without AI, the GPT Base group scored **17% lower** than students who had never used AI, while the GPT Tutor group scored about the same as them ([Knowledge at Wharton, 2024](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/without-guardrails-generative-ai-can-harm-education)).

The lesson: AI that gives answers can make practice look better while making learning worse. It works like a crutch. The study was with school students in maths, so results for adults and other subjects may differ, but the warning fits everything you have learned in this course.

### Why it happens

- **Retrieval is where learning happens.** When the AI produces the answer, you skip the effortful recall that strengthens memory (Module 3).
- **The fluency illusion.** A smooth AI explanation feels like understanding, just like a reread page (Module 7).
- **No struggle, no feedback.** If you never try first, you never find out what you can't do.

### Seven rules for learning with AI

1. **Try first.** Attempt the problem or recall the topic yourself, for at least 10 minutes or one full attempt, before asking.
2. **Ask for hints, not answers.** "Give me a hint for the next step" instead of "solve this".
3. **Explain back.** After any explanation, close the chat and explain it in your own words.
4. **No AI during retrieval practice, mocks or tests.** These measure and build what is in your head.
5. **Check facts** before learning them (LRN-M17-L02).
6. **Use AI where it adds thinking:** questioning you, judging your explanation, giving a different example, helping you plan. Not where it removes thinking: writing your notes, solving your practice sets, writing your answers.
7. **Track it.** Once a week, compare your AI minutes with your own practice minutes in the weekly review.

### AI for work, later

After PSC, AI tools can make your work much more productive, and the Free AI Generalist Course teaches that. The difference is purpose: at work you want the output; while learning you want the skill in your head. Keep the effort yours when the goal is learning.

## Local example

**Ashiq** noticed that his maths mock scores had dropped. For three weeks he had pasted every hard problem into an AI chat and read its neat solutions. It felt like progress.

He tried the experiment in this lesson. Set A: 10 time-and-distance problems, where he asked the AI for a full solution whenever he was stuck. Set B: 10 similar problems, where he tried each for at least five minutes and asked only for hints. Two days later he solved 10 new problems of the same types without any AI: 4 right from set A's types, 8 right from set B's.

He wrote his AI rules on a card: try first; hints, not answers; explain back; no AI in practice sets or mocks; facts checked; AI for questions and feedback. He kept a one-week AI log. His AI minutes fell from about 90 a week to 35, and his next maths mock score went back up.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer-giving AI can harm learning while improving practice | **Moderate** | One large field experiment (Bastani and others, reported by Wharton): exam scores 17% lower with answer-giving AI; school maths, so results may differ for adults. |
| Trying first and recalling yourself (retrieval) | **Strong** | The testing effect: effortful retrieval strengthens memory (Dunlosky and others, 2013). |
| Explaining back after an AI explanation | **Limited** | A practical safeguard based on self-explanation and retrieval; not directly tested with AI. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Knowledge at Wharton (27 August 2024): without guardrails, generative AI can harm education (Bastani et al.)](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/without-guardrails-generative-ai-can-harm-education) | Read the whole article on the study and its numbers | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenAI (29 July 2025): Introducing study mode in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-study-mode/) | Compare: how study mode is designed to avoid giving answers straight away | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write your AI rules for learning (start from the seven in this lesson and adapt them) on a card.
2. Run the experiment: set A of 10 problems or questions where you may ask AI for full answers; set B of 10 similar ones where you try first and ask only for hints. Note the time each set takes.
3. Two days later, without any AI, answer 10 new questions of the same types. Score which types you got right.
4. Keep a one-week AI log: what you used AI for, for how long, and whether you tried first.
5. In your weekly review, compare your AI minutes with your own practice minutes, and adjust your rules if needed.

**Proof to record:** Your AI rules card, the experiment with both sets and the two-day scores, and your one-week AI log.

## Template: my AI rules for learning

```
MY AI RULES (learning)                         Date: ______
1. Try first: at least ___ minutes or one full attempt before asking.
2. Hints, not answers.
3. Explain back in my own words after every explanation.
4. No AI in retrieval practice, practice sets, mocks or tests.
5. Every fact checked before it becomes a card or note.
6. AI for: questioning me, judging my explanation, other examples, planning.
   Not for: writing my notes, solving my practice, writing my answers.
7. Weekly: AI minutes ___ vs own practice minutes ___
```

## Template: AI use log

```
AI USE LOG     Week of ______
Day | What I used AI for              | Minutes | Tried first? | Hints or answers? | Rule kept?
Mon | ______________________________  | ___     | Y / N        | H / A             | Y / N
Tue | ______________________________  | ___     | Y / N        | H / A             | Y / N
...
Total AI minutes ___   Own practice minutes ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Opening AI before trying yourself.** Try first; the struggle is part of learning.
- **Copying AI-written notes.** Write notes in your own words (Module 9); use AI to question you on them.
- **Using AI during practice sets or mocks.** Those measure and build what is in your head. Keep them AI-free.
- **Outsourcing your English writing practice.** Write it yourself, then ask the AI for feedback.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In the study reported by Wharton, how did the answer-giving AI group do in the exam without AI?
    - A) 127% higher
    - B) About 17% lower than students who never used AI
    - C) About 48% higher
    - D) Exactly the same
2. What happened with the hint-based "GPT Tutor"?
    - A) It was not tested
    - B) Exam scores were about the same as students without AI
    - C) Exam scores fell by half
    - D) Students stopped practising
3. Why does answer-giving AI weaken learning?
    - A) It uses too much data
    - B) It is in English
    - C) It skips the effortful retrieval and struggle that build memory and skill
    - D) It is too slow
4. Which is a good use of AI while learning?
    - A) Copying its notes into your notebook
    - B) Asking it to solve your whole practice set
    - C) Using it during a mock test
    - D) Asking it to question you and judge your explanation

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Knowledge at Wharton article on the AI tutoring study
- **Action:** Write your AI rules, run the hints-versus-answers experiment on yourself and keep a one-week AI log. It is done when your proof is saved: your AI rules card, the experiment with both sets and the two-day scores, and your one-week AI log.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Practice looked better, but learning was worse: a crutch.
2. **B.** Hints and safeguards avoided the harm.
3. **C.** Learning comes from your own effortful recall and practice.
4. **D.** It adds thinking instead of removing it.

sections.title: Module 18: Personal knowledge management
sections.summary: Build a personal knowledge base that grows with you: atomic notes, links across subjects, index notes and a simple workflow, in a free app on your phone (Joplin or Logseq, both open source, or Obsidian if you already use it), connected to your review system.
sections.content:
## Overview

Your PSC preparation produces hundreds of notes. Without a system they end up scattered and unused. With one, every note has a home, connects to related ideas, and feeds your cards and revision schedule. The same knowledge base then carries everything you learn after PSC.

This module is honest that apps don't raise scores by themselves. The point is a single searchable place where notes are connected and turned into retrieval practice.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain atomic notes, links, backlinks, index notes and tags
- Write linked notes across subjects and find connections
- Choose and set up a free knowledge-base app on your phone
- Run the capture, process, connect, review, use workflow
- Keep the knowledge base backed up and tidy with a monthly check

## Time

About 3 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 20–21, with the module project due in week 21.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M18-L01: Linked notes: how a second brain works (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M18-L02: Your PSC knowledge base in Joplin or Logseq (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **atomic note** and **index note** templates
- The **topic note template** and your **knowledge base structure**
- The **monthly knowledge base check**

## Module project: My knowledge base

1. Grow your knowledge base to at least 30 notes, each with a source and at least two links.
2. Write an index note for every subject you have studied so far.
3. Use the knowledge base in one real task: preparing a Feynman explanation, a teaching session (Module 20) or a mock analysis.
4. Do the monthly check and a backup.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots showing 30 or more linked notes, your index notes, notes from the real task, and the monthly check with the backup file.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Notes | Long copied notes | Some atomic notes | 30 or more atomic notes in my own words, with sources |
| Links | Folders only | Some links within a subject | At least two links per note, including across subjects |
| Workflow | Notes added and forgotten | Processed sometimes | Inbox processed within 24 hours; facts feed cards and the Revision tab |
| Safety | No backup | Synced only | Monthly export to the Learning Folder |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use paper index cards with numbers and "links to" lines.
- Keep one index note per subject and process your inbox once a week.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Personal knowledge management | A system for capturing, organising, connecting and finding what you learn. |
| Atomic note | One idea, your own words, a clear title, a source. |
| Backlinks | A list, on each note, of other notes that link to it. |
| Index note | One note per subject that lists and links its key notes. |
| Open-source knowledge base apps in this course | Joplin and Logseq. |
| The workflow | Capture, process (24 hours), connect, feed the review system, use. |
| Why back up even if you sync | Sync copies mistakes too; a monthly export protects your notes. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Treating the knowledge base as the goal.** It serves your learning; retrieval still does the remembering.
- **Building a perfect system before using it.** Start small and improve it in your monthly check.

sections.title: LRN-M18-L01: Linked notes: how a second brain works
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain how a linked-notes system works (atomic notes, links, backlinks, index notes and tags), and turn ten notes on a PSC topic into a small linked network. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What personal knowledge management is

**Personal knowledge management (PKM)** is a system for capturing, organising, connecting and finding what you learn, so that it builds up over years instead of being scattered across notebooks, WhatsApp messages and PDFs. People sometimes call it a "second brain". For you it means one place where your PSC notes live now, and where your notes on AI, business or a new language will live later.

### Folders versus links

Folders put each note in **one** place: "Kerala history". Real knowledge doesn't fit in one place. The Vaikom Satyagraha belongs to Kerala history, but it also connects to Gandhi's visits to Kerala, to the Temple Entry Proclamation, to Article 17 of the Constitution and to the reformers involved. **Links** let one note connect to many others, across subjects. Following those links is elaboration (Module 3): it builds the connections that make facts easier to remember and understand.

### Five building blocks

1. **Atomic notes:** one idea per note, in your own words, with a clear title, often a statement or a question ("Why the Vaikom Satyagraha mattered").
2. **Links:** in Logseq and Obsidian you link to another note by typing its title in double square brackets, like `[[Temple Entry Proclamation]]`. Other apps, including Joplin, have their own way to link notes.
3. **Backlinks:** apps such as Logseq and Obsidian show, on each note, which other notes link to it. You discover connections you didn't plan.
4. **Index notes:** one note per subject that lists and links its key notes, like a table of contents you write yourself.
5. **Tags:** for status and purpose, not for topics: `#to-review`, `#pyq`, `#weak`, `#confirmed`.

### An old idea

A famous example of linked notes on paper is the slip-box (Zettelkasten) of the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, thousands of numbered index cards that referred to each other. You can do the same with paper index cards today; apps simply make links and search faster.

### Honest expectations

No research shows that a PKM app raises exam scores by itself. Its value is practical: everything in one place, connections you can see, and notes you can find in seconds. A beautiful note collection you never test yourself on is still forgetting with extra steps. Every important note should feed your retrieval system: cue questions, AnkiDroid cards and Revision-tab entries (Module 9).

## Local example

**Anu** had notes on the Kerala renaissance in three notebooks, a PDF and her phone's gallery. For this lesson she made ten atomic notes on paper index cards, one idea per card: one card each for four reformers, three organisations, two events (the Vaikom Satyagraha and the Temple Entry Proclamation) and one for Article 17.

On each card she wrote, at the bottom, "links to:" and the titles of at least two other cards: the reformer cards linked to their organisations and events; the Temple Entry Proclamation linked to the Vaikom and Guruvayur satyagrahas and to Article 17. She made an index card, "Kerala renaissance: start here", listing all ten.

When she drew the network on one page, she saw a connection she had never noticed: three of her ten notes linked to the struggle against untouchability, which tied the history topic to the Constitution topic. She now asks one cross-subject question in every weekly review: "What does this connect to in another subject?"

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linking new ideas to what you know (elaboration) | **Moderate** | Elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| PKM apps improving exam results | **Limited** | No research was found or checked for this course; their value is organisation and finding things. |
| Collecting notes without testing yourself | **No good evidence** | Collecting is not learning; memory needs retrieval and spacing (Modules 3 and 4). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Logseq: privacy-first, open-source knowledge management](https://logseq.com/) | Read the home page: what Logseq is for | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Joplin help: features, sync options, encryption and apps](https://joplinapp.org/help/) | Skim the Joplin features: notebooks, tags, search, sync | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Obsidian pricing: free without limits; optional paid sync (not open source)](https://obsidian.md/pricing) | Optional: if you already use Obsidian, check its current free and paid features | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose one PSC topic you have studied, with at least ten connected ideas.
2. Write ten atomic notes on it (on index cards or in any notes app): one idea each, your own words, a clear title, and the source.
3. Give every note at least two links to other notes, and at least one link to a note in a different subject.
4. Write one index note that lists and links all ten.
5. Draw the network of your ten notes on one page, and write the most surprising connection you found.

**Proof to record:** Photos or screenshots of your ten linked notes and the index note, and your network drawing with the connection you found.

## Template: atomic note

```
TITLE: ________________________________ (one idea, as a statement or question)
In my own words (3-6 lines):
____________________________________________________________________
Key facts (-> cards): ________________________________________________
Why it matters / how it connects: _____________________________________
Links to: [[__________]]  [[__________]]  [[__________ (other subject)]]
Source: ______________ page ___     Tags: #to-review #pyq
```

## Template: index note

```
INDEX: ______________ (subject or topic) - start here
Core ideas:      [[_______]]  [[_______]]  [[_______]]
People:          [[_______]]  [[_______]]
Events / dates:  [[_______]]  [[_______]]
Links to other subjects: [[_______]]  [[_______]]
Open questions: ____________________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Giant notes that hold a whole chapter.** One idea per note; link them together.
- **Relying only on folders.** Add links, especially across subjects.
- **Copying text into notes.** Write in your own words; copied notes are hard to link and hard to remember.
- **Collecting without reviewing.** Every important note feeds cards, questions or the Revision tab.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is an atomic note?
    - A) A note with a whole chapter
    - B) A note with one idea, in your own words, with a clear title
    - C) A note without a title
    - D) A copied paragraph
2. Why are links more powerful than folders?
    - A) One note can connect to many others, across subjects
    - B) Links delete old notes
    - C) Folders are not allowed
    - D) Links are faster to type
3. What is the honest evidence on PKM apps and exam scores?
    - A) They replace AnkiDroid
    - B) They harm memory
    - C) No research shows they raise scores by themselves; notes still need retrieval
    - D) They are proven to double scores
4. How do you link to a note called Temple Entry Proclamation in Logseq or Obsidian?
    - A) Type [[Temple Entry Proclamation]]
    - B) Underline the title
    - C) Type #Temple
    - D) Put it in a folder

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Logseq home page and the Joplin features list
- **Action:** Write ten atomic, linked notes on a PSC topic with an index note, and map the network. It is done when your proof is saved: photos or screenshots of your ten linked notes and the index note, and your network drawing with the connection you found.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Small notes can be linked and reused in many places.
2. **A.** Real knowledge connects across subjects; folders hold each note in one place.
3. **C.** Their value is organisation; memory still comes from retrieval and spacing.
4. **A.** Double square brackets create a link to that note.

sections.title: LRN-M18-L02: Your PSC knowledge base in Joplin or Logseq
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Set up a free knowledge base on your phone in Joplin or Logseq (or Obsidian if you already use it), organise it for PSC and later learning, and connect it to your review system. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 50 minutes setup and moving notes).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Choosing a tool

All the options below are free; the first two are open source.

| Tool | Best for | What you should know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joplin | Notebooks and tags, like a tidy filing cabinet | Open source; Android, Windows and Linux; notes in Markdown; full-text search; sync through Dropbox, OneDrive, Nextcloud or Joplin Cloud; end-to-end encryption; works offline |
| Logseq | Linking ideas, with a daily journal page | Open source (AGPL); built around [[links]] and backlinks; on Android through F-Droid |
| Obsidian | Linking ideas, if you already use it | Free without limits; optional paid sync; your data stays on your device; not open source |
| Paper index cards | No phone at all | Number the cards and write links as card numbers |

Sources: [Joplin](https://joplinapp.org/) and [its help pages](https://joplinapp.org/help/); [Logseq](https://logseq.com/) and [Logseq on F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.logseq.app/); [Obsidian pricing](https://obsidian.md/pricing) (check current rules).

**If you already use one of these, keep it.** The structure and workflow below matter more than the app. If you are starting fresh, choose Joplin if you prefer notebooks, Logseq if you want links first.

### A structure for PSC and after

```
Inbox            new notes waiting to be processed (24-hour rule)
Index            one index note per subject (start here)
Constitution     Kerala history     Indian history     Geography
Economics        Science            Current affairs (one note per month)
English          Malayalam          Maths and reasoning
Exam             syllabus map, 12-week plan, mock analyses
Learning system  your templates: planner, revision, card checklist, error log, Feynman, weekly review
Later            AI skills, business, a new language (one notebook or page each)
```

Each topic note follows the atomic note template (LRN-M18-L01): your own summary, key facts, why it matters, links, source and tags.

### The workflow

1. **Capture:** anything new goes into the Inbox: class notes, a fact from the news, a question.
2. **Process within 24 hours** (Module 9): turn it into an atomic note in the right place, with links.
3. **Connect:** add at least two links, and update the subject's index note.
4. **Feed your review system:** key facts become AnkiDroid cards, the topic goes into the Revision tab, why-questions go into the note.
5. **Use it:** before a Feynman explanation, a teaching session or a mock analysis, open the topic's index note.

### Keep it safe and simple

- **Back up** once a month with the app's export option or by copying its folder to your Learning Folder, even if you also sync.
- **Don't build for weeks.** Twenty minutes of setup, then move notes in as you study. The system serves your learning, not the other way round.
- **Sources on every note,** so you can check facts later (Module 16).

## Local example

**Ashiq** installed Logseq from F-Droid, because he wanted links first. He created the pages from this lesson's structure and an Inbox. His daily study notes went into Logseq's journal page for the day, then each evening he moved them into atomic topic pages with links: "[[Article 32]]" linked to "[[Writs]]", "[[Supreme Court]]" and "[[Fundamental Rights - start here]]".

In the first week he moved in 20 notes from his Cornell pages (Module 9) and his current-affairs note for the month. He added a "Learning system" page holding his six core templates, so he could copy them on his phone.

On the first Sunday of each month, Loop reminds him to back up: he exports the Logseq folder to his Learning Folder. The surprise for him was search: when a previous-year question mentioned "quo warranto", he found his own note and its links in five seconds.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connecting notes to cards and the Revision tab | **Strong** | This is what turns notes into retrieval and spaced practice. |
| A single, searchable place for all notes | **Limited** | Practical value (finding and linking), not tested learning research. |
| Any particular app being best | **Limited** | No evidence favours one app; the workflow matters more. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Joplin: free, open-source notes for Android, Windows and Linux](https://joplinapp.org/) | If you choose Joplin: install it and create the notebooks | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Joplin help: features, sync options, encryption and apps](https://joplinapp.org/help/) | Read about sync and encryption if you want to sync | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Logseq for Android on F-Droid (AGPL-3.0)](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.logseq.app/) | If you choose Logseq: install it from F-Droid | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Obsidian pricing: free without limits; optional paid sync (not open source)](https://obsidian.md/pricing) | If you already use Obsidian: check what is free and what is paid | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose your tool (or keep the one you already use) and install it.
2. Create the structure: Inbox, Index, your PSC subjects, Exam, Learning system and Later.
3. Move or process at least 20 notes into it: from your Cornell pages, your memory palace plan, your current-affairs notes and your Syllabus tab priorities. Give each note at least two links and a source.
4. Put your six core templates (from the Toolkit page) into the Learning system notebook or page.
5. Set a monthly backup reminder in Loop or your calendar, and do the first backup to your Learning Folder.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of your knowledge base structure, a topic note with its links and source, the Learning system page, and your first backup file in the Learning Folder.

## Template: topic note template

```
# [Topic title]
Summary (my words): ______________________________________________
Key facts -> cards: ______________________________________________
Why / how: _______________________________________________________
Links: [[______]] [[______]] [[______]]
PYQs on this topic: paper ______ Q ___ ; paper ______ Q ___
Source: ______________ page ___   Last reviewed: ______   Tags: #to-review
```

## Template: monthly knowledge base check

```
MONTHLY CHECK      Month: ______
[ ] Inbox empty (everything processed or deleted)
[ ] Index notes updated for subjects studied this month
[ ] Notes without links: ___ -> linked
[ ] Notes without sources: ___ -> sources added
[ ] Backup exported to the Learning Folder
```

## Common mistakes

- **Spending days designing the perfect system.** Twenty minutes of setup, then move notes in as you study.
- **Notes without sources.** Every note gets a source, so facts can be checked.
- **No backup.** Export once a month to your Learning Folder, even if you sync.
- **Switching apps every month.** Choose one, use it for three months, then decide.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which of these tools is open source?
    - A) Joplin and Logseq
    - B) None of them
    - C) Only paper cards
    - D) Only Obsidian
2. Where do new notes go first in the workflow?
    - A) Nowhere; keep them in your head
    - B) The Exam notebook
    - C) The Inbox, to be processed within 24 hours
    - D) Straight into AnkiDroid
3. How often should you back up your knowledge base?
    - A) Only when the phone breaks
    - B) Never, if it syncs
    - C) Once a year
    - D) At least once a month, to your Learning Folder
4. You already use Obsidian. What does the lesson suggest?
    - A) Keep it; the structure and workflow matter more than the app
    - B) Delete it and switch at once
    - C) Stop taking notes
    - D) Use three apps at the same time

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The help pages of the tool you choose (Joplin, Logseq or Obsidian)
- **Action:** Set up your PSC knowledge base, move in 20 linked notes and make your first backup. It is done when your proof is saved: screenshots of your knowledge base structure, a topic note with its links and source, the Learning system page, and your first backup file in the Learning Folder.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Joplin and Logseq are open source; Obsidian is free but not open source.
2. **C.** Capture first, then process, connect and feed the review system.
3. **D.** Sync is not a backup; a monthly export protects your notes.
4. **A.** No app is proven best; consistency matters.

Action: Set up your PSC knowledge base, move in 20 linked notes and make your first backup

sections.title: Module 19: Brain health
sections.summary: Look after the brain you study with: protect your sleep, move every day, take real breaks, eat simply following official guidance, and manage stress, with clear signs for when to get help.
sections.content:
## Overview

All the techniques in this course work better in a rested, active, calm brain, and worse in a tired, stressed one. This module uses official and open sources (the AASM sleep recommendation, WHO's activity guidance, the Indian Dietary Guidelines and OpenStax Psychology) and is honest about what is strongly supported (enough sleep, regular activity) and what is not (brain foods, supplements).

It is general guidance, not medical advice. If you have a health condition, follow your doctor.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain how sleep supports learning and keep a consistent sleep schedule
- Reach at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week
- Use movement breaks and simple food habits from official guidance
- Recognise stress and use exercise, relaxation, support and planning to manage it
- Know the signs that need help, and the Tele-MANAS and emergency numbers

## Time

About 3 hours 45 minutes in total: 3 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 21, with the module project due in week 21.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M19-L01: Sleep and learning (about 1 hour)
2. LRN-M19-L02: Exercise, food and breaks (about 1 hour)
3. LRN-M19-L03: Stress (about 1 hour)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **14-night sleep log** and **my sleep rules**
- The **weekly activity log** and **break menu**
- The **stress inventory** and **support plan**

## Module project: My brain-health plan

1. Put your sleep rules, activity plan, break menu, food change, stress tools and support plan on one page.
2. Show two weeks of the sleep log and the activity log with your averages and totals.
3. Write what changed in your Focus tab and AnkiDroid percentages over the same weeks, honestly, including if nothing did.
4. Add the plan's weekly items (walks, rest block) to your study planner for the next month.

**Proof to record:** Your one-page brain-health plan, two weeks of sleep and activity logs, and your honest note on what changed.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep | Not tracked | Tracked without rules | Two weeks tracked, rules set and kept most nights |
| Activity and breaks | Under 60 minutes a week | Some weeks at target | 150 minutes or more in both weeks, with movement breaks |
| Stress | No plan | Tools chosen, not practised | Three tools practised and a support plan written |
| Honesty | Claims miracles | Some reflection | Honest note on what changed and what didn't |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Keep three sleep rules and walk 30 minutes on five days a week.
- Save the Tele-MANAS number and name two people you can talk to.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Recommended sleep for adults (AASM and SRS) | 7 or more hours a night, regularly. |
| The night before an exam | Light review only, usual bedtime. |
| WHO activity target for adults | At least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. |
| Key messages of the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians | Be active; limit salt, sugar and fats; cut down on ultra-processed foods. |
| Evidence for "brain foods" and supplements for exams | This course found no good evidence. |
| Four ways to regulate stress (OpenStax 14.4) | Exercise, relaxation, biofeedback, social support. |
| Free mental health helpline | Tele-MANAS: 14416 or 1-800-891-4416, 24 hours. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Treating health as separate from study.** Sleep, movement and calm are what make the study methods work.
- **Waiting for a crisis before asking for help.** Talk to someone early; use Tele-MANAS if needed.

sections.title: LRN-M19-L01: Sleep and learning
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Protect the sleep that consolidates learning: track your sleep for two weeks, set a consistent schedule and fix the habits that cut it short. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 20 minutes setup plus a two-week log).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Sleep is part of studying

In Module 1 you saw that new memories are stabilised over the following hours, with sleep playing a part: stage 2 sleep spindles and REM sleep have been linked to learning and memory ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 4.3](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-3-stages-of-sleep)). Sleep also restores attention, mood and self-control, which every study method in this course depends on.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society recommend that **adults sleep 7 or more hours a night on a regular basis**. Sleeping less regularly is linked with impaired performance, more errors and a higher risk of accidents ([AASM and SRS consensus statement](https://www.aasm.org/resources/pdf/adultsleepdurationconsensus.pdf)).

For a PSC aspirant, cutting sleep to "study more" is usually a bad trade: you get extra hours with worse attention, and you lose part of the consolidation of what you studied.

### Habits that protect sleep

- **A consistent schedule:** the same bedtime and wake time every day, including weekends, as far as your life allows.
- **The phone outside the bedroom,** or at least in Bedtime mode with greyscale and Do Not Disturb (Module 5; [Android Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) (check current rules)).
- **A wind-down routine:** the last 30 minutes before bed without new study topics or screens. A short recall of the day's topic (Module 1) fits well here.
- **Tea and coffee:** if they affect your sleep, keep them to the earlier part of the day. Test it with your sleep log.
- **Light and noise:** a dark, quiet, cool room as far as you can manage.

### Exam season

The nights before mocks and exams matter most. Stop new topics the evening before, do a light review, and sleep at your usual time. An all-nighter before an exam usually costs more marks than it gains.

### When to see a doctor

See a doctor if you have trouble sleeping for weeks despite good habits, if you are very sleepy during the day even after enough hours in bed, or if someone notices loud snoring with pauses or gasping in your sleep. These can be signs of conditions that need treatment.

This lesson is general guidance, not medical advice.

## Local example

**Ashiq** started his sleep log without changing anything. The first five nights averaged 6 hours 10 minutes, with bedtimes between 11:40 p.m. and 2:15 a.m., and he scrolled Reels in bed most nights.

He set three rules: phone on the charger in the kitchen at 10:45 p.m., in bed by 11, up at 6:30 every day including Sunday. He moved his evening tea before 6 p.m. and did a 5-minute recall of the day's topic as his wind-down.

Over the second week his average rose to 7 hours 15 minutes. He also noticed in his log that his morning AnkiDroid percentage was lower after short nights, on average, which convinced him more than any article. Sunday was the hardest day to keep, so he wrote an if-then plan: "If my friends ask me out late on Saturday, then I will come home by 10:30."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adults sleeping 7 or more hours regularly | **Strong** | AASM and SRS consensus: less is linked with impaired performance, more errors and accidents. |
| Sleep helps consolidate new memories | **Moderate** | Sleep stages have been linked to learning and memory (OpenStax 4.3); the details are still being studied. |
| Specific habits (phone out of the bedroom, consistent times, no late tea) | **Limited** | Common, sensible advice; test each with your own sleep log. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AASM and Sleep Research Society (2015): recommended sleep for adults (PDF)](https://www.aasm.org/resources/pdf/adultsleepdurationconsensus.pdf) | Read the recommendation and the effects of short sleep | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 4.3 Stages of Sleep](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-3-stages-of-sleep) | Reread the stages of sleep and their links to memory | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Android Help: manage how you spend time with Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) | Set up or check Bedtime mode on your phone | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Keep a 14-night sleep log: time in bed, time up, hours slept, how rested you feel, and your morning AnkiDroid percentage correct.
2. After the first five nights, set your three sleep rules: a bedtime, a wake time (every day) and where the phone stays at night.
3. Set Bedtime mode on your phone for your new bedtime, and write a 30-minute wind-down routine.
4. At the end of 14 nights, work out your average hours for the first five and the last five nights, and compare your morning AnkiDroid percentages on short and long nights.
5. Write an if-then plan for the night you are most likely to break your rules.

**Proof to record:** Your 14-night sleep log with both averages and the AnkiDroid comparison, your three sleep rules and your if-then plan.

## Template: 14-night sleep log

```
Night | In bed | Up    | Hours | Rested (1-5) | AnkiDroid % next morning | Phone in bedroom?
1     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ___          | ___%                     | Y / N
2     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ___          | ___%                     | Y / N
...
14    | ______ | _____ | _____ | ___          | ___%                     | Y / N
Average hours: nights 1-5 ___   nights 10-14 ___
AnkiDroid % after nights under 7 hours ___  after 7 hours or more ___
```

## Template: my sleep rules

```
MY SLEEP RULES
1. In bed by ______, every day.
2. Up at ______, every day, including Sunday.
3. Phone charges in ______________ (or Bedtime mode from ______).
Wind-down (last 30 minutes): no new topics, no screens; 5-minute recall of today's topic.
Night before a mock or exam: light review only; usual bedtime.
If-then: If ______________________, then I will ______________________.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Trading sleep for study hours.** Seven hours or more makes the hours you do study count.
- **Sleeping late on Sunday to "catch up".** Keep wake times steady; large swings disturb the next week.
- **Scrolling in bed.** Charge the phone outside the bedroom or use Bedtime mode.
- **Ignoring long-lasting sleep problems.** See a doctor if problems last for weeks despite good habits.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. How much sleep do the AASM and the Sleep Research Society recommend for adults?
    - A) 7 or more hours a night, regularly
    - B) As little as possible during exams
    - C) 5 hours on study days
    - D) 4 hours plus a nap
2. What should the night before a mock or exam look like?
    - A) No sleep at all
    - B) An all-nighter on new topics
    - C) Three mocks in a row
    - D) A light review and your usual bedtime
3. Which habit best protects sleep from your phone?
    - A) Watching Reels until you feel sleepy
    - B) Keeping it under the pillow
    - C) Turning up the brightness
    - D) Charging it outside the bedroom, or using Bedtime mode
4. When should you see a doctor about sleep?
    - A) Only before exams
    - B) Never
    - C) When problems last for weeks despite good habits, or with loud snoring and gasping
    - D) After one bad night

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The AASM sleep recommendation and OpenStax 4.3 on sleep stages
- **Action:** Keep a 14-night sleep log, set three sleep rules and compare your averages. It is done when your proof is saved: your 14-night sleep log with both averages and the AnkiDroid comparison, your three sleep rules and your if-then plan.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Less is linked with impaired performance, errors and accidents.
2. **D.** Sleep supports attention and consolidation; new topics add little.
3. **D.** Distance and Bedtime mode reduce late scrolling.
4. **C.** These can be signs of conditions that need treatment.

sections.title: LRN-M19-L02: Exercise, food and breaks
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Add regular physical activity and real breaks to your study week, and make simple food choices that follow official Indian guidance. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 20 minutes planning plus two weeks of logging).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Movement

The World Health Organization recommends that adults do **at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week**, such as brisk walking, cycling or active housework, and says physical activity improves brain health, thinking and sleep, and reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety ([WHO physical activity fact sheet, 2024](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity)).

For a PSC aspirant, 150 minutes is 30 minutes on five days: a brisk walk to the library, an evening walk with family, cycling to the market, a yoga routine. It doesn't need a gym or money.

Be honest about what to expect: the evidence that activity is good for health, mood and sleep is strong; the evidence that a walk will directly raise your exam score is limited. Think of it as protecting the brain you study with.

### Breaks

Long stretches of sitting drain attention. In the study of Pomodoro-style breaks (Module 5), students who took short planned breaks reported less fatigue and more concentration than those who chose their own breaks ([Biwer and others, 2023](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/understanding-effort-regulation-comparing-pomodoro-breaks-and-sel)). Use breaks to **move**: stand, stretch, walk to the verandah, drink water. Don't spend them scrolling.

### Food

The Indian Council of Medical Research's National Institute of Nutrition released updated **Dietary Guidelines for Indians** in 2024. Its main messages, as reported by All India Radio News, include being physically active, limiting salt, sugar and fats, cutting down on ultra-processed foods and preventing obesity ([All India Radio News, May 2024](https://newsonair.gov.in/icmr-releases-updated-dietary-guidelines-for-indians-in-2024)).

For study days, that suggests simple habits:

- **Regular meals:** long gaps followed by a heavy meal tend to bring tiredness. Notice what happens to your focus after different meals in your Focus log.
- **Fewer fried and packaged snacks** during study: swap some for fruit, nuts or home-made snacks.
- **Water:** keep a bottle where you study, especially in Kerala's heat.

This course found no good evidence for special "brain foods" or supplements that improve exam performance; be wary of products that promise it. If you have a health condition, follow your doctor's advice.

## Local example

**Sreeja** spent most of her day either working at home or sitting with her books. Her weekly activity, when she counted it honestly, was about 40 minutes.

She planned 30-minute brisk walks with her children on five evenings, on the road to the temple and back, and a short stretching routine in every study break. In her two-week activity log she reached 160 minutes in week 1 and 175 in week 2. She also noticed in her Focus log that her worst blocks came after a large lunch with fried snacks, so she moved to a lighter lunch with a fruit at 4 p.m.

She can't prove that the walks raised her mock score. But she sleeps better, feels less heavy in her evening study slot, and her children now remind her when it is time to walk.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regular physical activity for health, mood and sleep | **Strong** | WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults, citing benefits for brain health, sleep and mood. |
| Exercise directly raising exam scores | **Limited** | Plausible, but direct evidence for exam results is limited. |
| Planned short breaks reduce fatigue | **Limited** | One study of 87 students (Biwer and others, 2023). |
| Special "brain foods" or supplements for exams | **Limited** | This course found no good evidence; official guidance stresses a balanced diet with less salt, sugar, fat and ultra-processed food. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [World Health Organization: physical activity fact sheet (26 June 2024)](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity) | Read the recommendations for adults and the listed benefits | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [All India Radio News (9 May 2024): ICMR releases updated Dietary Guidelines for Indians](https://newsonair.gov.in/icmr-releases-updated-dietary-guidelines-for-indians-in-2024) | Read the news report on the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Biwer et al. (2023), "Understanding effort regulation: Comparing Pomodoro breaks and self-regulated breaks"](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/understanding-effort-regulation-comparing-pomodoro-breaks-and-sel) | Reread the abstract on breaks and fatigue | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Count your physical activity for one normal week honestly (minutes of moderate activity).
2. Plan how you will reach at least 150 minutes a week, in sessions that fit your day (for example five 30-minute walks), and add them to your study planner.
3. Write a break menu of movements for study breaks, and use it in every break for two weeks.
4. Choose one food change for study days (a lighter lunch, fewer fried snacks, a water bottle at your desk) and keep it for two weeks.
5. Keep a two-week activity log with your minutes, and note your focus rating after meals in your Focus tab.

**Proof to record:** Your two-week activity log with weekly totals, your break menu, and a note on your food change and what you noticed.

## Template: weekly activity log

```
WEEKLY ACTIVITY      Week of ______   Target: 150 minutes of moderate activity
Day | Activity (brisk walk, cycling, yoga, active housework) | Minutes
Mon | __________________________________________________ | ___
Tue | __________________________________________________ | ___
...
Sun | __________________________________________________ | ___
Total ___ minutes   Target met? Y / N   Sleep this week (average) ___ h
```

## Template: break menu (5 minutes, no phone)

```
[ ] Stand and stretch: arms, neck, back
[ ] Walk to the verandah or courtyard and back, twice
[ ] Drink a glass of water
[ ] Look at something far away for a minute (rest the eyes)
[ ] Ten slow breaths
```

## Common mistakes

- **An all-or-nothing gym plan.** Walking 30 minutes on five days is enough to meet the WHO target.
- **Breaks spent scrolling.** Move in your breaks; keep the phone for later.
- **Buying "brain" supplements.** No good evidence was found for exam benefits; spend nothing.
- **Long gaps without food, then a heavy meal before study.** Regular, lighter meals keep energy steadier; check your Focus log.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. How much moderate physical activity does WHO recommend for adults each week?
    - A) None if you study
    - B) At least 150 minutes
    - C) Exactly 10 hours
    - D) At least 15 minutes
2. Which is a key message of the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians, as reported?
    - A) Eat as many sweets as you like before exams
    - B) Skip breakfast to focus
    - C) Limit salt, sugar and fats, and cut down on ultra-processed foods
    - D) Take daily brain supplements
3. What is the honest evidence on exercise and exam scores?
    - A) Proven to add 20 marks
    - B) Strong for health, mood and sleep; limited for exam scores directly
    - C) There is no evidence for any benefit
    - D) Proven harmful for studying
4. What is the best use of a 5-minute study break?
    - A) Check Instagram
    - B) Lie in bed with the phone
    - C) Stand, stretch, walk and drink water
    - D) Start another topic

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The WHO physical activity fact sheet and the report on the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians
- **Action:** Reach 150 minutes of activity a week for two weeks, use a movement break menu and make one food change. It is done when your proof is saved: your two-week activity log with weekly totals, your break menu, and a note on your food change and what you noticed.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** For example, 30 minutes of brisk walking on five days.
2. **C.** The guidelines also stress being physically active.
3. **B.** Treat activity as protecting the brain you study with.
4. **C.** Movement rests attention; scrolling pulls it away.

sections.title: LRN-M19-L03: Stress
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Recognise how stress affects learning, practise simple ways to manage it, and know when and where to get help. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 20 minutes planning plus two weeks of practice).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Stress and learning

Some stress is useful: a deadline sharpens focus. Long-lasting stress is different. It disturbs sleep, makes concentration harder, crowds working memory with worry and wears down motivation, so the same hours of study produce less.

PSC preparation has its own stresses: years of effort, uncertain notifications and results, family expectations, money worries, and constant comparison with "toppers" on social media.

### Ways to regulate stress

OpenStax *Psychology 2e* describes several ways people regulate stress, including **exercise**, **relaxation** methods such as the relaxation response, **biofeedback** and **social support** ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 14.4](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/14-4-regulation-of-stress)). In practice:

1. **Move every day** (LRN-M19-L02). WHO lists reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety among the benefits of physical activity ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity)).
2. **Slow breathing or relaxation,** 5 to 10 minutes a day: breathe in gently, breathe out more slowly, and let your shoulders drop.
3. **Talk to people.** Share how you feel with a family member, a friend or your study group. Social support is one of the most reliable buffers against stress.
4. **Control what you can:** your plan, your routines and today's blocks. Let go of what you can't: the date of a notification, other people's results.
5. **Limit comparison:** mute accounts that make you feel behind; compare yourself only with your own past (your Weekly tab).
6. **Put worries on paper:** a short daily "worry time" in a notebook, or the 10-minute writing before exams (LRN-M12-L06).
7. **Keep a life outside study:** one rest block a week, a hobby, time with people you love. A long preparation needs rest to last.

### When stress is more than stress

Talk to someone you trust and see a doctor if, for two weeks or more, you feel low or hopeless most of the time, lose interest in things you used to enjoy, sleep or eat very differently, have panic attacks, or have any thoughts of harming yourself.

**Tele-MANAS** is a free government mental health helpline, open 24 hours a day, in your language of choice: call **14416** or **1-800-891-4416** ([Tele-MANAS](https://ehrc.iiitb.ac.in/project/tele-manas)). In an emergency, call **112**.

Asking for help is a strength, and it is part of looking after the learner, which is the point of this module. This lesson is general guidance, not medical advice.

## Local example

**Joseph sir** noticed that Vinod had stopped coming to the study group after his name was missing from a rank list he had hoped for. When Joseph sir called him, Vinod said he couldn't sleep and felt there was no point.

Joseph sir listened, then shared what he had read in this module. Vinod agreed to two small things: a 30-minute walk each evening with a friend from the group, and coming back to the group on Saturday, without any study target. He also wrote down what he could control (his next 12-week plan, his routines) and what he couldn't (the rank list).

Joseph sir gave him the Tele-MANAS number and said there was no shame in calling, and that a doctor could help if the low mood stayed. Vinod called once. Two weeks later he was back at the group, sleeping better, and working on a new plan for the next notification.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exercise, relaxation and social support for stress | **Moderate** | Described in OpenStax Psychology 2e as ways to regulate stress; WHO lists reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety among the benefits of activity. Results vary between people. |
| Writing about worries | **Moderate** | Expressive writing before exams helped anxious students in two studies (Ramirez and Beilock, 2011). |
| Limiting social comparison and keeping rest time | **Limited** | Sensible advice with little direct research checked for this course. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 14.4 Regulation of Stress](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/14-4-regulation-of-stress) | Read the section on regulating stress | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [World Health Organization: physical activity fact sheet (26 June 2024)](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity) | Reread the benefits of activity for mental health | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Tele-MANAS: free 24x7 mental health helpline, 14416 or 1-800-891-4416](https://ehrc.iiitb.ac.in/project/tele-manas) | Save the helpline numbers in your phone | 2 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Fill in the stress inventory: your main sources of stress, how stress shows up in you (sleep, focus, mood, body), and what you can and can't control.
2. Choose three stress tools from this lesson and plan when you will use each.
3. Practise them for two weeks and keep a short daily log: stress level from 1 to 10 and which tools you used.
4. Write a support plan: two people you can talk to, when you will talk to them, and the Tele-MANAS and emergency numbers.
5. Put one rest block a week into your study planner.

**Proof to record:** Your stress inventory, the two-week tool log and your support plan (keep anything private to yourself; only the plan and log are needed as proof).

## Template: stress inventory

```
STRESS INVENTORY      Date: ______
Main sources of stress: 1. __________ 2. __________ 3. __________
How stress shows up in me: sleep ____ focus ____ mood ____ body ____
I CAN control: _______________________________________________
I CAN'T control: _____________________________________________
My three tools: 1. ______________ when: ______
                2. ______________ when: ______
                3. ______________ when: ______
```

## Template: support plan

```
SUPPORT PLAN
People I can talk to: 1. ______________  2. ______________
When I will talk to them: ____________________________________
Rest block each week: ______________ (day and time)
If low mood, hopelessness, panic or thoughts of self-harm last or worsen:
talk to someone I trust and see a doctor.
Tele-MANAS (free, 24 hours): 14416 or 1-800-891-4416
Emergency: 112
```

## Common mistakes

- **Hiding stress until it becomes a crisis.** Talk to someone early; small support now prevents bigger problems.
- **Comparing yourself with "toppers" every day.** Mute what makes you feel behind; compare with your own past.
- **No rest at all for months.** Plan one rest block a week; long preparations need rest to last.
- **Thinking help is only for "serious" cases.** Tele-MANAS is free and open 24 hours; asking early is wise.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which ways of regulating stress does OpenStax Psychology 2e describe?
    - A) Energy drinks
    - B) Avoiding all people
    - C) Exercise, relaxation, biofeedback and social support
    - D) Studying through the night
2. What is Tele-MANAS?
    - A) A paid counselling app
    - B) A free 24-hour government mental health helpline: 14416
    - C) A coaching centre
    - D) A PSC helpline for results
3. Which is something you can control during PSC preparation?
    - A) Other candidates' results
    - B) The date of the next notification
    - C) The cut-off marks
    - D) Your plan, routines and today's study blocks
4. When should you seek help from a doctor or helpline?
    - A) Never; push through alone
    - B) Only after an exam
    - C) If low mood, hopelessness, panic or thoughts of self-harm last or worsen
    - D) Only if your family insists

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax Psychology 2e 14.4 on regulating stress
- **Action:** Fill in a stress inventory, practise three stress tools for two weeks and write your support plan. It is done when your proof is saved: your stress inventory, the two-week tool log and your support plan (keep anything private to yourself; only the plan and log are needed as proof).
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Section 14.4 describes these methods.
2. **B.** It offers support in your language of choice.
3. **D.** Focusing on what you control reduces helpless worry.
4. **C.** These signs need support, and asking early is a strength.

sections.title: Module 20: Teaching others and study groups
sections.summary: Learn by teaching and learn with others: teach a PSC topic to a family member or study partner without notes, and run a study group whose meetings are built on quizzing, teach-backs and error swaps instead of chat.
sections.content:
## Overview

Explaining to someone else is one of the most effective ways to find out what you really know, especially without notes. And a well-run group adds what solo study lacks: accountability, other people's explanations, and other people's mistakes to learn from. This module gives both a structure.

The required teaching task of the course is in the first lesson; the second gives you a group format you can use until your exam and beyond.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain when learning by teaching helps, and why explaining without notes matters
- Plan and teach a 10-minute lesson with questions and an explain-back
- Use a learner's feedback to find and fix your gaps
- Set up a study group with roles, rules and a 60-minute meeting format
- Keep online study groups useful and free of unchecked forwards

## Time

About 3 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 21–22, with the module project due in week 22.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M20-L01: Learning by teaching (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M20-L02: Study groups that work (about 1 hour)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **10-minute lesson plan card** and **after the lesson** sheet
- The **study group charter** and **meeting log**

## Module project: Teach and be taught

1. Teach one more topic, to a different learner if you can, using the lesson card.
2. Run a third group meeting (or partner call) in which you are the explainer.
3. Compare your own scores on the topics you taught with similar topics you only studied, using your Revision tab or a short test.
4. Write half a page: what teaching showed you about your own knowledge, and how you will keep teaching in your routine.

**Proof to record:** Your second lesson card with feedback, the third meeting log with you as explainer, the score comparison and your half-page reflection.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Teaching | Read notes aloud | Taught with some notes | Taught from memory with questions, an explain-back and feedback |
| Gaps | None noted | Gaps noted but not fixed | Gaps noted, fixed from the source and retested |
| Group | Unstructured chat | Some structure | Charter agreed and meetings run with the format and rotating roles |
| Reflection | None | General comments | Scores compared and a plan to keep teaching |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Teach one 10-minute lesson to a family member and test both of you three days later.
- Find one accountability partner and have a 15-minute call each week: quiz each other on 10 questions.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| When learning by teaching works best (Fiorella) | When you actually explain, without notes, in a low-stakes setting. |
| Benefit of only preparing to teach | Modest and mixed. |
| The 10-minute lesson | Opening question, 3-4 points from memory, one example, one drawing, two checks, an explain-back, feedback. |
| Four rotating group roles | Quizmaster, explainer, fact-checker, timekeeper. |
| The 60-minute meeting | Check-in, quiz, teach-back, error swap, plan, buffer. |
| Online group rule for forwards | No forwards without a source; check before sharing. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Teaching only when preparing feels complete.** Teach early; the gaps it shows are the point.
- **Letting the group replace your own recall.** The group adds to your system; your daily retrieval stays yours.
